stories.Headline: Meta Expands AI Age-Estimation Tech to Protect Teens on Instagram
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms announced in a statement dated Nov. 9 that it is expanding its AI-powered age-estimation technology to find Instagram users it suspects are teenagers, even when they signed up with an adult birthdate. Suspected teens are automatically moved into Teen Account protections, which are built-in safeguards that limit the content they see, the time they spend on the app, and who can contact them. Meta said the change will bring those protections to millions more teenagers worldwide who use Instagram. The company is also continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook, and it said it will begin launching similar measures globally on Threads later this year. The announcement was reported on Nov. 10, 2026, by The Epoch Times and Biometric Update.

Starting this month, parents on Instagram in the United States will receive a notification explaining how Meta applies age-appropriate protections to teens and how they can help make sure their teenage child is logged in with the correct age. Teens aged 13 to 15 need parental permission before they can make some of their account protections less restrictive. Teens aged 16 and 17 have more freedom to update certain settings, though they still face restrictions such as content limitations that cannot be changed without parental permission. Meta said it has also started using Apple's age-range signal in Australia as an additional way to help determine users' ages. Under that method, when a parent sets up a smartphone for a teen, the app store can confirm who is using the device and assign an age range, which Apple passes to developers like Meta each time the teen downloads an app.

Meta says it uses AI and other signals to estimate a user's age, and it described the approach in a Nov. 6 post on its website written by Larry Magid, CEO of the nonprofit ConnectSafely. Magid wrote that those signals include information from profiles, comments, posts, captions and bios, such as references to school grades or birthdays. The company can also analyze visual patterns in photos and videos, which Magid said is not facial recognition but a search for general characteristics that suggest someone is underage. He said the idea is to estimate an age range, not to identify the person. Magid added that Meta deactivates suspected under-13 accounts and requires proof of age to prevent deletion.

Biometric Update, in an article by Joel R. McConvey, criticized the move, saying Meta is answering calls for platform accountability with an internally managed solution whose methods, accuracy and privacy implications are not subject to the same public scrutiny as independently evaluated third-party tools. The article noted that Meta already works with vendors such as Yoti for facial age estimation on Instagram. It argued that the approach erases user choice and amounts to profiling, which raises questions about transparency as the age assurance industry develops standards for privacy, accuracy and security. It also said Meta supports legislation requiring age verification and parental consent at the app store level, and quoted Meta saying one verified signal from a device is more effective and privacy-preserving than every platform verifying age individually. Meta warned that teens will receive inconsistent protections while collecting and sharing the signal stays optional for app stores and using it stays optional for developers, and it said its own AI system can serve as a backstop.

The expansion follows a roughly $18.1 billion settlement Meta reached in August with multiple U.S. jurisdictions over allegations of endangering children. The lawsuits accused the company of intentionally designing its platforms to be addictive, knowingly exposing children to mental harms, and misleading people about the safety of its products. Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion to settle suits brought by 47 U.S. states, territories and the District of Columbia, and $1 billion to settle a lawsuit from Texas. As part of the settlement, Meta agreed to institute age-verification protocols, content controls and time limits for children. Biometric Update described the agreement as involving 52 bipartisan attorneys general and said about 30 percent of the payments depend on TikTok and YouTube adopting comparable measures and making matching payments.

Meta, Google and TikTok filed separate lawsuits on Nov. 4 seeking to block California from enforcing Assembly Bill 1709, a new state law meant to protect children under 16 from the negative effects of social media. The bill bars platforms from offering underage children features deemed psychologically exploitative, such as autoplay videos and personal recommendations, and it obliges platforms to delete the accounts of children with such features. The companies allege the measure violates First Amendment free speech protections. The Electronic Privacy Information Center welcomed the bill in a Sept. 1 statement, and Megan Iorio, director of its platform governance and accountability program, said prohibiting manipulative design features is effective and does not infringe on kids' rights to access digital spaces. The articles do not say when courts will rule on the California suits, how Meta's AI estimation will be independently evaluated, or whether app stores will be required to share age signals.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Launches ChatGPT Business – What's New?
stories.Summary:
OpenAI launched ChatGPT Business on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, a beta feature meant to give companies a new way to reach the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week around the world. The company announced it in a release, and an OpenAI page dated November 10 also introduced the idea of businesses in ChatGPT. The first piece is Business Hub, where an eligible business can claim its organization in ChatGPT and, once verified, update key details. The second is Business Agents, which let a company talk directly with users inside the chatbot.

Under Business Hub, verified businesses can add self-service product feeds with pricing and availability, and they can see insights on how people engage with them on ChatGPT. OpenAI said this gives ChatGPT the most accurate and up-to-date details to help people explore products and services. Any eligible business in a market where ChatGPT is available can claim its profile, while existing OpenAI Enterprise customers and advertisers can work with their OpenAI representative to do so. Once a profile is claimed, eligible businesses can build, test and launch a Business Agent, and a user who finds a business in a ChatGPT answer can open its profile and start a conversation with the agent, if one exists. Customers can ask about products, compare features and work out which option suits them.

OpenAI stressed that users' chats, including conversations with Business Agents, will not be shared with businesses. For now, Business Agents are limited to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the US, though Business Hub is open in any market where ChatGPT is available. Both tools are free at the moment. Businesses can also sponsor their agents and use them as destinations for ChatGPT Ads, and OpenAI said sponsored placements will be clearly labelled and kept separate from regular ChatGPT responses.

OpenAI describes the launch as an early step and says it plans to expand to more countries and business categories, along with tools for organisations with more complex needs. The move builds on Sponsored Agents, which OpenAI began testing in September, according to The Next Web. Australian outlet SmartCompany reported that Australian businesses can now claim themselves in ChatGPT, in line with the Business Hub being open wherever the chatbot is offered. The articles do not say when Business Agents will reach other countries or when the beta will end.

stories.Headline: Mercor Raises $750M Series D at $20B Valuation to Expand AI Training
stories.Summary:
Mercor, a San Francisco-based AI data company, announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that it had closed a $750 million Series D funding round at a $20 billion valuation. The valuation is double the price of its previous round, which was a $350 million Series C at $10 billion in October 2025. The round included participation from Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, funds managed by affiliates of Apollo, G Squared, General Catalyst, Glade Brook Capital, NVIDIA, Salesforce, Sapphire Ventures, StepStone Group, XTX Ventures and Zoom. Business Model Analyst reported that the round also included a tender offer allowing employees to sell some of their shares. Mercor helps organisations train and evaluate AI using human expertise, and it was founded in 2023.

The funding will accelerate Mercor's research, evaluation and post-training infrastructure, including realistic environments where AI agents can learn professional workflows. The aim is to help companies measure and set standards for how reliably agents complete tasks and at what cost. Mercor says its network includes more than five million experts, serving frontier AI labs, technology companies, AI startups and Fortune 500 businesses. The company now has 700 employees, and it says the US has more than 800 occupations whose workflows AI models have not yet been evaluated against. Its customised evaluations, called evals, measure AI performance against an organisation's own standards and build on APEX, its public benchmark series for economically valuable professional work.

Mercor's co-founders and co-CEOs, Brendan Foody and Adarsh Hiremath, described the pitch in their own words. Foody said every job in the economy will need its own AI agents, and every company will need a way to train and evaluate them on its own work. Hiremath said every company deploying AI needs to know whether it works, and that the answer differs for each one. Mercor says it spent the past two years building this infrastructure alongside frontier AI labs and is now taking it to enterprises across industries. The company believes the next phase of AI adoption will come from applying existing models to professional work, not only from building new foundation models.

Jai Das, president, partner and co-founder at Sapphire Ventures, said Mercor has built something hard to replicate and that his firm is thrilled to help the team scale in the enterprise market. Das added that frontier labs have so far been the main buyers of expert-driven training data, and that enterprises will now want to evaluate and train agents on their own work. Business Model Analyst noted that Salesforce and Zoom, both software makers, are among the investors. AI models can perform well on public benchmarks yet still fail when navigating company-specific software, policies or operational exceptions, which is the gap customised evals address.

Reuters, citing Crunchbase, reported that AI startups pulled in $102 billion in the third quarter of 2026, 64% of all venture money raised worldwide. Brendan Foody, Adarsh Hiremath and Surya Midha founded Mercor in 2023, and it initially connected AI companies with professionals who supplied specialised knowledge to train advanced models. Business Model Analyst says it began as an AI hiring tool, and Benchmark led a $30 million Series A at a $250 million valuation in September 2024. A Series B of $100 million at $2 billion followed in February 2025, when the gross run rate was about $75 million.

In July 2026 Mercor announced an annualised revenue run rate above $2 billion, which Tech Funding News said is gross billings, with contractors keeping roughly 60% to 70%, implying net revenue of an estimated $600 million to $800 million. Earlier this year Mercor acquired Deeptune, whose team spent two years recreating hundreds of enterprise applications as training environments, and Business Model Analyst adds that it bought Sepal AI in February and launched Mercor Enterprise AI in March. Mercor operates in a growing market against rivals including Scale AI, which raised $1 billion at a valuation of nearly $14 billion in 2024, before Meta invested $14.3 billion for a 49% stake. Surge AI was reportedly weighing its first outside raise at a valuation above $25 billion, while Snorkel AI raised $350 million at $3.5 billion and micro1 raised $35 million at $500 million in September 2025.

Business Model Analyst reports that Mercor ended a Meta project called Musen in November 2025, that a March 2026 breach linked to LiteLLM software led to at least seven class actions, and that a May lawsuit alleges contractor misclassification. The articles say the challenge will be scaling the enterprise business against established AI data providers, and the opportunity is to become the layer that helps businesses deploy agents reliably. Tech Funding News described its July report as showing about 30,000 contractors in a rotating pool, set against the five million vetted candidates. Mercor says the new money will go toward building more simulated workplaces, though the articles give no timeline for when enterprise customers will adopt them.

stories.Headline: Anthropic expands Claude with workplace productivity tools
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on Tuesday that it is expanding its Claude platform with new tools for building spreadsheets, digital whiteboards and data dashboards. The move pushes Claude beyond answering questions and generating text into work usually done in office productivity software, and it places the company in the same space as Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. TechGig reported the news on Nov. 12. Separately, a Japanese company said it began offering Anthropic's newest model, Claude Fable 5.2, through its own gateway on Nov. 11, saying Anthropic released that model on Nov. 9.

The new workplace tools come in three parts. Claude Sheets handles spreadsheets, letting teams organize data together, write and edit formulas, and work across several tabs. Claude Whiteboards gives teams a shared space to gather ideas during meetings and ask Claude to summarize the discussion. Claude Data, previously called Dashboards, connects to services such as Snowflake and Salesforce and produces dashboards, visual data stories and narrated videos built on definitions certified by an organization's data team. Anthropic also said Claude can create custom tools such as account trackers, daily briefings, project status boards and contract review tables.

Businesses get additional features. Anthropic is adding interactive connectors that place partner applications inside Claude, including Adobe and Atlassian, along with plugins from Salesforce, NetSuite and Workday aimed at sales, finance and human resources teams. Administrators can manage employee access, limit what Claude is allowed to do and set spending limits for the organization. Enterprise data is encrypted in transit and at rest, and usage is tracked through audit logs.

On the model side, FlashLabs, a Tokyo company that exclusively offers the OrcaRouter AI gateway in Japan, said it now provides Claude Fable 5.2 through that service. It cited the third-party firm Artificial Analysis, whose Intelligence Index put the model first with a score of 65, ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon at 60 and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at 59. The company listed a context window of 1 million tokens, output of up to 128K tokens, and pricing of $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. It also launched a campaign that adds credit equal to 100% of a deposit of $10 or more, up to $200 per deposit, for the first 100 developers, open until Dec. 11, with the credit expiring Jan. 10, 2027.

Anthropic said Claude "works around you," drawing on the tools a team connects, producing ideas in whatever format is needed, and operating within the controls administrators set. TechGig noted that, unlike Microsoft and Google, which add AI across established suites, Anthropic builds these tools into Claude itself, so users can carry context between formats without repeating instructions. FlashLabs, for its part, said it plans to keep expanding model availability and running support campaigns for developers in Japan. The company noted that its benchmark figures come from Artificial Analysis and have not been independently verified.

stories.Headline: Google Expands Gemini 4 Carbon AI Access For Developers, Businesses With Advanced Coding, Cybersecurity And Research Capabilities
stories.Summary:
Google announced that Gemini 4 Carbon is now available, with the news published on November 10, 2026, on both the DeepMind site and the Google blog. The two pages carry the same headline, which describes an expansion of access to the model for developers and businesses. That headline points to advanced abilities in coding, cybersecurity and research as the main selling points of the release. The company behind the release is Google, through its DeepMind research arm and its main corporate blog.

The text supplied for both articles is almost entirely website navigation code and styling rules rather than reporting. Because of that, it does not spell out any specifics about what the release requires or changes. No pricing, usage limits, supported products or rollout schedule appear in the material provided. No model sizes, benchmark results or performance figures are given either, so there are no numbers to report beyond the November 10, 2026 publication date.

The material also contains no statements from named Google or DeepMind executives, researchers or spokespeople. Without any quoted or paraphrased remarks, there is nothing to say about how the company characterizes the model, its safeguards or its intended uses. The only attribution available is to the two organizations that published the announcement on their own sites. Responsibility for the release therefore rests with Google, which is the party making the model available.

The articles offer no background on earlier Gemini versions, on how Gemini 4 Carbon compares with competing systems, or on what happens next. Details about future updates, wider availability or additional features are not included in the text supplied. Readers who want the full terms of access and the technical description of the model's coding, cybersecurity and research capabilities would need to consult the complete announcement on the DeepMind and Google blog pages directly. Until that fuller information is available, the headline claim and the November 10 date are the only confirmed facts.

stories.Headline: How AI is changing procurement and supply chains
stories.Summary:
Sifted reported on November 12, 2026 that Magentic, a procurement and supply chain automation company, deploys AI agents to run procurement and supply chain processes for its customers. The same day, Seadronix announced that it had secured its first government vessel supply reference in the global defense market. Seadronix is an AI maritime solutions provider led by CEO Byeolteo Park, and its win concerns the NAVISS Bridge AI ship monitoring and navigation system. That system will be installed on the Republic of Singapore Navy's next-generation Sentinel-class Offshore Patrol Vessels, which are purpose-built for maritime security missions. The vessels are being built by Fassmer, a German shipbuilder that specializes in special-purpose and defense vessels.

Singapore's Ministry of Defence officially named Seadronix's AI system in the vessels' specifications, which it published on October 2. Seadronix is the only non-European company chosen for the vessels' sensor suite, listed alongside Thales, Saab, Safran and Terma. On the Magentic side, its agents extract data from emails, documents, files and CAD drawings, then use that data to verify pricing and purchase orders and secure cost savings within enterprise systems. The agents also identify and close value leakage, meaning the hidden loss of capital when a company overpays or fails to negotiate savings. For one client, Magentic ran agents on 1m purchase orders a year, checking pricing accuracy, supplier choice, renegotiation chances and rerouting to cheaper existing contracts.

Magentic's CEO, Robin Van Aeken, said everyone wants this work to run autonomously, but customers must first go on a human-in-the-loop journey in which agents learn from users. He said direct procurement is complex and localised, traditionally owned by manufacturing plants and by senior category managers who have known their three suppliers for 30 years. According to him, legacy ERP systems record only the final price paid, and none of the negotiation, context or supplier performance behind it. He said that in the first three months after one customer went live Magentic saved $1.2m, and that the total reached $4.2m over the six months after that. Seadronix's CTO, Hankeun Kim, called the Singapore selection a defining milestone, saying a place beside European suppliers shows its AI delivers the capabilities and reliability maritime security missions demand.

Boston Consulting Group data shows that only 35% of procurement teams have adopted AI, even though better supply chain management is crucial. According to LeanDNA, 64% of manufacturers spend 10% or more of their manufacturing budget reacting to supply chain disruptions, through last-minute production changes or emergency sourcing. Van Aeken said modernising procurement is critical for growth, including in European manufacturing, which competes aggressively with cheaper, lower-cost manufacturing. Magentic works with enterprises in the automotive, oil and gas, and food and beverage industries.

On the defense side, the article describes the selection as a strong endorsement, because equipment on government vessels must perform reliably over decades of service. Magentic's research on the cost of waste comes from World Commerce and Contracting, which found that value leakage costs enterprises that manage contracts and supply chains around 9% of annual turnover. To build trust with new clients, Magentic typically starts with outcome-based pricing, charging only a percentage of savings generated during a pilot phase. It then moves to a customised subscription model once daily operations are fully automated.

Seadronix's Singapore work extends beyond the patrol vessels, covering a smart port collaboration with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. It also includes a fireboat demonstration with the Singapore Civil Defence Force and a memorandum of understanding with the Defence Science and Technology Agency on an unmanned surface vessel. Seadronix describes the Sentinel-class win as a dual-use milestone, with AI proven on commercial and government vessels now extending into defense. Van Aeken expects procurement teams to change, with automation shifting them from administrative work to more strategic tasks.

He said the procurement team of the future finds more win-wins with suppliers, does more value engineering and pre-empts more disruptions. He hopes procurement will grow into a more strategic function, a partner to the CFO, to manufacturing and to engineering, rather than being too much of a cost centre. Seadronix's NAVISS Bridge is slated for installation on the Sentinel-class vessels, but the announcement gives no installation dates or number of vessels. The articles also give no delivery timetable for the vessels, no contract value for Seadronix, and no date by which Magentic's agents are expected to run fully autonomously.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA-KAIST Develop 1M Korean AI Training Data
stories.Summary:
Nvidia and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, known as KAIST, announced at a news conference at Nvidia Korea's Seoul office on Tuesday, November 10, that they will jointly develop sovereign artificial intelligence optimized for the Korean language. The two organizations laid out the research plans of their new joint AI laboratory, which will build Korean-language training datasets and make the resulting technologies freely available. It was the first detailed look at the lab's agenda since the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding in October to set it up. The aim is to overcome a shortage of Korean training data and to position South Korea as a research hub for AI serving languages with relatively few speakers.

The laboratory's initial work centers on high-quality Korean datasets and on methods for training AI models well with limited language data. Researchers plan to generate synthetic training material from existing data and to develop techniques for picking out the best examples. By the end of 2027, the lab aims to create and publicly release one million high-quality Korean-language data samples. South Korean AI companies will be able to use the datasets free of charge, which could lower the cost of building and improving domestic language models, and the lab also intends to share its sovereign AI training methods freely worldwide. The lab is currently recruiting full-time researchers, which organizers described as the first time a global technology giant has directly hired researchers in South Korea for such a joint operation.

The laboratory will be led by Kim Hyun-woo, a professor at KAIST's Kim Jaechul Graduate School of AI who is also a research manager at Nvidia. Kim joined KAIST in September and holds positions at both the university and the U.S. company. He said that AI performance is determined by data, but that South Korea has far less training data than English- or Chinese-speaking markets, so methods are needed to close that gap. He added that the first goal is to find ways to make the most of available data when training AI in languages with relatively few speakers.

The data gap is large. In a text dataset released by Google for AI training, Korean material amounted to just one-163rd of the English-language data. Such disparities can weaken the quality of AI answers in Korean and make it harder for domestic developers to build competitive models. Researchers describe the partnership as a shift in South Korea's role, from a major market for Nvidia's graphics processing units to a partner in advanced AI research. Nvidia and KAIST hope that techniques developed for Korean can be applied to other languages with limited training resources, supporting more locally developed AI systems and expanding the global sovereign AI ecosystem.

stories.Headline: Meta is launching its "smallest and most efficient" AI model: Muse Ember.
stories.Summary:
Meta Superintelligence Labs released Muse Ember on Nov. 9, 2026, describing it as the smallest and most efficient model the company has built so far. It is a hosted multimodal reasoning model made for the repetitive steps inside AI agents. Meta lists tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction and long document parsing as the main targets. The model scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort. Meta puts its cost at about $0.14 per index task.

Muse Ember has a context window of 1 million tokens and can produce up to 512,000 output tokens, four times the 128,000 cap on both rivals. It runs only on Meta's hosted infrastructure, through the Meta Model API and Muse Code, and its weights are private, so no local or quantized option exists. It accepts text, images, audio and video, and can operate desktop apps from screenshots. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.004 per million. Meta lists no long-context pricing tier for Ember, while Haiku 5.5 charges $0.50 and $2.50 above 100,000 prompt tokens.

Meta Superintelligence Labs is responsible for the release, and Meta describes Ember as a hosted model aimed at high-volume agent subtasks. Meta says the model takes repeatable coding and agent tasks at scale, and its own framing is that Muse Wonder plans while Muse Ember handles the volume. The company's pitch is that developers can use Wonder to plan a complicated job and hand the individual steps to Ember. Meta says Ember can read a scanned contract or pull details from a meeting recording without needing a separate model. Meta reports that Ember at max effort scores 35.8 for $0.136 per task, against 36.2 for $0.411 with Haiku 5.5.

Artificial Analysis summarised the result as matching Haiku at a third of the cost per task. Cloud storage company Box said in early testing shared by Meta that it used Ember to check contracts clause by clause against a company's negotiation rules and assign an overall risk rating. Developers building agents are the most directly affected, since Meta says Ember can run steps an agent might repeat dozens of times in one assignment. Ember wins on several benchmarks, scoring 37.8% on AutomationBench-AA, against 20.2% for GPT-6 Luna and 13.9% for Haiku. It trails Haiku on FrontierCode 2.0-AA, 27.2 to 34.9, and closed weights are listed as a downside.

Ember is the fourth model under the Muse brand, after Spark, Glimmer and Wonder, and it is the first Meta trained using Muse Wonder Full, its largest model. Meta positions it below its larger models, with Muse Wonder handling the hardest problems and Muse Spark covering coding and agentic workflows. Muse is also the name of the app with the avatar called Jolly, which Meta has promoted since September. That app passed 5 million downloads in 22 days, and last week Meta began rolling out voice conversations and animated avatars in the U.S. Claude Haiku 5.5 was released Oct. 7, 2026, and GPT-6 Luna on Sep. 22, 2026.

The articles say Ember is available now through Muse Code and the developer API, and they describe no further rollout plans. They do not say how many parameters Ember has, and the parameter counts for Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna are also undisclosed. No local, laptop or quantized option is offered, because the weights stay private. Ember's gap behind Haiku on FrontierCode 2.0-AA, which tests mergeable real-repo code, remains a listed weakness with no fix described. The articles give no word on whether Meta will release open weights or add a long-context pricing tier.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Stock Surges After Earnings. Its Debt Pivot Eases AI Fears.
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported third-quarter results on the morning of November 11, 2026, and its shares rose about 17.6 percent to $60.77 as investors reacted. The Nvidia-backed cloud provider posted revenue of $3.66 billion, up 168 percent from a year earlier and ahead of the $3.54 billion Wall Street expected. Memory chip stocks rallied with it, as Micron Technology, Sandisk and South Korea's SK Hynix all advanced. Micron jumped more than 10 percent that day, trading near $820, while Yahoo Finance reported premarket gains of about 6 percent for both Micron and Sandisk. The results eased fears that the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom was losing momentum after a volatile stretch of concern about heavy spending, rising debt and stretched valuations.

CoreWeave's contracted revenue backlog climbed to roughly $132.5 billion as of September 30, up from about $104 billion three months earlier. Revenue growth accelerated from 112 percent in the second quarter to 168 percent in the third. The company raised its full-year revenue forecast to a range of $13 billion to $13.3 billion, above the $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion range it gave in August. It also projected capital expenditures of $37 billion to $39 billion for the year. Debt reached about $46.9 billion and quarterly interest expense rose to $846 million, with fourth-quarter interest expense projected at $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion.

Chief executive Michael Intrator said CoreWeave has ten times as much qualified demand as available capacity through the end of 2027. He said pricing kept rising in the fourth quarter, more than offsetting cost increases. CoreWeave had raised prices by about 25 percent in July and by another 10 percent later in the third quarter. Intrator also addressed a worry about delays, saying the company sees no material risks to its 2027 deliveries based on ongoing construction at fully permitted sites. The Motley Fool writer noted that CoreWeave did not mention memory once during the earnings call.

The Motley Fool analysis argued that the link between CoreWeave and Micron's sales is less direct than the stock's jump implies. CoreWeave rents computing power built mainly on Nvidia hardware, so any Micron memory in its data centers probably arrives inside gear made by others. When CoreWeave secured storage supply in August, it signed a multiyear deal for priority access to enterprise solid-state drives from Solidigm, a subsidiary of SK Hynix. Micron's two data center business units took in $34.3 billion in fiscal fourth quarter 2026, which ended September 3, and made up about 63 percent of revenue.

GuruFocus said investors should watch high-bandwidth memory demand, DRAM contract prices and manufacturing capacity, and that delayed deployments, weaker pricing or reduced hyperscaler spending could quickly undermine the sector's recovery. The Motley Fool piece said Micron shares had fallen about 23 percent over November 4 and 5, when data center stocks dropped as traders braced for a slower build-out after Democrats' midterm wins, according to CNBC. Even after the jump, Micron trades about a third below its record closing high of $1,213.56, reached on June 25. It trades at under 5 times the earnings analysts expect for fiscal 2027, against a forward price-to-earnings ratio of around 18 for the S&P 500.

Micron's chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra said on September 30 that the company sees server unit growth in the high teens in both 2026 and 2027, with a modestly lower rate of content growth amid tight memory supply. Micron has signed deals for the vast majority of its calendar 2027 high-bandwidth memory supply, at much higher prices than a year earlier. Micron expects industry DRAM bit shipments to grow at a low-20s percentage rate in both 2027 and 2028, with the industry still short on supply through 2028. The Motley Fool writer said more demand from CoreWeave probably cannot turn into many more Micron chips in 2027, and is more likely to show up in what Micron can charge and how long the shortage lasts.

The articles leave open whether continued AI infrastructure expansion will translate into sustained memory pricing power and stronger margins for Micron. They also leave open whether Sandisk will see lasting gains in enterprise SSD demand and NAND pricing as cloud providers expand storage infrastructure. CoreWeave's rising financing costs remain something investors are told to watch. The articles do not say when the shortage will end, and the Motley Fool writer notes that CoreWeave's report does not change a single number in Micron's own outlook.

stories.Headline: AMD Showcases 6th Gen AMD EPYC Processors to Lead Next Era of AI and Enterprise Computing
stories.Summary:
AMD announced on November 10, 2026, from Santa Clara, California, that its 6th Gen EPYC SP7 server processors, built on the new Zen 6 architecture, are now generally available. Systems powered by the chips are already shipping from leading server vendors, and cloud instances from Microsoft Azure and OCI will become generally available soon. The chips were formerly codenamed "Venice" and belong to the EPYC 9006 Series. On November 11, 2026, Super Micro Computer, Inc. said from San Jose, California, that its H15 generation server portfolio built on these processors is now shipping. Both announcements were carried by The Manila Times through newswire services.

AMD says the 6th Gen EPYC 9996 delivers up to 3.7 times the performance of a system based on the Nvidia Vera CPU and up to 2.2 times the performance of an Intel Xeon 6980P system. It also claims 2.0 times the performance per dollar of that Intel system. High-frequency host-node processors reach up to 5.3 GHz and can deliver up to 1.8 times the LLM output throughput of the previous generation. AMD also says its high-density processors offer about 3.3 times the agents per CPU watt of Nvidia Vera and about 2.5 times that of the Intel Xeon 6980P. Supermicro lists up to 33% more cores, double the PCIe bandwidth and 1.6 TB/s of memory bandwidth per socket for its H15 servers.

AMD says the 9996 supports about 1.18 times as many agents per rack within the same 35 kilowatt envelope, compared with systems using default power-management settings. AMD has also developed the Helion agentic AI rack with partners across the server ecosystem, with some configurations reaching up to 73,728 threads in one rack. Customers can choose three Helion options, namely Helion Liquid, Helion Air and Helion Air Inference. Supermicro's portfolio spans more than 20 systems and uses SP7 and SP8 sockets. Its Petascale Storage platforms support up to 4.8 PB per system, and its Helios and Helion rack-scale solutions are built on its Data Center Building Block Solutions architecture.

Dan McNamara, AMD's senior vice president and general manager for Compute and Enterprise AI, said AI is expanding the role of the CPU across every layer of the data center. He said customers can standardize on the proven x86 foundation while choosing a workload-optimized solution to run more agents and keep accelerated infrastructure fed. Speaking about the Supermicro launch, he said platforms combining EPYC with Instinct GPUs and Pensando networking help organizations deploy AI infrastructure faster. He added that they improve utilization, reduce energy use and lower total cost of ownership while running more concurrent agents. Michael McNerney, Supermicro's senior vice president of Marketing, said the shipping H15 portfolio gives customers a faster, more efficient path to agentic AI infrastructure.

McNerney also said Supermicro's close engineering collaboration with AMD gives customers the flexibility to scale AI, cloud and enterprise workloads with confidence. AMD says 6th Gen EPYC CPUs are expected to power cloud instances at all major global cloud service providers, with recent announcements from Microsoft Azure and OCI. Meta is working with AMD as a lead customer and has been validating the new platforms as the companies prepare for deployment at scale. Microsoft Azure is bringing the processors to customers across its AI infrastructure. Supermicro says its Hyper and CloudDC platforms set multiple SPEC CPU world records, and that its servers give enterprise customers 1.8 times higher tokens per second for frontier-model host nodes.

AMD says five generations of EPYC processors have repeatedly raised the standard for server CPU performance, energy efficiency and platform choice. The 5th Gen processors became the fastest-ramping and highest-volume EPYC generation in the company's history. The Zen 6 chips form a broad portfolio spanning agentic AI, enterprise, cloud computing, HPC and general-purpose computing. AMD describes agentic AI as adding diversity to the data center, because one workflow can run agents, call models, retrieve data, execute code and use existing databases and applications. Supermicro, founded and based in San Jose, makes its products in the US, Asia, Malaysia and the Netherlands.

Supermicro says its Helios rack, powered by AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs, targets frontier model training and high-throughput inference. The Helion rack, built on the 6th Gen EPYC CPUs, is designed for compute performance and deployment flexibility, and the companies are bringing both to market together. AMD says the Azure and OCI cloud instances will be generally available soon, but the articles give no dates. The articles also give no pricing for the processors or the H15 servers. Meta's deployment at scale is described only as being prepared, with no timeline given.

stories.Headline: FuelCell Energy Advances AI Data Center Power With New Testbed
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy, a Nasdaq-listed company, announced on November 10, 2026, that it is taking part in StabilityMax, a three-year collaborative project led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratory of the Rockies. The announcement came from Danbury, Connecticut, in a press release distributed through GlobeNewswire. The project will develop and validate integrated power system architectures meant to support the rapidly changing energy needs of artificial intelligence data centers. Argonne National Laboratory also participates in the project alongside the National Laboratory of the Rockies, which is abbreviated NLR. The press release says data centers are driving unprecedented demand for electricity and causing rapid fluctuations in power consumption as AI adoption accelerates.

StabilityMax will build and validate a testing and modeling framework to evaluate how fuel cells, energy storage, advanced controls, and power electronics can work together. The aim of that framework is to deliver reliable and responsive power for AI data centers. Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Connecticut, creating a national laboratory-supported testbed for evaluating integrated power solutions. NLR will develop data center load profiles and simulation models that capture the dynamic power demands of modern computing infrastructure. Argonne National Laboratory will add techno-economic and lifecycle analyses to help identify commercially appealing and cost effective deployment strategies.

Shankar Achanta, FuelCell Energy's Chief Product and Technology Officer, said AI infrastructure is creating unprecedented demand for reliable, flexible, and resilient power. He said the project brings the company's operating experience and fuel cell technology together with leading national laboratories to understand how integrated power systems can serve AI data centers. According to Achanta, the insights from the work will help optimize system designs, validate performance under real-world conditions, and support future deployment of fuel cell-based solutions. Eric Strayer, the company's Head of Global Sales, said FuelCell Energy is actively working with customers and partners deploying power solutions for digital infrastructure. He said the project will provide valuable data and operating experience that can inform those future deployments.

Zhiwen Ma, Principal Investigator at NLR, said fuel cells collocated with data centers provide unique solutions to meet the power demands of AI infrastructure. He said NLR will help demonstrate how integrated fuel cell systems can respond rapidly to data center power needs while limiting impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers. The articles describe the affected parties as AI data centers and, through the grid and ratepayer point, the utility grid and the customers who pay for it. Strayer noted that load profiles evolve with each new generation of chips, which is part of why the company expects the project to refine system designs. The Quiver Quantitative page, which carries an AI-generated summary of the release, lists FuelCell Energy shares at 10.02 on Markets Insider, down 7.44 percent in midday trading on the day.

StabilityMax is part of a broader NLR initiative to support the growing energy needs of AI-enabled digital infrastructure. Through new modeling tools, planning platforms, and test environments, NLR is helping accelerate the development and deployment of the power systems needed for efficient fuel cell-powered data centers. The project also builds on FuelCell Energy's ongoing development of integrated power solutions for digital infrastructure, including an earlier collaboration with Siemens announced this year. That collaboration aims to advance a layered architecture that combines multiple technologies operating across different timescales to meet the evolving power needs of AI data centers. FuelCell Energy describes itself as a U.S. clean energy technology company with global deployments approaching one gigawatt, and its systems generate electricity on-site at the point of use.

The articles state that insights from StabilityMax are expected to further inform system design and deployment strategies for future digital infrastructure applications. The project runs for three years, but the articles give no specific milestones, interim deliverables, or completion date for the Connecticut test facility. They do not say how much the project costs, who is paying for it, or how much FuelCell Energy is contributing. Nothing in the articles states when the testbed will begin operating or which customers might use it. The Quiver Quantitative page notes that the release does not disclose timelines or milestones, which leaves the pace of development and delivery of the integrated power solutions uncertain.

stories.Headline: AMD vs. Intel: Which Is the Better Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chip Stock to Buy Right Now?
stories.Summary:
Harsh Chauhan, writing for The Motley Fool, published an article on November 10, 2026, comparing Advanced Micro Devices and Intel as artificial intelligence chip stocks and concluding that AMD is the better buy. Both companies have benefited from healthy demand for AI-oriented chips, which major hyperscalers deploy in data centers to handle both training and inference workloads. Both semiconductor stocks have delivered healthy gains to investors this year, despite the brutal sell-off they have experienced lately. AMD shares have jumped 137% in 2026, while Intel has clocked respectable gains of 60%, as of the time of writing. A second Motley Fool piece, published on November 11, 2026, argued separately that SpaceX could join the $5 trillion club by 2029, helped by a possible merger with Tesla.

Intel's data center and AI segment revenue increased by 78% year over year in the third quarter, reaching $7.3 billion, and its growth has been accelerating in recent quarters. AMD posted a much stronger 97% year-over-year increase in its data center segment, to $8.5 billion in the previous quarter, so it now outsells Intel there. AMD guides to a 66% year-over-year revenue increase in the current quarter, to $17 billion at the midpoint, while Intel's $15.5 billion guidance implies a jump of just 13%. AMD is also projecting revenue growth of more than 80% in 2027, which is more than twice the company's long-term growth forecast. In the second article, SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% from a year earlier, with net income of $4.4 billion against a $1.1 billion loss a year before.

AMD CEO Lisa Su said on the latest earnings call that visibility into 2027 continues to strengthen. She recalled that last quarter the company expected annual server revenue to grow more than 70% and data center segment revenue to more than double for the year. Since then, she said, customers have expanded their EPYC and Instinct deployment plans, and AMD has secured more supply to support that growth. AMD now expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027, and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than projected 90 days earlier. On the SpaceX side, Elon Musk announced in October that SpaceX and Tesla had established independent committees to explore a potential merger, and Musk is not participating in the negotiations because his ownership stakes in both companies create a conflict of interest.

Intel management noted on its latest earnings call that it expects server CPU industry shipments to increase by more than 30% in both 2026 and 2027. Because AMD is growing significantly faster than that end market, the author concludes it is taking market share from Intel. On valuation, Morningstar data show AMD trading at 30 times forward earnings, while Intel is slightly more expensive at 35 times. AMD's earnings per share are projected to increase by 118% in 2027, well above Intel's estimated growth rate of 20%, and analysts have become significantly more bullish on AMD's long-term earnings growth after its latest report. In the SpaceX article, the author says a merger is not guaranteed, that combining two enormous companies would complicate matters for shareholders, and that both businesses are investing heavily in technologies yet to show their full profit potential.

AMD sells both server central processing units and graphics processing units, which helps explain its lead in the data center market. Intel appears more inclined toward server CPUs, after its Gaudi series of data center GPUs failed to find much favor among customers. AMD's growth is being driven by its latest MI455X graphics cards, which it has begun shipping in volume, along with its Epyc server CPUs. In the SpaceX article, the company went public in June, raising a record $85.7 billion in the largest initial public offering in history. Its AI division, which it now calls super intelligence, generated $7.56 billion in third-quarter revenue, surpassing the $5.25 billion from its connectivity business, which includes Starlink, even though those AI operations were losing billions of dollars a year earlier.

Looking ahead, AMD expects stronger data center growth driven by the MI455X cards and Epyc server CPUs, and it expects server revenue to double in 2027 with data center AI revenue growing even faster. SpaceX and Tesla still have to complete the merger exploration, and the article says a combined market value near $3.4 trillion would need about 47% appreciation to reach $5 trillion by 2029. That figure rests on SpaceX's market cap of $1.8 trillion and Tesla's of $1.6 trillion, before any merger-related adjustments. SpaceX capital expenditures reached $19.6 billion in the third quarter, and its June agreement worth up to $6.3 billion with Reflection AI includes termination provisions, so the full value is not guaranteed. The articles leave open whether the merger will happen, and whether SpaceX will reach the $5 trillion mark by 2029.

stories.Headline: Nebius Stock Sinks as AI Cloud Provider Lowers Revenue Outlook, Lifts Capital Spending Guidance
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group, the Nasdaq-listed AI cloud infrastructure provider trading as NBIS, saw its shares fall 10% on Thursday, November 12, 2026, after it released third-quarter results. The company reported revenue above analyst expectations but gave a weaker outlook and sharply higher capital spending forecasts. Third-quarter revenue rose 571% from a year earlier to $980.8 million, compared with an analyst consensus of $907.5 million. Net loss narrowed to $37.5 million, or $0.13 per share, from $119.6 million, or $0.50 per share, in the third quarter of 2025. The beinsure.com article reports that investors gave more weight to the revised guidance and future capital needs than to the revenue and adjusted earnings beats.

Nebius now expects 2026 revenue near the lower end of its earlier range of $3 billion to $3.4 billion, against a $3.35 billion analyst forecast. For 2027 it introduced revenue guidance of $12 billion to $13 billion, compared with a consensus of $12.09 billion. Capital expenditure guidance for 2026 rose to $27 billion, above the earlier range of $20 billion to $25 billion and the analyst estimate of $23.85 billion. For 2027 the company expects capital spending of $40 billion to $45 billion, against a market consensus of $28.77 billion. That range sits roughly 39% to 56% above consensus, and at the top end it exceeds analyst expectations by more than $16 billion.

Chief Executive Officer Arkady Volozh told shareholders that Nebius expects fiscal 2026 revenue near the lower end of its existing $3 billion to $3.4 billion forecast. Management expects revenue of about $3 billion for 2026, and the guidance for 2027 implies substantial growth from that level. The company says the 2027 outlook reflects planned expansion of its AI computing infrastructure, which requires considerable investment before new capacity can generate revenue. Management projects revenue growth to accelerate substantially in 2027, with infrastructure expansion central to reaching the $12 billion to $13 billion target. The articles do not give a direct statement from the company explaining the decision to raise capital spending beyond these points.

The principal concern for investors is the relationship between Nebius's rapid revenue growth and the capital required to deliver it. Beinsure.com says the 2027 outlook is broadly consistent with market expectations at the lower end but leaves significant uncertainty around infrastructure deployment and the timing of capacity additions. Before the results, 15 of 22 analysts rated the stock Buy or higher, six recommended Hold and one rated it Sell, with an average price target of $278.05. That target was about 80% above the November 11 closing price, and beinsure.com notes it preceded the new outlook and may change. The higher investment forecasts could also prompt analysts to revise earnings, cash flow and valuation assumptions.

Adjusted EBITDA reached $465.8 million in the quarter, reversing an adjusted EBITDA loss of $5.2 million a year earlier, when quarterly revenue was $146.1 million. Adjusted earnings were $0.30 per share, against an adjusted loss of $0.61 expected in a separate analyst consensus. For the nine months to September 30, revenue rose 549% to $1.96 billion from $302.1 million, and adjusted EBITDA reached $831.5 million, compared with a loss of $79.9 million. Operating costs and expenses rose 237% to $930.4 million in the quarter, including depreciation and amortization of $354.7 million and selling, general and administrative expenses of $237.4 million. Spending on property, equipment and intangible assets reached $7.30 billion in the quarter, against $955.5 million a year earlier, and total assets rose to $38.74 billion from $12.43 billion at the end of 2025.

Nebius shares had gained about 85% since the start of 2026 before the results, and they rose 15.4% on November 11 to close at $154.69 after strong earnings from competitor CoreWeave. Nebius operates alongside CoreWeave and IREN, and its other holdings include autonomous vehicle company Avride, education technology provider TripleTen and equity interests in ClickHouse and Toloka. Simply Wall St reported that investors were focused on whether Nebius's large Microsoft contract, GPU build out and funding arrangements can turn sector demand into scalable operations. It also noted a $3.5 billion financing facility to expand GPU and data center capacity. A community investor named Womble put fair value at $259.97 per share, based on revenue growth of 21.8% a year and an eventual profit margin of 3.1%.

Nebius says its stock performance will increasingly depend on whether revenue growth can justify an investment program that may exceed $40 billion annually. Investors are watching deployment of data center capacity, securing of customer demand and conversion of infrastructure spending into future revenue. Simply Wall St listed utilisation, cash burn, drawdowns under the $3.5 billion facility and Microsoft related workloads as the details to watch. Net cash used in operating activities from continuing operations was $273 million in the quarter, while operating cash flow for the first nine months was positive at $4.23 billion. The articles do not say how analysts will revise targets after the guidance, nor how the company will fund the $40 billion to $45 billion spending planned for 2027.

stories.Headline: Nscale considers delaying its New York IPO until next year, The Telegraph reports
stories.Summary:
Nscale, a London-based AI cloud company backed by the chip maker Nvidia, is considering delaying its planned New York stock market listing, according to a report in The Telegraph published on Tuesday, November 10. Executives at the data-centre developer are weighing whether to pause their efforts to go public until next year, the newspaper said. Reuters passed the report on, and it described Nscale as a British cloud provider backed by Nvidia. Nscale did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment, which was sent outside regular business hours. Reuters did not report any reason for the possible delay, so the decision has not been explained publicly.

The listing at the centre of the report is one the company filed for in September, when it sought about $3.5 billion in funding, including $2 billion from Nvidia. Nscale plans to list on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol NSCL, and Reuters gave the possible value of the listing as $35 billion. The Telegraph has put the listing's possible value as high as $35 billion, while Bloomberg reported in October that the company was seeking a valuation of roughly $30 billion. Some investors told Bloomberg that a valuation of $16 billion to $19 billion would attract more buyers than the roughly $30 billion Nscale was seeking. If the pause goes ahead, the flotation would move from this year into next year.

The people responsible for the decision are Nscale's executives, who the Telegraph says are assessing whether to hold off on going public until next year. No named executive has been quoted, and the company has made no public statement about the review. Nscale did not immediately respond when Reuters asked for comment outside regular business hours, so the company's own position remains unknown. Nscale filed for the offering in September, and its plans to list under the symbol NSCL were still in place when the report appeared. The reports describe the delay only as an option under consideration, not as a settled plan.

Investors have been the main outside voice, with some telling Bloomberg in October that a lower valuation of $16 billion to $19 billion would draw more buyers. They cited construction delays and a cooling market for AI infrastructure listings as reasons for their caution. Microsoft is also affected, having declined an option to expand its existing agreement with Nscale to rent more computing power at a Texas data center, a move Reuters reported days earlier. Microsoft withdrew as anchor tenant of Nscale's planned data center in Loughton, Essex, where grid operators do not expect to supply power until the 2030s. Financing for the sector has also tightened, with lenders pulling back from AI debt, and the broader pullback by Microsoft has exposed the neoclouds built on its contracts.

Nscale's last private round valued it at about $15 billion, well below the figure now being discussed for the listing. Microsoft and Anthropic accounted for about 85% of the $103.4 billion in signed and active contracts the company reported at the end of August. Nscale's site in Norway is reportedly about six months behind schedule, adding to the construction delays that investors raised. The Telegraph's report came as CoreWeave, the largest listed neocloud, was due to report its third-quarter results after the market closed on Tuesday. Reuters tied the Nscale report to Anthropic's own listing plans, noting that the AI company filed an updated prospectus on Tuesday seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, slightly short of some investors' expectations.

What happens next depends on a decision that Nscale's executives have not yet made, since the reports say only that they are assessing whether to pause their efforts until next year. The company has not yet responded to the Reuters request for comment, so any confirmation or denial is still awaited. The reports do not say whether Nscale would keep its September filing in place, or how a delay would affect the roughly $3.5 billion in funding it sought, which included $2 billion from Nvidia. It is also unclear whether investors would accept a valuation closer to the $16 billion to $19 billion they favored, or whether the company would hold out for around $30 billion. Anthropic's listing, which Reuters called a key test of Wall Street's faith in the AI boom, is moving ahead, and its outcome may bear on whatever Nscale decides.

stories.Headline: Google Unveils Gemini Decision 1: Its First-Ever Decision-Making AI Model That Tops 7 Out of 9 Benchmarks With Up to 92.2% Accuracy
stories.Summary:
Google has released Gemini Decision 1, its first decision-making model, together with the Gemini Decisions API that runs on it. The announcement came on 11 and 12 November 2026, and Google CEO Sundar Pichai introduced the model in a post on X. The model does not write text token by token, and instead scores pre-set candidate answers in a single forward pass. Google says it took first place in 7 of 9 benchmark tests, reaching an accuracy of up to 92.2%. The API is launching in Google AI Studio, and Google's internal teams have already started using the technology.

The API supports three kinds of decision: yes or no judgments, multiple choice with 2 to 255 candidate options, and scoring against ordered grading rubrics. A single request can score up to 1000 questions, and the three kinds of task can be mixed within one request. Inputs can be text, images, audio, video or PDF, with a maximum multimodal context of 256K tokens. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens with no charge for output tokens, roughly one-fifth of the cost of Flash-Lite. End-to-end latency is about 150 to 250 milliseconds, with model computation at a median of 50 to 100 milliseconds for contexts up to 16K tokens.

Google is responsible for the release, and Pichai described the model as built for decision tasks within a closed set of options. Google says developers only need to supply the input, the questions and the candidate options, and the model returns the judgment, its probability and a confidence level. Each decision carries a confidence between 0 and 1, so uncertain results can be passed to other models or to manual review. Google says the model leads on multiple benchmarks while showing the lowest calibration error. Google also says dynamic routing with the API can cut latency for everyday queries by up to 40% in Gemini Notebook.

For comparison, Google chose OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, TypeSafe Jev 1.14 and its own Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, and the scorecard shows rivals ahead in places. On Mind2Web Multimodal, TypeSafe Jev 1.14 scored 86.8% against 86.2% for Gemini Decision 1. On When2Call, which tests tool invocation judgment, TypeSafe Jev led with 82.0% against 79.9%. Competitors also did better on total invocation cost in some cases. On JevBench, Gemini Decision 1 reached 92.2%, ahead of GPT-6 Luna at 90.9%, TypeSafe Jev at 90.0% and Flash-Lite at 86.6%.

The article gives more scores on other tests. In the Amazon ESCI product search test, the model's Macro-F1 of 58.7% beat GPT-6 Luna by 4 points and Flash-Lite by 11.5 points. On the New Yorker Caption test it scored 79.7% against 68.4% for GPT-6 Luna, while on PubMedQA it scored 79.8% against 74.4%. On Global-MMLU-Lite it reached 86.0% against 79.6%, and on MMAU and Video-MME it scored 71.8% and 69.1%, both above Flash-Lite. For Top-1 expected calibration error, it scored 0.0250, against 0.0721 for GPT-6 Luna, 0.0494 for TypeSafe Jev 1.14 and 0.2104 for Flash-Lite.

Previously, developers who wanted AI to flag spam or pick the agent for a task called a generative model and extracted the result from its text. Gemini Decision 1 removes that word-by-word decoding step, so classification, scoring and selection tasks skip full text generation. Google has applied it to AI model routing, agent tool selection, product design and safety detection. In Gemini Notebook it works as a real-time router that picks the model tier and reasoning intensity from the complexity of each request. In Google Stitch, the experimental Rapid Canvas feature uses it to generate interactive product flow wireframes in seconds, and in the Google Labs product CC it picks emoji reactions from more than 200 options.

Google Search also uses the API as a safety detection layer for MCP tools, identifying potential adversarial behavior and content. Developers can now call the Gemini Decisions API in Google AI Studio. In Google Stitch, once users confirm a design direction, the page can move into the full Stitch workflow for further improvement. The articles give no wider rollout dates or availability beyond Google AI Studio. They also leave open whether the gaps against TypeSafe Jev on Mind2Web Multimodal and When2Call will close.

stories.Headline: ModelOp Named a Market Shaper in the 2026 Gartner® Emerging Market Quadrant for AI FinOps Tools - Startup Vendors
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, ModelOp announced from Park City, Utah that Gartner had positioned it as a Market Shaper in its Emerging Market Quadrant for AI FinOps Tools for Startup Vendors. Gartner published the report on October 28, 2026, and ModelOp describes itself as the Enterprise AI Command Center for Fortune 500 and Global 2000 organizations. On the same day, Coralogix announced from Boston that it too had been recognized as a Market Shaper in the same quadrant, which it dates to October 2026. Coralogix calls itself the data and AI platform for observability. Both announcements appeared on the Manila Times newswire section, distributed through GlobeNewswire.

ModelOp says it is one of four vendors positioned in the Market Shapers quadrant, among 18 vendors recognized in the report. The Emerging Market Quadrant examines vendors in fast-changing technology markets, judging their Potential for Market Disruption and their Potential to Execute. Gartner defines AI FinOps tools as solutions that measure, attribute, forecast, control and optimize AI costs. The report characterizes Market Shapers as vendors with strong cost optimization insights and automation, pursuing end-to-end proactive AI cost management. ModelOp's capabilities are delivered through its Enterprise AI Command Center, powered by the ModelOp AI Delivery Engine, known as MADE, and include use case cost attribution, a usage and FinOps dashboard, portfolio analysis, AI discovery and business value monitoring.

ModelOp chief executive Dave Trier said enterprise AI faces a financial accountability crisis, because companies deploy more models and autonomous agents than ever while counting tokens and tracking invoices fails to show chief executives or finance chiefs whether investments pay off. He argued that the real question is what business value specific use cases deliver, which is why ModelOp ties costs to the use case, the business owner and the expected outcome. Trier added that AI FinOps must be part of how enterprises govern and operate AI, rather than a dashboard added afterward. He also said the next phase of enterprise AI will be defined by measurable returns rather than the number of agents deployed. Coralogix chief executive and co-founder Ariel Assaraf said AI is fundamentally changing the economics of running modern software, and that managing AI spending requires visibility into the systems and workflows driving it.

Assaraf said Coralogix believes its recognition reflects the growing importance of connecting AI observability with the financial accountability enterprises need as they operationalize AI at scale. He added that as agents grow more autonomous, enterprises must connect performance, resource consumption and business outcomes, and that observability provides a critical foundation for that understanding. Coralogix cites Gartner as saying the market is shifting beyond cost reporting toward AI economics management, and that organizations must connect token consumption, compute and other costs to measurable business outcomes. Among customers, a global professional services firm uses Coralogix to monitor approximately 19,500 coding-agent users, tracking consumption and spending across users, models and repositories. ModelOp's integrations include Microsoft Agent 365, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Quick, OpenAI and Model Context Protocol-based tools, supporting oversight across heterogeneous enterprise environments.

ModelOp says this is its third Gartner recognition since June 2026, following two earlier research placements that year. In June, it was named a Visionary in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Governance Platforms. In the accompanying Critical Capabilities report for AI Governance Platforms, ModelOp received the highest score for the AI Agent Governance use case. ModelOp says it has been building its enterprise AI delivery and governance foundation since 2018, spanning lifecycle automation, risk management, policy enforcement, operational monitoring and AI FinOps. Coralogix says traditional cost management, which monitors usage and reviews spending after it occurs, grows harder to sustain as AI workloads scale, while enterprises move from experimentation to production deployments with autonomous agents, multi-model environments and expanding token consumption.

Coralogix says its platform is built on a streaming-first architecture that brings together logs, metrics, traces and AI observability capabilities. It offers budget controls, consumption forecasting and automated safeguards against unexpected spending, and says it continues to invest in AI-native observability, real-time data infrastructure and autonomous investigation capabilities. The full Gartner report is available for download from a Coralogix web page, while ModelOp directs readers to its website and blog for more on its AI FinOps capabilities. Both companies add that Gartner does not endorse any vendor and that its publications reflect opinion rather than statements of fact. The articles do not name the other two vendors in the Market Shapers quadrant, and they do not list the 18 vendors recognized in the report.

stories.Headline: IBM and Microsoft Launch AI Agent Platform
stories.Summary:
IBM and Microsoft announced Imagine Enterprise on Tuesday, November 10, an artificial intelligence agent platform meant to help companies build, run and govern agents that carry out industry-specific business processes. The two companies describe it as an agentic platform that combines IBM Consulting's technologies and expertise with Microsoft's AI, data, cloud and security systems. The announcement was issued from Armonk, New York, and Redmond, Washington, and coverage followed from PYMNTS and the EdTech Innovation Hub. PYMNTS said the platform targets banks, insurers and retailers that want to automate their business processes. The EdTech Innovation Hub said it initially targets financial services, insurance and retail.

The platform brings together more than 6,000 prebuilt AI agents and related assets from IBM Consulting with Microsoft's cloud infrastructure and security tools. Forward-deployed engineers from both companies will work directly with qualifying customers to connect agents to existing software and move them from testing into production. Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio and GitHub Copilot provide the tools for developing and coordinating agents, according to PYMNTS. Microsoft Fabric connects enterprise data, Entra manages identities and access permissions, Purview supports data governance, and Defender provides security capabilities. On IBM's side, Process Studio, Context Studio and Advantage Core support configuring, deploying and overseeing agents, and the EdTech Innovation Hub adds that Azure also forms part of the supporting technology.

IBM and Microsoft are the two companies responsible for the platform, and IBM's contribution comes from Consulting Advantage, its existing platform for developing and deploying AI applications. Mohamad Ali, Senior Vice President and Head of IBM Consulting, said clients are no longer looking for AI that simply helps people do the same work a little faster. He said they want to build an agentic business. Ali added that the two companies are helping organizations bring human expertise and digital labor together in a way that can scale across the enterprise. In his words, the aim is to turn AI from a productivity aid into a real competitive advantage.

SEI, a financial technology, operations and asset management provider, is working with IBM Consulting, supported by Microsoft, to explore emerging and agentic technologies. Sneha Shah, Chief AI Strategist and Head of SEI Next, said the work is helping SEI explore how new capabilities could support critical processes and be responsibly scaled over time. She said the goal is better experiences for SEI's employees and clients. The EdTech Innovation Hub stressed that this example describes exploratory transformation work and that the announcement identifies no completed Imagine Enterprise deployment at SEI and no measured results. The platform particularly targets organizations in regulated industries, where its controls, observability and AI-compliance support are meant to help customers manage industry-specific deployments.

PYMNTS noted that the 6,000 figure includes agents and other assets, rather than exclusively deployable agents. It said the partnership extends Microsoft's efforts to expand AI adoption across its existing enterprise software customer base. In September, PYMNTS reported that Microsoft has 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats, but fewer than 7% carry paid Copilot licenses. Microsoft 365 Copilot costs $30 per user monthly, while newer agent capabilities are billed according to usage. Microsoft has also introduced agents that operate within corporate Microsoft 365 environments, with their own identities, memory and email addresses.

The launch arrives as businesses increase their AI investments but remain cautious about granting software independent authority. PYMNTS Intelligence's November report, titled The Agentic Edge Index, found agentic AI in use at 89% of large U.S. enterprises. Yet 78% of them would restrict agents to read-only access to company directories, while another 18% would allow tasks with human approval and 2% would permit independent execution. The same report found that 51% of executives consider organizational barriers, including staffing, business processes and corporate culture, greater obstacles to AI adoption than technology. The articles do not say when customers will begin production deployments, how many will qualify for engineering support, or what the platform will cost.

stories.Headline: SpaceX to Invest More Than $74 Billion in AI Data Centers in Texas, Arizona
stories.Summary:
SpaceX announced on November 12 that it will invest more than $74 billion in two artificial intelligence data centers, one in Texas and one in Arizona. The company also committed to funding its own electricity and water infrastructure for both projects. The Texas project is a supercomputer campus at Starbase in South Texas, with an estimated cost above $24 billion. The Arizona project is a campus of roughly $50 billion in Cochise County. SpaceX said the work would benefit nearby communities by creating jobs and by building new power generation and water supply networks.

The Texas data center will sit on 444 acres of land controlled by Starbase, near the Port of Brownsville and the city's landfill. SpaceX said the facility will generate its own electricity without drawing power from the public grid. The Arizona campus is expected to create about 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs for local workers. In Texas, the project has already generated more than 3,000 construction jobs and will support more than 500 permanent workers. The Arizona campus will use dry cooling, with no planned industrial groundwater consumption, and the site remains subject to approval by local authorities.

SpaceX is the company behind both projects, and it made the announcement on November 12 while describing the benefits to surrounding communities. For Arizona, it said it is working with local electric cooperatives to win approval for a power project built on existing renewable resources. The company said that project could lower cooperative members' electricity bills by as much as 20 percent. For Brownsville, SpaceX said that relying on traditional public financing to close the $220 million funding gap would have cost ratepayers $370 million over 25 years, including interest. The city of Brownsville, which struck the land deal, said it stands by the agreement and stressed the importance of securing the $220 million in water funding.

The South Texas Environmental Justice Network organized a protest against the Texas project, arguing that the new facilities would pollute the air, use up water, and raise energy bills for residents. Brownsville said in a message to residents that it remains committed to evaluating those concerns and protecting water resources. The city also pledged to evaluate infrastructure impacts and to ensure responsible growth serving its long-term interests. Residents of Brownsville are directly affected, since roughly three-quarters of the city's primary water supply comes from two Rio Grande reservoirs. SpaceX said both reservoirs have faced critically low water levels, which is part of why water use has drawn scrutiny.

Earlier this year, Brownsville voted to remove the land from its city boundaries at SpaceX's request, in exchange for up to $220 million toward water and wastewater infrastructure. That change placed the land outside the reach of a 90-day moratorium on data center applications within the city's jurisdiction, which took effect on November 5. The articles also describe dry cooling as a closed-loop system that circulates cooling fluid into a device exposed to outside air. As long as the ambient air is cooler than the fluid, the system can run without drawing water to replace evaporation. Separate coverage of SpaceX's finances said its AI business brought in $7.6 billion last quarter and its connectivity business brought in $5.2 billion.

Across Texas, data center developers are expected to face stronger headwinds under Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on halting new data center approvals. She said approvals should stay halted until the state adopts additional rules governing electricity costs, water use, and the role of local communities. The Arizona campus still needs approval from local authorities, and SpaceX is working with local electric cooperatives to win approval for its power project. The articles do not say when construction would finish on either campus or when the Arizona site might receive its approvals. They also leave open how the incoming governor's rules would apply to the Texas site, which sits on land outside the city's boundaries.
