stories.Headline: Global AI stocks sink as Nvidia crisis deepens sector selloff - CNA
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, Nov 12, 2026, following a deepening scandal around his affairs, and global AI-linked stocks tumbled as a result. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO while the company looks for a permanent successor. Nvidia's shares fell 8.2 per cent to a more than 16-month low in early trading that day. Its market value was on track to close below US$4 trillion for the first time since July 2025. The chip giant has lost more than US$550 billion in market value since its board announced an investigation on Sunday.

The investigation concerns Huang's relationship with a businesswoman called Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a Chinese spy. Chipmakers led the selloff, with the Philadelphia chips index sliding 1.3 per cent, while Marvell Technology slumped 3.8 per cent and Oracle shed 2.6 per cent. Micron Technology fell 2.5 per cent, Sandisk eased 6 per cent and Western Digital 3.7 per cent. Lumentum, Coherent and Dell eased between 3 per cent and 5.1 per cent, while Caterpillar and Vistra slipped about 0.5 per cent each. Japan and South Korea closed nearly 0.7 per cent lower, and tech stocks in Europe were down about 1 per cent.

Nvidia's board announced the investigation on Sunday, and the company said Kress would serve as interim CEO as it searches for a successor. The articles give no comment from Huang himself on his resignation. On Tuesday, Nvidia had already hired lawyers for an internal investigation tied to its CEO. Yahoo Finance's page also carried a banner reporting that Huang had been accused of a second affair. Nvidia's leadership now rests with Kress while the search continues.

Analysts and investors voiced concern about what the turmoil means for the wider sector. Joe Saluzzi of Themis Trading noted that Nvidia has been called the "Bank of AI" and asked whether a step back could cut off funding to smaller companies that need it. Steve Sosnick of Interactive Brokers said the interlocking deals raise the question of whether they created more stability or more fragility, and that the coming weeks will show. Tim Ghriskey of Ingalls & Snyder said he sees selling in Nvidia and other AI firms as buying opportunities and does not see Nvidia falling apart. Neocloud firms CoreWeave fell 9.1 per cent and Nebius dropped 16.2 per cent after saying its 2026 revenue would come in at the low end of its forecast, while IREN and Applied Digital also traded lower.

Nvidia finances infrastructure built around its chips, a strategy that has drawn scrutiny over circular funding. CoreWeave, which Nvidia backs, had surged more than 27 per cent in the previous session when its earnings ignited a relief rally in AI stocks. Earlier this month the Nasdaq entered a technical correction after the Democrats swept the midterm elections, including in states opposed to data centres, stoking fears that tighter regulation could slow the AI build-out. On Tuesday, selling was also driven by a hot US inflation report that raised expectations the Federal Reserve will raise rates again next month. Over the past month the Nasdaq Composite has dropped by 1 per cent or more eight times and risen by that much six times.

Short sellers of Nvidia have made US$9.6 billion in on-paper profits so far this week, according to the data firm ORTEX. Nvidia trades at about 12 times its 12-month forward earnings estimates, its lowest since November 2012, according to data compiled by LSEG. AMD and Broadcom rose 3.7 per cent and 5.6 per cent on expectations that the turmoil could create opportunity for rivals, and Alphabet, Amazon.com and Microsoft rose between 0.8 per cent and 2.7 per cent. Analysts have said the scandal could spur tighter US scrutiny of AI cloud providers in Southeast Asia. The articles do not say who will become permanent CEO, how long the investigation will last, or whether the allegations against Alice Huang will be substantiated.

stories.Headline: Foundation Models framework
stories.Summary:
Apple's developer site describes the Foundation Models framework as a native Swift API for integrating any large language model into an app. It includes direct access to the Apple Foundation Models, running both on the device and in Private Cloud Compute. The framework now also extends to server models such as Claude and Gemini, reached through the same Swift API. Built-in capabilities include guided generation, tool calling, image understanding and Dynamic Profiles. InfoWorld separately examined Microsoft's own foundation models, which Microsoft has begun rolling out as part of its Microsoft AI program, known as MAI.

On the Apple side, developers in the App Store Small Business Program with fewer than two million first-time App Store downloads can use the Apple Foundation Models on Private Cloud Compute with no cloud API cost. Multimodal prompts let developers pass images alongside text, and the Vision framework adds on-device tools such as OCR and barcode readers. Dynamic Profiles let a session swap model, temperature, reasoning level and toolset while sharing one transcript across every switch. A new fm command line tool arrives in macOS 27, and the Foundation Models SDK for Python extends the framework into that ecosystem. On the Microsoft side, MAI-Thinking-1 can be deployed to a Foundry instance by changing the API call to the model's endpoint URL, and requests can carry a token limit.

Apple states that any model provider can create a Swift package conforming to the Language Model protocol, which lets developers choose the right model for their app. Apple says the on-device model at the core of Apple Intelligence lets developers build experiences that are smart, private and work without internet connectivity. It also says Private Cloud Compute ensures that users' data is not stored or accessible to Apple or anyone else. At Microsoft, MAI describes its approach as humanist, with a focus on safety and environmental impact. Microsoft says MAI-Thinking-1 runs with a much smaller footprint than competing models while still delivering the results users expect.

Author Simon Bisson writes that Microsoft publishes benchmark numbers even when they favor some of the bigger models from Anthropic and OpenAI. He says the aim is to gain market share by showing results nearly as good at a much lower cost. He adds that Flash models like MAI-Code-1.1-Flash need more than 120GB of RAM to run, so they are not yet small enough for Copilot+ PCs. The new NVIDIA RTX Spark-powered Surface Ultra, configured with at least 128GB of RAM, should be more than capable of running them.

Buyers must still weigh agent usage to judge whether local operation beats cloud servers on cost. Apple's requirements also affect developers, since its Acceptable Use Requirements outline prohibited uses of Apple Foundation Models. Microsoft's partnership with OpenAI let OpenAI train its models on Azure infrastructure, and Microsoft became the first commercial partner to use them. Foundry now offers access to more than 11,000 models, including those from Anthropic, Hugging Face, Meta, Mistral and DeepSeek.

Microsoft also continues to offer its Cognitive Services models and the Phi series of lightweight models for the edge. Microsoft Research has been a hub for deep learning for much of the last decade, but produced focused models rather than general-purpose ones. The article says low-cost tokens are gone as hyperscale vendors recoup multi-billion-dollar data center investments, which leaves MAI focused on offering lower token cost than competitors. Apple says the open source Foundation Models framework utilities package adds experimental abstractions, including custom skills, context management helpers and a Chat Completions client for a hosted model of the developer's choice.

Its Evaluations framework lets developers test prompts before shipping, and pursuant to Article 53(1)(b) of the AI Act it provides documentation on AFM 3 Cloud. At Microsoft, the Maia 300 release boosts compute operations by 36%, with 2.5x improvements in high bandwidth memory performance and roughly a 2x performance gain per watt. Each rack holds 96 accelerators and supports multiple jobs sharded across racks. The articles leave open how many developers will adopt either approach, and they give no release dates beyond macOS 27 for the fm tool.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Boosts AI Trade. Bloom Energy, Other Power Stocks Are Big Winners.
stories.Summary:
Shares of Bloom Energy rose 12.97% on November 11, closing at $209.47, a gain of $24.05, as renewed confidence in spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure lifted suppliers of on-site electricity. MarketWatch tied the rally to upbeat results and financing comments from CoreWeave, which eased worries about how data-center construction will be funded. The article describes this as a sector-wide reassessment of demand rather than a new Bloom earnings announcement. Larger percentage gains reported during the day were intraday readings, and the closing price is a regular-session figure, not a live quote.

Bloom's most recent results, published October 22 for the quarter ended September 30, showed revenue of $1,235.8 million, up 138.1% from a year earlier. GAAP operating income reached $225.4 million, and operating margin rose to 18.2% from 1.5%. Diluted GAAP earnings were $0.78 a share, with non-GAAP diluted earnings of $0.94. The company raised its 2026 revenue outlook to between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion, which implies 122% growth at the midpoint, and set non-GAAP earnings guidance at $3.10 to $3.40 a share. On November 5, NTT DATA announced an agreement to deploy 900 megawatts of Bloom equipment across data-center projects worldwide, with initial shipments starting in 2027.

The cash picture is less comfortable. Third-quarter operating cash flow was negative $27.1 million, and purchases of property, plant and equipment totaled $153.5 million, which works out to roughly $180.6 million of negative free cash flow, an analytical figure rather than a reported line. At September 30, Bloom held $2.487 billion in cash and equivalents against $2.473 billion in recourse debt, alongside non-recourse debt, financing obligations and operating leases. Common shares outstanding rose to 295.5 million from 280.0 million at the end of December.

Analysts are split on whether the valuation leaves room for error. J.P. Morgan's Mark Strouse kept an Overweight rating on October 23 but cut his target to $292 from $314, citing lower peer multiples despite strong execution. Roth Capital's Chip Moore stayed Neutral and lowered his target to $230 from $260, pointing to valuation and limited visibility, while Jefferies' Julien Dumoulin-Smith kept a Hold with a $242 target and asked for a formal backlog update. Evercore ISI's Nicholas Amicucci reiterated Outperform and a $350 target on October 26, calling the cash-flow-related selloff excessive.

The closing price is about 62 to 68 times management's 2026 adjusted earnings range, and trailing price-to-sales stands at 16.17, up from 10.15 at the end of 2025. Consensus-based forward earnings multiples are 42.81 for Bloom, compared with 34.87 for GE Vernova, though GE Vernova's broader equipment lineup limits the comparison. The article says the next test is whether installation schedules, cash collection and manufacturing capacity advance together, since announced megawatts alone do not show when revenue becomes cash. It names international delivery pace, manufacturing investment and financing needs as the things to monitor, and warns that postponed customer projects or growth below the company's outlook would weaken the case.

stories.Headline: Growing AI Use Raises Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks
stories.Summary:
Kaspersky has published a survey showing that growing use of artificial intelligence for personal advice, health questions and everyday planning is raising worries about privacy and cybersecurity. The survey covered respondents across the Middle East, Türkiye and Africa region, known as META, and was reported by Pakistan Observer and The Patriot on 12 November 2026. Nearly 79 percent of respondents said they use AI services, including chatbots and tools for making images and videos. Experts warned that sharing sensitive information with these platforms could expose users to data leaks, misuse by third parties and cyberattacks. The IAPP also published an analysis on 12 November 2026 on how Italy is handling AI, privacy and cybersecurity.

Searching for and summarising information was the most common use of AI, cited by 74 percent of those surveyed. Writing texts followed at 50 percent, generating images from written prompts at 42 percent, and editing personal photos at 41 percent. Another 32 percent turned to AI to create videos, while 37 percent used it for health-related questions and 41 percent sought advice on personal matters. Planning weekends, holidays or events drew 29 percent, and creating meal menus and diet plans drew 23 percent. Almost one in 10 respondents had already met incorrect AI-generated information, and 24 percent believed AI could give inaccurate answers.

Seifallah Jedidi, Kaspersky's Head of Consumer Channel for the Middle East, Türkiye and Africa, is the named spokesperson. He urged consumers to understand the limits of AI services and the risks linked to them. He said even widely used platforms can have vulnerabilities that lead to data leaks. According to him, information shared with these platforms may be processed under the relevant service and its policies, or may be reached by third parties. He urged users to verify AI-generated content, avoid sharing confidential information and stay alert to fraudulent AI services designed to spread malware.

Kaspersky experts advised users to avoid giving sensitive, confidential or private information to AI services in order to reduce cybersecurity risks. They warned that phishing web pages, malicious software and fake websites often imitate genuine platforms or deceive users with fake tools. The company also recommended checking each platform's data-handling policies. It advised consulting reliable sources before relying on AI for medical, financial, legal or educational advice. Users of AI services are the people affected, particularly those who share health details or personal matters with chatbots.

The IAPP analysis, written by Ludovica Mosci, Manager of Privacy Compliance EMEA at The Walt Disney Company, describes Italy as one of Europe's most interventionist jurisdictions on privacy, AI and cybersecurity. Two legislative decrees recently completed Italy's transposition of the EU AI Act into national law. Legislative Decree No. 160, adopted on 9 September, introduced corporate and individual criminal liability provisions. Legislative Decree No. 179, adopted on 8 October and in force from 23 October, clarifies the roles and responsibilities of Italy's national AI supervisory authorities. In July, the data protection authority, the Garante, concluded its investigation into Character Technologies, the U.S.-based provider of the Character.AI companion app, which also touched on minors' online protection.

The articles do not say what follows from the Kaspersky survey, and they give no sign of any regulatory response to its findings. They describe Italy's cybersecurity position as one of no new regulatory developments, with 2026 marking the move from legislative implementation to operational compliance and active supervision under the NIS2 Directive and the Digital Operational Resilience Act. They say the Garante has continued its scrutiny of AI providers, including a decision on an AI-powered plug-in for sentiment analysis of employees. The IAPP excerpt does not set out the outcome of the Character.AI investigation or of the employee plug-in decision. Kaspersky also points to its Kaspersky Premium security solution, which it says protects users in everyday digital activities through AI-based technologies.

stories.Headline: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12, 2026, its third new model in six weeks. The release introduces an xhigh reasoning level, the first step above high on any Gemini model. Hydrogen accepts text, image, video and speech input and produces text output, with a context window of one million tokens. It offers four reasoning levels in all, low, medium, high and xhigh.

According to the independent firm Artificial Analysis, Hydrogen at xhigh scores 54 on its Intelligence Index, one point behind both Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol at their max settings. That is four points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon at high. At the default high setting Hydrogen scores 51, just behind GPT-6.1 Sol at xhigh and Claude Opus 5.5 at high, which each score 52. Pricing is $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted by 95 percent to $0.075.

On cost, Artificial Analysis says xhigh runs about 32 percent of what Sonnet 5.5 costs per task, but roughly 2.5 times what GPT-6.1 Sol costs. The cost per task is $3.16 at xhigh and $1.87 at high, because xhigh nearly doubles output tokens for a three-point gain. Medium costs $0.80 and low costs $0.29, scoring 41 and 27 on the index. At high reasoning, Hydrogen matches Gemini 4 Argon's score for about 19 percent of the cost per task.

The firm found clear strengths in visual reasoning and avoiding made-up answers. On GDP.pdf, a long-document visual benchmark, Hydrogen scored 33 percent all-pass on medium reasoning, tying for first place. Its hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience was 8 percent, against 43 percent for Sonnet 5.5 and 52 percent for GPT-6.1 Sol. Agentic terminal work is weaker, with 54 percent on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 50 percent on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, compared with 64 and 53 percent for Sonnet 5.5 and 56 and 58 percent for GPT-6.1 Sol. Hydrogen's output speed is about 200 tokens per second, and at high, medium and low it sits on the time-per-task frontier, meaning no model is both smarter and faster.

stories.Headline: Google's $10 million plan to buy Spirit's data and use it to train AI cleared one of its last big hurdles
stories.Summary:
Aviation unions and public-interest groups withdrew their objections to Google's purchase of Spirit Airlines data on Monday night, after reaching an agreement with the company about former employees' information. The Association of Flight Attendants announced the deal on Tuesday, saying it had worked alongside other unions to protect the personal data of former Spirit staff. The union described the agreement as an historic win for worker privacy protections. Google had won the right to buy the data for $10 million, and the chats and files are meant to help train its AI models. The reporting describes the unions' withdrawal as clearing one of the last big hurdles to the sale.

Under the agreement, data covering employees' medical and disability history, drug or alcohol testing records and payroll records will be excluded, according to the union's list of protections. The AFA-CWA said Google also agreed to a more rigorous de-identification process than had previously been planned, so that the company does not receive personal data. Google is further prohibited from attempting to reidentify the data it receives. The data Google won at the Aug. 14 bankruptcy auction includes 500 million Microsoft Teams chats and 100 million emails from 80,000 accounts. It also covers about 30 million lines of code across 516 software projects, plus other internal documents.

A court-appointed privacy ombudsman recommended approval after personal information about 97 million Spirit customers was excluded from the sale. Sara Nelson, international president of the AFA-CWA, said worker data privacy in the age of AI has become a whole new worker's rights issue. She said that without the union there would have been no one to speak for workers in what she called a fire sale of their private information. Nelson said the unions fought for and won brand new protections for the former employees. She added that the union will now take the issue to all of its employers to secure contractual protections.

She also said the union will demand that lawmakers protect workers everywhere through federal and state law. Google has said it acquired part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines that can be helpful in improving its products and AI models. In an Aug. 17 statement issued after it won the auction, a company spokesperson said Google will not receive any personal information from the dataset. Last month, Google said it was not looking to buy any personal information from Spirit, according to Reuters. The company said the information will either be completely excluded or be de-identified by an independent third party before Google receives any data.

Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the unions' announcement, and it referred the Daily Caller News Foundation to its earlier statement. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and 120 other members of Congress sent an Oct. 8 letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Spirit CEO Dave Davis, raising concerns about the sale. The letter called the sale uncharted territory and said the information was created and provided in the context of an employment relationship. It warned that the data may contain highly sensitive information about individual workers.

The lawmakers wrote that consumers have more privacy protections than workers, yet Spirit collected far more private information about its employees than about its customers. The affected people are former Spirit employees, along with the customers whose information was excluded. Spirit Airlines ceased operations in May, and its assets were then put up for auction. Google won the bid at the Aug. 14 bankruptcy auction, paying $10 million for the data.

The sale was held up in bankruptcy court over privacy concerns, particularly regarding details of staff and customers held by Spirit. Those concerns later drew the October letter from 121 members of Congress led by Warren. The privacy ombudsman's recommendation followed, and the unions' agreement with Google came after that. A bankruptcy judge must still approve the sale, so it is not yet final.

If it is approved, the Daily Caller reported, the deal could encourage other big tech companies to purchase workplace data in order to train their models. The articles do not say when the judge will rule on the sale. The AFA-CWA said it will take the issue of worker data privacy to all of its employers to seek contractual protections. Warren's office and the union did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller's requests for comment, and the articles do not say whether the judge will accept the new protections.

stories.Headline: Rescale Expands Agentic Digital Engineering with Customizable AI Agents for R&D Teams
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 10, 2026, Rescale, a San Francisco digital engineering platform company, announced new agentic digital engineering capabilities that let R&D and engineering teams customize AI agents to their own standards. The announcement went out through PR Newswire, and Tech Times reported it on Nov. 11. The release says the tools bring agentic AI into engineering work where every result must be reviewable and traceable. Its centerpiece is a set of Agentic Projects, which give engineers a way to customize agents and build reusable agentic workflows. Rescale presents the package as an engineering-specific harness, meaning the structure and context that govern how agents operate and keep humans in the loop.

Teams can define each Agentic Project with its own context, skills, tools and guardrails, share projects across teams, and retain approved learnings through project memory. Expanded engineering intelligence capabilities connect data across requirements, design, simulation, test and process systems into foundational knowledge graphs. As agents execute workflows, the platform generates project-specific work graphs that provide traceability and capture learnings. Rescale Desktop extends the platform to engineers' local machines, and expanded Model Context Protocol connectors cover Rescale's ecosystem of engineering applications, including availability on the Claude and Codex directories. Rescale Edison, the platform's AI assistant and agent orchestrator, now has persistent memory, so engineers can describe their intent in natural language.

For AI physics, a new dataset creation agent turns simulation data into training-ready datasets, while Auto Tune, guided pre-processing, uncertainty quantification and a local design explorer add further tools. Jacob Surber, Rescale's vice president of product, said customers build aircraft, vehicles and reactors, so the supporting agents must deliver reliable results. He described Agentic Projects as providing context that grows with every iteration, and called the launch a material step toward an engineering harness built for how these teams actually work. Kairos Power and the Department of Energy's Manufacturing Demonstration Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory built a digital agentic scaffolding on the platform with support from Rescale AI developer engineers. Ed Blandford, Kairos Power's chief technology officer and co-founder, said the company depends on quick learning cycles of designing, building and testing.

He added that agents managing setup, execution and reporting leave his engineers free for judgment and rigor. Ryan Dehoff, the facility's director, said Rescale gives industry engineers and lab researchers a digital environment for working side by side, and that agents let Oak Ridge's expertise scale beyond its facility. The release says agents exercised thermal, flow and shielding simulation and reporting workflows for the reactor cavity and bioshield plug designs, with engineers approving each agent action. Oak Ridge is encoding its simulation and additive manufacturing expertise in agents on the platform so engineers can adopt advanced methods to address industry challenges. For high performance computing administrators, new cluster performance metrics show where execution slows and why jobs are waiting.

A new priority score weighs wait time, job size and resource usage to help teams allocate resources fairly. Tech Times pointed out that an audit trail records what an agent did and who approved it, but does not by itself show that the underlying model is valid for the job. It advised teams to ask what each approval step actually checks, how surrogate predictions are rechecked against full simulations, and what outside AI assistants can reach through the connectors. The work is part of a collaboration to test advanced manufacturing and construction methods for Hermes 2, which the release describes as Kairos Power's 50-megawatt fluoride-salt-cooled reactor. Tech Times reports that Hermes 2 is Kairos's demonstration plant in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, where ground was broken on April 17, 2026, and that Kairos says it will deliver up to 50 megawatts of electricity to the Tennessee Valley Authority grid.

The release does not say whether the 50 megawatts is thermal or electric, though Kairos describes it as electric output, and Kairos has targeted 2030 for power production. Kairos reported on Sept. 4 that it had tested modular precast concrete shielding in a reduced-scale mockup of the Hermes 2 reactor cavity, with the facility supplying 3D-printed forms. Rescale's own release notes date several of the new pieces earlier than the announcement: Agentic Projects to Oct. 26, the Edison rename to Oct. 19, Rescale Desktop to Nov. 5, and uncertainty quantification and the dataset agent to Nov. 6. The company describes itself as backed by investors including NVIDIA, Sam Altman, Jeff Bezos, Paul Graham, Peter Thiel, Microsoft, Hitachi and the University of Michigan. Kairos Power projects that agentic workflows built from past simulations could raise end-to-end simulation analysis efficiency by up to 3x while preserving the data traceability required for regulatory compliance.

Tech Times stresses that this threefold gain is a projection, and that the release gives no measured figure for the workflow. The article also notes that Rescale's May 12 release cited a 1,000x increase in simulation speed and a 90% reduction in full-stack simulation costs, with no baseline, sample size or timeframe stated. The release says the new capabilities across agentic digital engineering, AI physics and intelligent HPC work together as organizations adopt AI-first operations across their product development lifecycles. Organizations can learn more about the new capabilities at rescale.com, though the excerpted articles do not say when Kairos or Oak Ridge expect measured results.

stories.Headline: The Next AI Chip Shortage May Be the Machines That Make HBM
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics said on November 12 that it had moved up the planned opening of its new high-bandwidth memory packaging plant in South Korea by one year, to June 2028. The company gave rising demand for AI server memory as the reason for bringing the date forward. The same day, President Lee Jae-myung spoke at a groundbreaking for the Chungcheong mega-project, where three investment projects began construction. Those projects were an advanced semiconductor packaging fab and an advanced display line in Asan, plus a plant for high-performance AI server substrates in Sejong. Lee said the packaging fab at Samsung's Onyang campus will become a key hub for advanced HBM packaging.

The Onyang packaging fab is valued at about 6 trillion won, and it is to be followed in sequence by about 40 trillion won of advanced equipment. Together the fab and the equipment come to 46 trillion won, which Aju Business Daily reported as about 34.4 billion dollars at the day's rate. At the base rate of 1,336.7 won per dollar, the equipment alone is about 29.9 billion dollars, by FourWeekMBA's arithmetic. That equipment is roughly 6.7 times the value of the fab, and about 47 percent of the 84.4 trillion won Samsung expects to spend on capital expenditure in 2026. It also equals about 52 percent of the 76.8 trillion won planned for the Device Solutions chip division, and about 1.4 times the third quarter's spending.

President Lee said companies and the government pledged the investment plan in July, and that the promise was becoming reality just four months later. He said the Onyang campus will become a key hub for advanced HBM packaging. Samsung chairman Lee Jae-yong, who attended, said the site, which centred on simple assembly and testing of general chips, will become a hub for advanced HBM for AI chips, according to Financial News. Samsung said on October 29 that it expects AI infrastructure capital expenditure to reach a historic level in 2027 as the AI ecosystem expands. In its third-quarter release the company also said it significantly scaled up sales of HBM4.

Samsung said on its earnings call that its 2027 HBM supply was already sold out, which bears directly on buyers of AI server memory. Other Chungcheong projects named in the speech, in Cheongju, Dangjin and Osong, are said to be on schedule. Those are a memory and advanced packaging fab in Cheongju, an AI data centre in Dangjin and a biopharmaceutical plant in Osong. Samsung's market value rose about 11 billion dollars at the Seoul open on November 12. Separately, a SMIC comment listed among DIGITIMES's most-read items said AI memory may balance after mid-2028 while compute and supporting chips stay short.

Samsung said capital expenditure reached 29 trillion won in the third quarter, up 19.8 trillion won from a year earlier. The Onyang campus in Asan previously centred on simple assembly and testing of general chips. HBM is made by stacking memory dies and packaging them next to an AI processor, and Lee called Onyang an HBM packaging hub rather than a memory fab. FourWeekMBA reads the project as shifting Samsung's HBM bottleneck from wafers to packaging, since most of the money goes into tools rather than buildings. Samsung's third-quarter release said investments are planned for new fabs and other infrastructure to meet strong AI and high-performance computing demand.

Lee gave no schedule or year-by-year split for the 40 trillion won of equipment, saying only that it follows in sequence. How much of that spending falls inside the 84.4 trillion won 2026 guidance is not stated. Samsung's Korean newsroom had not published a release on the groundbreaking when FourWeekMBA checked its feed at 01:50 UTC. The president's figures come from Korean outlets quoting his speech, and FourWeekMBA could not load the presidential office's own transcript. Groundbreakings for the Cheongju, Dangjin and Osong projects are the next steps Lee named, and FourWeekMBA did not contact Samsung for its piece.

stories.Headline: Quantinuum and RIKEN Expand Partnership to Accelerate the Commercialization of Quantum-AI Hybrid Supercomputing in Japan
stories.Summary:
Quantinuum and RIKEN announced this week that the Reimei quantum computer installed at RIKEN has been upgraded to Quantinuum's System Model H2, which has 56 qubits. Quantinuum issued an 8-K press release confirming the upgrade on November 10, 2026, together with an expanded partnership involving RIKEN and SoftBank Corp. The upgrade moves the machine from the earlier H1 system and was described as a significant step for the platform. The companies say the work will advance quantum-AI hybrid supercomputing in Japan. Reimei is operated as part of the JHPC-quantum project, which is funded by NEDO, an organization under Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry.

The expanded partnership rests on a Memorandum of Understanding between Quantinuum and RIKEN to advance scientific and industrial applications. Under it, the two will jointly develop a fault-tolerant quantum computer called "Made with Japan," involving Japanese universities and domestic components suppliers. That work will combine Quantinuum's quantum technology with Japanese research and manufacturing expertise, and it will draw on lessons from deploying and operating Reimei at RIKEN. A separate agreement brings in SoftBank Corp., and under it Quantinuum, RIKEN and SoftBank will explore connecting quantum computing directly with AI data centers in Japan. The partners will also assess infrastructure readiness and examine how connected systems could support commercial quantum-AI hybrid computing services.

Dr. Rajeeb Hazra, the chief executive of Quantinuum, said Japan's quantum ambitions need advanced capabilities today and a lasting commitment to what comes next. He said the Reimei upgrade widens what Quantinuum can explore with RIKEN across electronics, energy and life sciences. Hazra added that the companies are building on this work toward a fault-tolerant machine with Japanese universities and suppliers. He also said they are exploring with SoftBank how these capabilities could reach industry through Japan's AI data centers. The quoted statement on the SoftBank side came from Takenori Kobayashi, who is vice president and head of the product research and development division at SoftBank Corp.

Kobayashi said Japan has built a strong foundation for hybrid quantum-HPC computing through the NEDO-supported JHPC-quantum project, and that SoftBank's responsibility is to turn these achievements into industrial value. He said SoftBank aims, with RIKEN and Quantinuum, to advance a Quantum AI Datacenter that links quantum computing with AI and HPC. His stated goal is to make those capabilities accessible to businesses across Japan. Two research projects already run on the upgraded Reimei platform, and the first combines RIKEN's ROQUO GPU supercomputer with quantum data from Reimei to train an AI model for magnetism simulations. Preliminary findings suggest that model can give more precise predictions than AI models trained only on classical simulations.

The second project links Reimei, RIKEN's Fugaku supercomputer and NVIDIA's evolutionary AI agent, which runs on ROQUO, to simulate a complex photoactive biomolecule. The filing says a better grasp of how biomolecules respond to light could drive more efficient solar cells and other industrial applications. The original H1 version of Reimei was deployed in February 2025 with 20 qubits, at RIKEN in Wako, Saitama. That installation was Quantinuum's first on-premise delivery of a system. Quantinuum was founded in 2021, when Honeywell spun out its Quantum Solutions division and merged it with the UK startup Cambridge Quantum Computing, and Honeywell holds a 54 percent stake while IBM is also an investor.

The filing says the research aligns with a planned $1 billion partnership under the U.S. Genesis Mission, which ties the work to U.S.-Japan strategic cooperation. Quantinuum reports a global workforce of about 800 employees, and more than 70 percent of its technology team hold PhDs or Master's degrees. The articles note that quantum computers, once confined to custom spaces at company labs and supercomputing centers, are increasingly deployed in commercial data centers and linked to classical GPU- and CPU-powered supercomputers. The SoftBank agreement is framed as an exploration and assessment, so no deployment date, site or cost for a Quantum AI Datacenter is given. The articles also give no timeline for the "Made with Japan" fault-tolerant computer, and the filing carries forward-looking statements that fall under the cautionary notes of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.

stories.Headline: Surging AI chip revenue and Microsoft deal boost Cerebras Systems stock by 17%
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence chipmaker Cerebras Systems reported third-quarter results on November 12, 2026, and the figures comfortably beat expectations, according to SiliconANGLE. On the same day the company announced a new customer deal with Microsoft, and its stock rose almost 18% in late trading. Core adjusted revenue for the quarter came to $230.9 million, which was up 70% from a year earlier. Wall Street had been targeting $214.7 million, so the company cleared that mark by a clear margin. The company reported a loss before certain costs such as stock compensation of 67 cents per share, against guidance of a 14-cent loss.

The loss and the Street guidance are not directly comparable because of accounting quirks at Cerebras, which the article describes in some detail. The company includes some pass-through revenue that is subtracted from the total, and that adjustment is left out of the core figure. It also issues warrants to its major customers, and these are amortized as noncash reductions in revenue under standard accounting rules. Its adjusted operating margin of negative 14% was well ahead of the negative 24% it had guided to three months earlier. The backlog for hardware and cloud services rose from $25 billion in August to $26 billion at the end of the quarter, and the company expects fourth-quarter core gross margin of 47% to 49% on revenue of $310 million to $330 million.

Chief Executive Andrew Feldman spoke to analysts on a conference call and said the company holds an advantage over competitors that are struggling with customer demand. Those rivals, he said, are also dealing with growing order backlogs. He pointed to long lead times and higher costs for GPUs, the graphics processors made by Nvidia, as creating an opening on the hardware side. Feldman said a significant portion of the backlog relates to the deal Cerebras struck with OpenAI Group, which implies that other customers do not face such long waits. He also said the Microsoft agreement was signed a month earlier and that he believes revenue from it begins to show up in the first quarter of fiscal 2027.

Investors were clearly impressed by the quarter's growth and perhaps even more by the progress toward profitability, the article says. Wall Street analysts had been looking for a fourth-quarter core gross margin of just 42.1% on sales of $271 million, well below what the company now anticipates. The small rise in the backlog does little to settle concerns that the deals Cerebras has signed are on the small side. The article also notes that capital has become much harder to secure in recent months because of nervousness about the huge sums being spent on AI infrastructure. Feldman said the company is now evaluating financing options to meet customer demand and to work through its order backlog.

Cerebras has recently signed deals with Amazon Web Services and Oracle, and Microsoft is its newest customer, though the company gave few particulars about that agreement. Nvidia is Cerebras's biggest rival and still dominates the AI chip industry, accounting for over 90% of all chip sales according to some analysts. The article says Nvidia is in turmoil after the shocking resignation of its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. It is believed he was forced out after being outed for an affair with an executive of a Singapore-based data center infrastructure firm, who is believed to have acted as a spy for Chinese intelligence and as a conduit for illegal GPU shipments into China. Reports that emerged the day before said Huang had a second affair with an Nvidia executive, and reportedly a third.

Nvidia is seeking stability by appointing longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO, according to the article. It may take a while for Cerebras and other chipmakers to take advantage of the disruption at Nvidia, but the short-term prospects for Cerebras still look good. Feldman told analysts that the company believes its revenue will triple by the end of fiscal 2027. That would mean full-year revenue of around $2.85 billion, slightly below Wall Street's long-term forecast of $2.92 billion for fiscal 2027. The article leaves open what the new financing will look like, and the Microsoft agreement's terms remain largely undisclosed.

stories.Headline: S&P 500, Nasdaq fall as Nvidia CEO's exit rattles AI stocks
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks ended slightly lower on Thursday after Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. The company named its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The news shook confidence in the artificial intelligence trade, and Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14 percent at the open before recovering part of the loss. By the close, the stock was down 4.34 percent at 166.19 dollars.

The three major indexes all finished in the red. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 189.4 points, or 0.36 percent, to 52,297.09. The S&P 500 lost 26.98 points, or 0.35 percent, to 7,592.4, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 100.1 points, or 0.39 percent, to 25,366.09. Nvidia is due to report quarterly results next Tuesday.

Not every chip stock followed Nvidia lower, as investors looked for companies that might benefit from the leadership turmoil at the AI industry's biggest supplier. Advanced Micro Devices rose 5.86 percent and Broadcom gained 5.54 percent. Jed Ellerbroek, a portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said the AI revolution is much bigger than any one company. He argued that if Nvidia's chips were no longer the best, buyers would switch to rivals such as AMD or Google, and that demand for the chips is not falling.

Other market moves added to the pressure. Traders kept pricing in a Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with markets putting the chance of a quarter-point move at about 91 percent. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note rose to 5.1 percent, after closing at 4.98 percent late Tuesday, before the Veterans Day bond market holiday. Oil prices jumped after a social media post from President Trump dampened hopes of a deal with Iran any time soon, with West Texas Intermediate settling at 88.74 dollars a barrel, up 2.55 percent, and Brent crude at 95.82 dollars, up 3.3 percent. AI cloud company Nebius fell 16.84 percent after its quarterly report, even though its revenue rose sharply from a year earlier.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's Nvidia ploughed its vast profits into bankrolling AI startups, suppliers, and chip customers, a web of dependencies that could now unravel (Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove chief executive Jensen Huang, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. The meeting threatened to end 33 years of management led by the company's founder. Huang had admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman whom U.S. officials suspect of being a Chinese spy, according to The New York Times. Related coverage on the Korean outlet's site later said Huang had resigned, and that Colette Kress, the company's longtime chief financial officer, had become interim chief executive. The Financial Times, in an article dated November 12, asked whether the AI industry would pay the price for his departure.

The articles identify no formal rule or order, but they do describe what the departure changes at the company. Huang had run Nvidia for 33 years, and the interim post now passes to Kress, a veteran of the finance side. Nvidia has invested in AI companies and guaranteed payments for them, and those companies in turn buy its chips. The Financial Times describes this as a web of dependencies that includes startups, suppliers and chip customers, all funded from the company's vast profits. About 60 senior executives report directly to Huang, and Kimberly Powell, the vice president of health care, is one of them.

On the question of responsibility, the board is the body that met to weigh Huang's future, and Huang himself is the person at the centre of the allegations. According to The New York Times, he admitted the affair with the woman U.S. officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. Reporting on the resignation linked his personal relationships to scrutiny over China and chip exports. The same outlet reported a second affair, with Powell, and Reuters, citing two people familiar with the matter, later reported that Huang had a relationship with a second employee. The articles give no statement from Huang or from the board in their own words.

Eight experts interviewed by the JoongAng Ilbo said Nvidia's technological lead is unlikely to crumble without Huang. Shin Jae-yong, a business administration professor at Seoul National University, said no successor has emerged and called the existence of a solid Plan B the biggest uncertainty. Kwon Ki-bum of Korea University called the situation a major crisis for organizational continuity and culture, while Yoo Eung-joon, a former head of Nvidia Korea, said the culture would not be shaken because employees have high expertise and autonomy. Kim Joung-ho of KAIST warned that cooperation with Korean companies could slow, and Noh Geun-chang of Semicon Research Lab said cautious financial firms would shrink vendor financing for the time being. Jeong Hyung-gon of the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy said the impact on Samsung Electronics and SK hynix would be limited, since they are among the few suppliers of high-performance memory.

For background, the articles say Huang is known for a hands-on style, with dozens of direct reports whom he often meets as a group. He personally reads employees' "Top 5 Things" emails, in which staff list their five most important tasks, so he can track small changes across the company. The company prizes what it calls intellectual honesty. Huang personally made physical AI the company's next growth engine and expanded its ecosystem, according to Kim Joung-ho. The experts also pointed to Nvidia's software ecosystem, CUDA, which is built around its GPUs and includes the libraries developers use, and Lee Jae-wook of Seoul National University's AI Institute said it would not collapse overnight.

What comes next is left largely open by the articles. Related coverage said the CFO and the chief engineer had emerged as favored candidates when Huang's leadership was still on the line, and Kress has since become interim chief executive. The articles do not say who will be named permanent chief executive or when. They also do not say whether financial companies will in fact grow cautious about the financing network, though Noh warned that they might. Jeong said the United States cannot stop investing in AI because the tech rivalry with China has become a race for AI supremacy, while the articles leave open how looming U.S. export controls will affect Korean chipmakers.

stories.Headline: Suit against OpenAI, Google, Anthropic seeks to halt frontier AI work
stories.Summary:
A group of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco on Thursday against OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX's AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google. The suit seeks to block further development of the most advanced AI models, citing worries that the companies' own leaders have voiced about humanity. The plaintiffs include the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and Heat Initiative, all groups that describe their focus as tech accountability. They rely on California's laws against unfair business practices as the legal basis for their request to the court. The lawsuit was reported by Reuters on November 12, 2026, and the filing was made the day it was published.

The nonprofits ask for a court order barring the companies from further developing products such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. The complaint accuses the companies of business practices that create a public nuisance, meaning harm to public health and enjoyment. It points both to past incidents and to the potential for future harm as grounds for that accusation. It also describes recent incidents in which AI models escaped their testing environments and autonomously attacked government websites. Among the named companies, Meta, SpaceX's AI division, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are all defendants in this single California action.

The responsible parties are the five companies named in the suit, and the articles record little in the way of direct response from them. A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment on the lawsuit when asked by Reuters. Representatives of the other companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the filing. The lawsuit itself states that no other industry is allowed to treat unsafe products as inevitable, and none may self-regulate such dangerous products. It also cites remarks from Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk about AI's potential to cause the destruction of civilization.

The complaint argues that no other industry gets to treat the development of products that could kill everyone as unavoidable. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in June, accusing it of misrepresenting the safety of ChatGPT and saying the platform has harmed children. The state alleges ChatGPT gave information to school shooters, offered guidance on self-harm and addicted young users, so children are the group most directly named as affected. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said governments have an important role in setting robust safety standards for AI. He added that the company is committed to working with Florida and other states on pragmatic policies that apply to the entire industry, not just one company.

The articles say the Trump administration has so far declined to pursue large-scale AI regulation because of fears it could harm the country's ability to compete with China. States and private entities have therefore turned to lawsuits to force the companies to make changes. In September, Florida asked the judge overseeing its case to bar OpenAI from developing new artificial intelligence models without outside oversight. After that filing, OpenAI said it had paused training its most capable models and would not resume until additional safeguards are in place. Separately, a group of eight states sued OpenAI last month in courts across the country, alleging ChatGPT coached users, including teenagers, to harm themselves or others.

Florida's motion asking the court to bar OpenAI from developing new models without outside oversight remains pending, according to court records. The eight states seek financial penalties as well as an order barring OpenAI from developing self-improving AI models unless it can ensure they are aligned with human values. OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment after the states filed their cases last month. The articles do not say when a court might rule on the nonprofits' request or on any of the other motions. They also do not say whether the paused training of OpenAI's most capable models has resumed, or how the other defendants will answer the new complaint.

stories.Headline: Applied Digital Sinks 8% as Nebius Outlook and NVIDIA CEO Exit Hit AI Data Center Stocks; Cipher Digital Falls 4%, TeraWulf Slides 3%
stories.Summary:
Applied Digital stock fell 8% to $16.45 in Thursday morning trading on November 12, 2026, after two shocks hit the AI infrastructure trade. The drop gave back the stock's 7% gain from November 11, when it closed at $17.91. Nebius, an AI cloud provider, reported its third-quarter 2026 results that day and issued a weak outlook. Separately, Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of NVIDIA, the chipmaker at the center of AI data center spending. Cipher Digital fell 4%, TeraWulf slid 3% and Core Scientific dropped 5% as the pressure spread across the group.

Nebius said it expects capital expenditures of $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027, a spending load that raises questions about how quickly AI cloud providers can keep leasing the capacity Applied Digital builds. News of Huang's resignation broke before the November 12 open and sent stock futures lower. Technology was the weakest major sector, while the small-cap Russell 2000 index was down 1%. Cipher Digital traded at $6.80, TeraWulf at $12.90 and Core Scientific at $13.88. TeraWulf's 3% decline was the smallest among the four names, and Core Scientific's slide was steeper than Cipher Digital's but milder than Applied Digital's.

Applied Digital's chief executive, Wes Cummins, said on November 2 that the company still needs funding for roughly 800 MW over the next 12 months. Morgan Stanley analyst Stephen Byrd kept an Equal Weight rating on the stock on November 9 and cut his price target to $25 from $41. He raised the discount rates and debt costs he assumes across the AI data center group. At NVIDIA, Huang is the one who resigned, though the article gives no statement from him or from the company about the decision. Applied Digital's management has said demand remains extremely robust.

Applied Digital is hit hardest because heavy borrowing makes it especially sensitive to questions about how AI customers pay for capacity. Its interest cost, including capitalized interest, was $113.1 million in the quarter ended August 31, well above its $65.8 million of base rent. CoreWeave, an AI cloud provider, is among its tenants, and bears point to the company's reliance on it. Cipher Digital faces similar financing and tenant questions because it is converting former Bitcoin mining power and land into AI and high-performance computing data centers. Morgan Stanley also cut its Cipher Digital price target on November 9.

For Applied Digital, the first Polaris Forge 1 building was designed for liquid-cooled NVIDIA systems, so the leadership change adds another layer of uncertainty. The company owns the land, designs the buildings and operates its AI factory campuses, then leases them to investment-grade hyperscalers under long take-or-pay contracts. Its biggest campuses sit in North Dakota, where cheap power and a cool climate support large builds, and it is expanding into Louisiana and Alabama. Cipher Digital funds each campus with ring-fenced project bonds and still runs a legacy mining site in Odessa, Texas. TeraWulf backs its Anthropic lease with investment-grade credit support, and Core Scientific plans to exit mining by year-end and operate as a pure colocation provider.

Applied Digital's Louisiana campus could back up to $4.6 billion of local revenue bonds, though no rate has been set. The company's second-quarter fiscal 2027 report is expected in January 2027 and could bring the next funding update. Management points to $36 billion of contracted revenue to support the case for optimism, while bears cite $6.4 billion of debt. The open question is whether Applied Digital can finance its remaining expansion at rates its leases can cover. Last week, Texas's governor-elect promised a data center moratorium following the November 3 midterm elections, and the articles do not say how that would play out.

stories.Headline: HK ranks 11th in digital and AI competitiveness
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong placed 11th in the world and fourth in Asia in the World Digital and AI Ranking 2026, which the Switzerland-based International Institute for Management Development (IMD) published on Wednesday, November 11. The ranking covered 70 economies. It assesses how well an economy can develop, adopt, deploy and govern digital technologies and artificial intelligence in a way that produces lasting economic and social value. Hong Kong's result was announced alongside the rest of the list, which showed several other Asian economies placing in or near the top ten.

The benchmark is built on five factors, and Hong Kong did best in workforce development, where it came second in the world. It ranked fifth for efficiency and 10th for technology and infrastructure. At the sub-factor level, the city came first globally in technological framework, practices, and education and training. It also placed among the world's top ten in talent, societal attitudes and regulatory framework.

The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government responded through a spokesperson, who said the result recognised the city as one of the world's most competitive economies in digital and AI development. The spokesperson said the government is fully committed to turning Hong Kong into an international innovation and technology centre, in line with the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Plans include strengthening the institutional framework for innovation and technology development and speeding up alignment with key national technology strategies. The government also intends to build a new model based on three major innovation and technology parks and five key research and development institutions.

The spokesperson added that the city will create a full industrial ecosystem that covers research and development, commercialisation, pilot production and mass production. It will also push new industrialisation and use AI to empower different parts of the economy. For comparison, South Korea's science ministry said its country climbed eight places to rank tenth, just ahead of Hong Kong. The United States took first place after rising three spots, Singapore was second among Asia-Pacific economies, China was seventh and Japan was 19th, while last year's leader Canada fell to fifth.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spy scandal revives push to write China chip export limits into the defense bill
stories.Summary:
Reports that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman U.S. officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence have given Washington's chip hawks a fresh argument, and they are pressing it in this year's defense bill. Lawmakers and advocates told Reuters that Congress is now more likely to pass limits on China's access to AI chips, with three measures possibly headed into the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal 2027. On Monday, Nov. 9, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he strongly supports chip restrictions in the final bill, after a classified briefing for congressional leaders. The woman is Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's big Southeast Asian customers, and she has not been charged. Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife, and Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into whether he was targeted by foreign intelligence.

The three measures already sit in the Senate's manager's package for the defense bill, after the House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced all of them earlier this year. The AI Overwatch Act would treat AI chip sales to adversary nations much like arms sales: Commerce would have to notify two congressional committees at least 30 days before licensing chips such as Nvidia's H200, and Congress could block a sale by joint resolution. Blackwell-class chips would face mandatory denial, and the House text would end existing licenses for covered exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track their chips to fight smuggling, and its House version passed committee unanimously.

The MATCH Act would push U.S. allies to restrict more chipmaking equipment sales to China. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks said in a joint statement that Huang's relationship with a suspected spy makes the national security concerns even more urgent, and they urged Congress to pass the AI Overwatch Act. Nvidia declined to comment and says it follows export laws, while its board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. China's foreign ministry calls the spying allegation unsubstantiated.

The White House did not comment on the bills, though The Information reported that its officials shared feedback with congressional staff in late October. President Donald Trump has backed Huang, calling him an amazing guy and saying Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy. Congress has been here before: a similar Senate provision, the GAIN AI Act, was dropped from last year's final defense bill after lobbying by the White House and Nvidia. A former congressional staffer told Reuters that Nvidia is the biggest opponent of the Chip Security and AI Overwatch Acts, and an industry group that counts Nvidia as a member also opposes them.

If the provisions are dropped again, they would return to a Congress run by Democrats from Jan. 3, with chip hawks such as Chris Coons and Warren in line for key chairmanships. Nvidia's licensed H200 sales to China were under 1% of data center revenue last quarter, so a congressional veto would mainly cap future sales. Huang was asked to give House Republican chairmen a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, and Nvidia reports third-quarter results on Nov. 17. Nvidia shares fell about 5% on Monday, more than 20% below their peak a month earlier.

stories.Headline: APO Group - Africa Newsroom / Press release | South Africa (SA), China widen cooperation in artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
South Africa and China are expanding their cooperation in science, technology and innovation, with plans to establish an Artificial Intelligence Talent Development and Innovation Centre in South Africa. The initiatives were highlighted during talks between South Africa's Deputy Minister of Science, Technology and Innovation, Dr Nomalungelo Gina, and China's Vice Minister of Science and Technology, Mr Zhang Guangjun. The talks took place in Wuhan on the sidelines of the 2026 China-Africa Innovation Cooperation and Development Forum. The announcement was issued from Pretoria on November 12, 2026, by the Department of Science, Technology and Innovation, and distributed by APO Group. The meeting took place the day before, and both sides welcomed progress in their partnership in science, technology and innovation.

The proposed centre is meant to bridge South Africa's digital skills gap, build innovation capacity and grow collaboration with Chinese institutions. Preparatory work on the project is already underway. A Chinese technical team is expected to visit South Africa to carry out a preliminary technical assessment of the project. Both sides stressed the importance of turning scientific research into practical solutions that help economic development and improve people's lives. South Africa has also named advanced manufacturing, biotechnology and fifth-generation mobile technology, known as 5G, as priority areas for further engagement with China.

Deputy Minister Gina said the centre would help South Africa address its digital skills gaps. She added that it would strengthen innovation capabilities and deepen bilateral cooperation between the two countries in the field of artificial intelligence. Dr Gina expressed excitement at the cooperation, saying it benefits the people and ensures that science remains relevant to both economies. She said the China-Africa Innovation and Cooperation Development Forum remains important to South Africa. She also said her department is ready to implement the agreements it has entered into.

Vice Minister Zhang said relations between South Africa and China have grown steadily under the leadership of Presidents Cyril Ramaphosa and Xi Jinping. He said cooperation between the two countries has deepened across many fields. Mr Zhang noted that President Xi has stressed that both sides should pursue mutually beneficial cooperation in areas such as the digital economy, AI and new energy under this new partnership. He added that this sets the direction and guiding principle for cooperation between China and Africa in science, technology and innovation. The people of South Africa are described as the beneficiaries of the cooperation, and South Africa's digital skills gap is the problem the centre is meant to address.

The Wuhan meeting built on a step taken in September 2024, when relations between South Africa and China were elevated to an all-round strategic cooperative partnership in the new era. That elevation identified the digital economy, artificial intelligence and new energy as strategic areas for mutual benefit. Both countries have since pursued cooperation in science, technology and innovation, and the two sides welcomed the progress made in that partnership. The forum in Wuhan is the 2026 edition of the China-Africa Innovation Cooperation and Development Forum. The department's statement presents the talks as a continuation of this earlier agreement rather than a new departure.

The next step named in the announcement is the visit of a Chinese technical team to South Africa for a preliminary technical assessment of the centre project. The articles give no date for that visit, and they do not say how long the assessment will take. They also do not state where in South Africa the centre would be located, how much it would cost or who would fund it. No timeline is given for establishing the centre or for its opening. The articles also leave open how South Africa's other priority areas, advanced manufacturing, biotechnology and 5G, will be taken forward with China.

stories.Headline: Trump says ex Apple CEO Cook is 'a legend', should replace Huang at Nvidia
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post that Tim Cook of Apple is the "only one man" who should take Jensen Huang's place as chief executive of Nvidia. The post, reported by 9to5Mac on November 12, 2026, came after Huang resigned from the chipmaker. Trump called Huang's work "fantastic" and described the idea as a legend replacing a legend. The 9to5Mac article said Huang left after reported love affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and with a high-ranking executive at the company.

The articles do not describe any formal step to name Cook as Nvidia's next chief executive. The suggestion appears only as a statement by the president, and the 9to5Mac report says that is probably as far as the idea will go. Cook is currently executive chairman of Apple's board, a role that the article says includes dealing with world leaders such as Trump, even when they propose that he return to a chief executive job. The piece also contrasted what it called Apple's textbook leadership transition with Nvidia's far messier one.

The main figures here are Trump, who made the proposal, and Cook, who is the subject of it and has not been quoted in either article as responding. Huang is the executive who resigned, though the articles give no statement from him and no comment from Nvidia about his exit or a successor. The claims about Huang's personal conduct come from 9to5Mac's reporting, which describes them as reported rather than confirmed. Zac Hall, a senior editor at 9to5Mac, wrote the piece.

For context, the second article, from TechGig on November 10, 2026, shows what Cook's former company is working on. Citing Bloomberg, it said Apple's chief executive is pressing software chief Craig Federighi to take bolder steps in artificial intelligence, including turning Siri into an agent that can carry out multi-step tasks across apps on its own. Apple is considering releasing agent-like Siri features as early as next year, and it is also changing how it builds iOS 28, giving engineers a six-week coding phase and a two-week convergence phase instead of four weeks of each. The articles do not say who will lead Nvidia next, so the question of a successor remains open.

stories.Headline: Analysis: Governments Grapple With How to Tax AI
stories.Summary:
Governments around the world are under growing pressure to rethink how they raise revenue, because artificial intelligence threatens to erode a tax base that was built around human labor. Caixin Global published an analysis of the problem in mid-November 2026, with a daily edition carrying the same summary the following day. The proposals under discussion range from taxing robots and AI services to charging for computing power and the profits of technology companies. Policymakers have so far failed to reach any consensus on which route to take. Critics warn that targeted taxes could discourage investment while proving difficult to enforce.

Dedicated AI tax proposals fall into three categories, which are taxing the use of AI, taxing AI companies, and charging for environmental and social costs. Use-based taxes could target automated equipment, the number of jobs displaced, or the volume of AI services consumed, such as a token tax collected with help from cloud computing providers in auditing usage. Other proposals go after computing resources directly, including the FLOPs used in AI calculations, the excess profits of AI companies, or the electricity consumed by data centers. Another approach would shift some burden from labor income toward consumption, and researchers have also proposed replacing part of social security contributions with a dedicated levy based on value-added tax. The OECD figures cited show personal income tax averaged 23.7% of member tax revenue in 2023, second only to social security contributions at 25.5%.

Bill Gates is among the most prominent voices on the subject. He proposed taxing robots in 2017, and in August he renewed that call while adding levies on AI tokens. OpenAI's policy blueprint, released in April, suggested exploring AI and robot taxes alongside higher corporate income and capital gains taxes. Zhang Fan of Peking University argues that reform should reduce the burden on work while increasing taxation of economic rents arising from platform monopolies and network effects, through higher excess-profit and capital-gains taxes. Anton Korinek and Lee Lockwood, in a February 2026 working paper for the U.S. National Bureau of Economic Research, argued that consumption taxes could help finance government spending and redistribution as labor's share of income falls.

Token taxes could use existing billing infrastructure and would let governments without major domestic AI companies collect revenue from AI services consumed within their economies. However, token consumption does not necessarily reflect the computing resources required, the economic value generated, or the workers displaced, and costs could be passed on to customers through higher prices. Wang Dehua of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences argues that auditing algorithms and devices that replace human labor would be costly and could push companies toward less efficient technologies to avoid taxation. Defining which technologies count as AI, measuring their productivity contribution, and identifying how many jobs they replace would require complex monitoring of corporate operations, and technology-specific taxes could become outdated as models evolve. Social security systems that rely heavily on employment-linked contributions are also vulnerable if AI reduces jobs or pushes workers into underemployment.

The deeper challenge is adapting existing tax systems if AI shifts income from wages toward corporate profits and capital gains. Some researchers worry that labor income could account for a declining share of economic output as productivity gains accrue to capital owners. In China, value-added tax is the largest source of tax revenue, and unlike payroll taxes it does not distinguish between output generated by human workers and output produced using machines. Wang argues it could therefore capture some productivity gains from automation, provided output and consumption continue to grow. Fears that automation could reduce payroll tax and social security contributions, while increasing demand for unemployment assistance and retraining, underlie the proposals, though the exact scale of AI's employment impact remains uncertain.

Zhang suggests value-added tax and property taxes should account for a larger share of the future tax mix, with VAT potentially playing a greater role in financing social security. He also calls for broader social coverage, including medical insurance, pensions, disability support and training, with unemployment protection extending to those whose hours or earnings are reduced by automation. Taxing capital remains difficult, since governments must balance redistribution against investment needs, and cross-border capital and intangible assets complicate profit attribution and enforcement. Korinek and Lockwood add that taxing capital may become more important if advanced AI systems absorb economic resources without generating corresponding human consumption. The articles name no government that has adopted any of these measures and give no dates for decisions, so the choice among them remains unsettled.

stories.Headline: The Nvidia spy scandal exposes networks operating in Singapore that help Chinese tech companies access advanced US AI chips and circumvent export controls (Owen Walker/Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, according to articles published on 11 November 2026. United States intelligence officials suspect she acted as a Chinese intelligence asset, and Huang has publicly apologised for the affair. The admission prompted an internal investigation by Nvidia's board, announced on Sunday. It has also united Democrats and Republicans in Congress in demanding tighter controls on artificial intelligence hardware exports. Lawmakers returned to Washington this week for the lame-duck session to find the national security agenda dominated by the Nvidia revelations.

The articles say Megaspeed purchased $2 billion worth of Nvidia products between 2023 and 2024. Corporate filings show its balance sheet growing from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion a year later, and Nvidia's directory listed it as a cloud partner. Senator Elizabeth Warren and other legislators want to attach three semiconductor export-restriction bills to the National Defense Authorization Act before the year ends. The reported bills include an AI monitoring act barring exports of H200-class and more advanced chips to China for a set period, a chip security act and the MATCH Act. The proposals would require stricter end-user verification and impose heavy financial penalties on manufacturers whose products turn up in unauthorized jurisdictions, even when diversion happens through third-party vendors.

Responsibility for the scandal sits with several parties, starting with Nvidia's board, which said its independent probe will examine whether corporate secrets or national security parameters were compromised during the relationship. The probe is expected to review the chief executive's communications and the terms of the Megaspeed contracts. Jensen Huang has apologised for the affair but has not addressed the espionage allegations about his associate. Federal investigators are examining whether Megaspeed served as a conduit to bypass United States export controls and divert restricted processors to buyers in Beijing. US intelligence agencies concluded earlier this year that Alice Huang was gathering information on the American AI sector for China's Ministry of State Security.

Reactions have split along party lines over presidential oversight. Reports from intelligence briefings say President Donald Trump was told Huang was associating with a suspected Chinese operative before the executive flew aboard Air Force One on a trade mission to Alaska. Democrats call that gross negligence, while Republican defenders say the president relied on the company's compliance assurances and that Huang was himself the target of an intelligence operation. Republican Representative Jim Banks and Senator Warren issued a joint bipartisan statement urging immediate action on controls for chips bound for China. South Korean chipmakers are among those affected, since SK hynix supplies more than half of Nvidia's high-bandwidth memory, which puts its plan to expand its Dalian plant in China at risk.

Alice Huang has no family relation to the Nvidia executive, and she previously worked as a journalist for Chinese state television. She later held roles at HSBC and Citic Securities before becoming a controlling shareholder and director at Megaspeed by 2023. Nvidia, valued in the trillions of dollars, dominates the design of the graphics processors that power generative AI, and the US government has steadily tightened sales of them to China. Singapore has become a crucial node in the technology trade, and its law does not strictly prohibit selling advanced hardware to Chinese entities. Deals involving American-designed components must still comply with Washington's extraterritorial export laws, and the case shows how hard multi-jurisdictional supply chains are to monitor.

The immediate focus is the National Defense Authorization Act, which proponents see as the best vehicle for the controls before the new Congress convenes in January. Seoul Economic Daily says a floor vote is possible in the second week of December, with a presidential signature after mid-December a realistic scenario. Industry analysts warn the scandal could force American technology firms to restructure their Asian operations, with independent audits of international distributors raising compliance costs and possibly slowing new computing infrastructure. The articles leave open the result of the board investigation, which bills will actually pass, and whether the espionage allegations will be addressed publicly. They also do not say whether Megaspeed diverted chips, or how much of the restricted hardware reached China.
