stories.Headline: Mavria raises $130 million for factory-built AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Mavria, a company building industrial infrastructure for artificial intelligence, has raised a total of $130 million across pre-seed and seed funding rounds. Crypto Briefing reports that the Houston-area startup launched on November 9, 2026, and that the money is meant to scale manufacturing of its factory-built data centers. The latest round values the company at $1 billion, which Crypto Briefing describes as a post-money valuation. Paradigm led the round, and AMP PBC, Liquid 2, Critical Frontier and Dream Ventures also took part. The company wants to build data centers and related infrastructure across the United States, according to the reports published between November 9 and November 11, 2026.

Crypto Briefing says the $130 million includes a $100 million round led by Paradigm that sets the $1 billion valuation. Mavria plans to use the money to secure critical supply chains, expand manufacturing capacity and grow its workforce, according to its company announcement. The first product line is called Terrain, and each unit is a standardized 5 MW block bundling power, cooling and IT infrastructure into one package. The blocks are designed for high-density artificial intelligence workloads. The first unit, Terrain 01, is currently in production in Houston, though Mavria has not said which customers will deploy Terrain or where the units will go.

Adam Blake, the chief executive of Mavria, said in the company announcement that America sets the pace at the intelligence frontier. He said the race is moving from the laboratory into the physical world, because intelligence needs data centers and data centers need power. According to Blake, power in turn needs factories, equipment, supply chains and skilled workers. He added that much of this infrastructure is still built one custom project at a time, on timelines measured in years. Mavria's stated approach is to produce infrastructure through standardized manufacturing rather than individually designed construction projects, which can take years to complete.

Crypto Briefing notes that a $1 billion valuation before any disclosed customer deployment sets a high bar, because investors are pricing in the factory's future output rather than its current one. It also points out that a finished 5 MW block still needs 5 MW of electricity waiting for it at its destination. The outlet suggests the founders' energy policy experience may help with grid access and energy infrastructure. Mavria's launch comes as the expansion of AI computing capacity increases demand for electricity, data centers and industrial equipment. W.Media adds that investment in computing capacity continues to grow, while the manufacturing capabilities, energy equipment and supply chains needed to support it have not kept pace.

Mavria was founded by former colleagues from the U.S. Department of Energy. Co-founders Nick Poradek and Adam Blake previously served as senior advisors to the U.S. Secretary of Energy, and co-founder Seth Cohen was the department's head of nuclear law and policy. Crypto Briefing says the trio came from an unusual place for a hardware startup, and that conventional data center construction is site-specific, with every project designed and built more or less from scratch. The company's bet is that AI infrastructure should move toward an industrialized model, where one block is designed, perfected and then built over and over. That rollout is currently running into two obstacles, power constraints and construction constraints.

The company is developing a standardized manufacturing model that it hopes to apply to a broader range of infrastructure projects beyond data centers. Although data centers are its initial focus, Mavria plans to expand into other areas of physical infrastructure needed to support AI development. Crypto Briefing says the first thing to watch is when Terrain 01 leaves the Houston production line and where it ends up. The second is whether Mavria names its first customers, since a disclosed deployment would turn a promising pitch into a proven product. The third is how quickly the company can move from a single unit to repeatable volume, since raising $130 million to scale manufacturing means the scaling must now actually happen.

stories.Headline: Immaculate Kassait Ends Six‑Year Term as Kenya's First Data Protection Commissioner
stories.Summary:
President William Ruto nominated lawyer Lydia Sitienei Chelagat as Kenya's next Data Protection Commissioner, with the nomination announced on Monday, 9 November 2026. Government spokesperson Charles Owino made the announcement and said the president acted on advice from the Public Service Commission, the state body that recruits for senior public posts. Chelagat is currently the Director of Legal Services and Corporation Secretary at the Communications Authority of Kenya, the telecoms regulator. The nomination has gone to the National Assembly, which must approve her before she can take office. Immaculate Kassait, the first person to hold the post, is ending her six-year term after serving since November 2020.

The recruitment drew 152 applications, and 13 candidates were shortlisted for consideration. Chelagat is expected to succeed Kassait, which would make this the first leadership change at the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner since the regulator was set up. Her appointment is subject to vetting and approval by the National Assembly, where lawmakers normally examine nominees in a committee before a vote in the full house. The announcement also named five new chief executives for state corporations, whose boards appointed them after competitive recruitment. That process is separate from the Data Commissioner nomination, and the date for her parliamentary hearing has not been announced.

Government spokesperson Charles Owino, speaking for the president, said the nomination followed the recommendation of the Public Service Commission. Under the Data Protection Act, the president nominates the commissioner and makes the appointment once the National Assembly approves. The president has therefore acted on his part of the process and forwarded the nomination to the assembly. The announcement framed the nomination as the result of a competitive recruitment process rather than a direct presidential choice. The Public Service Commission is the body the president relied on for the recommendation, and Owino delivered the statement on Monday.

The articles report the nomination and the process rather than named reactions from other parties. The regulator Chelagat would lead has more than 15,000 registered data controllers and processors, all of whom fall under its authority. Its enforcement mandate covers financial institutions, telecommunications companies, technology platforms, healthcare providers and government agencies. The commissioner polices how any company, local or foreign, handles the personal data of people in Kenya, including banks, mobile-money services and AI tools. Kenyans who give their personal information to those organisations are the people the regulator exists to protect.

The Office of the Data Protection Commissioner was established under the Data Protection Act of 2019 to regulate the processing of personal data and to protect individuals' privacy rights. The law gives the commissioner a single six-year term with no right to be reappointed, which is why Kassait is leaving. Under Kassait, the regulator introduced registration requirements for qualifying data controllers and processors, set up mechanisms for complaints and investigations, and began imposing administrative penalties on violators. One of its best-known disputes involved Worldcoin, the cryptocurrency-linked digital identity project that collected biometric information from Kenyans in exchange for digital tokens. In May 2025 the High Court ordered the deletion of biometric data unlawfully collected through the project, and the regulator confirmed in January 2026 that the data had been deleted.

The regulator has also investigated complaints involving digital lenders, businesses accused of sharing customers' personal information without consent, and institutions alleged to have failed to safeguard sensitive data. Chelagat's nomination now goes to the National Assembly for vetting and approval, after which she would take over from Kassait. Her experience at the Communications Authority comes as the data protection regime faces complex questions about artificial intelligence, biometric identification, digital financial services and cross-border transfers of personal information. The articles do not say when the National Assembly will hold the hearing or vote on the nomination. They also do not say how soon Chelagat would take office if approved, or what happens at the regulator in the interval after Kassait's term ends.

stories.Headline: New Australian AI Safety And Security Protections
stories.Summary:
The Albanese Government announced on 10 November 2026 that it will write mandatory Artificial Intelligence safety and security protections into Australian AI Standards legislation. The announcement was published as a government release on that date, with the Prime Minister named as its source. The protections will apply to all frontier AI companies that wish to operate in Australia, according to the release. The government says it chose to announce its safety approach first, ahead of a range of major international talks. Those talks will cover AI development and investment, and the announcement is placed within the government's AI in Australia's Interests agenda.

The release says the protections will be legislated through the AI Standards, and the government will propose a new targeted regulator for AI safety to enforce them. That regulator would work with the Australian AI Safety Institute, which would provide technical expertise and oversight as global standards evolve. The regulator would be able to enforce significant penalties against AI companies that fail to meet the mandatory obligations. Companies would be required to maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment, and to identify and manage serious risks associated with their models. They would also have to allow independent evaluation of their models and notify the Australian Government of incidents rapidly.

Two further obligations complete the list the release sets out for companies. Firms must maintain and publish safety and security frameworks, which the release says will ensure good governance, risk management and transparency. They must also respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change. The release defines frontier AI as the term for the most sophisticated models at the cutting edge of current technological capability. No dollar amounts, penalty figures or commencement dates are given in the material, and the only date it supplies is the announcement itself on 10 November 2026.

The Albanese Government is the party responsible for the announcement, and the release describes the protections as world leading. It says Australia has the chance to secure and shape the generational opportunities of AI in the national interest while keeping Australians safe. The government says it wants AI investors to come to Australia, but first and foremost it wants to keep Australians safe. It argues that safety and security are the foundation for building trust in frontier AI. It also says frontier AI offers huge opportunities but carries the highest risks to the community if it is not used safely, which is why it is acting now.

The release attributes no statements to outside groups, companies or experts, so the articles do not report any reaction from industry, regulators or the public. The people and organisations affected are the frontier AI companies that wish to operate in Australia, which would face the mandatory obligations and the possibility of significant penalties. The wider community is also named as a beneficiary, since the stated aim is to keep Australians safe. The release says the measures will give earlier warning of emerging risks from rogue AI agents. It adds that they will enable faster, coordinated action when serious AI incidents occur.

The release gives some background to the government's position, saying Australia has a world leading reputation for setting standards on digital safety. It says the approach to AI continues to keep Australian values at the forefront. It describes AI as offering Australia huge opportunities, whether in boosting productivity, building economic resilience or revolutionising healthcare. To seize those opportunities, the government says it must ensure social licence for AI, safety for Australians and security for the national interest. The protections are also described as aligned with interim report recommendations from the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence.

What follows from the announcement is that the protections are to be legislated through the AI Standards, and the government will propose the new regulator. The articles do not say when legislation will be introduced, when the protections would take effect, or what the penalties would be. They do not name which companies count as frontier AI companies, or say how the new regulator would be funded and set up. They also do not identify the international talks that the announcement was timed to precede, nor give their dates or locations. Finally, the material says nothing about how the regulator would divide its work with the Australian AI Safety Institute beyond the institute supplying technical expertise and oversight.

stories.Headline: Social media posts twisted in AI phishing scams
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington have shown how widely available AI tools can gather personal details from public social media accounts and turn them into convincing phishing emails. Fox News reported the findings on November 10, 2026. The technique is called context-aware spear phishing, which means using details about someone's everyday life to build a scam that feels written for them. The researchers found the technology can produce these personalized messages at a scale that once demanded far more time and effort. A scammer might use a concert post to send a fake ticket confirmation, or a delayed-flight complaint to offer false compensation.

The study examined 200 public Instagram accounts and found that as few as 10 posts from one person could supply enough information for highly targeted messages. The team evaluated more than 18,000 AI-generated emails and compared them with thousands of real-world phishing messages. The AI tools drew on travel photos, public updates about upcoming events and personal concerns that people had shared online. The researchers also tested how AI could customize subject lines, sender names and links to make the messages more believable. In a separate piece, Larry Magid wrote on November 12, 2026 that a Common Sense Media survey released in October 2026 found half of American children ages 9 to 12 used social media on a given day.

The study was led by Shirin Nilizadeh, an associate professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Texas at Arlington. Her team included graduate student Elham Pourabbas Vafa and researcher Sayak Saha Roy. Nilizadeh said that anyone can be the attacker, and that this possibility makes the findings scarier. The article notes that someone using these tools may need very little personal knowledge about a target, since public posts can supply much of what is needed. Magid, writing about age assurance, noted that most online services for 28 years simply asked for a date of birth, with little or no effective verification.

In a user study, participants generally rated the AI-generated emails as more convincing and less suspicious than the real-world phishing examples used for comparison. The researchers did not measure how many people would actually click malicious links in a real attack, and they tested reactions only in a controlled setting. Fox News said scammers may never need to hack an account, because a public profile already offers details people have shared with the world. The article added that AI can produce professional-sounding emails, so traditional warning signs such as spelling mistakes and awkward wording may be missing. Magid reported that the Common Sense Media survey found tweens using platforms at least monthly included TikTok at 32%, Snapchat at 16%, Facebook at 15% and Instagram at 13%.

The Fox News article points to common phishing patterns, such as claims of a bank account problem or an undelivered package, which many people have learned to spot. It also notes that AI companies already have safeguards meant to stop their tools from being used to create phishing scams. Magid recalled that in 2011 danah boyd, then a researcher at Microsoft, reported millions of children under 13 on Facebook despite its minimum age of 13. She also found that many parents knew their children used Facebook and that some helped them misrepresent their ages. In 1998 Congress passed the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, which requires verifiable parental consent before covered services collect personal information from children under 13, and many services instead simply prohibit younger users.

Magid said that in 2008 he served on the Internet Safety Technical Task Force convened by Harvard University's Berkman Center for Internet & Society. The task force spent nearly a year examining proposed online safety technologies, including age verification systems, and found none it could endorse because of accuracy, effectiveness, privacy and legal limitations. There are now reasonably effective technologies that estimate a user's age, including AI-powered facial age estimation, systems that read profile and behavior clues, and services that check identification, financial records or digital IDs. Magid cautioned that estimates can be wrong, especially near age thresholds, and that people challenging an incorrect estimate may be asked for government ID or other personal information. The Fox News excerpt breaks off just as it says the researchers found that AI companies' safeguards had significant weaknesses, so the full details of that finding are not given.

stories.Headline: China's trade surplus soars past $1 trillion as AI boom powers exports
stories.Summary:
China's customs data released on Tuesday, November 10, showed that the country's trade surplus surged past US$1 trillion in the first 10 months of the year. A global race to build artificial intelligence infrastructure buoyed sales of Chinese high-tech products and helped offset weak demand at home. Exports rose by 35.2 per cent in October from the same month a year earlier, measured in US dollar terms. The surplus for the period reached US$1.04 trillion, which the articles say is likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners. Imports also grew quickly, rising 41.6 per cent and outpacing the pace of exports.

The surplus topped US$1 trillion for a second consecutive year, and China reached the milestone a month earlier than it did in 2025. October's export growth was only slightly slower than the 36.3 per cent surge recorded in September. It was also ahead of economists' forecast for an increase of 33.5 per cent. Imports beat the median forecast in a Reuters poll for a 32 per cent rise, and they accelerated from the 31 per cent growth seen in September. China's car exports kept a solid pace of growth in October, while domestic vehicle sales fell for a twelfth straight month, according to separate data from an industry association.

Responsibility for the figures lies with Chinese manufacturers and exporters, whose sales of technology products drove the result, with customs data providing the official count. On the trade truce with Washington, China on Monday officially announced a two-month extension of the arrangement, which was due to expire on November 10. Beijing also said last week that any expansion of its purchases of US farm goods would depend on implementation of the reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement the two sides agreed. The articles carry no further comment from Chinese officials on the surplus itself, and they describe Beijing as increasingly reliant on overseas demand to support its economy.

Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China, said the risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will stay elevated in 2027. He pointed to Chinese manufacturers continuing to expand their presence in overseas markets. Analysts at Macquarie wrote that the outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last. They expect Chinese exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before slowing from the first quarter of 2027. Consumers in China are among those affected, as they remain reluctant to spend, held back by a property downturn that has battered household wealth and dented confidence in the economic outlook.

The articles describe an economy hobbled by subdued consumption and a protracted property slump, which has left Beijing leaning on overseas demand. Sluggish demand at home has pushed Chinese automakers to seek sales in overseas markets. The global AI investment boom is expected to keep demand for Chinese technology products strong into 2027. The articles warn that it risks deepening domestic imbalances and fuelling trade frictions with partners including the European Union. In the EU, leaders have called for more trade curbs on China after reaching an agreement with Beijing to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc over the next few years.

Because the EU measures on hybrid vehicles have yet to take effect, factories are expected to bring forward shipments, which should bolster exports in the near term. Macquarie expects exports to accelerate further in the fourth quarter before they begin to slow from the first quarter of 2027. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit will take place next week in Shenzhen, a southern Chinese hub for technology and innovation. Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet there for the third time so far this year. Greater reliance on exports leaves China's economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand, and the articles do not say how long the AI boom will last.

stories.Headline: Rackspace and Together AI Announce Strategic Agreement to Support Enterprise AI Inference
stories.Summary:
Rackspace, which trades on NASDAQ as RXT, and Together AI, described as the AI Native Cloud, announced an initial multiyear strategic AI infrastructure agreement on November 10, 2026. Under it, Rackspace expects to provide and operate dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 infrastructure, connected with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, to support Together AI inference workloads. Deployment is planned for 2027, and it is subject to the satisfaction of certain conditions set out in the definitive agreement. The two companies also entered into a separate, non-binding letter of intent to explore a joint go-to-market approach for enterprise-focused AI solutions. Under that approach, Together AI would provide inference capabilities while Rackspace would provide the supporting AI infrastructure, platforms, solutions and forward-deployed engineering expertise.

Rackspace expects to provide and operate the dedicated NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra infrastructure, including the associated power, liquid cooling, networking and storage. Together AI expects to provide the managed cloud platform running on that infrastructure, including access to open source models, inference optimizations and developer tools. Rackspace plans to run the deployment in a purpose-built, liquid-cooled facility using dedicated GB300 NVL72 systems, supported by NVIDIA networking. Effective November 6, 2026, Rackspace entered into a share purchase agreement with an investor group led by Voss Capital, LP for an aggregate $66 million private placement of its common stock. Rackspace expects to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, working capital, capital expenditures and growth capital, including funding for GPU-related initiatives.

Gajen Kandiah, Chief Executive Officer of Rackspace, said enterprise AI needs more than access to compute, because success depends on bringing compute into production and operating it reliably. He said that requires deep infrastructure and engineering expertise combined with operational accountability, and that Rackspace brings more than 25 years of experience operating complex enterprise environments. He described the announcement as a chance to apply that experience to the dedicated infrastructure behind Together AI's inference platform. Kandiah added that the company believes the relationship advances its strategy to be the operator of the full enterprise AI stack. Rackspace says it intends to build a repeatable model to support AI platform companies, systems integrators and enterprises while they retain control of their technology and customer relationships.

Vipul Ved Prakash, founder and CEO of Together AI, said scaling in the enterprise requires infrastructure that can grow with the company's ambitions while delivering the performance and reliability customers expect. He said Rackspace brings the infrastructure engineering and operational expertise to support that growth, and that Together AI looks forward to exploring additional opportunities together. Raj Mirpuri, Vice President of Global AI Clouds and Infrastructure Ecosystem at NVIDIA, said enterprises need infrastructure that turns AI advances into services they can deploy at scale. He said NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra lets Rackspace and Together AI run inference workloads efficiently and bring the next wave of enterprise AI services to market. Rackspace is an NVIDIA Cloud Partner, and the companies say the arrangement may serve enterprises that need greater control, compliance and data sovereignty.

Rackspace describes the deployment as reflecting its strategy to become the operator of the full enterprise AI stack, drawing on decades of experience operating mission-critical environments. It says that experience lets it offer compute solutions meeting the security, trust and governance needs of regulated, production environments. Its approach to scaling AI infrastructure is to seek contractual commitments for dedicated capacity and to manage related financing and capital commitments, aiming to align with expected customer demand and the useful life of the hardware. Rackspace says its experience with regulated industries, together with its expertise across private cloud, hyperscaler and edge environments, may create opportunities to bring Together AI's cloud closer to enterprise data and workloads. A separate HFS Research study with Rackspace, published November 12, 2026, surveyed 502 senior AI decision makers and found that only 33% of enterprises have met or exceeded the business case for their most significant AI program.

Rackspace expects to seek separate financing for the purchase of the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems and says it is in active discussions with potential lenders. No definitive GPU financing commitment had been obtained as of the date of the release, and there is no assurance it will be obtained on acceptable terms or at all. Rackspace's obligations to proceed with the deployment are subject to that financing condition and other conditions in the definitive agreement. The companies also plan to evaluate additional security, governance and compliance controls for future offerings, depending on end-customer requirements and agreed configurations. Any joint offerings under the letter of intent would depend on further agreement between the parties, and the availability and features of any deployment configurations, including data residency, security and compliance, would be set by the specific offering and customer arrangement.

stories.Headline: Google Acquires Crusoe’s Wyoming Data Center Site
stories.Summary:
Google has acquired Crusoe's data center site in southeast Wyoming, Crusoe announced on November 6, 2026, from Denver. The sale ends Crusoe's pre-development work on the project, which covered site selection, governmental approvals and a power strategy. Crusoe's co-founder and CEO, Chase Lochmiller, said the pre-construction effort of origination, entitlement and de-risking has set the project up for construction and eventual operation. Crusoe is a Denver-based developer recently valued at $30.9 billion. Google did not disclose the price.

Google said it will invest $17 billion to develop the campus, which is in Laramie County. The site is planned to use air cooling and 702 megawatts of Bloom Energy fuel cells. It was announced in July 2025 at 1.8 gigawatts, expandable up to 10 gigawatts. The power strategy was developed with Tallgrass Energy and combines fuel cells, grid power and natural gas turbines. It also carries a long-term roadmap for carbon capture through Tallgrass's regional CO2 sequestration hub.

Crusoe and Tallgrass started the campus through joint development of power and data center infrastructure. That parallel process required simultaneous coordination across energy systems design, data center engineering, site development and hyperscaler engagement. Tallgrass is backed by Blackstone. Lochmiller said Crusoe is in the business of activating gigawatts for intelligence, with more than 6 GW contracted and over 40 GW in its pipeline.

One report said Crusoe had tried and failed to sign Google as a customer for the site. It added that Google is taking over development after reportedly raising concerns about cost and construction timelines under Crusoe's management. The same report said the deal underlines how hard it is for independent developers to deliver massive AI projects on time and on budget. It pointed to challenges in securing equipment and power and to growing local opposition. Another report said the transaction separates Crusoe's technical preparation from Google's investment, which must still turn the site into construction and operation.

Google and Crusoe continue to work together elsewhere. Crusoe recently announced that it is the developer of Google's data center campus under construction in Armstrong County, outside Amarillo, Texas. Crusoe also serves Oracle and OpenAI at its Abilene, Texas, campus and is building a 900-megawatt campus for Microsoft. Meta is a customer, and Jane Street reportedly signed a $13 billion cloud deal with the company. Crusoe was founded by Lochmiller and Cully Cavness, secured $3.9 billion in September and added Redwood Materials founder JB Straubel to its board.

stories.Headline: Samsung SDI's backup battery for AI data centers wins CES award
stories.Summary:
Samsung SDI is set to receive a CES 2027 Innovation Award for a battery system that supplies emergency power to artificial intelligence data centers. The company said on Tuesday, the 10th, that its SDI U8A3-UPS prismatic battery solution was selected in the Enterprise Tech category. The Consumer Technology Association announced the selection on the 9th, local time, which was a Monday. The award marks Samsung SDI's third consecutive year of recognition at CES, counted from its first showing at the event in 2025. The Korea Herald reported the story on November 10, 2026, and the Kyunghyang Shinmun ran its own account the same day.

CES 2027 will take place in Las Vegas in the United States in January next year, and the award falls in the Enterprise Tech category. The product uses prismatic battery cells with a lithium manganese oxide chemistry, which deliver ultra-high output and high energy density together. Samsung SDI says this improves space efficiency by 33 percent compared with its existing products. The company says data centers can therefore maintain stable power with a smaller number of batteries. The system also underwent a large-scale indoor fire test administered by the global safety certification body UL Solutions, which is the other basis for the recognition.

A Samsung SDI representative said the award recognizes the innovativeness of a core power solution for the AI era. The company says its product was the first in the world to meet every evaluation criterion in the UL Solutions fire test. The representative added that Samsung SDI will keep leading the market with products combining the performance and safety that customers require. The Korea Herald attributed a similar statement to a Samsung SDI official, who described the award as reflecting the technology's potential as a power solution for the AI era. That official also said the company will continue developing products that meet market demands for performance and safety.

The Consumer Technology Association, which organizes CES, is the body that announced the selection, and it made the announcement on the 9th, local time. The batteries are aimed at data centers, where surging electricity demand is increasing the need for stable power supplies. A separate report from The Elec said the Korean firm Naintech won CES 2027 Innovation Awards in two categories, Enterprise Tech and Energy Transition and Sustainability, for a different AI server cooling system. Naintech's chiller-free thermoelectric rack cooling system combines air, liquid and thermoelectric cooling in a single server rack and achieves a power usage effectiveness of about 1.2. Its chief executive, Park Geun-no, said the company will expand in the global AI data center cooling market.

An uninterruptible power supply is a battery system that supplies emergency power to key facilities such as data centers when a blackout suddenly cuts the main supply. According to Samsung SDI, the new product also supplies auxiliary power when demand surges during AI computation. This is meant to prevent server failures and data damage during such spikes. At CES 2026, Samsung SDI received a Best of Innovation award for its ultra-high-output cylindrical battery, the SDI 25U-Power. The same year it also won an Innovation Award for its No TP thermal propagation blocking technology, which is designed to prevent fires from spreading between battery cells.

CES 2027 opens in Las Vegas in January, where the SDI U8A3-UPS will carry its Innovation Award in the Enterprise Tech category. The articles do not give the exact dates of the exhibition or say how Samsung SDI will present the product there. They do not state a price, a launch date or the customers who might buy the battery solution. They also do not say how many data centers could adopt it or how the 33 percent space efficiency gain was measured. Samsung SDI has said only that it will continue developing products that meet market demands for performance and safety.

stories.Headline: Paras Semiconductors partners with US firm BroadPak for advanced chip packaging in India
stories.Summary:
Paras Semiconductors, a subsidiary of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, has announced a technology partnership with US-based BroadPak Corporation to develop advanced semiconductor packaging capabilities in India. The announcement came in a company release on Monday, November 10, 2026, as reported by PTI and by Electronics For You. Through the tie-up, Paras Semiconductors aims to set up an advanced heterogeneous integration and 3D packaging facility in the country. The proposed facility is an OSAT unit, meaning an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test operation. Electronics For You described the partnership as one that gives Paras Semiconductors access to specialised technology expertise from the American firm.

The proposed unit will focus on 2.5D and 3D packaging, chiplet integration, hybrid bonding, wafer-level and panel-level fan-out packaging, co-packaged optics, and testing and qualification. Paras Semiconductors will gain access to BroadPak's design, manufacturing and integration intellectual property, along with technology transfer and process know-how. The two firms will also explore joint development of packaging platforms for AI and high-performance computing applications. They plan to collaborate on training and skill development programmes for Indian engineers. The planned manufacturing unit will incorporate through-silicon vias, micro-bumping, advanced interposers and redistribution layer technologies, along with wafer-level processing and reliability testing.

Munjal Sharad Shah, Managing Director of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, described the company's entry into the semiconductor sector as a strategic expansion into a technology domain that is increasingly critical. He said it matters for India's AI, data centre and industrial capabilities. He added that the collaboration would help build advanced packaging capabilities that complement the company's existing strengths in optics, optronics and critical electronics. Santosh Kumar, CEO of Paras Semiconductors, said the company intends to build a packaging platform that can meet the performance, connectivity and thermal needs of next-generation applications. He said the collaboration would support capabilities in heterogeneous integration, chiplet architectures, hybrid bonding and advanced system-in-package technologies.

Shah also said the initiative would address India's strategic domestic requirements as well as the wider needs of the semiconductor industry. BroadPak Founder and CEO Farhang Yazdani said India's growing semiconductor ecosystem offers an important opportunity to develop capabilities in heterogeneous integration and system-level packaging. He noted that this opportunity is especially strong as demand for AI and high-performance computing increases. The facility is meant to serve applications in artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, networking, data centres and strategic electronics.

It will also address high-volume manufacturing needs, including devices for optical and optronic systems. Through the partnership, Paras Semiconductors aims to strengthen its presence in India's domestic semiconductor packaging ecosystem and to support emerging computing and strategic electronics applications. BroadPak is headquartered in San Jose, California, and was founded in 2007. According to the release, it brings specialised expertise across advanced packaging design, manufacturing and system integration.

Its capabilities cover 2.5D and 3D IC packaging, heterogeneous integration, multi-die architectures, high-speed interconnects, thermal management and co-packaged optics. Electronics For You said the rising demand for advanced packaging technologies, including chiplets, 2.5D and 3D integration and hybrid bonding, made the decision to collaborate stronger. Paras Semiconductors is a subsidiary of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, whose existing strengths lie in optics, optronics and critical electronics. The articles do not say when the proposed facility will be built or begin operating.

They give no location for it, and they state no investment amount or capacity figure. They also do not say how many engineers will be trained or when the training will start. The two firms have said they will explore joint development of packaging platforms for AI and high-performance computing, so those platforms remain at an early stage. The financial terms of the partnership and any regulatory approvals the facility may need are not stated.

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s Claude Tops AI Rankings as OpenAI Limits Cyber Model
stories.Summary:
Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 on Monday, Nov. 9, and it moved to the top of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 65. The company launched it alongside Claude Mythos 5.2, a restricted sibling for vetted cybersecurity and life sciences organizations. Meta released its cheapest model yet, Muse Ember, on the same day, Nov. 9. OpenAI had already released GPT-6 Cyber on Nov. 5, but only to approved customers in its Daybreak Red security program, with no public access. Thinking Machines Lab and Baidu also released lower-cost models on Nov. 5, and Baidu published its model weights openly.

Fable 5.2 scored 65, ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon at 60 and Anthropic's own Claude Opus 5.5 at 59. Pricing is $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, while Meta's Muse Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens. Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small costs $0.30 per million input tokens and $1 per million output tokens. In testing, GPT-6 Cyber found 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox and built 948 working exploits against the Linux kernel. Google DeepMind released Gemini Robotics 2.5 to robotics partners on Tuesday, Nov. 10, and Ricursive Intelligence released Ripple-65B Preview on Nov. 4.

Anthropic says Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1, and that its safety filters block about 55% fewer legitimate requests. The company named Jump Trading, Balyasny Asset Management and XTX Markets as users for quantitative research. It said Box used the model to review loan application files and flag a mismatch between salary deposits and a bank statement balance. OpenAI rated GPT-6 Cyber Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, the first OpenAI model to reach that level, and that rating is why access is gated. OpenAI says the model stayed within researcher-set boundaries in 99.93% of tests.

Meta says Muse Ember costs less per task than Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Luna, and it accepts text, images and audio. Meta built it to pair with its larger Muse Wonder, which plans a task while Ember executes repetitive steps such as tool calls, data extraction and long-document parsing. Google says Gemini Robotics 2.5 resists jailbreak attempts 99.5% of the time, up from 82% for its predecessor, Gemini Robotics ER 2. In a pilot on live Mercedes-Benz lines in Hungary and Germany, Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid robots sorted metal brackets into trays in vehicle order with a 96% success rate. Boston Dynamics and Agile Robots are also deploying the model, and the pricing question for financial firms is shifting toward routing each task to the cheapest capable model.

Thinking Machines Lab was founded by former OpenAI Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, and Inkling 2 Small is the first model in its second generation. The model has 594 billion parameters but uses only 17 billion on any request, and the company says it will release the weights under an Apache 2.0 license after outside safety testing. Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base has 280 billion parameters, uses 14 billion per request, and supports a 1-million-token context window of roughly 1,500 pages. Baidu positions it as a base for companies to fine-tune on their own data rather than a finished assistant. Ricursive, a Palo Alto startup founded by former Google researchers to design AI chips with AI, says its 65-billion-parameter Ripple is the strongest U.S. open model for agentic coding, scoring 80.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 against 80.1 for Reflection AI's Beam.

Thinking Machines has not yet released the Inkling 2 Small weights, which depend on outside safety testing finishing first. A separate OpenRouter guide published Nov. 11 describes how developers can handle 429 rate limit errors from OpenAI, Anthropic and OpenRouter when running under real load. In its test, the OpenAI Python SDK's default retries left 23 of 60 requests failed, while a retry that waits for the reset time finished all 60 in 89 to 92 seconds in Python. A fallback model finished all 60 in 13 seconds, for $0.000066, with no waiting. The articles do not say whether OpenAI will widen access to GPT-6 Cyber, and Ricursive says its project cost $32 million, about a tenth of what it estimates Reflection spent on Beam.

stories.Headline: KT deploys AI-based email security service across KAIST
stories.Summary:
KT has been chosen by the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, known as KAIST, to provide a cloud-based AI email security service to the whole university. The service will cover all students, researchers and faculty and staff, rather than only a handful of key researchers or particular departments. KT announced the deployment on Tuesday, the 11th, and the news was reported on November 11, 2026. KAIST picked the service after its own technical evaluation of the technology. It also cleared a security review by the National Intelligence Service, which opened the way for a campus-wide rollout.

The service is KT's in-house AI Email Security product, a cloud security service that detects and blocks threats delivered by email, including ransomware and phishing messages. It applies a three-stage filtering system covering spam blocking, AI-based threat detection and in-depth analysis of advanced persistent threats, known as APTs. The system can spot phishing URLs and malicious files disguised as legitimate mail. KT will supply AI-based threat detection and an APT response system for every member of KAIST. The service runs on a software-as-a-service model and can be supplied according to the scale of use, so universities, research institutes and other organizations can adopt it.

KT is the party responsible for delivering and operating the service, and it described its aims in plain terms. It said the deployment is meant to shield KAIST's core research and education assets from increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks while also growing its AI security business. Seung-taek Baek, executive director and head of the Western Corporate Customer Headquarters in KT's Enterprise Division, said KT will use its AI security technology to protect KAIST members and the university's research and educational assets. He added that KT will build on this case to extend its AI security services to universities and research institutions. KT also said it will use the KAIST deployment to widen its AI email security business to major research and education institutions, including domestic universities and government-funded research institutes.

KAIST's own view came from Young-jin Kwon, head of the university's Academic Information Office. He said it is important that students, researchers and faculty and staff can concentrate on research and education in a safe environment. Kwon said the university will keep advancing its information security system so that all members can receive a high level of protection. The people directly affected are the students, researchers and faculty and staff of KAIST, all of whom fall under the new coverage. KT also said it intends to support institutions that feel burdened by specialist security staffing or infrastructure operations, so they can use AI-based threat detection and APT analysis.

The articles give some background on how the service differs from earlier approaches and on its certification. Unlike existing on-premises APT security solutions, KT's service integrates spam, AI and APT security functions through a cloud-based software-as-a-service model. Because of this, an institution does not need to build a separate large-scale security infrastructure, which reduces its operational burden. KT obtained Cloud Security Assurance Program certification for the solution's cloud service in June. The articles also note that the AI security solution was developed in-house by KT, and that the service is scaled to the size of each deployment.

Looking ahead, KT says it will use the KAIST case to expand its AI email security business to major research and education institutions, including domestic universities and government-funded research institutes. KAIST says it will continue to advance its information security system so all members can receive a high level of security protection. The articles do not give a start date for the campus-wide rollout or a timetable for the planned expansion to other institutions. They also do not state the contract value, the contract length, or the number of KAIST users who will be covered. Nor do they name which other universities or research institutes KT intends to approach next.

stories.Headline: AI-era trade challenges demand cooperation
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, China's General Administration of Customs reported that foreign trade in goods kept growing strongly in the first 10 months of the year. Total imports and exports grew 20 percent year on year to 44.81 trillion yuan, about 6.67 trillion U.S. dollars, accelerating from 18.8 percent over the first nine months. Imports surged 23.6 percent, while exports rose 17.6 percent during the January to October period. Booming artificial intelligence demand lifted exports of electronic components, and imports posted especially robust gains. Both imports and exports have now recorded double-digit growth for six consecutive months through October.

Goods trade in October alone expanded 31.2 percent. Mechanical and electrical products rose 25.2 percent over the period and accounted for 64.7 percent of total exports, up 3.9 percentage points from a year earlier. Exports of integrated circuits and memory components surged 101.9 percent and 132.5 percent, while 3D printers, digital cameras and industrial robots rose 104.8 percent, 41.4 percent and 17.8 percent. Exports of the so-called new three, electric vehicles, photovoltaic products and lithium batteries, grew 46.5 percent, electric motorcycles and bicycles rose 33.3 percent, and wind turbines and their components gained 19.7 percent. By trading partner, trade with ASEAN grew 24.2 percent, trade with the European Union rose 8.5 percent, and trade with the United States expanded 6.3 percent, while trade with Belt and Road participating countries grew 18.5 percent.

Lyu Daliang, director of the customs administration's Department of Statistics and Analysis, said China's foreign trade has kept up its momentum this year, showing greater resilience and vitality. He said imports from more than 150 countries and regions recorded growth in the first 10 months. Imports from ASEAN, Latin America and Africa all reached record highs for the same period. In his words, China's vast market continued to offer opportunities to the world. Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating, said several factors kept export growth elevated in October.

She noted that the global AI investment boom continued to push up prices of chips, other electronic components and computer parts, which drove strong growth in export value. She added that domestic manufacturing upgrades in recent years have also strengthened the competitiveness of new energy vehicles and high-tech products. Separately, Sierra Leone's President Julius Maada Bio told a high-level virtual meeting convened by French President Emmanuel Macron that African and other developing nations must have a meaningful voice in shaping global standards for frontier AI. He said no country can adequately address these challenges alone and that sovereignty means choosing the terms on which countries work together. The Sierra Leone presidency said the meeting, held on Monday, November 9, focused on strengthening international cooperation on frontier model security.

Attendees included the prime ministers of the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, Norway and the Netherlands, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Bahrain's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa also took part, along with technology leaders Brad Smith of Microsoft, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Arthur Mensch of Mistral AI. Bio recalled that Sierra Leone endorsed the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models at the AI Middle Powers Roundtable at the United Nations General Assembly in September, co-hosted by Kenya and Finland. He said the country has completed its National AI Readiness Assessment, which will inform its first National AI Strategy, and that it is exploring AI in agriculture, healthcare, education and public service delivery.

He also cited the proposed Regional Data Embassy Framework under ECOWAS, which aims to expand shared infrastructure while safeguarding national control over data. A commentary carried by China Daily Global Edition, drawing on interviews with Zhang Monan of the China Center for International Economic Exchanges and Wang Zhimin of the University of International Business and Economics, examined how AI demand moves along global supply chains. It said AI is spreading into manufacturing, automobiles, robotics and smart devices, and that it helps firms overcome language and information barriers in cross-border trade and improves logistics. It warned that AI could widen the digital divide because of gaps in technology, infrastructure and talent, and said China has worked with various countries on digital infrastructure and smart cities through the Digital Silk Road.

It also said data, algorithms and intelligent services are raising questions about market access, cross-border data flows, privacy, intellectual property and security certification. Bio told the meeting that common standards for evaluating advanced models, clear accountability for developers and deployers, and mechanisms for reporting serious incidents are essential, and that countries should not simply adopt standards set elsewhere. Experts quoted by Xinhua expect strong exports to continue through the end of the year. Zhang Di, a macro analyst at China Galaxy Securities, said that as the AI cycle remains in an upswing, China will keep benefiting as a global hub of electronics supply chains.

She added that the global green and low-carbon transition, combined with China's rising competitiveness in mechanical equipment, will sustain strong growth in new energy vehicles, ships and other transport machinery. Bio welcomed the proposed Paris Declaration and called for its commitments on common evaluation standards, accountability and incident reporting to become practical measures. He said Sierra Leone is ready to work with international partners and wants greater investment in scientific expertise, institutional capacity and evaluation tools for developing countries. The articles do not say when the Paris Declaration will be finalized, and the China Daily commentary does not name specific rules or agreements that would follow its call for cooperation.

stories.Headline: WhatsApp to make connections richer, use AI to save time; privacy unchanged: CEO Kunal Shah
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday, November 11, WhatsApp chief executive Kunal Shah set out three priorities for the Meta-owned messaging platform in a post on X, speaking from New Delhi. He said WhatsApp will make connections richer, let users finish tasks such as paying bills inside chats, and use artificial intelligence to improve efficiency. He promised that personal messages and calls will stay end-to-end encrypted while these changes arrive. Shah took charge of the platform in June this year, and he said he spent the last few months listening to users. He summed up what he heard as a wish to stay close to those who matter and to get more done on the app.

On the first priority, Shah said users send over 10 billion voice messages and over 4 billion stickers on WhatsApp every day. He said WhatsApp will make voice notes, groups, stickers and video simpler and more expressive, because the ways people feel close keep changing. The second priority is to cut the extra steps needed when a task begins in a chat, such as paying a bill, borrowing money or staying connected while travelling. Shah said WhatsApp is working with financial services and telecom partners so that finishing something feels as easy as starting it. The third priority is AI that quietly finds what users need, gets things done and ensures they never miss a booking or an appointment.

Shah is the person responsible, and he presented the plan in his own words on X. He said the best technology saves people time, so they can return to the connections that matter. He noted that WhatsApp handles over 100 billion messages and 2 billion calls every day, and that the platform must remain simple, reliable and private. Shah said trust takes years to earn and a moment to lose, and that he does not take that lightly. He added that the quality bar would not change and that these long-held principles are not changing.

Inc42 reported that the post signals WhatsApp's intent to expand beyond messaging into payments, financial services and commerce, building on its existing payments and business offerings. It noted that in India WhatsApp has expanded its payments capabilities through WhatsApp Pay, though adoption has stayed limited compared with established UPI players. Inc42 also pointed out that Shah did not say which AI capabilities will be introduced or whether they will involve more advanced agentic features. It added that he did not disclose specific partnerships or timelines for the integrations with financial and telecom partners. The users affected include India, WhatsApp's largest market, with an estimated 535 million to 550 million monthly active users, some databases putting it as high as 853.8 million, and more than 3 billion users worldwide.

Shah is the founder of the fintech platform CRED, and Meta appointed him WhatsApp's global head in June. He succeeded Will Cathcart, who had led WhatsApp since 2019 and moved to a new role within Meta. Shah announced in June 2026 that he would step down from day-to-day operations at CRED, where cofounder Miten Sampat became interim chief executive. Shah kept his personal shareholding in CRED, and Meta led a funding round of about Rs 8,550 crore, or about USD 900 million, in the Bengaluru-headquartered firm. That Series H round valued CRED at Rs 43,239 crore post-money, or USD 4.5 billion, and his remarks came nearly five months after the move.

Shah now faces the challenge of widening WhatsApp's usefulness beyond communication while keeping its simplicity and privacy standards. Driving adoption of its payments, financial services and other offerings is expected to remain a key challenge for the platform. The articles leave open which AI features will be introduced, and whether they will include advanced agentic tools. They also leave open which financial services and telecom partners will be involved, and when the planned changes will reach users. Meta AI currently offers AI-powered features on WhatsApp, including help with queries and content generation, and Shah described no timeline beyond his stated priorities.

stories.Headline: Cognizant commits 25,000 staff to Claude AI deployment
stories.Summary:
Cognizant announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, the formation of the Claude Frontier Capability Group, a dedicated global organization of more than 25,000 professionals committed to delivering Anthropic's Claude for clients. The Nasdaq-listed company, with its base in Teaneck, New Jersey, made the announcement through a PR Newswire release. The group is built around execution excellence, transformation and client success. It has the scale to take AI from pilot to production across the core operations of enterprises. Cognizant also introduced a managed services model for Claude, under which it runs Claude-powered systems in production on behalf of clients.

The managed services model combines dedicated talent, licensed access to Claude and Cognizant's own intellectual property, including its AI Delivery Operating System. It gives clients more predictable AI spend and runs every engagement within enterprise-grade security and governance controls. Those controls are customized to each client's connectivity, architecture and risk requirements. The new group will initially focus on four areas, starting with redesigning business domains around AI and building and modernizing the systems that support them. The other two areas are operating agents securely at scale and establishing AI-native software engineering as a core delivery capability, and for modernization Cognizant brings purpose-built Claude agents that speed analysis and refactoring of legacy and mainframe code.

Ravi Kumar S, Cognizant's chief executive, said clients want a partner who will take responsibility for delivery once AI is running inside their business. He said the company is putting more than 25,000 of its people on Claude and taking on the job of running it for clients through managed services. Kumar described this as a significant bet on Claude and on what enterprises can achieve with it in their core operations. Both initiatives draw on Cognizant's Frontier workforce model, through which it is developing Frontier Certified Engineers and Frontier Business Operators credentialed directly by frontier-model companies. Cognizant did not disclose the commercial terms of the offering, according to TechGig.

Paul Smith, Anthropic's Chief Commercial Officer, said every enterprise is racing to bring AI into its organization, but people with the skills to make it work inside a real business have become the hardest talent to find. He said Cognizant is working to address that gap by committing more than 25,000 people to help customers put Claude to work across their businesses. Cognizant cited client results from the work already underway, including a global pharmaceutical manufacturer where Claude-powered shop-floor agents cut downtime by 35%. At that manufacturer, troubleshooting time fell from 90 to 120 minutes down to 10 to 15 minutes. A media and entertainment company cut time to market from three to four weeks to about 15 minutes by automating requirement data sheet creation, and a North American insurer accelerated campaign brief generation and retirement plan support by 40% to 60%.

Cognizant has built Claude skills across its workforce, with more than 44,000 associates in business units and corporate functions already trained or certified on Claude. The company holds more than 26,000 Claude certifications and ranks first globally for Claude Certified Architect: Foundations. It is deploying Claude across its workforce, including corporate functions, engineering and delivery teams, as announced in November 2025. TechGig reports that the latest announcement builds on an expanded partnership with Anthropic in July, when Cognizant outlined plans to integrate Claude into its engineering platforms. stories.Headline: Chinese AI firms rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity as spy scandal stirs fear of US curbs
stories.Summary:
Chinese artificial intelligence companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centres outside China, according to three people familiar with the matter. They are worried that a scandal involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang could push Washington to tighten limits on their remote use of advanced processors. A major Chinese cloud provider has discussed internally whether to lock in overseas Nvidia chip capacity, while some firms have contacted data centre operators about reserving it. Smaller AI labs are considering similar steps, including approaching major providers of rented computing power in South-east Asia, two of the people said. The article was published on November 12, 2026, and the sources declined to be named, or to name the cloud provider, because of the sensitivity of the matter.

Washington restricts exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips, but Chinese firms can reach such processors remotely by renting computing power at overseas data centres. The companies fear the controversy could add momentum to the Remote Access Security Act, known as Rasa, a US bill that would let the Commerce Department regulate remote, cloud-based access to restricted technology. The House of Representatives passed the bill in January by a vote of 369 to 22, and it now awaits action in the Senate. Restricting overseas cloud access would make it harder for Chinese developers to obtain high-end computing power without importing the chips directly. The prospect of tougher enforcement has also fuelled demand for restricted Nvidia chips in China's grey market, prompting traders and intermediaries to start stockpiling them.

Huang said on Sunday, November 8, that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The New York Times reported that the woman involved was Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed, and that US authorities had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Reuters could not independently verify that allegation, which China has denied. Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting chips to China, while Nvidia, Megaspeed and the US Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tencent and Alibaba also did not immediately respond when asked about Alice Huang's dealings with them.

Alice Huang had business dealings and investment ties with several leading Chinese technology companies, including Tencent and Alibaba, according to two people familiar with the matter. Singapore business filings show that Apex Enterprise Solutions, an Alibaba subsidiary, provided financing to Speedmatrix, a Malaysian company linked to Megaspeed. Seoul Economic Daily, citing foreign media, said Speedmatrix pledged servers and intellectual property to Apex as collateral, which secured Alibaba as a client. In the grey market, buyers fear a broader US crackdown on the smuggling of advanced chips and AI servers into China, according to two of the people. Smaller AI labs and traders are among those now acting in response to the controversy.

Megaspeed has faced scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Chinese customers gain access to advanced Nvidia chips subject to US export controls. Seoul Economic Daily reported that Alice Huang built a structure linking China, Singapore and Malaysia, using Shanghai Century Litong, launched in June 2023, Megaspeed, and its Malaysian subsidiary SpeedMatrix. It said the chips she smuggled or leased out as data centre capacity were estimated at about 240,000 units, including H100, H200 and A100 processors. A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia H200 chips in October despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show. In March, US prosecutors charged Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and two others with conspiring to divert servers containing Nvidia chips to China through a South-east Asia-based company.

Prosecutors said that company bought about US$2.5 billion of servers from Super Micro between 2024 and 2025, and that a substantial portion was diverted to China. The defendants have not been convicted. Seoul Economic Daily reported that Singapore authorities summoned Alice Huang over suspicions of false import declarations but closed the investigation for lack of evidence. It also said she later left for Shanghai, while Megaspeed's business continues and figures linked to her have reportedly pressed ahead with data centre construction in Malaysia. The Rasa bill still awaits Senate action, and the articles do not say whether or when the Senate will vote on it.

stories.Headline: Nvidia loses its 'Godfather of AI' and now faces first big test without him
stories.Summary:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the company on Thursday, after reports of two extramarital affairs and a board investigation that followed. One of the relationships was with a Chinese businesswoman whom United States authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. Nvidia announced that Colette Kress, its veteran chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive. The news roiled the company's stock as investors and analysts weighed the path ahead for the artificial intelligence chip giant. Earlier reports had said the board was preparing to oust Huang, and the stock had already fallen on those reports.

Nvidia shares fell roughly 14% from Wednesday's closing price, reaching an intraday low of $148.80 per share before paring those losses. By early afternoon the stock was down only 4.3%, and the latest quote showed it at $166.19, a fall of $7.54. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it to the forefront of the artificial intelligence trade. Nvidia reports its earnings next week, and investors will examine the results closely for a fresh read on demand. The company is also expected to face continued scrutiny over its business dealings with China and any loopholes in export controls.

Nvidia's board of directors is the body that investigated the affairs and now steers the company through the transition. Kress, as interim chief executive, takes responsibility for running the company while it works out its future leadership. The articles quote no direct statement from Huang, from Kress or from the board beyond the announcement of her interim role. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said the resignation lets the board remove the problem quickly and take Nvidia into its next chapter without Huang. Ives added that the company already has a strategic roadmap built around its next family of chips, which Nvidia hopes will keep powering the artificial intelligence boom.

Bret Kenwell, an investment analyst at eToro, said Huang was more than a chief executive and was part of the investment thesis, which will bring greater scrutiny to next week's earnings report. Kenwell added that leadership questions do not erase Nvidia's position as a best-in-class technology company during a transformational period for the sector. James McCann, a senior economist at Edward Jones, pointed to the lack of a clear succession plan and to the financial role Nvidia has played in backing other parts of the artificial intelligence sector. McCann said the corporate fundamentals are unchanged, and the firm advises investors to avoid over-concentration in technology companies and to hold well-diversified exposure across large and midcap American stocks. Inc42 reported that the scandal adds uncertainty for India's neocloud providers, firms that rent out graphics processing units and depend on Nvidia's ecosystem.

Investors had already been selling shares of American neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN suffering sharp corrections that intensified through October and into November. McCann noted that the Nasdaq had delivered gains or losses greater than 1% in seven of the past 10 trading days. Ives said Nvidia remains the clear leader in graphics chips for the artificial intelligence revolution, roughly two to three years ahead of the nearest competitor. His firm holds a price target of $225 a share and an outperform rating on the stock. Inc42 said Nvidia's influence now extends beyond chip supply to financing and strategic partnerships, and that India's neoclouds rely on international customers, government-backed demand and evolving financing arrangements.

The most immediate event is next week's earnings report, when shareholders will look to Nvidia for stability, a fresh read on demand and a reason to regain confidence. The articles do not say who will become the permanent chief executive, and Kress serves only on an interim basis. McCann said it remains to be seen whether a change at the top will materially affect strategy and execution. Ives said the outlook assumes continued headwinds from China-related scrutiny, which he considers already factored into the stock at current valuation. Inc42 left open whether Indian neoclouds will keep the financial backing and customer commitments needed to withstand a global market correction, including CoreWeave's plan to be sole tenant of a 240 megawatt AdaniConneX data centre campus in India.

stories.Headline: Firms can cash in on clients’ AI itch
stories.Summary:
Parachute co-founder and chief executive Vivienne Chan said law firms could respond to clients' growing use of chatbots by offering their own branded AI tools, according to a Lawyers Weekly article dated November 11, 2026. Chan made the remarks during a recent AI Innovate live stream, where she said clients' chatbot use was creating friction around billing and AI-generated confusion. The article was written by Naomi Neilson and was also published in a later version the same day. Chan said firm leaders were reporting growing tensions with clients who believed they were doing much of the work with these tools themselves. Those clients, she said, expected lower fees or faster turnaround from their lawyers.

Chan said the friction was real because lawyers did not want to take on the risk of a client's AI output. She said lawyers had no idea where such output came from or how verified it was. She also said both sides were using AI far more, but the end-to-end process had not become smoother for anyone. Chan recounted how one customer first reported hallucinations in Parachute, but further investigation showed the errors came from Claude. She said Parachute verifies every piece of source material, which it said makes its output legitimate, up-to-date and actual source material.

Parachute has introduced an extension that clients can access themselves, and the chatbot has been fully white-labelled to look as though it sits within the client portal. Chan said the tool becomes a safe space for clients to get round-the-clock legal support and immediate answers. Questions that need further strategy or discussion are pushed up to the law firm to investigate and respond to. Chan said the tool can be packaged up for billing, and that clients feel they are getting more value for their money. She said the chatbot scratches the itch to check everything with AI within a safe environment co-sponsored with the law firm.

Chan said the arrangement ensures lawyers are not wasting time on low-value legal work, and that it promotes better relationships that can lead to retention or referrals. She said trust is elevated when firms are transparent about their use of AI and sponsor clients' use of it. Chan said this helps clients find a way to use AI safely together with their lawyers. The affected parties named in the article are law firms and their clients, who are the ones facing the friction over billing and AI output. The article does not describe any change in the wider profession beyond these comments.

The article's background is the rise of clients' chatbot use, which Chan described as creating friction around billing and AI-generated confusion. It also gives the context of Parachute's own guardrails, which Chan contrasted with Claude and other OpenAI models. The article does not give further history of the dispute between firms and clients. It does not provide any figures on how many firms or clients have adopted such tools. The article's only other background is the publication details and the author's own role at Lawyers Weekly.

The article does not say whether any firm has adopted Parachute's branded chatbot or what results it has produced. It does not report any figures on fees, turnaround times or client retention after such tools are used. It also does not say how the billing packaging works in practice or how the errors Chan described were resolved. The article leaves open whether clients will accept firm-sponsored tools in place of their own AI use. It gives no timetable for further developments.

stories.Headline: The AI industry faces intense strain as lawsuits, protests, scandals pile up
stories.Summary:
The Alliance for Secure AI, together with Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and the Heat Initiative, filed a lawsuit on November 12, 2026, in San Francisco Superior Court against five AI developers. The suit names Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI (SpaceX Super Intelligence) as defendants. The groups allege these companies knowingly built technology that poses catastrophic risks to humanity. They ask the court to block further development of AI models. The filing comes amid a broader wave of strain on the industry, including scandals and protests.

The plaintiffs argue that existing law, specifically California's Unfair Competition Law, allows the court to find the companies' practices unlawful and halt further development. The groups contend that the companies are releasing products they have admitted could be potentially harmful. The suit also raises concern about "recursive self-improvement," in which AI models are used to develop future platforms without human intervention. It says the defendants know their systems do not consistently act as intended and that no reliable control method exists. The complaint seeks to freeze AI development in the name of public safety.

The Public Citizen co-president, Robert Weissman, said in a press release that AI executives are rushing to deploy ever-more advanced systems despite warnings. The Alliance for Secure AI's CEO, Brendan Steinhauser, said executives have warned that their own frontier models pose catastrophic risks. The defendants did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have previously agreed on the need to slow the growth of advanced AI systems. In a September essay, Amodei proposed a three-point plan to "pace the frontier" of AI, which Altman later signaled support for.

Child advocacy groups say children have already been harmed by Big Tech's priorities. Heat Initiative CEO Brooke Istook said chatbots have pushed kids toward suicide and that AI tools have turned ordinary photos into abusive material. Dozens of survivor parent-advocates sent a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings. The letter urges them to compel OpenAI to restructure its corporate structure and board membership. The two states led a joint investigation into OpenAI's recent restructuring.

In a separate matter, a family is arguing that their teen's access to AI on school-issued Chromebooks posed a life-threatening risk to her mental health. Background from the articles includes Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO, which ended the company's first CEO change in 33 years. Voters approved more than 40 measures to slow or ban data center growth in the midterm elections. On November 11, a coalition of school and child safety groups led nationwide protests over Google's new policies for schools. Google announced that its AI tools would be opt-in by default, and because AI-powered Search cannot be turned off, districts with AI bans face a choice.

The articles also report that in October, AI company leaders including Altman, Amodei and Elon Musk voiced support for an industrywide slowdown in AI development. The companies had not responded to requests for comment at the time of the reporting, and the articles do not say how the court will rule on the suit. The articles do not say whether the attorneys general will act on the parents' letter. They also do not say whether the incoming Democratic Congress will take up the issues raised. Whether Google's schools policy will change after the protests is not addressed in the articles.
