stories.Headline: AI – Master and Commander: Lessons from graduate student projects and the need for an AI-enriched contract
stories.Summary:
The seminar was held in the spring of 2026 at Goethe University, where 31 master's students used AI to investigate why the EU appears more exposed to international shocks and political, financial and industrial vulnerabilities than before. Students examined defence and security, migration and labour markets, energy and the green transition, strategic autonomy and industrial policy, the Single Market, and monetary policy under uncertainty. The authors describe the seminar as an experiment in how AI might be used in graduate education without displacing students' independent judgement. The question was whether AI could help students without outsourcing the thinking that graduate study is meant to develop. The work ran over six weeks as a graduate seminar, with the authors acknowledging the importance of this challenge in assessment.

The authors note that views on AI range widely, and they cite concerns in the literature about unreliable outputs, including hallucinations and fabricated references. They also describe cognitive offloading, where people delegate tasks to technology, and cognitive surrender, where people stop thinking for themselves. Employers are expected to value people who can reason critically as AI takes over routine tasks. The Guardian reported that 92% of UK students already use AI, and universities were urged to stress-test their assessments. The seminar adopted a pragmatic, optimistic stance in line with UNESCO's human-centred guidance and the OECD's view that assessment should measure learning rather than polished output.

The seminar required each group to submit three elements: a pre-AI outline with a research question, motivation, initial sources and analytical plan, written before any AI use; a core presentation enriched by AI; and a transparency statement listing the tools used, the prompts, and what worked or failed. The authors describe this as an AI-enriched contract designed to keep ownership of ideas with students and to make AI use visible. The final lecture refined research questions and helped students present strategically. The assessment rested on three dimensions set out in a table in the source article. Students were expected to show judgement, not just output, in the final presentations.

Thirteen groups presented, covering defence, migration, energy, industrial policy, the Single Market and monetary policy. Several projects examined how Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the 2022 energy crisis and renewed trade tensions exposed gaps in Europe's architecture, while others assessed whether REPowerEU, the Green Deal and the Critical Raw Materials Act were on track. Methods ranged from policy analysis and surveys to panel regressions, difference-in-differences and text analysis. The authors report that the groups drew the line in the same place, reserving the research question, economic reasoning and final interpretation for themselves while verifying what AI produced. Students and graduate programmes, the authors suggest, face the same tension between speed and understanding.

The authors observed five recurring patterns: AI sped up routine work such as cleaning data, debugging code, formatting charts and translating sources; it helped students use methods they did not previously know; it allowed exploration within a six-week seminar; humans kept judgement, interpretation and fact-checking; and students developed new literacies, including careful prompting and critical checking of sources. The authors conclude that AI behaved as a capable subordinate rather than a master and commander, with students keeping command of questions and conclusions. Each student presented and answered questions for well over 15 minutes on average. The authors note that the phrase master and commander refers to 18th-century Royal Navy officers who captained sloops-of-war.

The authors acknowledge limitations: the cohort was small, self-selected and not random, much evidence came from student reflections, and there was no control group working without AI. Reported gains in speed and ambition therefore cannot be causally attributed to AI or the contract, and durable learning was not measured. Future pilot studies are planned to assess outlines and final outputs separately, require systematic prompt logs, and track whether critical questioning persists. The authors also note that the AI landscape and graduate education are changing continuously. The article is a CEPR/VoxEU piece, and the authors thank Goethe University for financial support and a workshop audience for comments.

stories.Headline: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills, study shows - CNA
stories.Summary:
Nearly six in ten senior executives at large companies plan to increase their use of cheaper open-weight AI models over the next year, according to a Capgemini study released on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The shift comes as AI bills have overshot budgets for many firms. The survey of 500 executives at enterprises with annual revenue above $1 billion across 10 countries found that open-weight models handled 72 per cent of traffic on the OpenRouter multi-AI provider in September. Those models, however, accounted for only 27 per cent of AI spending. Capgemini also said open-weight tokens were on average 87 per cent cheaper than closed ones.

Fifty-nine per cent of the executives said their AI spending over the past year had run significantly above their expectations or budgets, by 24 per cent on average. Another 53 per cent said they were worried about AI costs, up from 45 per cent the previous year. Half of the respondents said they would keep closed models where the complexity of a task justified the extra cost. The findings point to a mixed approach rather than a full move away from proprietary systems.

Companies appear to be weighing price against performance task by task. Capgemini, the IT consulting firm that helps companies embed AI into their existing platforms, conducted the study. The report reflects its own survey findings and its view of where enterprise spending is heading. The trend echoes a decision by SAP, whose finance chief said last month that the company was replacing some of its costliest AI models with cheaper ones where performance held up.

Anthropic, which launched its IPO roadshow this week, also warned in its prospectus that customers may shift to cheaper options, including open-weight models. Open-weight models, such as those from DeepSeek or Mistral, can be downloaded and run anywhere, while closed options such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini are accessible only from the cloud. The survey indicates that enterprises are likely to keep expanding their use of cheaper models while retaining premium closed systems for demanding work. The articles do not say how the spending pattern will change beyond the next year.

stories.Headline: AI productivity gains need to be shared — but how?
stories.Summary:
The Australian government has released a draft "Best practice guide on the adoption of AI in the workplace," announced by Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth this week. The release comes as AI is already contributing to job losses across the country, including at Qantas, Canva and Australia's big banks. Rishworth discussed the guide with POLITICO's Amanda Copp on the Canberra Playbook Podcast. The guidance is aimed at helping business owners and workers prepare for disruption from AI.

The guide advises employers to involve workers when they deploy AI, to redesign jobs and to build skills among their staff. It also calls for clear accountability and ongoing checks to make sure AI systems are safe and fair. The government's position, as the article reports it, is that AI can benefit both businesses and workers. The guidelines are not enforceable, however, so they set out expectations rather than binding rules. The article's headline frames the central question as how the productivity gains from AI should be shared.

Rishworth's office is responsible for the guide, and the minister spoke about how the government is trying to help the business community and workers adjust. The article paraphrases her approach as one of preparation, not compulsion. The Labor government's view, as relayed in the piece, is that well-managed AI adoption can serve both sides of the workplace. The article gives no timeline for when the draft will be finalised or whether any part of it will become law.

The piece places the guidance within a broader Australian policy debate, noting that Canberra is weighing questions about technology regulation alongside other pressures. The article describes Australia as a middle power with major resources, including a large share of the world's uranium and lithium. It also references the AUKUS defence program and the country's energy transition. The article does not say what steps will follow the draft guide or how employers and unions are expected to respond.

stories.Headline: Judge Says Fake AI Case Citations Warrant Sanctions
stories.Summary:
A federal magistrate judge in Pennsylvania has recommended dismissing with prejudice a pro se couple's lawsuit over a mortgage foreclosure, and said their continued use of fictitious case citations warrants sanctions. The recommendation came in a November 4 report in Torres v. Freedom Mortgage Corp., issued by U.S. Magistrate Judge Martin C. Carlson of the Middle District of Pennsylvania. Carlson said Hericson and Leigh Torres kept citing cases that do not exist after both a bankruptcy court and the federal court had warned them. The recommendation now goes to Judge Karoline Mehalchick, and the parties have 14 days to file objections.

The Torres filing is a report and recommendation, so the district judge may accept, modify, or reject it. Freedom Mortgage obtained a default judgment against Hericson Torres in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, in December 2023, with damages assessed at $308,604. State courts denied two petitions to open that judgment. On February 26, 2026, the day the sheriff sold the property, Leigh Torres filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. On March 31, the bankruptcy court found that Leigh Torres had cited nonexistent or inaccurate case law and ordered her to certify any future use of generative AI in filings.

Three days later, the couple filed a federal complaint asserting 13 counts, including claims under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, RESPA and the CARES Act. Carlson said the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, claim preclusion, and the Anti-Injunction Act barred the attempt to relitigate the foreclosure. He wrote that there was no bankruptcy stay to violate, because two earlier bankruptcy cases had been dismissed within the previous year. He also found that private lenders are not state actors for constitutional claims, and that the sheriff has quasi-judicial immunity for carrying out a court-ordered sale. Carlson noted that the FDCPA's one-year limitations period bars any claim based on conduct before April 3, 2025.

He wrote that once a foreclosure judgment is entered, the mortgage merges into the judgment and there is no servicer for RESPA purposes. In their opposition brief, the plaintiffs cited Caban v. Caban, 259 A.3d 527, to argue that void judgments are legal nullities. Carlson said that citation points to a criminal case, Commonwealth v. Sanders, that does not address civil judgments, and he could find no Pennsylvania case by that name on the point.

He wrote that the plaintiffs' briefs persisted in citing cases and quotations that do not exist, despite having been admonished. He also noted that Rule 11 applies to unrepresented parties, citing a 2025 Middle District of Pennsylvania decision, Kholod v. Nationstar Mortgage. Carlson concluded the conduct warrants the imposition of sanctions, but his recommendation does not specify a penalty. Attorneys Manny Newburger and Brit Suttell of Barron & Newburger, P.C. noted in a legal alert that pro se litigants are more likely than attorneys to abuse the legal system with generative AI.

According to Damien Charlotin's AI Hallucination Cases database, courts worldwide had documented nearly 2,000 cases of AI-fabricated content in filings as of late August 2026, including more than 1,300 in the U.S. The reasoning gives collection agencies and their counsel a roadmap for the kind of serial, AI-assisted filings they increasingly see. Earlier ACA-tracked rulings include Harris v. Pinnacle Bank in Mississippi and Owens v. Select Portfolio Servicing in New York.

Separately, a federal judge in Mississippi, U.S. District Judge Sharion Aycock, issued sanctions on June 8, 2026, in a contract dispute between Louisiana attorney Tom Withers III and the City of Aberdeen. She removed all four attorneys from the case, imposed $8,000 in fines, and barred two lawyers from appearing in the Northern District of Mississippi for two years. Kathleen Wilson, who used the AI program First Drafts, told the judge she had used the software for about six months and was unaware AI could invent authorities. Aycock called that explanation "insufficient and incredulous," and she extended the proceedings' suspension for 60 days, with the parties given until August 7 to secure new representation.

stories.Headline: See what AI looks like in production at Microsoft Ignite
stories.Summary:
I can't write this to the spec as stated, because the articles don't contain enough facts for thirty sentences of 20 to 30 words each, and the request also asks for six paragraphs of five sentences that conflicts with the later note about four to five sentences per paragraph. The supplied material is also mostly navigation text, a newsletter signup form, and article listings, with only one substantive story. Here is a version using only the facts the articles give, in five paragraphs of five sentences each. Armanino, an accounting, consulting, and technology firm headquartered in San Ramon, California, built an AI App Factory on Microsoft Foundry, using GitHub Copilot to standardize and accelerate application delivery. The firm set out to grow its business by meeting rising customer demand for AI solutions.

It needed to scale innovation faster without proportionally increasing resources, and to deliver enterprise-grade AI capabilities to mid-market customers. The factory provides a highly secure, reusable foundation that gives teams a way to build and deploy AI solutions faster. The story is presented as a Microsoft customer story published on November 11, 2026. Armanino cut production time for new AI applications by 89 percent and reduced version revision cycles by 90 percent. Its consultants now turn a two-hour client session into finished requirements in 30 minutes.

The firm can now build solutions it once found too costly to attempt. The company says the gains come from reengineering its delivery workflows to be AI-native rather than only adopting AI tools. The article identifies this as the basis for the reduction in production time per new application. Carmel Wynkoop, Partner, Artificial Intelligence Solutions at Armanino, said the firm recognized early that meeting the opportunity required deep reengineering of delivery workflows. Drew Armanino, Lead, Artificial Intelligence Solutions at Armanino, said the firm's core developer team is small while its business is large.

He said the ambition to reengineer workflows across the entire firm meant a small team had to produce strong output. He described that constraint as the catalyst for the effort. The article says mid-market companies are asking service providers for AI that can reach production rather than remaining pilots. It states that in professional services, shipping a scalable solution is harder than proving a model can do the work. It says a prototype can take days to create, while a governed, audited application for a regulated client can take months.

The article notes this lag is a common reason AI programs fail to move from pilot to production. The article describes two technical challenges that stood between Armanino's ambition and delivery. The first was extensibility, since a talent acquisition tool, a technical accounting memo drafter, and a client intelligence engine each have different user workflows and domain logic. The second challenge is not described in the portion of the article provided. The articles supplied do not state a timeline beyond the published date, nor do they give further details of the second challenge or the firm's outcomes beyond those listed.

stories.Headline: Japan explores options as it moves to put penalties behind AI law
stories.Summary:
Japan's government is considering penalties for artificial intelligence businesses that refuse to cooperate with authorities or fail to ensure safety, according to a source familiar with the matter who spoke on Wednesday, November 11, 2026. The proposal was presented at a closed-door working group meeting on AI-related legal systems in Tokyo. It comes amid growing concern that advanced AI models may behave unpredictably and after several high-profile data leaks and unauthorized access incidents suspected to involve misuse of AI. The government is weighing a system in which it could issue legally binding orders to businesses that do not cooperate after an AI-related incident. Noncompliance would be punishable, with penalties expected to apply only to incidents involving advanced AI.

Under the approach being considered, the government would examine which types of firms should be covered, since AI businesses range from research firms to developers of foundation models and service providers to end users. The working group aims to present an overall outline of its review of the law, including possible revisions, by the end of 2026. Japan's AI law, enacted in May 2025, lets the government investigate businesses and issue guidance when malicious conduct occurs. However, that law contains no penalty provisions, and its measures are nonbinding. The planned reform is aimed largely at U.S. frontier developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI, whose advanced systems Japan uses but cannot currently compel to share information.

Japan's AI Promotion Act took full effect in September 2025 and states that when AI misuse harms someone's rights, the government can investigate and give guidance. A group within the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, led by former digital minister Masaaki Taira, warned in a draft proposal that Japan may be unable to obtain information that other governments can get from AI companies. The draft noted that the European Union already fines AI companies that refuse to hand over information. A private working group has confirmed that the government wants AI companies to take on safety duties and is considering penalties for the risk of advanced AI going out of control or being used in cyberattacks. Officials also want the power to act against companies that refuse to help after something goes wrong.

Some participants have suggested that Japan proceed with caution, because other countries are not all considering tighter AI rules. South Korea's AI Basic Act took effect in January 2026 and allows regulators to fine companies up to 30 million won, about $21,000, for refusing inspections or ignoring corrective orders. Analysts note that such a fine would be negligible for a large U.S. AI company and unlikely to change its behavior. Japan's first AI law was passed without penalties as part of an effort to make the country the "most AI-friendly country," so that cautious firms would not be discouraged from using AI. That law was meant to work through social pressure and voluntary compliance, and analysts assumed that a company seeking access to Japan's market would have to follow local rules.

The digital minister, Toshiharu Furukawa, told an expert panel reviewing the AI Promotion Act on October 26 that Japan needs closer work with partner countries on AI safety. A group of academics held its first meeting two days later, and the panel hopes to settle on a direction by the end of the year. It remains unclear whether the penalties will survive this process and how large any fines would be. Japan's Financial Services Agency set up a 36-member group in May 2026 to study cyber threats linked to Anthropic's Mythos model, with the Japanese branches of Anthropic and OpenAI taking part. The outcome by year-end will determine whether Japan adopts any fines at all.

stories.Headline: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
stories.Summary:
Researcher Will DePue published a report on November 12, 2026, saying six AI models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group carry a hardware fingerprint matching NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs. The models include DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1-Pro, MiniMax-M3 and Ant Group's Ling-3.1-flash. The report says the models were released between April and October 2026. Blackwell chips are restricted from export to China under U.S. rules, and the report says no export license has been reported for them.

The fingerprint is read from the published weights, the adjustable numbers that determine how a model works. The report describes how those starting values depend on a random seed and on the number of processing units, called streaming multiprocessors, on a chip. The B200 and B300 have 148 of these units, while the GB200 and GB300 have 152. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match the B200 or B300, and the other four match the GB200 or GB300. The report says the method was checked against 24 models whose developers had publicly disclosed their hardware, and it agreed in every case.

DePue says the six models were likely trained on Blackwell hardware, and he estimates roughly 12,000 GPUs were used across the five largest training runs. He writes that the cost of those GPUs would be more than half a billion dollars, based on a price of about $70,000 per chip. He says the estimate rests on assumptions the weights cannot confirm, including how efficiently each lab used its GPUs. The report says the fingerprint establishes how the starting weights were created, and that training on Blackwell is a supported inference rather than a proven fact. It adds that the figures cover only final training runs, not experiments or serving.

The report states that it cannot establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. It notes that Blackwell systems can be rented from data centers outside China. A companion article from Startup Fortune reports that DePue posted on X that he had "conclusive forensic evidence," and that no lab has responded to the findings. Earlier, U.S. officials and press reports had alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI used Blackwell chips, but without publishing technical evidence.

Several other Chinese labs appear to have stayed on NVIDIA's older Hopper generation. The report says the newest models examined from Alibaba, Zhipu, Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan said its LongCat-2.0 was trained on "AI ASIC superpods," and the report found no NVIDIA fingerprint in that model's weights. The report notes that NVIDIA's own Nemotron-3 Ultra reads as 152 streaming multiprocessors, matching Kimi K3.

Chinese labs began training on Blackwell relatively recently, according to the report. DeepSeek's models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3, released in December 2024, and as Blackwell from V4, released in April 2026. Moonshot's models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 in January 2026 and as Blackwell from K3 in July 2026, while MiniMax's shift came with M3 in June 2026. The report says Ant Group's Ling-3.0-flash in August 2026 read as Hopper, and its Ling-3.1-flash in October 2026 read as Blackwell.

The report leaves several questions open, including where the chips were located and how the labs obtained them. It also does not establish whether export controls were violated. The article from Startup Fortune notes that the claim has not been verified by outside reviewers, and the report names no outside reviewer. The findings are DePue's own, and the article says the report does not mention Singapore or Megaspeed. Whether the labs or U.S. regulators will respond to the report is not stated in the articles.

stories.Headline: OpenAI faces civil racketeering charges over $30bn data center planned in Effingham County, Georgia
stories.Summary:
The civil racketeering lawsuit over OpenAI's planned Project Camellia data center in Effingham County, Georgia was filed by residents against the company, two of its affiliates and several county officials. The complaint alleges that the defendants kept residents in the dark about the project. It is the third lawsuit related to Project Camellia filed since the 3.2 GW campus was announced in July. Among the allegations are civil conspiracy, improper zoning procedures, and civil racketeering involving false statements, perjury, and forgery. The complaint does not detail specific statements that might constitute racketeering.

The project is a $30 billion data center campus planned on a 1,440-acre parcel at the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub near Rincon. It would have four data center buildings with a total footprint of 4.4 million square feet, or 408,775 square meters. Construction could start in 2028 if final permission is granted. A Supervisors' board decision that had been due on November 4 has been shifted to November 19. Tom's Hardware reports the site is expected to cost between $20 billion and $30 billion, built across five phases.

The lawsuit was filed by the law firm Savage Turner Pinkney Savage Sprouse & Gilluly on behalf of three Effingham County residents, identified as Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr. and Raymond Carver. The named defendants include county commissioners Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly and Phil Kieffer, County Manager Tim Callanan, and Industrial Development Authority CEO Brandt Herndon. Also named are the Industrial Development Authority, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, which operates the data center for OpenAI, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC. OpenAI was contacted for comment, and the articles do not report a response.

The plaintiffs say offers to buy nearby properties have been reduced or withdrawn, and that the project has affected their property values, so they seek civil damages. The complaint alleges the defendants used non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements to keep residents unaware of the project's nature for as long as possible. Residents say the county tried to secure land, tax incentives and zoning approvals without informing them until key decisions were final and contracts signed. The plaintiffs describe the actions as affecting residents of Effingham County, whose property values they say have declined.

OpenAI has promised that the project will not raise the community's utility costs, since it will pay for all required infrastructure upgrades, and that it will use minimal water through a closed-loop system. The Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act was originally conceived to counter organized crime, but Georgia's version is less stringent than the federal one. Georgia's RICO statute was used in the 2023 election case against Donald Trump and 18 others over the 2020 presidential election results in the state, and in Young Thug's trial. Georgia State University professor Volkan Topalli, quoted in Atlanta Magazine, said critics consider the state version too encompassing. Developers say they use NDAs to avoid running afoul of insider trading rules, though West Feliciana Parish in Louisiana closed a data center deal without one.

Two other lawsuits related to the project were filed earlier this year, one over zoning and another over the Effingham County Industrial Development Authority's role in advancing the development. None of the three cases has yet reached court. The articles do not say whether the November 19 board decision will proceed as scheduled or how the courts will rule on the claims. They also do not report whether OpenAI or the county has responded to the allegations in court.

stories.Headline: Exploring How Autistic Individuals Interact With Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Stony Brook University and the University of Cincinnati studied how autistic people use ChatGPT, and published their findings in the ACM Interactive Health Conference. The article was posted by news.stonybrook.edu on November 11, 2026. The lead author, Renkai Ma, is an assistant professor at the University of Cincinnati's School of Information Technology. Coauthor Ben Zhang is an assistant professor in the Department of Technology, AI and Society at Stony Brook University. The study builds on earlier research the team published in the proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026.

The research team gathered 3,984 posts from Reddit, X, and Tumblr published between January 2023 and September 2025. The analysis focused on firsthand accounts from individuals who identified as autistic and discussed their experiences with ChatGPT. The article describes four ways autistic users benefited from the chatbot, including communication, planning and emotional support. Some users also said it helped them find words to describe what it feels like to be autistic. The article states that these benefits are inextricably linked to risks, which the researchers examined alongside them.

Ma said that autistic users turned to ChatGPT in moments of acute distress, and that large language models can provide perceived patience and understanding. Ma also said these models risk making users too reliant on that assistance. Zhang said some autistic users use the chatbot to get unstuck on tasks, manage overwhelm and translate between autistic and neurotypical communication. The researchers recommend separating emotional validation from factual verification, so a chatbot can acknowledge distress while checking the facts behind a fear. The article quotes both researchers on these points.

Autistic users described the chatbot as a bi-directional translator between neurodivergent and neurotypical people, helping them adapt messages and interpret replies. Some users felt this rewriting amounted to automated masking, because their messages sounded less like them. Users also relied on ChatGPT to offload executive tasks such as planning, organizing and getting started, which helped them begin tasks. The researchers caution that repeated outsourcing could create over-reliance and make starting tasks harder without the chatbot. Ma said autistic individuals felt the people reading their messages were connecting with ChatGPT rather than with them.

The article proposes what the authors call beneficial frictions, such as a chatbot asking users to set their priorities before it suggests a plan. The researchers also proposed tools to help neurotypical readers interpret direct messages from autistic colleagues. The article says these ideas will direct the team's future research. It does not say what those studies will examine or when they will begin. The article also does not detail how many users in the study were affected in each way, or whether any of the proposed tools have been built or tested.

Articles.Title: Exploring How Autistic Individuals Interact With Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Stony Brook FinTech Workshop Explores AI’s Impact on Finance, Announces New Industry Partnership
stories.Summary:
Stony Brook University held its FinTech Workshop on November 6 in the New Computer Science Building, where researchers and industry leaders discussed how artificial intelligence is changing financial analysis, software development and investment decisions. The event was organized by Karina Torres Castro, manager of research and innovation and assistant research professor in mechanical engineering, and it included the announcement of a new AI Innovation Lab in partnership with the financial technology company Broadridge. Students and faculty will work alongside industry experts in the lab to tackle challenges in AI and finance. The workshop included academic research presentations, industry perspectives and a panel discussion, and it was sponsored by the College of Engineering and Applied Sciences, the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, the Center of Excellence in Wireless and Information Technology and the AI Innovation Institute.

Amy Erickson, executive director of the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, said AI-driven financial modeling can help small and mid-sized manufacturers reduce waste and make better investment decisions without replacing skilled workers. She described the workshop as the first of several AI-focused programs her organization is rolling out for regional manufacturers. Andrew C. Singer, dean of the college, welcomed participants and introduced keynote speaker Robert J. Frey, research professor and founder of the university's Quantitative Finance Program. Frey, who has held leadership roles at Renaissance Technologies and other financial firms, compared the rise of AI with earlier technological advances that disrupted industries, saying some adjustments can be painful in the short term. He argued that stagnation is not the answer.

At Broadridge, AI is taking on more complex software development tasks, including some once assigned to entry-level employees. Roger Burkhardt, the company's chief technology officer of capital markets and AI, said the career ladder is changing and that new employees may be expected to define problems, evaluate AI-generated code and recognize security vulnerabilities. He encouraged students to experiment with AI development tools while learning to assess their output, and he said critical thinking and communicating with users are lasting skills. Jill Scher, managing director at CBIZ Advisors, began her accounting career in 1994 working with paper ledgers and red pencils, and she now uses AI to analyze financial statements and prepare for client meetings. Frey said that when AI is used properly, students will see it as a force multiplier that increases productivity rather than replacing them.

Pawel Polak, a faculty member in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, presented research on an international competition that attracted more than 1,000 registered participants to develop AI agents capable of writing code, forecasting financial trends and simulating markets. Some agents significantly improved the speed of existing software, but others struggled with unfamiliar problems. Teams that incorporated financial knowledge and agents required to explain their predictions generally performed better on new tasks, and Polak said human involvement definitely helps. Lav Varshney, professor of electrical and computer engineering and inaugural director of the AI Innovation Institute, argued that opaque "black box" AI may be less helpful because its inner workings are unknown. He described research using explicit, verifiable rules, with one possible application being financial transactions that fail to settle as expected, a context where traceability matters in regulated industries.

The afternoon panel, moderated by Yvette Wohn, inaugural chair of the Department of Technology, AI and Society, included Polak, Burkhardt, Scher and Melissa Brown, managing director of investment decision research at SimCorp. Brown said her team helps investors understand how unexpected economic developments might affect their portfolios, and she described an exercise considering what could happen if the Federal Reserve lost its independence. She said that work once took hours of searching historical data but now can be done by asking AI to identify similar past circumstances, which "takes five minutes rather than a day." Scher said some clients arrive with AI-generated tax analyses and ask her to confirm them, even when those analyses may overlook changing regulations or individual circumstances. Samir Das, chair of the Department of Computer Science, closed the workshop by announcing the AI Innovation Lab, which he said will focus on experiential learning and on how universities and industry can work together.

stories.Headline: Ulster County Bans Government Use of AI Surveillance
stories.Summary:
Ulster County Executive Jen Metzger issued an executive order on October 22 banning the use of Flock cameras and other AI-assisted video surveillance technologies in county government. The order, titled "Prohibiting the Use of Flock Cameras and other AI-Assisted Video Surveillance Technologies" and designated Executive Order No. 5, took effect immediately upon its announcement. It bars any department or employee under the county executive's office from buying or deploying such systems, from helping to develop them, and from aiding private individuals or corporations in implementing them. Flock systems, made by Flock Safety, include security cameras, license plate readers and data-sharing networks, many of which use generative AI and machine learning to identify people, track them and build databases.

The ban covers buildings and property under the county executive's authority, including the Ulster County Courthouse, the Sheriff's Office, UCAT public transit facilities, county public works departments and public recreational areas such as rail trails. It does not reach facilities controlled by towns and villages, such as the New Paltz Town Hall, the New Paltz Courthouse or the New Paltz Police Headquarters, and it does not apply to private individuals or businesses. In her order, Metzger argued that protecting public safety and individual rights go hand in hand in a democracy and that the rapid, unregulated growth of the AI sector threatens that balance. She wrote that tech companies dominate AI development without independent oversight, that multiple security breaches have occurred in these companies' systems, and that collected information could be shared outside county government without authorization.

New Paltz Town Supervisor Tim Rogers said he agrees with Metzger's assessment that unregulated AI in security matters can weaken public safety and democratic principles, and he warned that civil liberties could be trampled if for-profit companies are left to operate without limits. He also said the town has no current plan to adopt Flock technology, citing its high cost, and that to his knowledge the New Paltz Police Department does not use it. Rogers acknowledged that surveillance can deliver local benefits, arguing that cameras like those Lowe's operates on Route 299 help deter shoplifting and theft. The New Paltz Oracle reports that the town has three AI surveillance systems in and around its territory, two of them Flock cameras owned by Lowe's facing its parking lot, and that the owner of the third remains undisclosed. Rogers said Lowe's is not required to register these cameras with the town and that no site plan or building review involves Flock cameras, so private companies remain outside local regulation, just as they do at the county level.

Articles.Title: Ulster County Bans Government Use of AI Surveillance - The New Paltz Oracle

stories.Headline: SMX Brings American Innovation to the Next Frontier of Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
SMX (Security Matters) PLC announced on November 12, 2026 a new artificial intelligence platform called SMX Scientific Intelligence, or SMX SCI, in a release issued from New York City. The company is developing the platform to help industries solve complex material challenges and create new technological opportunities. Unlike general-purpose AI tools, SMX SCI is being designed for industrial material development, chemical compatibility, manufacturing and material verification. The announcement frames the initiative as an application of American entrepreneurial tradition, in which technology is valued when it solves practical problems. The company described the project in its release as a platform meant to move AI beyond theory into real industrial use.

The platform aims to build a comprehensive scientific codex covering chemical agents, additives, molecular markers and supplementary materials. It combines AI-powered analysis with SMX's accumulated scientific knowledge to evaluate chemical properties, production requirements, manufacturing conditions and potential industrial applications. SMX expects to introduce the platform into its internal operations during the first quarter of 2027, with full operations anticipated during the second quarter of 2027. The company also plans a limited commercial edition in the second quarter of 2027, making selected capabilities available to customers worldwide. The planned service would support material identification, additive selection, product enhancement and preliminary regulatory and compatibility assessments, with the United States and other major international markets named as relevant requirements.

SMX is the company responsible for the platform, and its release presents SMX SCI as an extension of the company's existing business. The company's molecular marking technology gives physical materials persistent identification, while its Digital Material Passport infrastructure records composition, quality, origin and lifecycle history. The release states that final material suitability and compliance decisions will continue to require appropriate testing, validation and regulatory review. SMX describes the platform as being developed by its internal team in collaboration with specialized subcontractors. The company's stated aim is to connect scientific research with real-world manufacturing, distribution, recovery and recycling.

The release says manufacturers could gain faster assessments of material suitability, more efficient product development and shorter response times when technical challenges arise. It says the infrastructure could have potential applications across plastics, packaging, precious metals, electronics, semiconductors and other industries important to modern supply chains. The release does not name specific customers or other parties who have commented on the platform. It also does not identify any group that would be harmed by the platform, and it contains no outside assessments of its performance.

The release describes SMX as a company that provides molecular marking, tracking, measurement and digital platform technologies designed for material authentication, supply chain transparency and circular economy applications. It also says SMX is working toward trusted global standards for certified and graded recycled plastics. The company has said that SMX SCI could support AI-enabled capabilities tied to its planned Plastic Circularity Credits. The release also notes that SMX's shares trade on NASDAQ under the ticker SMX. The articles do not provide further history of the platform's development.

The release states that the platform's capabilities and commercial potential depend on successful testing, validation and adoption. It does not say whether the internal rollout will meet its first-quarter 2027 target, or whether the limited commercial edition will reach customers on schedule. The articles also leave open the pricing of the service, the identity of its customers and the outcome of the planned Plastic Circularity Credits. The standards and commercial mechanisms tied to recycled plastics are described as still under development. No independent confirmation of the platform's effectiveness appears in the articles.

stories.Headline: Rajnath Singh calls for stronger defensive capabilities to maintain 'element of surprise' in future warfare; launches UDAAN-developed AI applications
stories.Summary:
The Indian Air Force has introduced a set of homegrown artificial intelligence applications to automate tasks across operations, administration and aerospace safety. The launch was announced by defence minister Rajnath Singh at the Air Force Commanders' Conference in New Delhi on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The applications were developed in-house by the IAF's AI Centre of Excellence under the Unit for Digitisation, Automation, Artificial Intelligence and Application Networking, known as UDAAN. They are deployed on the Air Force's secure network and are aimed at expediting tasks in three areas: military operations, administrative functions and aerospace safety. The initiative is part of the IAF's wider effort to integrate artificial intelligence into its functioning and improve efficiency through technology-driven solutions.

At the conference, Singh called on the armed forces to strengthen both offensive and defensive capabilities to maintain the element of surprise against conventional and emerging threats. He said forces must develop capabilities and methods that leave an adversary no time to react or recover. He also said India must never be caught off guard by an unexpected enemy move. Singh called for stronger intelligence and surveillance mechanisms, better integration among military systems and early identification of potential threats. He said operational preparedness must be enhanced so that personnel remain alert, agile and ready to respond to emerging challenges.

Singh, the defence minister, made these remarks and announced the launch of the applications. According to an official ministry of defence release, the applications were built by the IAF itself rather than sourced from outside. Singh told IAF commanders to prepare for emerging threats and pointed to the growing importance of drones and air defence systems. He said future victories would depend on more than the number of aircraft deployed. The release, as cited in the articles, describes the applications as indigenous and developed in-house, and it names the AI Centre of Excellence as the developer.

The articles say the applications are intended to benefit the Air Force's operations, administration and aerospace safety work. They state that the military's personnel must remain alert and equipped to respond to emerging challenges. The articles do not describe any specific group of people outside the armed forces who are affected by the launch. The conference was attended by IAF commanders, to whom Singh directed his call for preparedness.

Singh said warfare was increasingly extending beyond traditional battlefields, with missiles, drones and advanced weapon systems playing a significant role. He referred to the Russia-Ukraine and Israel-Hamas conflicts as examples of this shift. He called for dedicated doctrines and architectures for emerging domains of warfare, including electronic, cyber and space. The articles note that the IAF's move to integrate artificial intelligence is presented as a step toward improving efficiency. They do not give further history of the IAF's AI programme beyond this initiative.

It remains unclear from the articles how the applications will be rolled out across units or what specific capabilities they will provide in practice. The articles do not say when the doctrines Singh called for will be written or what form they will take. They also do not give the cost of the applications or details of any further funding. The articles provide no timeline for the stronger intelligence and surveillance mechanisms Singh requested.

stories.Headline: Global powers head to Asia with trade, AI, security in focus
stories.Summary:
Global leaders are heading to Asia for a series of high-stakes meetings covering AI, trade and possibly nuclear disarmament. The 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations opens its final leaders' summit of the year on Sunday in Manila. French President Emmanuel Macron attends a Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh. The annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference then moves to Shenzhen, with Russian President Vladimir Putin expected to be a key figure there. US President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will travel to both the ASEAN and APEC meetings.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will attend the ASEAN meeting. A proposed sit-down between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Trump and Putin may take place at APEC, though its agenda remains unclear. A pause in the China-US trade war was extended through January 10 during Xi's September visit to the White House. Analysts told AFP that Trump's recent midterm election defeat will not change how the region sees him.

Siew Mun Tang, a former head of the ASEAN Studies Centre at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, said Trump has two more years in office. Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution said the symbolism of the talks will account for much of their substance. Artificial intelligence will be a major topic at APEC, after Xi and Trump agreed in September to set up a communication channel for AI incidents. Xi said in September that Washington and Beijing have a responsibility to keep AI under human control.

Meanwhile, a spying scandal involving Nvidia boss Jensen Huang threatens to overshadow AI discussions, with US officials accusing him of a relationship with a woman they claim worked for Beijing. The Philippines' year as ASEAN chair looks set to end without a South China Sea Code of Conduct with China, according to one Southeast Asian diplomat involved in summit preparations. Philippine and Chinese sailors clashed a day before a July summit, and a diplomatic row erupted at an October defence meeting. Tang said the code may have lost its purpose because conditions on the ground have changed, citing the militarisation of islands by China and Vietnam.

Trade will feature at both summits, but advancing regional free-trade frameworks remains complicated by China-US tensions and Trump's tariff war. Oxford Economics economist Harry Murphy Cruise warned that reversing existing US tariff mechanisms would require legislation the president could veto. Separately, a deepfake network of more than 3,000 videos, identified by McGill University researchers, drew about 20 million views in three months. stories.Headline: Warby Parker bets on Google AI glasses for growth, but privacy fears still loom
stories.Summary:
Warby Parker is entering the smart glasses market in partnership with Google and Samsung, betting that demand for artificial intelligence wearables will balloon in the coming years. The New York-based fashion brand, known for affordable eyewear, is also seeking to head off privacy concerns that have weighed on existing producers of the glasses. Warby Parker shoppers will start placing pre-orders on Thursday, November 12, 2026. The Warby Parker glasses are broadly similar to Meta smart glasses already available from Ray-Ban and Oakley maker EssilorLuxottica, which have faced regulatory scrutiny from Norway to Australia. Like the Meta glasses, they will connect to an AI assistant, in this case Google's Gemini, for tasks such as directions and language translation.

The main difference from existing versions on the market is the privacy framework built into the glasses from the outset, according to Warby Parker Co-CEO Neil Blumenthal. Google will not use visuals captured with the glasses to train its AI, and the glasses will bar facial recognition of bystanders. A small white notification light on the front turns on automatically when a user starts recording video. Google says it will embed privacy guardrails to prevent tampering with that light, redact people's faces from video footage before it is sent to Gemini, and ban targeted advertising on the glasses. Shares of Warby Parker have rallied nearly 40% this year, compared with a 10% gain in the S&P 500.

Warby Parker's Co-CEO Neil Blumenthal said that as long as the tools provide utility to customers, the company will be successful. Juston Payne, who leads extended reality products at Google, acknowledged that public skepticism could be a risk to growth and said trust was lost in this area. Payne said Google is trying to raise the bar and change the conversation about the technology. Meta's spokesperson said input from safety experts helped inform the privacy features on its own glasses, which also include a camera notification light. Google and Warby Parker did not say how the privacy measures would be enforced beyond the listed guardrails.

Ray-Ban's Meta glasses still dominate the market, representing 81.3% of AI glasses shipments in the first half of 2026, according to tech research group Omdia. Global AI glasses shipments more than doubled in the first half of 2026 from a year earlier, though growth has slowed since the second half of last year. Luxury group Kering is also poised to release glasses in partnership with Google. One of Britain's biggest pub chains has restricted the use of the frames, Norway's government is planning a temporary ban on AI glasses in certain locations, and Australia is considering barring camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces. Calli Schroeder, who leads the AI and human rights program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said she was happy footage is not automatically fed into AI training.

Schroeder said that still leaves open the concern that a stranger may have footage of a child on their phone, which is concerning however it is phrased. Analysts at TD Cowen wrote in a research note that smart glasses are poised to be an increasingly important driver of Warby Parker's growth outlook. Warby Parker executives said on an earnings call earlier this month that the new wearable technology would add several percentage points to fourth-quarter revenue growth. Google said it wants to rebuild trust, while the articles do not say whether the guardrails will ease concern about widespread surveillance if the glasses become ubiquitous. The articles also do not say how far Warby Parker's glasses will sell or whether the regulatory moves in Norway and Australia will extend further.

stories.Headline: Kazakhstan-linked hackers used AI to steal Tajik government documents, researchers say
stories.Summary:
A hacking group linked to Kazakhstan used an artificial intelligence agent to steal more than 2,000 national security-related documents from Tajikistan, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Singapore-based cybersecurity company CloudSEK. The firm said it found the operation after the attackers accidentally left a server exposed to the internet. The group, which researchers call Silent Lynx, relied on Hermes, an open-source framework for autonomous AI agents, and the data CloudSEK recovered shows the hackers began reconnaissance around mid-August before breaking into Tajikistan's electronic document system a couple of weeks later. The server also held more than a dozen gigabytes of material, including stolen government files, hacking tools and records of how the agent was used.

According to CloudSEK, the hackers configured the agent to act as an offensive security expert, and it handled reconnaissance, data collection and the erasing of traces from compromised systems. The agent was also set up to run certain potentially destructive commands without additional approval, and the operator issued instructions in Russian through a Telegram bot, which let them direct it from a phone. The AI models behind the system were mainly developed by the Chinese company DeepSeek. Once inside Tajikistan's systems, the group used the credentials of a single railway employee to log into the national platform that ministries use to exchange official correspondence, then built tools to download large volumes of files, including thousands sent to or processed by the Defense Ministry in 2026. The stolen material also reportedly touched the National Guard, the State Committee for National Security and the State Investment Committee, and information about more than 100 government organizations.

CloudSEK said it assessed with medium confidence that Silent Lynx has ties to Kazakhstan, pointing to Russian-language communications and test connections from a residential internet provider in the country. The company's findings align with earlier assessments that the group is probably based there, though they do not establish any link to the Kazakh government, and Kazakh and Tajik officials did not respond to requests for comment. The researchers also found evidence of a compromised server supporting Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative and malicious files posing as official Turkmenistan documents that were created in October, which suggests another phishing campaign was being prepared. Silent Lynx, also known as Cavalry Werewolf and YoroTrooper, has been active since at least 2022 and has previously targeted government and diplomatic bodies across Central Asia, Russia and Europe. Efforts to reach the group were unsuccessful, and the researchers did not determine whether the Turkmenistan attacks succeeded.

stories.Headline: Norway, Britain agree to deepen AI cooperation
stories.Summary:
Norway and Britain signed a letter of intent in Oslo on Thursday, 12 November 2026, to deepen cooperation on artificial intelligence. The agreement opens the way for joint work on computing infrastructure, model safety testing and international oversight of advanced AI systems. Norwegian Minister for Digitalisation and Public Governance Torgeir Micaelsen and British Minister for Artificial Intelligence Kanishka Narayan announced the cooperation in a joint statement. They made the announcement on the sidelines of the Atlantic Futures Forum, held aboard the British aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales, which was making a port call in Oslo. The statement was published by the UK government on the same day.

The statement commits both sides to explore several areas of collaboration. They plan to speed up cooperation on compute infrastructure and hardware integration, including possibilities for semiconductors and novel AI hardware from either country. Britain's Taskforce RAID and Norway's Defence Centre for Data and AI would work more closely on AI-enabled defence capabilities. AI Norway, a national hub within the Norwegian Digitalisation Agency, would share best practices on AI security, testing and evaluation with Britain's AI Security Institute, including on cybersecurity through the NCSC and NSM. The ministers also agreed to coordinate on international AI governance, research and innovation policy, and the convergence of AI with quantum technologies, biotechnology and robotics.

Both ministers are responsible for the statement, which the two governments describe as a new area of bilateral cooperation. The UK Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade and the Norwegian Ministry of Digitalisation and Public Governance will coordinate the work. Narayan and Micaelsen agreed to remain in regular contact with the relevant ministries and authorities in both countries. The ministers recognised the complementary strengths of the two countries in AI, research, secure digital infrastructure and clean energy. They described the partnership as one that could support their respective industrial policy ambitions.

The statement recalls the Joint Declaration on the Norwegian-UK Strategic Partnership, agreed by Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer on 16 December 2024. The ministers said the relationship is rooted in shared democratic values and a commitment to open, secure and resilient societies. They recognised the potential of artificial intelligence to improve lives, support economic growth, scientific discovery and public services. They also stressed the importance of understanding and addressing safety and security risks from increasingly capable AI systems. The statement complements existing cooperation under the Green Industrial Partnership, the Lunna House Agreement and the UK-Norway Security Dialogue.

The statement is nonbinding and expresses intentions only, creating no rights or obligations under international or domestic law. Cooperation will be subject to each country's laws, policies and available resources. Norway's government said the two sides aim to follow it with a memorandum of understanding to specify future cooperation. The articles do not give a timetable for that memorandum. They also do not say what specific projects, funding or commitments will follow from the statement, or how the proposed work will be measured.

stories.Headline: AI spending helps lift UK growth to fastest since early 2024
stories.Summary:
Britain's economy grew 0.7% in the July-to-September quarter of 2026, its fastest quarterly expansion in two-and-a-half years, helped by investment in artificial intelligence. The Office for National Statistics announced the figure on Thursday, and the growth extended a strong first half of the year. Growth had been expected to slow after the Iran war began, so the result defied those predictions. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the quarterly rate, but output in September alone rose 0.2%, beating expectations of no change for the month. Annual growth picked up to 1.9% in the third quarter, the strongest reading since the fourth quarter of 2024.

Monthly GDP has now beaten consensus forecasts for the fifth month in a row and seven times in the last eight months. Rob Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said these figures strengthened the chances of another Bank of England rate hike next month. Growth over the three months to September was the fastest since May, on a rolling basis. Growth so far this year has been the strongest since 2017, excluding the post-pandemic rebound. British growth in the third quarter was the second-fastest among the Group of Seven advanced economies, behind only the United States.

The Office for National Statistics said there was widespread strength in industries that may be related to artificial intelligence. Computer programming, consultancy and related activity made the largest single contribution to growth in the third quarter. Computer manufacturing made the biggest contribution to industrial production, which rose 4.6% in the three months to September. The economy had expanded by 0.6% in the first quarter of 2026, showing resilience in the first half of the year. Business investment, however, grew just 0.4% on the quarter, half of what economists expected, and was the weakest growth since the start of the year.

Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JP Morgan Personal Investing, said the UK economy has been relatively resilient since the conflict started, but that strength will be tested in the months ahead. He said nervousness before the autumn budget and continued uncertainty from the Middle East war are expected to weigh on confidence and activity in coming GDP readings. The Bank of England last week raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.6%, against the 1.2% forecast by the government's Office for Budget Responsibility after finance minister John Healey's October 28 budget. The central bank attributed some of the strength to spending on AI and a small, temporary boost from Healey's fiscal plan. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey welcomed the data.

The data is likely to increase pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates again. The central bank warned last week that inflation will near 5% in 2027, and investors see a 73% chance of a back-to-back hike in December after November's increase. Wood said that with growth and inflation both strong, he expects at least two more hikes from the Monetary Policy Committee, and that today's figures make a December hike more likely. Household gas and electricity bills are still set to rise by about 25% when the energy price cap changes in January. Britain's government has offered limited support to help families absorb the energy price shock.

Some economists expect slower growth in the final quarter of the year as higher energy prices and borrowing costs weigh on activity. There have been recent signs of weakening consumer and business demand, with retail sales volumes falling in September. Consumer confidence also suffered its sharpest month-on-month fall since April 2020 before the budget. The articles do not say how large the fourth-quarter slowdown will be or whether the Bank of England will raise rates in December. They also do not give the outcome of the autumn budget, which Gardner described as a source of nervousness for confidence and activity.

stories.Headline: Databricks Launches New Always-on Genie: Autonomous AI for Complex Enterprise Work
stories.Summary:
Databricks announced on November 11, 2026, the second generation of Genie, which it describes as an always-on, autonomous agent for enterprise work. The announcement came from San Francisco and was published by SD Times on the same day. Employees can give Genie a goal and rely on it to keep work moving without constant prompting. Genie takes ownership of tasks, delegates to subagents when needed, tracks progress, and follows up on missing inputs.

The new version runs in autonomous mode in the background using its own compute, and it opens to a priority inbox that shows which items need attention. Genie sends each new alert as its own unread email, with later updates placed in the same thread, and each email links back into the Genie app. Genie Search now indexes content in tools such as Google Drive, Jira, and Confluence without moving or copying it, and Databricks offers more than 100 connectors for key business applications. Every action stays within Unity Catalog permissions and Unity Gateway approval rules and budgets, and is fully auditable.

Databricks says Genie is built to operate within existing company controls and the Databricks environment, not beside them. The company states that enterprise work often spans multiple platforms and exists in people's heads, so an assistant needs business context, system access, and correct permissions to act. Genie Ontology captures a company's definitions, metrics, people, and processes, and it keeps that context current as the business changes. Genie Search, which uses this ontology, lets people and agents search the lakehouse and business-app documents, tickets, and chats through one governed interface with inspectable sources.

Ali Ghodsi, Co-founder and CEO of Databricks, said Genie has made him a 10x more productive CEO and that it no longer waits for him to ask. He said it keeps up with his inbox, prepares him for meetings, and runs in the background, returning only when it needs a decision. Ghodsi credited the product's knowledge of what the company means by revenue, which numbers are official, and who can see what. The articles say the capabilities are aimed at enterprise teams, including marketers monitoring GEO performance, customer success teams tracking usage patterns, and executives tracking revenue trends and customer feature requests.

Other new capabilities include an Ontology Manager that flags frequently asked concepts needing refinement, expanded Genie Ontology sources drawing business logic from external BI tools, and an organizational structure connector for people and reporting relationships. Genie can generate live, governed slides, dashboards, and interactive reports that update as data changes, and it can work across PDFs, contracts, and slides in Unity Catalog Volumes without a separate vector index. Teams can reach Genie through web browsers, mobile apps, email, and tools including ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot Cowork, and Grok Bot. The articles do not give pricing or availability dates for these features.

The articles provide little background beyond the company's own description of the product. Databricks states that work is moving faster and that enterprises now expect AI to take real tasks off their plates. The SD Times article is a newswire item that also carries unrelated stories about Apache Kafka, OpenSilver, SmartBear, and Microsoft's cybersecurity data. The Databricks page presents the release alongside its broader platform offerings, including data engineering, data warehousing, governance, and security products. The articles do not describe customer results beyond Ghodsi's own statements, nor do they report independent evaluations of Genie.

The articles do not say when the new Genie will reach general availability or how it will be priced. They also do not describe the results of any trials, customer deployments, or security reviews beyond the stated governance controls. Databricks says Genie works across all data, structured or unstructured, inside or outside Databricks, but the articles do not detail how well that performs in practice. Whether competitors will offer comparable autonomous agents is not addressed. The articles also leave open how users will balance Genie's autonomous actions against the approval rules and budgets that govern them.

The announcement was reported by The Canadian Press in Edmonton and first published on November 12, 2026. The government says the decision followed a successful pilot program that began last year. That pilot led to almost 12,000 more MRIs being done in the province. The articles give no further detail on the timing of the announcement itself.

The technology is installed directly on MRI machines in hospitals. According to the government, it improves image clarity while also shortening examination times. The government expects the technology to be installed provincewide by 2028. The money is intended to increase the province's testing capacity. Alberta's Hospitals Minister, Adriana LaGrange, is responsible for the program and spoke about it publicly. She said a record number of MRIs were completed in Alberta last year. Patients waiting for MRI scans in Alberta are the group the articles describe as likely to benefit from shorter wait times. The government says the technology does not transmit individual records or information to outside networks. Patients whose scans are processed on the equipped machines are the people whose data the government says will stay protected. The articles do not name any other groups affected by the expansion. Reactions from patients, health professionals or other officials are not reported.

The articles report that a record number of MRIs were completed in Alberta last year. The pilot program that produced the 12,000 additional scans began last year. The articles do not describe earlier MRI capacity problems in the province beyond the reduced wait times that the funding is meant to address. No other history of the technology or the pilot is given in the articles. The reports do not say which hospitals took part in the pilot.

The articles do not say when the funding will be released or how it will be divided among hospitals. They do not give a timeline for installation beyond the expectation of provincewide coverage by 2028. stories.Headline: Naver clinches $1.5 bil. AI computing deal with US firm
stories.Summary:
Naver, the South Korean internet company, has signed a 2 trillion-won ($1.5 billion) computing services supply contract with a U.S. artificial intelligence inference company, its first customer for its AI infrastructure business. The deal was announced on Thursday, November 12, 2026, during the company's third-quarter earnings call, and it comes ahead of a commercial launch planned for the first half of next year. The contract covers computing services using next-generation graphics processing units, with the initial supply scheduled to begin in 2027. Naver's chief executive, Choi Soo-yeon, described the agreement as confirming real market demand and the early commercial viability of the AI factory business. Naver also said it had reported record quarterly revenue alongside weaker operating profit.

The contract covers about 20 megawatts of capacity over four to five years, according to reporting on the deal. Naver plans to expand its AI factory capacity from 55 megawatts next year to 200 megawatts by 2028. The company said its contracted data center capacity already exceeds that 200-megawatt target for 2028. Naver is in talks with more than 10 prospective customers outside Asia, including major AI model developers, for the remaining capacity. Separately, the company plans to set up a dedicated logistics subsidiary and expand its leased fulfillment centers, with investment expected to approach 1 trillion won through 2030.

Choi said the AI factory is being developed in partnership with the Canadian asset manager Brookfield and the U.S. chipmaker Nvidia. Choi said Naver was pursuing long-term contracts with major customers while widening its customer base to include global AI companies with strong growth potential. She said this would reduce reliance on individual clients and help the company seek stable, higher-margin business. Choi also said the company would seek appropriate financing and revenue structures to limit the impact of logistics spending on cash flow and earnings. Naver's chief financial officer, Kim Hee-cheol, spoke about the negotiations with prospective customers.

The company reported third-quarter sales of 3.47 trillion won, up 10.7 percent from a year earlier, marking its sixth consecutive quarterly revenue record. Operating profit fell 20.9 percent to 451.3 billion won, giving an operating margin of 13 percent, as AI-related investment and content spending weighed on earnings. Platform revenue rose 7.3 percent to 1.95 trillion won, while financial platform revenue increased 14.1 percent to 487.7 billion won. Global business revenue climbed 15.9 percent to 1.04 trillion won, driven by consumer-to-consumer businesses including Wallapop and Poshmark. Naver also plans to launch a personal AI agent app by the end of this year that can carry out tasks such as shopping and making reservations.

Naver is also planning robotic delivery services at residential complexes in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in the first half of 2027, combining its digital-twin mapping technology with Naver Labs' Nuri robot. Choi said traffic from the AI Tab to shopping and local services has nearly doubled since its launch, with transaction value also growing. The expansion of AI infrastructure and logistics is aimed at reducing reliance on search and e-commerce as revenue sources. Naver's global business and Saudi digital-twin projects also contributed to the growth in its global ventures revenue. The company's stated plans cover the coming years, but the articles do not say how the logistics investment will be financed.

Naver has not named the U.S. customer, and the articles do not say which specific AI models will run on the capacity. The articles also do not say how much revenue the AI factory will generate once commercial services begin in the first half of next year. Whether Naver will sign contracts with the more than 10 companies it is negotiating with remains unknown from the reporting. The articles also leave open how quickly the logistics subsidiary will be established and how the personal AI agent app will perform once launched.

stories.Headline: Cohesity Expands Cyber Resilience and AI Data Capabilities for Microsoft Environments
stories.Summary:
Cohesity announced expanded cyber resilience and AI data capabilities for Microsoft environments in a press release distributed via PR Newswire, dated November 13, 2026. The announcement, issued from Singapore, describes recent innovations across Azure, Microsoft 365 and DevOps environments that the company says strengthen data security and recovery. It also extends to AI and analytics through a Cohesity Gaia Catalog integration with Azure Databricks. The company describes its work as advancing data protection and resilience across the Microsoft ecosystem.

The enhancements extend protection to Azure Blob Storage, Azure Data Lake Storage and Azure Kubernetes Service, with application-consistent backups and granular recovery for Kubernetes resources. In Azure Government, Cohesity extended cloud-native protection to Azure SQL Database, SQL Managed Instance, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Table Storage and Cosmos DB. A preview of new capabilities for GitHub and Azure DevOps covers GitHub repositories and complete Azure DevOps organizations, including pull requests, boards, wikis and pipelines. Microsoft 365 recovery adds threat scanning across Exchange, SharePoint and OneDrive, and protection of the Preservation Hold Library. For Microsoft Entra ID, recovery of permanently deleted objects synced to on-premises Active Directory is supported, and administrators can assign a new password when restoring a user account.

Cohesity's Microsoft 365 data optimization capabilities discover redundant, obsolete and trivial data and automatically tier it to archive storage based on policy. Cohesity DSPM identifies that data, and Cohesity Cloud Services can stub it, keeping active environments focused on current data for use with AI tools such as Microsoft Copilot. The Gaia Catalog integration lets organizations publish curated enterprise data directly into Azure Databricks as an external data source, while the underlying data remains in Cohesity Data Cloud. This avoids new extract, transform and load pipelines, and it builds on Gaia's existing integration with Microsoft 365 Copilot, which enforces role-based and file-level access controls.

Cohesity's chief product officer, Vasu Murthy, said organizations depend on more applications and data than ever, making resilience across those environments increasingly critical. Murthy said the company's work with Microsoft aims to give customers greater confidence in their systems and data while creating opportunities to use that data as AI becomes more central to business. The company describes itself as the leader in AI and data security, and says its Cohesity Data Cloud is trusted by customers in more than 140 countries, including two-thirds of the Global 500. The press release names Microsoft, which is listed in the release's ticker references.

The announcement is aimed at organizations that run Azure, Microsoft 365, Entra ID and DevOps workloads and that need recovery from cyber incidents. It is also aimed at public sector customers using Azure Government. A separate Dark Reading article from November 11, 2026, reported on Commvault's SHIFT 2026 conference in Nashville, Tennessee, where executives argued that data recovery must become a continuous operational discipline. Sanjay Mirchandani, president and CEO of Commvault, said resilience will be the new competitive advantage in the AI era. Rajeev Kottomtharayil, chief products officer at Commvault, said recovery is becoming less about speed and more about bringing back clean data.

Cohesity will exhibit at booth 5215 in the Microsoft Ignite Hub at Moscone Center in San Francisco. It will also take part in a session titled "Build resilience and recover Microsoft operations after compromise" on Thursday, November 19, from 10:45 to 11:10 a.m. PT. The articles do not state when the preview capabilities for GitHub and Azure DevOps will become generally available. They also do not state the pricing, the availability of the Gaia Catalog integration beyond the announcement, or whether the Commvault and Cohesity developments are connected.
