stories.Headline: From AI Native Advertising to Marketing System Delivery: BlueMedia launches partnership with ChatGPT Ads
stories.Summary:
BlueMedia, a China-based provider of international marketing services, officially launched its partnership with ChatGPT Ads in Shanghai on November 12, 2026, according to a PR Newswire release. The partnership focuses on helping Chinese brands enter AI-powered conversational and decision-making scenarios and on exploring AI Native advertising in global marketing. The release frames generative AI as a new gateway connecting user needs with commercial information, as more people use ChatGPT to search, compare products and choose services. The release says ChatGPT now has more than 1.2 billion weekly active users worldwide. ChatGPT Ads first launched in the U.S. in February of that year and has since expanded to more than 89 markets across several regions.

BlueMedia says it has served more than 100,000 clients across consumer electronics, gaming, e-commerce, internet services and automotive. Its local service networks cover the United States, Singapore, Vietnam, Thailand, the Netherlands, Brazil, Indonesia, the United Kingdom and Malaysia. Under its "AI + Globalization 2.0" strategy, the company integrates AI into market intelligence, creative production, media buying and performance optimization. Its Blue AI platform runs across end-to-end marketing workflows, moving toward autonomous decision-making and execution. The company reports more than 1,000 AI agents deployed in live business operations.

The company says its AI-driven international operations, which use Agent-to-Agent interactions and autonomous decision-making, have generated revenue exceeding RMB 300 million. For ChatGPT Ads, BlueMedia built a full-stack framework covering user intent insights, product analysis, advertising strategy, landing page review and development, data monitoring, campaign execution and performance analysis. The company has launched ChatGPT Ads campaigns for its first group of brand clients, and it reports that preliminary data shows performance exceeding industry averages. It has also introduced tailored solutions for e-commerce, travel and AI applications. BlueMedia states that it will refine its standardized advertising service framework and move AI native advertising toward deployment at scale.

BlueMedia's chairman and company statement describe the partnership's aim as connecting AI Native advertising, model capabilities and marketing systems. The company says long-term data feedback and real-world practice will help AI learn and improve in live marketing scenarios. The release states that the value of AI goes beyond efficiency and is reshaping how marketing is produced, delivered and monetized. Chinese companies going global, which BlueMedia describes as its focus, are the audience the company says it serves. The release presents these claims as the company's own assessment.

A separate Business Insider report, published November 11, 2026, examines the results advertisers are seeing from ChatGPT Ads, which has attracted more than 100,000 advertisers. Reporter Lara O'Reilly writes that the platform must now prove it moves hard business metrics to become a permanent part of media plans. A working paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze, covering 102 advertiser sites, found ChatGPT Ads generated $0.89 in revenue per U.S. session, against $2.45 for Google search ads. Adthena reported that 52% of 30 enterprise brands struggled to recoup ChatGPT ad spend from July through September, while 26% matched or beat Google ads. OpenAI cited an Evernote case study showing a trial-to-paid conversion rate about 10% to 20% above its historical average.

The report says OpenAI launched ChatGPT Ads about nine months earlier and reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate by the summer. Growth is limited by the size of ChatGPT's free user base, the scarcity of ad-relevant conversations and how many ads users will tolerate. Qualcomm CMO Don McGuire said it is hard for LLMs to find audiences, which raises the ROI question. Adthena CMO Ashley Fletcher called measurement a sore point and said new measurement pixels and conversion bidding could help, though he warned results may show mostly early-stage nudging. Natural Intelligence, which runs comparison sites including Top10.com and BestMoney.com, moved ChatGPT Ads from its test budget to its growth budget.

Whether ChatGPT Ads can move from experimental spending into permanent media plans remains unresolved in the articles. The Business Insider report describes the verdict from marketers so far as mixed, with Twilio and Intuit still experimenting. The BlueMedia release gives preliminary performance data without specific figures. Fletcher said Black Friday would be a major moment to watch. The articles do not say whether BlueMedia's early results will hold, or how many of the advertisers that tested ChatGPT Ads will continue using the platform.

stories.Headline: From Nuclear Weapons to Artificial Intelligence, a New Test of Humanity's Restraint
stories.Summary:
Eight decades after atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the world faces a new question: what happens when decisions involving human life increasingly pass from people to machines? That concern ran through an international peace gathering in Assisi, Italy, organized by the Community of Sant'Egidio from October 25 to 27, where religious leaders, nuclear disarmament campaigners and technology specialists examined the risks of nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence. The meeting marked 40 years since Pope John Paul II brought representatives of the world's major religions to Assisi to pray for peace. Its theme, "Unarmed and Disarming Peace," carried particular urgency because nuclear arms control has weakened and military spending has reached record levels. The central question, according to the articles, was no longer only whether humanity could destroy itself, but whether governments retained the judgment to prevent those means from being used.

The human consequences of nuclear warfare formed the moral foundation of a forum on disarmament and proliferation. Hiroshima survivor Katsuko Tanaka, also known as Toshiko Tanaka, recalled the bombing of August 6, 1945, when she was six years old. Her account described a catastrophe that killed indiscriminately and left survivors with physical and psychological wounds for decades. Archbishop Peter Michiaki Nakamura of Nagasaki, in published remarks, drew on the legacy of Takashi Nagai, a physician and atomic bomb survivor who devoted his later life to peace. Together, the speakers challenged the language of nuclear deterrence, which measures security by military capabilities rather than by the lives potentially lost.

Susi Snyder of the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, or ICAN, addressed the danger posed by the modernization of nuclear arsenals and the erosion of arms control. The New START treaty between the United States and Russia expired in February, and the 2026 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference failed to reach consensus, reinforcing concerns about nuclear restraint. Attention now turns to the first Review Conference of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, scheduled to begin in late November. Disarmament advocates face a persistent obstacle, however, because the governments possessing nuclear weapons largely remain outside that treaty. For the Italian Soka Gakkai, a Buddhist organization engaged in nuclear abolition campaigns, education has become an essential part of the response.

Alessja Trama, representing the Be The Hope Foundation, described the work of Senzatomica, an initiative that has organized exhibitions and educational activities on nuclear weapons across Italy. The campaign traces its inspiration to a 1957 declaration by Josei Toda, the second president of the Soka Gakkai, calling for the abolition of nuclear weapons. Its premise is that remembering Hiroshima and Nagasaki must lead to public responsibility, particularly among younger generations with no personal connection to the war. Advances in artificial intelligence are also transforming the nature of military power. At a separate forum titled "Humanity in the Age of Technology," Archbishop Vincenzo Paglia warned that technological capabilities were advancing faster than the institutions meant to govern them.

Tiziana Catarci, an Italian artificial intelligence researcher, distinguished between placing a human in a decision-making process and exercising meaningful control over it. An operator may formally approve a machine-generated recommendation without understanding how it was produced or being able to challenge it. In military operations, that gap could become deadly, she said. Catarci called for stronger oversight of AI systems and the prohibition of autonomous weapons capable of making lethal decisions without meaningful human control.

Yoshiyuki Nagaoka, executive director of the Office of Public Affairs of Soka Gakkai, approached the problem through Buddhist teachings on the dignity of life. He cited a case in Japan of an elderly woman who turned to generative AI for advice about the treatment of her terminally ill husband. Other participants cautioned against viewing artificial intelligence solely as a threat. Matt Vasey of the Gates Foundation argued that AI could improve access to healthcare, education and agricultural knowledge, especially in communities historically neglected by technological development.

He also warned that people could voluntarily surrender moral responsibility to systems designed to make decisions easier. Cisco executive Gianpaolo Barozzi emphasized redesigning work around human capabilities, while Rabbi Noam Marans of the American Jewish Committee distinguished the accumulation of information from the exercise of wisdom. The closing Peace Appeal urged that resources devoted to weapons be redirected toward food, water, education, healthcare and decent work. The message from Assisi, as the articles frame it, was that security must be measured not only by what humanity can build but by what it is prepared to refuse.

stories.Headline: ASUS Expands Access to Local AI Across DIY PCs, Gaming Systems, Creator Workstations, and Professional Desktops
stories.Summary:
ASUS announced on November 12, 2026, that it is broadening access to advanced AI through an ecosystem of AI-ready hardware and software for gamers, creators, developers and enterprise organizations. The company, based in Fremont, California, framed the effort as the ASUS Agent Computer initiative, which lets users deploy AI locally, in the cloud or through hybrid models. The move gives users control over performance, data privacy and operational costs. ASUS said its hardware and software can lower the overall cost of ownership and operation. The company also said existing ASUS devices can be used as Agent Computers.

The hardware portfolio ranges from DIY PC builds with AI-ready motherboards to mini-PCs, workstations, external accelerators and enterprise supercomputers. Motherboards span the PRIME, TUF Gaming, ROG and ProArt series, and the ET900A X9 is among the ExpertCenter Pro workstations. Builds can use NVIDIA GeForce RTX or AMD Radeon AI GPUs, and the ProArt GR1X Mini PC targets creator applications. A "Find Your ASUS Agent Computer" tool recommends hardware based on workloads, performance needs and local, cloud or hybrid preferences. The portfolio is designed to give users full visibility into total operating costs.

Press contact Juan Jose Guerrero, Public Relations Manager, provided the company's statements in the release. ASUS, listed as 2357.TW, describes itself as an innovative technology leader across infrastructure, physical AI, AI PCs and devices. The company's "Ubiquitous AI. Incredible Possibilities" strategy guides the initiative, and its ROG and ProArt sub-brands serve gamers and creators worldwide. ASUS said it aims to bring enterprise-to-edge AI to life through this strategy.

The release sets out these statements without independent verification in the articles. The initiative also covers software meant to make local AI and agent-based computing easier to use. ASUS Zenni Claw is designed to make agentic AI practical on consumer devices, while ASUS Multi-LM Tuner helps users deploy optimized large language models across ASUS platforms. ASUS DisplayWidget Center acts as a bridge between ASUS displays and emerging agentic AI workflows. The company said its solutions balance performance, scalability, security and long-term cost efficiency across local, cloud and hybrid environments.

Users are directed to the ASUS Agent Computer hub for further information. Separately, China's National Development and Reform Commission said at a Beijing news conference on Tuesday that China will deepen its "AI Plus" initiative during the 15th Five-Year Plan period from 2026 to 2030. Deputy director Wang Ruomeng said China has built more than 10,000 advanced-level smart factories, where AI is used in quality inspection, production monitoring and fault diagnosis. Deputy director Ren Zhongbao said six emerging pillar industries, including integrated circuits, aerospace and biomedicine, will be prioritized. Their combined output approached 6 trillion yuan in 2025 and is expected to exceed 10 trillion yuan by 2030.

The China Daily report says China will also build national AI application pilot bases in manufacturing, energy, transportation and healthcare. Luan Jie of the National Data Administration said China will develop high-quality datasets and strengthen data labeling. Yang Chao, a researcher at the Development Research Center of the State Council, said strict data and reliability requirements, varied production scenarios and cost considerations hinder large-scale AI adoption in manufacturing. He said AI's contribution to economic growth would depend on computing infrastructure investment in the short term. Wang said China will promote open-source AI.

China is working to make the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization operational, and 38 countries have joined as founding members. Wang said China will coordinate with other countries on AI development strategies, governance rules and technical standards. Lu Chuanying, a professor at Tongji University, said turning these efforts into lasting results requires moving beyond broad agreement on governance principles to sustained practical cooperation. He said the organization aims to integrate AI governance with development and narrow the AI divide. The articles leave open how the organization's work will be carried out in practice.

stories.Headline: Mondrio Raises $3.75 Million Round Led by Heartcore Capital for Its Agentic Pricing Platform
stories.Summary:
Mondrio, an agentic B2B pricing management platform, announced on November 12, 2026 that it had raised a $3.75 million round led by Heartcore Capital. Pretiosum VC, Hersir Ventures, Cambrena Capital and Momo VC also joined the round, alongside angel investors with experience in pricing, CPQ, AI and payments. The company said the funding will expand its AI and engineering teams, grow its pricing experts and strengthen its commercial presence in the U.S. and Europe. Mondrio is headquartered in San Francisco and Amsterdam, and its co-founder and CEO is Gregor Biljardt. The announcement was distributed by GlobeNewswire.

Mondrio's platform is built to help businesses create a pricing team in which AI agents handle much of the daily work in pricing strategy and deal execution. Companies can equip existing pricing teams with AI capabilities or draw on Mondrio's pricing experts when needed. The platform analyzes product changes, customer behavior, competitive intelligence and market signals to recommend pricing changes. It also provides quote and discount guidance, automates quoting and approvals, and feeds insights from individual deals back into pricing strategy. The platform consists of two products, Pricing Studio for pricing design and Deal Engine for pricing execution.

Biljardt, Mondrio's co-founder and CEO, said AI is moving beyond answering questions to identifying opportunities and taking action. He said the company can now build agents that combine quantitative data with qualitative insights such as customer conversations and market feedback. Co-founder Joep van den Nieuwenhoff serves as chief commercial officer, and the company's executive team also includes Joe Cainey, Ife Ajiboye, Isabelle van Keulen and Roos Offerhaus. The announcement describes Mondrio's leadership and the founders' pricing experience, but it does not name any other person responsible for the company's decisions.

Heartcore Capital partner Yacine Ghalim said most companies set a price once and refresh it through consulting projects every few years. He said AI is making that model untenable and that Mondrio turns pricing into a continuous function. G2 CEO Godard Abel, who is also an investor in Mondrio, said AI agents will increasingly represent both buyers and sellers. Onno Oldeman, former Managing Partner at Simon-Kucher and a Mondrio investor, said the next competitive advantage lies in the speed of pricing adaptation. Threekit chief operating officer Joachim Klein also praised the company.

The announcement says AI has accelerated product innovation and that pricing has become the next bottleneck to growth. It cites McKinsey as finding that roughly three-quarters of software companies lack a centralized pricing function. A McKinsey survey of more than 400 B2B pricing executives found that 65% to 85% of organizations expect to adopt generative or agentic AI in pricing within one to three years, while only 5% to 10% have fully scaled agentic AI in any pricing use case. G2's 2026 Buyer Behavior Report found that more than 80% of B2B software buyers have used AI chatbots to source software recommendations in the past two years.

Mondrio said it plans to use the funding for three priorities: product development, pricing expertise and go-to-market expansion. It intends to significantly grow its workforce across its San Francisco and Amsterdam offices over the next year, adding pricing architects. It also plans to deepen relationships with B2B technology companies and private equity firms in the U.S. and Europe, and to lay groundwork for serving manufacturing and professional services firms. The announcement does not state the timing of the go-to-market expansion beyond the next year, nor the number of new hires.

stories.Headline: Consumer-first thinking, enterprise AI: Why Tencent Cloud wants adoption to feel like ‘turning on a light’
stories.Summary:
Tencent Cloud wants businesses to adopt AI as easily as switching on a light, according to a branded content piece published by The Business Times on November 13, 2026. Its WorkBuddy office productivity agent helps employees analyse information, prepare documents and complete tasks across applications. Behind the scenes, WorkBuddy selects a suitable large language model for each task, so employees do not have to make that choice themselves. WorkBuddy was launched in March 2026 and has rolled out more than 100 updates. The approach draws on Tencent's more than 20 years of building consumer services, including Weixin and WeChat, which together have 1.4 billion monthly users.

Tencent Cloud reported in October 2026 that its active overseas customer base had doubled over the preceding year. International demand for its AI solutions had grown at a triple-digit rate over the same period. In Singapore, local company Weesware applied Tencent Cloud's PalmAI to senior activity centres through its CaritaHub platform. Contactless palm recognition now lets more than 10,000 seniors sign in without cards or passcodes. In Indonesia, Tencent Cloud was the strategic technology partner for telecommunications operator XLSMART on a large-scale cloud migration.

Poshu Yeung, senior vice president of Tencent Cloud and head of Tencent Cloud International, compared the goal to electricity, saying users flip a switch without asking where the power comes from. He said the company's consumer-first thinking helps make AI adoption easier for businesses. Yeung also said the company's priority is deploying AI practically to create real, positive impact for the communities it serves. He described Tencent Cloud's Consulting-as-a-Service as high-touch, giving businesses an expert to call about their AI needs and strategy. He said the company aims to make adoption of advanced technologies seamless at the right price performance.

Many companies in Asia-Pacific are still working out where AI can improve their operations, while grappling with ageing IT systems, fragmented data and regulatory requirements. Potential applications include repetitive processes in human resources, finance, procurement and legal operations. Tencent Cloud's consultants across Asia-Pacific markets work alongside businesses to identify suitable AI applications. Its AI CAN DO IT hackathon programme drew more than 10,000 participants across five markets in the past six months. The Singapore edition, co-organised with AI Singapore, had participants tackle challenges from partners including DBS, Keppel, Aspire, Ryde and NTU's Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine.

Tencent Cloud's parent company has been developing and deploying its AI capabilities since 2016. Tencent Cloud says its experience developing and operating digital platforms at scale helps drive its international demand. The company built more than 20 AI-assisted migration tools for the XLSMART project, moving 1,200 microservices and over 15 terabytes of core data in four and a half months with zero downtime. CodeBuddy, the AI coding assistant used in that project, was first developed and tested internally by employees. Looking to 2027, Tencent Cloud plans to expand its international AI solutions and strengthen their global infrastructure.

stories.Headline: U.S. finalizing rule to block China’s remote AI chip access- The Information
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Commerce Department is preparing to finalize a rule that would stop Chinese artificial intelligence companies from remotely using advanced AI chips through data centers in other countries, according to a report from The Information on Wednesday. The report cited two people familiar with the matter. The rule could be announced this month. It would expand existing semiconductor controls from the department's Bureau of Industry and Security.

The expanded controls would reach seven additional countries, including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. The measure is aimed at blocking remote access and chip smuggling into China. The Commerce Department is consulting with other government agencies before the rule can be finalized. Earlier on Wednesday, Axios reported that President Donald Trump had pushed for tighter export controls to curb illegal chip smuggling, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had opposed the measure.

The rule comes amid a growing controversy over Nvidia's potential links to China after its CEO, Jensen Huang, admitted to an affair with a suspected Beijing spy. Chinese internet companies including Tencent, Alibaba and Bytedance have signed offshore data center agreements that give them access to Nvidia's top chips for training their artificial intelligence models. Those arrangements are drawing more scrutiny both abroad and at home, particularly as Beijing pushes companies to use more domestic chips. Shares of Alibaba and Tencent fell after the report.

stories.Headline: From College Projects to Job Interviews: How AI Tools Support Students at Every Stage
stories.Summary:
AI writing and resume tools are now appearing at almost every stage of student life, from college assignments to job interviews, according to a Hindu feature published on November 12, 2026. The article follows a composite student, an electronics BTech graduate, whose use of the tools grew from small helpers in her first year to heavy use by her final year. In first year she used a Summarizer, Grammar Checker, Paraphraser, Citation Generator and Translator, mostly from Quillbot. The tools handled small tasks while the argument of each essay remained her own work. Her first-year marks, the article says, tracked how much she had read.

In her second year, the group project was a low-cost water quality sensor built by four students, with a shared document of about 3,000 words. She was given the presentation slides with four days to go, and she used Quillbot's AI presentation maker to build a ten-slide deck for a ten-minute slot. The prompt she wrote asked for plain, technical language, slides under 35 words each, and a suggested chart for the cost breakdown. She attached two photos of the circuit board and corrected the first draft, which had promoted a literature-review sentence into a claim about their own sensor. The deck was exported as a PPTX for the seminar hall and a PDF for the submission portal, and the presentation maker lacks animations and speaker notes.

Quillbot's presentation maker is still labelled Beta and is free to use, with a Premium plan that adds unlimited presentations and faster generation. In her third year, she used Quillbot's AI Resume Builder for an internship at an eleven-person fintech startup in Bengaluru, importing her LinkedIn profile and pasting in project and fest details. She chose the student template, moved her projects and education above her part-time job, and rewrote her tutoring bullet with facts she supplied, including eight students and two years. The founder later said the sponsorship bullet made him open her file. In her final year she used the ATS-friendly template, which the product page describes as parse-safe, while noting that no builder can guarantee a pass through every applicant tracking screen.

The article's author writes that such tools are useful when the student supplies the facts, and that the student must check every line before applying. It lists common failures, including submitting unedited first drafts, using default generic decks, and inventing achievements such as percentage improvements that the student cannot explain. Lecturers recognise these problems quickly, the article says, and interviewers may ask how a stated figure was measured. The student used Quillbot's AI Chat to generate fifteen likely interview questions from the job description and her resume, and she recorded practice answers herself. She did not ask the tool to write her answers, because scripted replies sound scripted on a video call.

A separate KSAT report published November 11, 2026, from San Antonio, Texas, carries a similar message from Jason Pasola, who works for Robert Half, a worldwide staffing company. Pasola said many companies first run applications through software that scans for buzzwords taken from the job posting, with a human or HR professional reviewing them afterward. He said this practice had grown over the last two years, and he advised tailoring a resume to the job description without copying it word for word. He recommended using AI to organise and format a resume but never to claim skills a candidate lacks. He named Microsoft and Claude as tools that work well, and he said he "absolutely" believes qualified candidates are missing out by not showing their skills.

Pasola's view is that employers are increasingly screened by technology before people read applications, so qualified candidates who do not present their skills clearly may be overlooked. The student's story suggests that the same screening can be passed by a clean, one-page layout that matches the posting, though the article notes that the rest depends on whether the experience fits. The KSAT report mentions Texas's new governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, who is searching for her team through a digital portal rather than paper resumes. Both articles place this shift in the hiring process within the last few years. Neither article reports data on how many employers use these screening systems or what share of applicants they reject.

stories.Headline: IIT Madras Pravartak offers free online courses in AI, electric vehicles and future skills for Classes 7 to 12
stories.Summary:
IIT Madras Pravartak Technologies Foundation, working with BodhBridge Education, has opened registrations for free online courses for school students and teachers. The programmes cover Artificial Intelligence, electric vehicles, future mobility, entrepreneurship and other emerging fields. Applications are open for the November 2026 to January 2027 batches, and the courses are aimed at students in Classes 7 to 12. Interested learners can register through the BodhBridge portal at bodhbridge.iitmpravartak.org.in. The offering was reported on November 12, 2026.

Students can enrol in courses on AI, electric vehicles, future mobility, entrepreneurship, design thinking and innovation. The courses are delivered online through live classes, practical activities and real-world examples. Sessions are conducted monthly, between November 2026 and January 2027. All courses are free, but students who want a certificate can opt for an additional certification from IIT Madras Pravartak. Teachers can also take courses in career counselling certification, leadership development for educators, and classroom management and student engagement.

IIT Madras Pravartak Technologies Foundation is a Section 8 company and a Technology Innovation Hub hosted by IIT Madras. It operates in Sensors, Networking, Actuators and Control Systems under the National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems. Dhanalakshmi Sampath, Manager of the Digital Skills Academy at the foundation, said the programmes act as a stepping stone from classroom education to industry needs. She said they build skills in AI, financial literacy and entrepreneurship. The foundation says the programmes give students, teachers and institutions practical tools for a forward-looking learning environment.

The sessions will be led by experts from the IIT Madras alumni network, start-ups and various industries. Students will learn how emerging technologies function and how they are used across industries. The initiative is aimed at school students and educators who want practical exposure to these fields. The foundation says more than 45,000 teachers have already benefited from its free training initiatives. The collaboration seeks to make emerging technology education more accessible to school students and educators.

BodhBridge Education is an educational platform founded by IIT Madras alumni that works to provide learning opportunities and support to students, teachers and parents. The two organisations are working together on this initiative. The programme aims to connect classroom learning with the practical skills increasingly required across industries. The foundation has delivered free training to teachers before, and this initiative extends that approach to students.

The articles do not say how many students or teachers will be admitted to each batch. They do not give the fees for the optional certificate or its exact cost. They also do not specify the number of sessions in each course or the schedule of individual classes. Whether the programme will run beyond January 2027 is not stated. Applicants should check the official portal for enrolment details, certification options and the applicable terms before registering.

stories.Headline: AI Spending Lifts Global Trade to 30-Year High, Raising Bust Risk
stories.Summary:
AI spending by U.S. Big Tech is driving global trade to its strongest growth since the early 1990s, excluding rebounds after the pandemic and the global financial crisis, according to the articles. Up to 80% of the recent rise in global exports is concentrated in AI-related goods, and analysts warn that Asian exporters including South Korea, Taiwan and China would take an immediate hit if U.S. investment cools. The Wall Street Journal reported on the 11th, citing analysis by Capital Economics, that a cooling of the AI investment boom could tip the world economy into recession. In October, South Korea's total exports rose 93.7% from a year earlier and semiconductor exports soared 259.4%, while Chinese exports rose 35%. Moody's Analytics head of international economics Gaurav Ganguly said a sharp drop in AI-related stocks combined with other shocks could lead to a global recession.

The U.S. government is finishing a plan to extend export restrictions to Southeast Asia, which has been identified as a detour route for AI chips bound for China. The Bureau of Industry and Security at the U.S. Commerce Department is pushing to add Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, Norway and South Africa to its semiconductor export control list, The Information reported on the 11th. Under the proposed rules, imports of Blackwell-class or more advanced chips would require U.S. government approval, with end users and intended uses also subject to disclosure. Singapore accounted for 18% of Nvidia's total revenue in fiscal 2025 on a billing basis, but chips actually shipped into Singapore generated only 2% of revenue. Congress is seeking to attach the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act to the National Defense Authorization Act.

Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang's future is uncertain, and Wall Street has cut ratings and price targets on the company as a result of the possibility that he steps down. Baird on the 11th lowered its rating to neutral from outperform and cut its price target 60% to $200 from $500, while Bernstein halved its target to $200 from $400. Nvidia shares fell 9.51% over two days after Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on the 8th. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning pushed back, saying the United States should stop fabricating spy narratives. Nvidia has provided a combined $300 billion in financial support to customers over the past three years, according to Bloomberg, and in August it unveiled a $500 billion AI infrastructure investment vehicle with BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and others.

South Korea has announced at least $510 billion, about 680 trillion won, in joint projects with Nvidia over the past year, and SK Group signed a letter of intent worth more than $500 billion in July. NAVER received $1 billion from Nvidia in exchange for a 4.13% stake. According to the Korea Securities Depository, domestic investors held $13.64744 billion worth of Nvidia shares as of the 10th, or about 18 trillion won, the second most held foreign stock after Tesla. Advantest, the Japanese chip test equipment maker, reported second-quarter revenue up 81.7% from a year earlier to 477.7 billion yen. Its gross margin reached a record 71.1%, and it raised full-year revenue guidance to 1.863 trillion yen.

Huang's exit and the U.S. chip curbs are the two risks that the articles frame as threatening Nvidia and the broader AI supply chain. stories.Headline: The promise and peril of AI in government
stories.Summary:
Taoyuan, Taiwan's industrial hub home to 200 semiconductor facilities, is using AI to manage its fast growth under Mayor San-Cheng Chang. The city runs an AI-powered lung cancer screening program for residents over 40 with risk factors such as occupational exposure or family history. The program began in March 2023 and screened over 400,000 residents within two years. Chang previously served as Taiwan's first nonpartisan premier and held leadership roles at Google and Acer. The Post and Courier separately argues that AI's potential benefits, such as a phone app describing scenes for blind users, deserve attention alongside its risks.

Taoyuan, which is home to Taiwan's international airport and 2.2 million residents, must handle heavy truck traffic, air pollution, population growth and constant construction. The screening program detected 233 lung cancer cases, with 90% at an early stage, and saved NT$500 million, about $17 million, through AI-aided diagnostics. The software predicts cancer risk from a single low-dose CT scan without requiring additional clinical data. The city also built a system that analyzes exhaust pipe images against a database of legal configurations, and complaints about illegal exhausts fell 20% over last year. AI cameras monitor construction sites and factory chimneys, and traffic lights now shave about 10 seconds off each wait.

Mayor Chang is responsible for these projects and has been selective about which AI tools his administration adopts. He has said he will not sanction generative AI chatbots that could hallucinate. He distinguishes between machine learning that detects existing conditions and machine learning that predicts future outcomes, favoring the former. The Taoyuan administration uses AI to locate potholes and to identify wheelchair users at train station elevators so assistance can be ready. The article presents these uses as ones where AI sees what is already present without automating human decisions.

The article's author, Beth Simone Noveck, warns that predictive AI is being relied on for decisions such as sentencing, parole, credit scoring and hiring. Princeton researcher Arvind Narayanan is quoted as warning that predicting job performance or recidivism involves countless unpredictable variables. Fraud-detection systems may misclassify a struggling single parent with irregular gig income as a fraud risk. The Post and Courier editorial, meanwhile, says the public conversation about AI has been largely negative and that Democrats are taking control of Congress partly by pointing to AI's dangers. Students at the College of Charleston, including Saif Chaundry, have built an app that narrates surroundings for visually impaired users.

Narayanan identifies five ways predictive systems break down, including models that miss crucial context, systems that can be gamed, and overreliance on automated outputs. A sepsis prediction system sold by Epic was trained on national data and proved ineffective for local patient populations. The author distinguishes population-level forecasting, such as for forest fires, from judgments about individuals, which she says should be advisory and contestable rather than automated. Labor disputes in Taiwan's semiconductor industry and worries about cost and context for non-English languages also appear in the coverage. The Post and Courier argues that the federal government has declined to restrict AI development or require public disclosure of its use.

The articles leave open how Taoyuan's screening and traffic programs will be evaluated over the long term and whether other governments will adopt similar limits on predictive tools. They do not say whether the federal government will impose the restrictions the Post and Courier calls for once Democrats take control of Congress. The College of Charleston app's release and wider adoption are not described, and the outcomes of the Taiwanese labor disputes are not reported. The articles also do not say whether individual-level predictive systems will be restricted or made contestable in practice.

stories.Headline: 65% of Australian Frontline Workers Are Using AI, but Almost Half Have Had No Employer Guidance
stories.Summary:
Humanforce research released on November 12, 2026 found that 65% of Australian frontline workers have used AI or an AI-enabled tool at work in the past year. The same survey of 501 workers in Sydney-based research found that 46% had received no employer training, briefing or written rules on AI. The survey covered healthcare, hospitality and tourism, and retail and wholesale trade workers across Australia. Among workers who had used tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude or Copilot for work, almost one in four said their employer did not allow it or they did not know. In healthcare that figure rose to more than one in three, and only 13% of all workers said they had received comprehensive training.

Humanforce's findings describe a gap between how widely AI is used in frontline jobs and the guidance employers give about it. Paperwork and administration ranked first in every sector as the task workers most wanted technology or AI to ease, cited by 43% overall. Rostering and managing shifts came next at 31%. Nearly half of respondents, 49%, estimated spending at least two hours a week on forms, timesheets, shift changes and pay or leave issues, while 28% spent four hours or more. Pay accuracy was also a concern, with 41% saying their pay had been wrong at least once in the past 12 months and 27% saying it had happened two or more times.

Clayton Pyne, CEO of Humanforce, said guidance has not kept pace with frontline workers already using AI on the job. He said workers should know what information they can share with general-purpose AI tools, what they can rely on, and when an answer needs checking. Pyne argued that organisations providing this clarity early would reduce risk and gain more from AI, including less paperwork and easier shift management. On pay, he said AI must work within clear permissions, with every action traceable and explainable, on top of a core system that holds awards, rosters and pay records. He said nobody should have to take AI's word for what they are owed.

The survey found that the effects of AI would be felt most by frontline workers, including carers, hospitality staff and retail employees. Losing human contact was the top concern across frontline workplaces, selected by 47% of respondents. Healthcare workers reported the heaviest administrative load, with 58% spending two hours or more a week on admin, and 40% named misuse of personal information as their top AI concern. Hospitality and tourism workers reported the highest pay error rate at 48%, compared with 33% in retail and wholesale, and 29% in hospitality worried AI could mean fewer shifts or hours.

Humanforce describes itself as an operating platform for frontline workforce operations, serving more than 1,500 customers and one million employees across more than 90 countries. It was founded in 2002 and has offices in Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, the Philippines and the United States. The survey was commissioned by Humanforce and conducted by Zoho in Q3 2026. Respondents were split across healthcare (151), hospitality and tourism (200), and retail and wholesale trade (150). Retail and wholesale workers were the most likely to have received some AI guidance, though 37% still reported none.

The articles do not say what regulatory or employer steps will follow the findings. They also do not state whether employers plan to introduce AI training or written rules. Support for AI use was conditional, with 49% wanting a person to review important AI decisions and 39% wanting the right to question or appeal AI-assisted decisions. Only 8% said no additional safeguards were needed. The articles leave open how far those safeguards will be adopted across the sectors surveyed.

stories.Headline: Shopify (SHOP) Earnings And AI Commerce Story Put Valuation Back In Focus
stories.Summary:
Shopify reported its third quarter 2026 earnings, which drew renewed investor attention to the company's valuation. The articles report revenue of US$3.74b and net income of US$462m for the quarter, with guidance for low-30% revenue growth in the next quarter. Shopify also filed an omnibus shelf registration covering equity, debt, warrants and units. The coverage points to a stock that has slipped about 17% over the past month and is down around 5% year to date. Analysts' targets cluster near US$177, while the share price was changing hands around US$149.

The shelf registration gives Shopify flexibility to raise capital quickly if it needs funds for products, AI infrastructure or payments. The quarter also highlighted a heavier tilt toward merchant solutions and AI-driven commerce tools. A partnership with Meta's Muse agent ties Shop Pay more directly to transaction volume on major social platforms. The articles say the shelf filing does not change operations by itself, but it could dilute existing shareholders if future equity issuance does not improve earnings power. One article's narrative assumes revenue grows 19.9% a year and eventually reaches a 20.0% profit margin.

The articles name Shopify as the company responsible, and its disclosures contain the revenue, net income, guidance and filing details. The articles cite QuanD, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, who built a fair value estimate of US$210.47 per share on an 8.89% discount rate. QuanD argues that Shopify's commerce platform and app ecosystem keep merchants loyal as their businesses expand. The articles attribute the view that AI is the main swing factor to some of the most optimistic analysts. They say these analysts projected revenue rising about 37.1% a year and earnings reaching roughly US$5.3b by 2029.

Investors holding Shopify shares are the group the articles identify as affected by these developments. The articles say the stock trades on a P/E of 90.3x, compared with a fair ratio of 55.7x, a US IT sector average of 22x and direct peers at 45.4x. One article warns that the gap points to meaningful valuation risk if sentiment cools or growth expectations are tested. Another says the story could wobble if merchant activity slows or valuation expectations compress further. The articles also note that Shopify's three-year total shareholder return is up about 120%.

The articles report that Shopify's share price had slipped after the earnings miss and the fresh shelf registration filing. They describe the company's long-term momentum as intact despite more recent pressure. The articles say Shopify has built an ecosystem in which more merchants attract more developers, and more integrations attract still more merchants. They describe this network as increasingly difficult to replicate. The articles give no further detail on the earnings miss beyond the figures already cited.

Looking ahead, the articles say the key short-term catalyst is execution around merchant solutions and AI-driven tools such as the Meta Muse partnership. They leave open whether Shopify will use the shelf registration and, if it does, how much capital it would raise. The articles also do not say whether the fourth quarter guidance will be met or whether AI products will generate monetisation. Nor do they say whether analysts will revise their targets from the current cluster near US$177.

stories.Headline: AI Expert, Spelman College President’s New Book Offers a New Vision for the Future of Artificial Intelligence - Carroll County Mirror-Democrat
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, Spelman College in Atlanta hosted an event to launch Spelman President Ayanna Howard's new book about the future of artificial intelligence. The book, titled REBOOTING THE MACHINES: A New Human Vision for Artificial Intelligence, was celebrated with a fireside chat, an audience question-and-answer session, and a book signing. All proceeds from the event went toward Spelman scholarships. The press release announcing the event was issued on November 12, 2026, through GlobeNewswire, and the same text appeared in other outlets. Howard's book is presented as a new vision for AI that centers human values, ethics, and diverse perspectives.

Howard draws on her experience as an AI and robotics expert, entrepreneur, and academic leader to examine how human values shape AI's future. In the book she argues that AI, including robotics, is not built with a moral center, so people must supply that moral compass if the technology is to serve all humanity. An excerpt quotes her saying that people must take stock of AI's influence on their lives to thrive in an AI-infused world. She also says society has the power both to build AI that reflects society as it is and to build AI that fosters the society people aspire to have. The book offers a practical roadmap for deciding what to demand from tech companies, what to resist, and how to build ethical human values into machines.

Howard, who became president of Spelman in August 2026, wrote the book as the author and speaker in the launch. The press release attributes the book's message to her and quotes her directly. The release does not describe any other person as responsible for the book's arguments. Its contents are presented as her own views on AI's moral foundations and its social role. The release frames the book as her contribution to the discussion, supported by the launch event.

The release says that students in higher education worry that AI will erase the futures they worked hard to build. Howard's arrival at Spelman comes during this period of anxiety, according to the release. At the launch, engineer and policy scholar Dr. Kamau Bobb and WABE's Rose Scot joined Howard in a conversation about AI's changing effect on the workforce. They also discussed the importance of diversity among AI developers, ways to address bias in new technologies, and shared responsibility for a more equitable AI future. Spelman students and the wider public are the groups the release identifies as affected by these concerns.

Spelman College was founded in 1881 and is located in Atlanta, where it has 2,700 students. The release describes Spelman as a liberal arts college focused on educating women of African descent, and it says the college leads the country in producing Black women who complete Ph.D.s in STEM fields. U.S. News & World Report ranked Spelman No. 34 among liberal arts colleges and No. 1 among historically Black colleges and universities for the 20th year. Recent initiatives include a Department of Defense designation as a Center of Excellence for Minority Women in STEM and collaborations with MIT's Media Lab, the Broad Institute, and the Army Research Lab on AI and machine learning. The release also lists notable alumnae such as Marian Wright Edelman, Rosalind Brewer, Stacey Abrams, and Tayari Jones.

The articles do not say whether a second printing, further events, or policy steps will follow the book's launch. They also do not state the book's sales figures or how much money the scholarships will ultimately receive. Readers can learn more or buy the book at www.broadleafbooks.com, and the release directs media questions to Spelman's public relations office. The articles do not describe any response from tech companies or government bodies to Howard's proposals.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) Blowout Quarter Signals Robust AI Infrastructure Demand, Lifting Nasdaq 1.6%
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, listed on the Nasdaq as CRWV, reported record quarterly revenue of $3.66 billion on Wednesday, November 11, and the results lifted the broader market. The company also raised its full-year 2026 revenue outlook, which eased worries that corporate demand for computing capacity might not justify the heavy spending required to build it. Its shares jumped 24.71% during the session, and the stock has risen 52% since it went public in 2025. The results gave a lift to technology stocks as well, with the Nasdaq Composite climbing 1.60% to close at 25,466 after declines caused by Tuesday's inflation concerns. The S&P 500 gained 1.29% to finish at 7,618.

The rally was concentrated in technology and semiconductor names rather than spread evenly across sectors. Micron Technology rose 11.89% as chipmakers recovered from losses earlier in the week. Nebius Group closed 15.44% higher and Applied Digital finished up 7.37%, as investors reassessed the near-term earnings potential of companies tied to AI infrastructure. The article describes CoreWeave's report as a confidence reset for a part of the market that had been pressured by valuation worries and doubts about how long AI-related capital spending could last.

The story frames the gains as a reaction to that single catalyst. Several risks remained after the rally, according to the article. The 10-year Treasury yield kept moving toward the 5% level, which the piece notes has historically created headwinds for growth stocks. Higher yields raise the discount rate applied to future earnings, which can leave richly valued technology shares more exposed if the upward drift continues.

The article also questions whether the gains reflect broad market strength, since they were confined to a narrow group of AI and semiconductor companies. The article's author, David Prior, a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, presents CoreWeave's results as having restored credibility to the AI trade for now. He says investors will be watching whether that momentum holds as macroeconomic pressures build. The piece does not specify any further scheduled events or outcomes beyond that.

stories.Headline: AWS releases AWS Emulator, a free tool that simulates 200+ of its services locally, saying AI agents wrote it and its team hasn't written or reviewed any code (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)
stories.Summary:
AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free local tool that simulates more than 200 of its cloud services on a developer's own machine. The emulator works with the AWS CLI and SDKs, so no AWS account or service fee is needed to run it. The release, announced in November 2026, stands out because autonomous AI agents wrote all of its code, and AWS says its team has not written or reviewed any of it. Developers and coding agents can use the tool to run quick, low-cost tests against AWS-style APIs. The emulator is built from 438 AWS API models and ships as one Rust crate per service.

It runs on Linux through RPM or Debian packages, or in Docker on macOS and Windows with a 2 GiB memory limit. Building it from source requires 100 GB of free disk space. In release v1.0.322, it passed 24,243 of 42,857 scored fidelity tests, or 56.6 percent. Its strongest result was AWS KMS at 93.9 percent, while AWS CloudFormation was the weakest at 15.8 percent. Resources live in memory and disappear when the program stops.

AWS attributes the work to a coordinated group of AI agents. The project began with a prompt to Kiro, which produced a basic Amazon SQS emulator in about 15 minutes, and the work was then split among three agent teams that wrote test scenarios, found failures and submitted fixes. Every change must pass a merge gate covering build, code review, security and fidelity checks, and several security agents run adversarial reviews. Matthew Goldberg is cited as reporting that hundreds of agents work at once on thousands of issues each day. The articles say the release pipeline runs on AWS Developer Tools, with CodeCommit as the agents' repository and GitHub receiving the code last.

The articles place the emulator among competing tools such as LocalStack, Moto and Floci, which differ in licensing, pricing and service coverage. AWS publishes a scores file with each release, so outside observers can review the test results. Its published fidelity figures show that control-plane operations match AWS most closely, while support for data-plane services, CloudFormation, Terraform and CDK varies widely. Operations not yet implemented return an HTTP 501 response, and the failing tests remain public in the evaluation suite.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave stock: up 39.2% in AI rebound since Nov 5
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave's stock has climbed 39.2% since the November 5 close, leading a rebound in AI-linked shares that has pushed the broader market higher. The strongest gains have come from smaller AI names, with AMD up 36.7%, Nebius up 28.5% and Micron up 23.6%. Over the same period the S&P 500 rose 3.6% and the Nasdaq gained 4.7%. Nvidia is the only name on the chart still below its November 5 close, down 4.3%. November 5 itself was the S&P 500's worst day since April 4, 2025.

On Wednesday, November 11, U.S. stocks rebounded as a strong quarterly report from CoreWeave revived confidence in AI spending. CoreWeave shares soared 24.71% after the company reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 168% from a year earlier. It also raised its full-year revenue forecast to between $13 billion and $13.3 billion. The Dow rose 0.49% to 52,486.49, the S&P 500 gained 1.31% to 7,619.38, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.6% to 25,466.19. Technology led the gainers with a 2.71% rise, while consumer discretionary was the only sector to fall.

Shares of Micron Technology and SanDisk each jumped more than 11%, and Advanced Micro Devices, Intel and Broadcom posted significant gains. Nvidia recovered part of its two-day slide, rising 2.87%, even after Baird cut its rating on the stock to neutral. An amended filing from Anthropic, which is preparing to go public, showed AMD and Micron among seven technology companies that agreed to buy a combined $26 billion of its shares. Kevin Rippey, a technology analyst at Evercore ISI, said sentiment around the frontier AI companies is the core driver of the AI trade and that he sees a bullish outlook into December.

The rally came as oil prices rose from two-month lows, with West Texas Intermediate settling at $86.53 a barrel, up 0.57%, amid doubts about a diplomatic settlement with Iran. The U.S. bond market was closed for Veterans Day, so there was no Treasury trading, a day after the 10-year yield topped 5% on hotter-than-expected inflation data. Traders still see a December rate hike as near-certain, with odds of a quarter-point move at about 90%, according to CME FedWatch. Investors next turn to weekly jobless claims and Nebius earnings on Thursday.

stories.Headline: Arctera Helps Companies Bring Business Information into Microsoft Copilot Workflows with Governance Controls in Place
stories.Summary:
Arctera, a business unit of Cloud Software Group, announced on November 12, 2026, new Model Context Protocol connectivity for Microsoft 365 Copilot from its base in San Ramon, California. The connectivity lets organizations bring enterprise information governed through Arctera into supported Copilot workflows. The capability gives employees access to more of their company's information for AI-assisted work while keeping established governance and compliance controls in place. The new connectivity is part of Arctera AI Converge, which uses MCP to link AI models with enterprise information that Arctera governs. The company said the connectivity is available now.

Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications with external data sources and tools. Through a custom federated connector, Microsoft 365 Copilot can reach Arctera's MCP server and interact with enterprise information governed through the platform. Organizations keep control over who can access the information, how it can be used, and how long it must be kept. The connectivity supports Arctera's Modern Compliance Intelligence strategy and builds on the Arctera Unified Platform's communications governance, compliance, and eDiscovery capabilities. Arctera's platform can capture data from more than 130 content sources and includes more than 280 AI policies.

Irfan Shuttari, product manager at Arctera, said that connecting enterprise information to Copilot requires preserving the governance controls built into that content. He said that pairing MCP connectivity with years of secure collaboration data managed within Arctera can accelerate regulatory inquiries and legal investigations while maintaining full compliance. Soniya Bopache, SVP and GM at Arctera, said that much of an organization's knowledge sits outside the workflows where employees could use it. She said the Copilot connectivity brings that information into work while preserving the governance controls businesses have established. Bopache added that leaders can get more value from information they already manage and from their AI investments.

The articles present the Arctera announcement as aimed at organizations that hold valuable information spread across systems and want their workforce to get more useful output from AI tools. Arctera is described as helping the biggest companies in the world monitor and control how their information is accessed, used and shared. Arctera was created in 2024 from Veritas Technologies. A separate article from ITWeb, dated November 12, 2026 and written by Joanne Carew for CloudZA in Johannesburg, covers AI governance for businesses. It recalls that in April South Africa's Draft National Artificial Intelligence Policy was officially withdrawn by Communications and Digital Technologies Minister Solly Malatsi because it contained fake, AI-generated academic references.

Jonathan Oaker, founder and CEO of CloudZA, advises that good AI governance starts with understanding the data a business holds and sorting it into categories. He recommends assessing AI tools by where each model gets its data, how it was trained and what access it has to business information. Oaker suggests weighing return on investment for the next six months or year and embracing Open Telemetry from day one. He says a business that cannot fail and handles identifiable data should consult a service provider or partner, and he warns that retrofitting governance later is complex and costly. Failing to consider governance can expose businesses to data breaches, legal liability and reputational damage.

The articles do not say when or how the Arctera connectivity will be adopted by specific customers, nor what results organizations have achieved with it. They also do not give pricing for the Arctera connectivity or detail how supported Copilot experiences are defined. The ITWeb article does not link its governance advice to the Arctera product. Whether Microsoft or other AI providers will expand similar connectivity is not addressed in the articles. The articles leave open how South Africa's AI policy will be revised after its withdrawal.

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind Releases AlphaGenome 2 for Cell-Type-Specific Variant Effects
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, a DNA model that predicts how genetic variants affect specific cell types. The company announced it on November 11, 2026, and the model is available through the AlphaGenome API for non-commercial research. Unlike its predecessor, which averaged results across bulk tissues, the new model resolves closely related cell types. It reads a 1 Mb window of human or mouse DNA together with a target cell state.

The model's input is a 1,048,576 base pair DNA window, and it is hosted only as an API for now, with weights to follow upon final publication. Training used 2,048 TPU v4 chips. The conditioning on cell state takes the form of a 256-dimensional embedding that modulates the network through FiLM layers. Outputs cover RNA coverage, CAGE, splicing, chromatin accessibility, histone marks, transcription factor binding, contact maps, and, as a new addition, CpG methylation. Researchers can pass raw single-cell counts, up to 256 cells per call, to obtain a condition embedding.

Google DeepMind is the developer, and the work was reported by researchers at the company, with Adam Gayoso, a research scientist at Google DeepMind involved in the project, describing the central advance. The company says the model turns static cell atlases into a predictive engine for human genetics. It also says the model identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells as its previous state-of-the-art model did. The company frames the work as a way to reveal disease-relevant effects in specific cells that broader models might miss.

The developers say the model is useful for scientists studying the causes of disease, because the same genetic variant can have different effects depending on the cell. Non-commercial researchers can use the API now, which limits commercial access. Anyone studying genetic variants in specific cell types, such as immune or heart muscle cells, stands to benefit from its finer-grained predictions. The model could also help scientists decide which gaps in experimental data to investigate next in the laboratory.

AlphaGenome 2 succeeds AlphaGenome, which DeepMind released last year, and the new model was built to address a gap in that earlier work. The earlier model predicted a fixed catalog of thousands of tracks in parallel, while the new one predicts outputs for one condition per call. Human cells carry the same DNA, yet heart muscle, skin and immune cells switch different genes on and off, which is why the variant effects differ. Across GTEx tissues, the model raised median Pearson correlation for cross-tissue expression changes from 0.61 to 0.71.

Several questions remain open in the articles. The parameter count and the final model weights have not been disclosed, and the articles do not say when the weights will be published. The sign prediction performance outside accessible chromatin reaches only 0.63 AUROC, and the articles do not explain why. Whether the model's predictions will translate into treatments is not established, since the articles only describe it as potentially pointing the way. The articles also do not say how the model will be used commercially after the non-commercial phase.

stories.Headline: KAIST Professor Predicts 100 AI Agents in Semiconductor Design
stories.Summary:
The two articles report that Kim Jung-ho, a KAIST professor who first proposed the core concept of HBM, unveiled a research system on November 11, 2026, at the online "TERA AI Agent Day" event. In his keynote, he described a setup in which a single human engineer commands about 100 AI agents to design semiconductors. The system is being developed by KAIST's TERA Lab, which he leads, and the goal is to demonstrate its core functions by the end of 2027. The articles say the system was tested in the design of next-generation HBM and high-bandwidth flash (HBF), and at the event researchers showed the AI producing performance results immediately after being asked.

Under the structure, a human enters only the design goal and the AI splits the work, runs commercial design tools and checks the results. A top-level "super agent" receives the goal in natural language, draws up a work plan, manages memory and access rights, and assigns tasks to specialized agents covering signal, power and thermal analysis before merging their output. Precise calculations such as signal integrity, voltage drop and resonant frequency are left to verified engineering tools, while language models are used only to interpret inputs and choose tools. The engineer keeps approval of critical steps such as tape-out. The articles also say the approach reuses the reasoning ability of existing AI models rather than training new ones, and they describe verification mechanisms intended to catch design errors.

Kim said the industry faces a triple challenge of shorter development cycles, rising design complexity and a shortage of skilled engineers, and he argued for agents that plan their own work and run specialized simulators rather than chatbots that only answer questions. Kim took part in core design and technical verification during HBM development in 2009 and contributed to SK Hynix commercializing the first HBM in December 2013, which is why he is called the "father of HBM." The articles also present TERA Lab's proposed tHBM and tHBF architectures, which place compute chips on top of memory stacks, and a uHBM structure that stacks memory on top of a GPU. The articles frame the work as aimed at industry bottlenecks, though they do not report a timeline beyond the 2027 demonstration target.

stories.Headline: Data443 Brings Convaa.ai™ to iPhone Duo: Live, Multi-Person AI Collaboration Now Available on the App Store for Apple's New Foldable
stories.Summary:
Data443 Risk Mitigation, Inc. announced on November 12, 2026, that its enterprise AI collaboration platform, Convaa.ai, is now available on the App Store and works with iPhone Duo, Apple's new foldable smartphone. The company said the app, version 1.5.0, lets teams work with AI together, live, including people from other companies. Convaa.ai brings employees and their partners, suppliers and customers into live sessions where several people prompt, review and refine AI work simultaneously. On the 7.6-inch inner display of iPhone Duo, the live AI session and the team conversation appear side by side. Separately, Google announced on November 11, 2026, that its Gemini Live assistant is coming to Apple CarPlay.

The enterprise decides who participates, which models are used and what data those models can reach, and all models run locally using native enterprise compute. Sessions are protected by Vaikora. On the 5.4-inch outer display, users can follow session activity and respond without unfolding the device. Apple's iPhone Duo became available in more than 70 countries and regions at launch on October 23, 2026, with 28 more beginning October 30, according to Apple. The Gemini integration lets drivers hold back-and-forth conversations through the vehicle's display by tapping the Gemini icon, and users must update the Gemini app, enable microphone permissions and have used Gemini Live on their phone at least once.

Jason Remillard, Chief Executive Officer and Founder of Data443, said that more of the work people do with AI happens on the phone than anyone plans for, and that it is rarely done alone. He said the company moved quickly to bring Convaa.ai to iPhone Duo with the same IT controls enterprises rely on elsewhere. Data443 Risk Mitigation, Inc., trading as OTCPK: ATDS, is headquartered in Research Triangle Park, North Carolina, and says it has more than 10,000 customers in over 100 countries. Google said the Gemini rollout is designed to let drivers accomplish more during commutes while minimizing distractions, and that users can interrupt Gemini or pause conversations when they need to concentrate on driving.

Apple cited Zoom and Slack among the third-party apps already taking advantage of the folding design of iPhone Duo. Data443 says its customers include organizations in more than 100 countries and that Convaa.ai is built on the same data classification, discovery and policy foundation as its other products. Through Google Workspace applications such as Gmail and Google Calendar, drivers can ask Gemini to summarize unread emails, check appointments and prepare for meetings. Gemini is available globally to iOS users in all languages supported by Gemini Live. Gemini already supports Android Auto and vehicles with Google built-in, and its earlier CarPlay integration was limited to Google Maps.

Other AI assistants have also been added to CarPlay, including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft's Copilot, Perplexity and xAI's Grok. Google said in September that its Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking models were designed to power more capable voice agents. The Gemini app surpassed 1 billion monthly active users in August, becoming Google's fastest-growing product to reach that milestone, according to the company. The Data443 announcement also notes that video and audio capabilities for Convaa.ai are expected to be released shortly. stories.Headline: AI Scams: What families should know this holiday season
stories.Summary:
Veriff, an identity platform company, issued a warning on November 12, 2026, through GlobeNewswire from New York, saying that scams driven by artificial intelligence are set to target holiday shoppers. Its fraud expert Ira Bondar-Mucci shared tips to help shoppers stay ahead of increasingly convincing scams as Black Friday, Cyber Monday and the rest of the holiday sales season approach. The same day, the Alabama station WALA published a segment from Mobile in which gerontologist Rodnée Warr explained what families should watch for this holiday season. The WALA piece said artificial intelligence is making familiar scams more convincing, with deepfake calls, videos and images that can seem to come from loved ones or other trusted people. Both pieces were published on November 12, 2026, and both focus on how AI is changing fraud before the busiest shopping weeks of the year.

The Veriff release lists four habits for safer holiday shopping. The first is to start at the source, entering the retailer's address or opening its app instead of tapping an ad, text or social post, and the second is to treat any celebrity or influencer endorsement as unconfirmed until the same offer appears on the retailer's own website. The third is to keep one-time passcodes private and avoid completing an ID or selfie check through a link someone sent you, on the rule that if you did not start it, you should stop. The fourth is to stay on the platform, pay by credit card for the strongest protection, and treat any request to switch to a bank transfer, gift cards or crypto as a red flag. International Fraud Prevention Week runs from November 15 to 21, and WALA said Warr would explain what to do when something does not seem right.

Bondar-Mucci, who is Fraud Platform Lead at Veriff, said sales events squeeze the time people take to decide, so shoppers click on things they would normally question, and fraudsters build their campaigns around that habit. She said the tricks themselves are familiar, such as fake deals, bogus delivery notices and phony customer support, but AI has made them cheaper to create, more believable and much easier to run at scale. She argued that shoppers should not have to carry this alone and that organizations relying on manual review, or on customers vouching for themselves, are exposed. In her view, retailers, marketplaces and payment providers need checks that do not hinge on what the human eye can see, including confirming a live person is present, making sure the camera feed has not been tampered with, and linking signals across sessions so a reused face or device is noticed. She added that protection should not end at sign-up, because some of the riskiest moments come later, such as a password reset, a new payout account or a large order placed mid-sale, and she said the deepfake arms race is an AI problem that will take AI to solve.

Those most affected include parents, grandparents, neighbors and older loved ones, according to WALA, and the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center 2025 Annual Report found that Americans aged 60 and older reported more than $7.7 billion in fraud losses in 2025, a 59% increase from the previous year. Veriff's Deepfakes Report 2026, produced with Kantar, found that Americans and Britons do only slightly better than chance at telling real visuals from AI-generated ones, and video proved the trickiest format for both groups. Roughly half of Americans, and slightly fewer Britons, said they could reliably spot manipulated media, yet their actual results were close to random guessing, and in the UK more than one in five admit they do not try to verify suspicious content online. About 7% of people fall into an especially high-risk group who struggle to identify fakes, feel sure of themselves anyway, and seldom check a second source. Bondar-Mucci said that is exactly who a well-made deepfake ad is aimed at, because once people feel they cannot be fooled they stop looking for warning signs.

The release explains that scam shops no longer have to rely on a polished website alone, because they can add a video of a familiar-looking face endorsing the offer, a support agent on a live video call, or a cloned voice saying an order is on hold until payment details are confirmed. Generative AI also lets a single fraudster produce hundreds of fake identities, each with a face, a document and a backstory, which are used to set up seller, payment and buy-now-pay-later accounts as well as mule accounts for moving stolen funds. Any one identity may pass inspection, and the giveaway is the pattern, such as the same face, device or network appearing across accounts that supposedly belong to different people. Some scams enlist genuine people instead, approaching targets through a bogus job offer, a prize or refund claim, or a romance or investment chat and asking them to complete an identity check for someone else. The report was an online survey by Kantar of 3,000 adults aged 18 to 64 in the US, the UK and Brazil, and Britons are the most familiar with the term deepfake among the countries surveyed, though that awareness has not sharpened detection.

International Fraud Prevention Week, running from November 15 to 21, falls ahead of the holiday sales season, and Warr's guidance on what to do when something does not seem right was set to be shared with families. Fraudsters often steer victims away from the shopping platform and toward a text thread, messaging app, bank transfer, gift cards or crypto, where buyer protections no longer apply, and the release says genuine retailers do not ask customers to move a conversation or payment off-platform. Neither article says how many shoppers will be targeted this season or how much money these scams may cost them. WALA does not detail the specific steps Warr recommends beyond saying she would explain them. Veriff's release likewise gives no timetable for when retailers, marketplaces and payment providers might adopt the checks Bondar-Mucci calls for.
