stories.Headline: Putting AI on pause: South Portland schools consider moratorium
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 9, 2026, the South Portland School Board voted 6-1 against a proposed moratorium on student-facing generative AI use for the remainder of the 2026-2027 school year. Only At-Large Board Member Claire Holman, who originally proposed the moratorium, voted in favor of it. The vote came at the board's regular meeting, which included several highly anticipated agenda items. WGME reported the result late that Monday evening, and its story was updated the following morning. The South Portland School Department remains without a specific AI policy after the failed vote.

Official city documents show the moratorium would have paused student-facing generative AI use in classrooms and assignments for students in grades PreK-8 across the South Portland School District. The pause was meant to give the board time to develop an appropriate AI policy. The proposal also stated that the school department would make sure all staff received two hours of AI awareness training and three hours of AI literacy training. After finishing that training, teachers would have been allowed to use only AI tools sanctioned by the South Portland School Department. Exceptions could have covered assistive technologies and centrally approved instructional uses.

Holman, who brought the proposal, told the meeting that nothing in it stops students from learning about AI or stops teachers from generating a whole curriculum with it. She said she knew some audience members were laughing at her. She voiced concern about the consequences of allowing student-facing AI use without a moratorium, asking what happens if kids cannot think, and saying simply that she does not like it. Board Chair Rosemarie DeAngelis said she would not support the moratorium that night, based on what she had heard, and stressed waiting for a more detailed plan on AI use. Superintendent Dr. Angela Atkinson Duina also opposed the proposal, saying she is confident in the judgment and oversight of the district's educators.

Board Vice Chair Tyler Smith and At-Large Board Member Eleni Richardson also spoke against the moratorium, and Richardson said many high school students she has spoken with are not excited about AI use. Student Representative Sarah Lupien said AI has not hurt her own learning, since many of her classes never discuss it, and she trusts her teachers to decide how to use it. Peter Wetzel, a middle school computer science teacher and South Portland resident, said it was his first time hearing of the moratorium and that it would directly affect a curriculum he worked hard to build. Cidney Mayes, who teaches digital literacy to fifth and sixth graders at South Portland Middle School, said AI literacy makes up a significant part of her curriculum and that the moratorium would cost her four weeks of instruction. She called the proposal an overstep and later thanked the board for rejecting it, saying something is wrong if she must justify her curriculum, while a Waldo T. Skillin Elementary School teacher said the board should have asked teachers who actually do this job.

Other speakers were split. One community member warned that using AI in certain ways weakens children's critical thinking, and the mother of a kindergartner at Frank I. Brown Elementary School supported the resolution but urged exceptions for classes that teach AI literacy. Brown School's librarian asked why she should not talk with children about AI when they already raise it with her. South Portland High School student Ian Archibald said some teachers weave AI into their courses, but that the repetition he has noticed has lowered his learning experience. WMTW had reported before the vote that the board would consider the ban over concerns about negative effects on children's cognitive development.

The moratorium was limited to students in grades PreK-8 and would have lasted only through the current school year. Mayes teaches students about what a language learning model is, about bias, about the upsides and downsides of AI, and about its environmental impacts. WGME's coverage tagged the story with topics including cybersecurity, student education, staff training and AI integration. Wetzel and Mayes both said they had not been consulted before the proposal came forward. The board's stated purpose for the pause was to buy time to write a policy, which the district still does not have.

Board members told WGME that the conversation is far from over, even though the ban failed to pass. Officials are now working on a comprehensive plan set to launch in January, which will address AI integration as well as broader cybersecurity issues in the district. DeAngelis tied her opposition to waiting for a more detailed plan addressing AI use. The articles do not say what the January plan will contain, whether it will limit student use, or how teachers will be consulted. They also do not say whether the proposed staff training will go ahead, or whether Holman or anyone else will bring back a new moratorium proposal.

stories.Headline: Hackers stole AI credentials to get $740,000 in free compute; Railway picked up the bill
stories.Summary:
Hackers exploited Railway, a cloud hosting provider, in an attack that began on October 20 and lasted nearly 26 hours. They first exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway's build infrastructure, evading filesystem isolation protections to obtain an internal credential. Using that credential, they accessed stored build histories and retrieved a copy of Railway's internal source code. They then used a misconfigured trust relationship to reach more of the infrastructure and obtain credentials that decrypt customer environment variables. Railway disclosed the incident on October 22 and posted a follow-up report the week of November 11.

The attackers were fully evicted on October 21, after they had decrypted a subset of roughly 100,000 customer variables, or at most 1.85 percent of workspaces. They generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges, with customers reporting that their keys answered coding questions and performed training-data tasks they never ran. The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to more than 1,850 users, including GitHub and OAuth tokens that Railway reset. Railway worked with GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Stripe and others to revoke potentially compromised keys. Customers were advised to revoke and reapply sensitive environment variables stored on Railway before October 21.

Railway is working to reimburse customers, including for charges that providers decline to refund. The company said it shut down potentially compromised internal tooling and rolled all keys after validating that intruders had been shut out. It moved to a new generation of infrastructure, rebuilt the tooling used to run its infrastructure, and added functionality to mass revoke app permissions after suspicious activity. Railway also said it is moving to short-lived credentials and logging every decryption. The company described the incident as a contest of agent speed, in which both attackers and defenders worked in parallel.

David Shipley of Beauceron Security said AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers, and that so-called LLMjacking is expected to displace cryptojacking. Frank Dickson of Dickson Research called Railway's report remarkably candid, noting that it owns its configuration mistake and admits it cannot be sure it found every account the attacker created. Dickson said stolen keys let thieves get cost-free compute while the key owners pay the bill. Customers of Railway, he advised, should treat every stored secret as stolen until rotated. The affected parties are Railway's customers, the 1,850-plus users with linked accounts, and the AI providers whose keys were misused.

AI credentials are cheap to harvest at scale, and attackers can resell access through so-called AI routers that provide models users otherwise could not afford. Such access is valuable for distillation, which transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one to cut costs. Dickson said training on another model's answers takes millions of questions, and stolen keys spread those questions across thousands of real customers. An investigation by Wiz found that stolen keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft, then flooded with traffic four to seven days later. Wiz also found that a key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles left most of the thief's traffic throttled.

Railway said it cannot yet share the specific details and scale of the exploits because the investigation is ongoing. Dickson advised customers to check AI provider bills and usage logs, rotate cloud, database and payment credentials, and set hard spending caps on every AI key. Customers were also advised to remove public network access to databases, check GitHub audit logs and Dockerhub registry logs, and review all app access. The articles do not say whether Railway has found every account the attacker created, nor whether all reimbursements will be paid. They also leave open whether providers will refund the disputed charges they have declined to reverse.

stories.Headline: Analysis: Paralegals Can Bridge the Gap Between AI and Legal Practice
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence now runs through legal practice, from automated research tools to predictive analytics and case management software. Megan Goor, a Fort Worth paralegal, argues that paralegals are well placed to lead its adoption because they are often the first to work with new tools. She cites former State Bar President Allan DuBois, who called paralegals the "first responders" to lawyers and law firms. In her article for Fort Worth Inc., published on November 12, 2026, she says the job is to ensure AI is used properly, efficiently and ethically. Her piece sets out what paralegals need to understand before they bring these tools into their daily work.

The gap she describes is one of confidence, understanding and accountable integration between legal professionals and AI. Many attorneys and staff know AI exists but are unsure how to use it safely, while others experiment without knowing its risks. Client data must stay confidential under the American Bar Association's guidance on generative AI, and paralegals should check whether a tool is closed or public. They should also confirm whether safeguards such as encryption, access controls and vendor audits are in place. Studies report that even legal-specific tools may hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time, so outputs and citations must be verified before reaching attorneys.

Paralegals should also watch for bias caused by incomplete or nonrepresentative training data. Goor places responsibility for supervision with attorneys, while noting that paralegals work under that supervision. ABA Formal Opinion 512, issued in July 2024, requires lawyers to understand the AI tools they use and to review outputs independently. The Texas Professional Ethics Committee issued Opinion 705 in 2025 after a request from the State Bar's Taskforce on Responsible AI in the Law Committee. An amendment to the Texas Disciplinary Rules added a duty of technological competence for attorneys.

Goor says these obligations extend derivatively to paralegals, who must ensure AI-related tasks are properly supervised and reviewed. She recommends continuing education, safe testing with non-confidential data, documentation of every AI-assisted task and participation in drafting firm AI policies. The article's audience is paralegals and the legal profession generally, and the practical effect is that every AI-assisted task must be logged and checked by a human. Goor writes that AI cannot replace the human skills that define strong paralegals, such as critical thinking, empathy, strategic judgment and advocacy.

She says paralegals become indispensable by guiding responsible use of the technology rather than being replaced by it. Her five tips tell readers never to put client names or privileged information into public or free tools. They also tell readers to treat AI as a helper that does not understand the law, verify all output, and check their firm's AI policy before use. The article gives background showing that the regulatory picture is still developing.

Goor points to ABA guidance from July 2024 and to Texas Opinion 705 from 2025 as the main ethics authorities for lawyers and paralegals. She also notes that Texas courts are issuing their own rules, citing a Southern District of Texas General Order 2025-04 dated May 7, 2025, and a standing order from the Denton County District Courts. Goor, a trial litigation paralegal at Cantey Hanger LLP who holds TBLS-BCP certification, has served as president of the Paralegal Division and sits on the State Bar's Emerging Technology Committee. She draws on a State Bar of Texas AI Toolkit and a Paralegal Ethics Handbook as resources.

The article does not say how courts or the State Bar will enforce the new duties or how quickly rules on AI disclosure will change. It leaves open how firms will resolve the conflicts between AI tools and confidentiality, and how much verification will be enough. Goor's closing argument is that paralegals should apply their long-standing role of helping lawyers work efficiently to AI through understanding and empowerment. The articles do not describe any specific next steps beyond that, and they give no timetable for further guidance.

stories.Headline: Nscale’s AI Data Center Plans Come With A Big Bill
stories.Summary:
Congress is weighing a bipartisan bill that critics say would speed the buildout of AI data centers. On Monday, November 9, 2026, the Senate voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, which aims to ease construction of new energy infrastructure. The bill has broad support, including from labor leaders who say it will produce thousands of jobs and from clean energy advocates who believe it could unlock wind and solar. Its sponsors hope to pass it before the current Congress ends in January. A growing coalition of anti-data center critics has pushed back hard, arguing it would accelerate an industry that Americans voted against in the midterm elections.

BAAJA would require data centers to pay the full cost of the upgrades they trigger and includes transmission reforms meant to modernize the grid. It would also strip back environmental protections and could lead to more data centers powered by gas and built on public lands. The bill would ease permitting, limiting judges' ability to halt construction over environmental review. Under one study, data centers would pay about $55 billion in transmission charges over ten years, roughly $35 billion more than under current policy. The bill also establishes protections so households and businesses are not left paying for failed projects.

Following Monday's cloture vote, the Senate must still vote to take up the legislation, and any Senate-passed version must pass the House in identical form before reaching Trump. Sponsors argue the bill addresses the public's main data center concerns, and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic sponsor, said last week that "the day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes." Donald Trump urged the Senate to pass the bill on Truth Social on Sunday, writing that "China will take any Data Center that we don't want." Allie Rosenbluth, U.S. campaigns manager at Oil Change International, called the bill a massive giveaway to the data center industry that creates a backdoor for fossil fuels. Holly Bender, chief program officer of the Sierra Club, said the data center industry is driving a historic and alarming investment in gas and fossil fuels.

Hundreds of local and national organizations, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, have signed letters urging Congress not to pass the bill as written. Critics say the bill would most directly affect communities, Tribal Nations and the public in places where data centers are proposed. A coalition of Tribal leaders wrote on Saturday that the bill would gut the ability of Tribal Nations and the public to protect historic and cultural places threatened by federally connected projects. Many industry trade groups support the bill, even though it would likely make building more expensive.

Meg Slattery, a staff scientist at Earthjustice, said more gas pipelines could increase data center demand and soak up new power. Michele Jawando, CEO of Omidyar Network, said that trying to pass the bill in a lame duck Congress before a hundred new House members arrive is never a good look. Critics also point to the protests against the CoreWeave AI data center in Kenilworth, New Jersey, in October. The articles describe a boom in gas power tied to data centers, with Global Energy Monitor data reported by Wired showing U.S. gas projects powering data centers rising from about 4 gigawatts in early 2024 to 189 gigawatts in development by mid-2026.

Many developers built their own gas plants rather than waiting to connect to the grid, and researchers say some plants worsened local pollution and asthma. The Trump administration signed an executive order in July 2025 directing the Interior and Energy departments to make federal sites available for data centers. At least 17 active applications for data center campuses on public land, covering thousands of acres in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada and other states, were found in one recent study. The Senate's next steps, and whether the bill passes before January, remain unresolved, and the articles do not say how the amendment process will turn out.

stories.Headline: AI Debt Under Pressure: Credit Spreads Widen as Democrats Target AI Regulation - News and Statistics
stories.Summary:
Bond investors have become more cautious about debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom, reflecting worries that a Democrat-controlled Congress will try to slow AI investment and data center expansion. Reuters reported the shift, and the articles place it in the week after the midterm elections. US high-yield credit spreads widened to 348 basis points during last Thursday's stock-market swoon, according to ICE BofA US Corporate Index data. That was the widest level since May 2025, one month after President Donald Trump imposed global tariffs. By Friday, the spreads had narrowed to 342 basis points.

Investment-grade spreads stood at 93 basis points last Thursday, compared with 91 basis points in the previous session. Single-B spreads widened 35 basis points to 367 basis points, which led the deterioration in the high-yield market and marked their highest levels since March. Galaxy Helios Data Center bonds fell to 89.25 cents on the dollar on November 5, lifting yields to 13 per cent. Those bonds carry a B+ rating and were sold by a wholly owned unit of Galaxy Digital in late July at a yield of 9.875 per cent. Many data center bonds sit in the BB and single-B tiers of the junk bond market, and they have faced fresh pressure in recent weeks, especially during the technology selloff.

Democrats plan to introduce a flood of new legislation targeting AI systems and data center development when they take control of Congress in January. Republican President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed calls to write mandatory rules for AI technology. Over the weekend, following a historic midterm loss for his party, he signaled openness to safeguards. The articles do not say what form those safeguards might take or when the president might act.

Larry Holzenthaler, a senior portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds in New York, said markets are definitely anxious and that he would not be surprised by continued volatility in high yield and loans. Ali Hassan, a portfolio manager at Thornburg Investment Management, said appetite is more cautious and discriminating, with scrutiny prompting a review of credits from developers to contractors to suppliers. Peter Yanulis, a multi-asset portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles, warned that a slowdown would have second-order effects on the supply chain, power producers, electrical contractors, equipment and machinery makers, and data center developers. Abiel Reinhart, a senior economist at J.P. Morgan, said any slowdown in data center development could materially slow overall business investment.

Healthy corporate fundamentals continue to support the market, according to analysts and portfolio managers. A deeper reassessment of AI-related risk could still push spreads wider in both high-yield and investment-grade debt, as investors anticipate stricter regulation. Investment in artificial intelligence and its supporting infrastructure has been a major engine of US expansion this year, helping keep growth resilient despite broad uncertainties. Some investors believe a slowdown could be healthy for the credit market and for AI companies, because stricter regulation would mean less bond issuance, which should support prices. Yanulis said the market can now digest a transition period over the next six to 12 months, after the open floodgates of AI supply.

Karen Choi, a portfolio manager at Capital Group, said political and regulatory uncertainty could affect the later years, 2028 to 2030 and beyond. She added that it is unlikely to change capex and issuance numbers for 2027 significantly, because many projects are underway and capital commitments have been made. Investors see little risk of an immediate pullback in borrowing or spending on projects already under construction. Ben Emons, chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors, argued that AI is not going to slow down, and that a slowdown in Texas would simply pop up in another state. The articles leave open how far spreads will move, what legislation Democrats will actually propose, and how the president's openness to safeguards will play out.

stories.Headline: Law Schools Take Varied Approaches in Adapting to AI
stories.Summary:
Law schools are rethinking how they train future lawyers as artificial intelligence takes over tasks that junior attorneys once learned by doing. Recent graduates in entry-level roles may now be asked to use AI for research and document review instead of building skills through repetition. A 2024 study found that AI-assisted highlighting cut the time law students spent on the task by 30 percent. Stanford research on AI legal research tools found hallucination rates ranging from 17 percent to 33 percent. Professors and researchers are therefore reconsidering how to teach students to use AI, assess its outputs, and understand its effects on the legal system.

Stanford law professor Julian Nyarko said that rote contract reading and due diligence were never an efficient way to build judgment, though they were the traditional route. He argued that if that work is disappearing, it could prompt a more careful look at other ways to teach legal and critical thinking. AI already handles much of the document-heavy work once given to junior lawyers. Homebuilder Century Communities asked an intern to use AI to review and summarize 87 land contracts without help from senior lawyers. The firm Ashurst Perkins Coie used generative AI to map document requests against a database of 400,000 previously produced documents, cutting the timeline from six weeks to three.

Maura Grossman, a professor at the University of Waterloo, said law schools face competing pressures about what to teach. Schools may want students to practice memos and document searches that they may no longer get on the job, while also focusing on critical thinking and judgment. She asked whether future partners would be people who can do more than enter questions into large language models and retrieve answers. Nyarko's research lab built an AI deposition simulator that lets attorneys practice questioning witnesses with traits such as forgetfulness or hostility.

An American Bar Association Task Force on Law and AI survey of 29 law school deans and faculty found that 55 percent of respondents' schools offered AI courses. The same survey found that 83 percent offered opportunities for students to learn about AI, and 69 percent had changed academic integrity policies because of the technology. The University of San Francisco School of Law introduced AI into its first-year curriculum in the 2024-25 academic year. Nyarko said instructors at Stanford set their own rules, banning devices during class in his early contracts course while encouraging outside experimentation.

Grossman asks students to use AI on some assignments and keep a reflection journal, which led one student who relied on AI summaries to reconsider skipping the assigned readings. Nyarko said AI now affects almost every class because it appears across many areas of law, including in the case Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Company, where Judge Kevin Newsom consulted ChatGPT on the meaning of "landscaping." Grossman said courts reviewing an employer's AI hiring screen would need to assess whether the system is reliable, valid, and unbiased, and whether its decisions can be independently tested.

Traditional standards for authenticating recordings may not be enough when AI can produce convincing deepfakes. Nyarko cautioned against glamorizing the legal system before AI, saying he sees enormous potential for better legal representation and access to justice. A separate November 10, 2026 release from K Altman Law reported that Google plans to turn off Gemini and AI search for kindergarten through twelfth-grade student accounts until schools enable them. The company announced those changes on November 3, with further school details promised in the coming months before rollout.

stories.Headline: New Report: The Impact of AI on Student Safety and Learning Needs Strong Guardrails and Support for Educators - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
Texas 2036, a nonpartisan public policy organization, released a report on November 10, 2026, titled "In Ctrl of AI in Schools." The report concludes that artificial intelligence can help or harm Texas students depending on the decisions people make around it. Its findings say AI benefits appear when tools are built with safeguards, when clear guidance governs their use, and when an educator controls how they are used in instruction. The report arrived as AI use in Texas schools is outpacing the rules governing it. Texas lawmakers were beginning to file legislation for the 2027 session when the report was released.

A fall 2025 survey of Texas school and district leaders, conducted by the University of Texas at Austin and the Texas Association of School Administrators, found that 86% said teachers were using AI. The same survey found that 61% reported student use. Only 29% of leaders reported a district policy governing student AI use, and just 20% had one for teachers and staff. The report offers insights for the state's efforts to give schools and teachers the resources they need. Its four priorities call for statewide guidance, student safety, equipped teachers and students prepared for an AI-driven future.

Renzo Soto, deputy director of education and workforce policy at Texas 2036 and the report's author, said that school leaders and teachers must control how AI appears in schools. Soto said the early research does not show that AI is simply good or bad for students. Mary Lynn Pruneda, director of education and workforce policy at Texas 2036, said parents should be able to trust that classroom technology is safe, protects privacy and helps students learn. Pruneda said safety and effectiveness must be the starting point for AI in classrooms, not an afterthought. The report does not advocate putting AI in every classroom or banning it entirely.

The report analyzes mixed evidence on AI and learning, in which some studies find real gains, others find real harms, and many find both. The difference often depends on how tools are designed, how teachers guide their use, and whether students can think critically and independently. Three laws passed in Texas in 2025 established a foundation for responsible AI governance, including requirements affecting public school districts. Those broad standards have yet to be translated into consistent, classroom-specific guidance. The report finds that 42 states have issued statewide AI guidance or model policies for schools, while Texas is among the eight that have not.

Texas 2036's 10th Texas Voter Poll found strong public support for protecting students as AI enters classrooms. Nearly 85% of Texas voters said protecting student data and privacy is extremely or very important if schools use AI. More than three-quarters prioritize safety and quality standards for AI tools, and 71% said teaching students to use AI responsibly and ethically is important. The report's four priorities are establishing statewide guidance, putting student safety first, equipping Texas teachers, and preparing students for an AI-driven future. Building on Texas 2036's recently released legislative agenda, these priorities target responsible AI use in K–12 education.

This report is the first installment of Texas 2036's research on artificial intelligence in K–12 education. A second report will analyze policies, guidance and resources from other states to help Texas build a statewide model policy. That model policy is intended to prioritize student safety and learning. The articles do not say when the second report will be released or whether Texas lawmakers will adopt any of the report's priorities in the 2027 session.

stories.Headline: 'Parents are concerned.' Norwalk Public Schools hosts community forum on rapidly evolving AI and screentime policy - News12
stories.Summary:
Norwalk Public Schools held a community forum on Tuesday night, November 10, 2026, where education leaders discussed how artificial intelligence should be used in classrooms and how much screen time students should have. The district already has some rules in place, but parents said more needs to be done before new policies take effect. One parent, John Demarco, asked the district to slow down and consider the possible consequences first. He wants the district to present a plan supported by data before introducing anything new. His concern is especially personal, since he has a first grader in the system and a 2-year-old who will attend later.

Ralph Valenzisi, the assistant superintendent of Digital Learning and Innovation, described the rules the district already follows. Daily screen time limits are set by grade level, screens are not allowed during recess, certain sites such as YouTube are blocked, and a bell-to-bell cellphone ban applies to grades K-8. He said the district is gathering more information so that an official policy can be written. Valenzisi acknowledged that parents are concerned and that the concern is justified. He also said the district needs time and some grace while staff work out how to approach AI, so that it can learn alongside everyone else.

The district hopes to have a more complete policy in place by March 2027. Valenzisi's comments make clear that the district is responsible for drafting that policy, and he framed the current effort as one of gathering data and building the policy carefully. Parents at the forum pressed for caution and for evidence before any change is made. The articles do not describe any specific new rule that has been adopted, and they do not say what the policy will ultimately require. Both News 12 versions of the story report the same forum and the same district statements.

stories.Headline: Arkansas governor embraces Trump, calls for AI guardrails in new book
stories.Summary:
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders released a new book on Tuesday in which she praises President Donald Trump's leadership. The book came out a week after Republicans suffered heavy losses in a midterm that was widely seen as a rebuke of Trump by voters. Sanders, who won reelection last week and is considered a potential 2028 presidential hopeful, also distanced herself from the president by calling for "commonsense" guardrails on artificial intelligence. The book is titled "Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy," and it covers her election and first term as Arkansas governor. In it she also writes about her family and her Christian faith, regularly quoting the Bible and authors such as C.S. Lewis.

The book arrives as Republicans grapple with an election in which they lost control of the U.S. House, the Senate and a majority of governorships. Sanders was first elected in 2022 and won a second term by double digits this year. Even so, Republicans lost the supermajority in the state House that is needed to pass most budget bills without Democratic support. On artificial intelligence, Sanders highlights her opposition to a provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill tax and spending cut law, signed last year, that would have prevented states from regulating the technology. The book also covers her stalled plan for a 3,000-bed prison in Franklin County, her 2022 thyroid cancer diagnosis, and her 2023 State of the Union rebuttal.

Sanders says in the book that she decided to run for governor with Trump's leadership style in mind, hoping to bring bold, new leadership to Arkansas. She writes that she loves Arkansas but was not blind to the problems the state faced. On artificial intelligence, she writes that Trump is right that the United States must win the AI race against China to survive. She adds that the race cannot become a race to the bottom that enriches billionaires in Silicon Valley and leaves the rest of America behind. She also wrote that conservatives should be skeptical of Big Tech when it comes to AI.

Trump has dismissed the calls for more guardrails around artificial intelligence, which is where Sanders parts ways with him. The provision that would have blocked state regulation of AI was stripped from the legislation after Sanders and other Republicans objected. On the prison plan, Sanders faced resistance from locals, from members of the Board of Corrections, and from lawmakers of both parties. She expresses frustration at opposition from her own party and labels those opponents, along with Democrats, the "coalition of the unwilling." She writes that she expected to fight the left over making communities safer, but had no idea some of the fiercest opposition would come from within her own party.

Sanders served as White House press secretary during Trump's first term and touted his endorsement when she first ran for governor. She has signed into law measures limiting youths' access to social media. She was diagnosed with thyroid cancer in 2022, just a couple of months before she was elected governor, and returned to the campaign trail after surgery and being declared cancer-free. Doctors had warned her that some patients suffer damage to their vocal chords or changes to their voice, which she says could have derailed her career, though the damage did not occur. Shortly after taking office in 2023, she hesitated before accepting an invitation to deliver the Republican response to President Joe Biden's State of the Union address.

Sanders put the Franklin County prison project on hold after the resistance she met. The articles do not say whether the project will resume or what will become of it. Her speech painted a bleak picture of life under Biden, but she says it only reached that form after she and First Gentleman Bryan Sanders revised a first draft that was too dark and heavy on policy. She says she and the unnamed speechwriter agreed to part ways after she rewrote the speech. The articles do not say what Sanders will do next, and they offer no announcement about a 2028 run beyond describing her as a potential hopeful.

stories.Headline: Ohio likely won’t pass AI regulations before year ends
stories.Summary:
Ohio currently has no substantial artificial intelligence regulations, and lawmakers from both parties are trying to change that before their December deadline arrives. One Republican leader is blocking those efforts, saying that none of the bills are ready for a vote. The chair of the House Technology and Innovation Committee, Thad Claggett of Licking County, spoke after hearing bills on Monday. Eight bills on artificial intelligence sit in his committee, and he has not advanced any of them toward a floor vote. As a result, Ohio will most likely reach the end of the year without passing any new rules on the technology.

House Bill 524 would establish penalties for developers whose artificial intelligence models generate content that encourages self-harm or violence. Under the bill, the state would be able to investigate such cases and impose civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation. The money collected would go to the state's 988 crisis hotline and to consumer protection enforcement. The bill was introduced by Democratic state Rep. Christine Cockley of Columbus, Republican state Rep. Ty Mathews of Findlay, and a bipartisan group of other legislators. Other measures in Claggett's committee would require watermarks on images altered by artificial intelligence, make it a crime to generate AI child sexual abuse material, and prevent AI marriage.

Claggett, a Republican, said he wants to write really good law rather than law that must be amended immediately after it passes. He told reporters that no bill in his committee is ready for a vote, and he is not aware of any that lack serious downsides. Those downsides, as he described them, include problems for liberty and burdens he considers unnecessary. He pushed back on the idea of targeting developers, arguing that the problem lies generations down the line from them, with a bot acting through its own systems. His comments referred to the president's use of the term Super Intelligence, and the articles do not explain that reference further.

Cockley said that Ohio is not preventing deaths right now, and she criticized the current supermajority for its priorities. In her view, the legislature is not putting a priority on helping people who are dying by suicide after making plans with chatbots. She disagrees with Claggett about the cause of the delay, saying that tech companies are spending money to hold back legislation. She pointed to a large amount of money in politics, which she believes makes legislators afraid to act, along with fear of big tech and of the status quo. She added that lawmakers also fear the unknown nature of the technology, and the parents of a 13-year-old girl agree that things should not have gotten this far.

As artificial intelligence chatbots become more mainstream, wrongful death lawsuits have started appearing across the country. Court documents say the victims come from all walks of life but share one thing, which is that each received help from a bot. The latest case involves a 13-year-old whose parents are suing after Google's AI chatbot Gemini allegedly helped the child form a suicide plan over a matter of weeks. She survived, according to the reporting. Lawmakers in Ohio have been trying to address artificial intelligence policy for years, yet the effort continues to stall, and Gov. Mike DeWine has repeatedly pushed for safety regulations.

Lawmakers have until mid-December to pass guardrails, and Claggett's statements suggest that is unlikely to happen. Cockley sees hope beyond that point, saying that if nothing is done this year, next year may bring a different result. She cited Governor-elect Amy Acton and a change in her party's position from superminority as reasons for that hope. She said there is hope for her bill either way, though the articles do not say whether it will be reintroduced or what its path would be. The articles also leave open whether any of the eight bills will receive a vote before the deadline, and whether Claggett will change his view.

stories.Headline: Banks seek to rein in soaring AI agent costs, McKinsey says - CNA
stories.Summary:
Banks around the world are trying to curb the rising cost of AI agents, according to McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review published on November 10, 2026. The consultancy warns that spending on the tokens that power these agents could reach as much as 20 percent of total labor costs. Banks have begun shifting responsibility for AI spending to new teams, which some institutions call AI FinOps. Early efforts to control expenses relied on routing employees to different AI models depending on how complex their queries were.

Those earlier methods do not work well once AI agents are active, because the agents communicate with one another and their token usage adds up quickly. As a result, banks are becoming more selective about where they deploy agentic AI, concentrating on areas with the strongest expected returns. Productivity savings are comparatively easy to measure, so banks are increasingly weighing AI-driven revenue growth when deciding whether higher spending is justified. Most banks currently block external AI agents from authorizing transactions within their systems, which has kept the effect on profits limited so far.

Vik Sohoni, a senior partner at McKinsey and one of the report's authors, explained the problem in an interview with Reuters. He said the model-routing systems banks first used are ineffective for agent-driven workloads. The report also finds that customers are adopting AI faster than they adopted earlier technologies. McKinsey expects AI agents to become widely used within three years, compared with the five to ten years it took mobile internet to reach broad adoption.

A McKinsey survey of 46,000 retail banking customers worldwide found that most already use AI to compare banking services, find higher-yield savings accounts, and refinance or consolidate debt. Of those who use AI, 72 percent said they would let a banking agent carry out one financial task, although they would cap autonomous approvals at $500. Meta's Muse agent was downloaded 5 million times in the United States during its first 22 days after launch. The report notes that AI agents could help banks grow revenue and cut costs, but they could also squeeze profits by moving deposits from non-interest-bearing accounts into higher-yielding ones.

stories.Headline: Sharp to Launch Second Poketomo AI Character in Japan and Taiwan on December 5
stories.Summary:
Sharp Corporation will launch the second Poketomo conversational AI character in Japan and Taiwan on December 5, 2026, the first anniversary of Poketomo. The launch coincides with a new feature that lets nearby Poketomo chat freely with each other, and a new pricing plan for owners of multiple units. Sharp announced the plan in a press release dated November 12, 2026, from Osaka. The company said the launch will bring more ways to enjoy life with multiple Poketomo. Special events will be held on December 5 and 6 to mark the launch and the first anniversary.

The new feature will be available from December 5 and requires two Poketomo registered in advance to the same app. It can be used with any combination of first- and second-generation Poketomo. The new Share Plan allows the number of conversations included in each plan to be shared among two to five Poketomo robots registered under a single Share Plan. Conversations that start automatically between Poketomo do not count toward each plan's conversation limit.

The Share Plan applies only to the robot version of Poketomo, not the app version. A campaign offers the Premium plan, priced at 990 yen per month including tax and allowing 800 conversations per month, free for three months, from December 5, 2026, to January 31, 2027. Sharp is the company responsible for the launch and the Poketomo brand, which it says are registered trademarks or trademarks of Sharp Corporation. The company describes the second character as a little gruff and not always straightforward, but truly caring toward its owner.

According to the release, the character may put on a tough front and struggle to be honest about its feelings, yet stays by its owner's side and expresses care through simple words. Sharp said the Poketomo developers will hold a talk event on December 5 covering the first year and the second character's development. Sharp directed readers to its Japanese-language website for details about the Tokyo event venue. The release says Poketomo is a conversational AI character that keeps its owner company whether the owner is happy, excited, or lonely.

It is available as both a robot and a smartphone app, and it grows more attuned to its owner the more they talk and spend time together. The two-day event in Tokyo will let visitors meet the second character and the first character, described as the "innocent" type. Sharp also gave the price and campaign terms only for the Japanese market, according to a footnote. The release gives no further details about the Taiwan launch, the Taiwan pricing, or how the Share Plan will work outside Japan.

stories.Headline: Proposed Outbound Investment Rule Bans Biotech and Chinese AI - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury has proposed a rule that would bar U.S. investors from certain investments in businesses working in sensitive strategic technologies tied to countries of concern, or require them to notify Treasury. The proposal, which Proskauer Rose LLP analyzed in a client alert dated November 11, 2026, targets investments with a nexus to China and its territories for most investors. Treasury's proposal builds on outbound investment rules in effect since early January 2025, and the articles describe the rule as a significant tightening for AI and biotechnology. Treasury is seeking comments on the proposed rule by December 7, 2026.

The Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act, signed into law on December 18, 2025, requires final regulations by March 2027. The proposed rules sort covered investments into notifiable transactions, which are allowed but must be reported, and prohibited transactions, which are barred outright. The proposal adds high-performance computing, hypersonics and biotechnology to the covered sectors, with biotechnology added under Treasury's authority to designate additional technology categories. The list of countries of concern now includes Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia and Venezuela, though Treasury says the Maduro regime no longer exists, so the Venezuela designation appears to have no current application. China and the Hong Kong and Macau Special Administrative Regions remain in scope.

The articles identify Treasury as the agency behind the proposal, and they note that Treasury itself wrote the rule's definitions and comment requests. Treasury says no single measure separates advanced AI models, because developers improve capability through synthetic data and new post-training techniques. Treasury also acknowledges that the proposed limits on biotechnology could create public health risks, and it has asked for comments on narrowing the pharmaceutical category to frontier technologies and on excluding certain biofuels. The authors of the client alert are Déborah Aléxis, John R Ingrassia and Eric S. Johnson, and they say the national interest exemption will largely be unavailable in practice.

The proposal would affect U.S. investors with holdings or pipeline deals touching AI or biotechnology, along with contract manufacturers and holding companies that could be treated as developers. The articles say that Chinese companies building their own AI models, or building agentic layers that extend third-party models, would be off-limits. The articles also say Treasury's first penalty under the existing program involved an unnotified investment by a U.S. company's foreign fund in a Chinese AI and robotics company, which would likely be banned outright under the proposal. Under the proposal, capital calls under commitments made before the effective date would likely be excepted, while transactions closing before that date would remain under the current rules.

The articles leave open whether simply incorporating a third-party model into a commercial product counts as development under the rule. They also leave open the final rule's effective date, which the authors expect to closely follow release of the final rule. Treasury's proposal may also require divestment of covered transactions in prohibited technologies, which would now include essentially every covered AI and biotech transaction. The articles do not say whether Treasury will adopt the proposed narrowing of the pharmaceutical category or the exclusion of certain biofuels. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Proposed Outbound Investment Rule Bans Biotech and Chinese AI - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Practical workshops on Artificial Intelligence Applied to Legal Research begin today - Universitat de València
stories.Summary:
The Regulation Research Group at the University of Valencia began a series of practical workshops on artificial intelligence applied to legal research today, 9 November 2026. The workshops are taught by Andrés Marzal Varó of the Universitat Jaume I. The programme runs on 9, 16 and 23 November 2026, with a final session on 14 December 2026, each from 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. In-person sessions are held in Room 3P12 of Administrative Law at the Faculty of Law of the University of Valencia, with online attendance also available. The course consists of four highly practical sessions in which participants work directly on their laptops to apply AI tools rigorously to legal research tasks.

The theoretical component builds a conceptual framework covering how generative AI systems learn, why they are not deterministic, what hallucinations are and how to mitigate them. It also covers what an AI agent is and how AI systems interact with the internet, databases and personal documents. Participants practise searching, summarising, organising, analysing, comparing, verifying and arguing as part of everyday academic research. Each session ends with a tangible output, including a configured AI assistant for research, a workflow for case-law summaries, an AI-assisted thematic research wiki and monitoring tools. To take part fully, attendees must hold an active Claude Pro subscription during November, which currently costs about €20 for one month and is separate from the free course.

The articles identify the Regulation Research Group, which organises the workshops, and Andrés Marzal Varó, who teaches them, as responsible for the programme. The group presents the course as a response to artificial intelligence becoming part of the work of anyone conducting legal research. The articles state that its importance is likely to increase in the short and medium term. Marzal Varó is described as teaching from the Universitat Jaume I. The articles do not give any further statement from either of them about the course.

The articles present the workshops as aimed at those who conduct legal research, including academics whose everyday work involves searching, summarising and verifying material. Participants are affected by the subscription requirement, since they must pay for a Claude Pro subscription that is not part of the course. The articles note that participants may cancel the subscription once the training period has ended. No other groups, reactions or objections are reported in the articles.

The workshops are listed on the University of Valencia website under the Regulation Research Group's training and teaching activities. The announcement was published on the university site on 9 November 2026, and an earlier version of the same item appeared that day. The articles also list other recent items from the group, including an international workshop on the proposed forestry law of the Valencian Community and specific postgraduate degrees for 2026/2027. The articles give no earlier history of the course itself.

The articles state the schedule of the remaining sessions but do not describe their content in detail beyond the general outline. They do not say how many participants may enrol or whether registration is still open. They also do not state how the online attendance link will be managed, nor whether the course will be repeated. The articles leave unstated whether the Claude Pro subscription cost may change during November.

Articles.Title: Practical workshops on Artificial Intelligence Applied to Legal Research begin today - Universitat de València

stories.Headline: SIU’s Health Law Moot Court Looks at AI, Also Honors Event’s ‘Pillars’ - Illinois State Bar Association
stories.Summary:
Southern Illinois University Simmons Law School is hosting its National Health Law Moot Court competition in Carbondale, with preliminary rounds on Friday, November 13, and the final round on Saturday, November 14, 2026. The event, which the article describes as the nation's only mock U.S. Supreme Court competition devoted exclusively to health law, is in its 35th year. It also honors four people whose work shaped the program: Cheryl Anderson and W. Eugene Basanta, emeriti law faculty, Dr. Marsha Ryan, an adjunct faculty member, and Ted LeBlang, an emeritus professor of law and medicine at the SIU School of Medicine. A celebration in their honor runs from 4:30 to 6 p.m. Friday at the law school.

This year's fictional case centers on artificial intelligence in medicine. It involves a retired steelworker in a rural county who relied for years on an AI diagnostic tool offered through a regional health system's telehealth portal. The tool repeatedly reported no sign of lung cancer, but it missed a growing tumor, and the man was later diagnosed with advanced cancer and died the following year. His widow sued both the health system and the tool's developer. Competitors will argue whether the health system can be held liable despite a disclaimer in its online terms, and whether the suit was filed too late under state law.

Associate professor Kaitlyn Poirer, who described the fictional case, is among those framing the issues for students. The competition is run mainly by second- and third-year students on the Moot Court Board, and the article says the school's moot court team serves as host and does not compete. Sponsors include the law school, the American College of Legal Medicine, the American Health Law Association and Southern Illinois Healthcare. The final round, at 4 p.m.

Saturday in the Rhode Covington Moot Court Room, will be livestreamed and posted to the law school's moot court YouTube channel. The final-round judges are Illinois Supreme Court Justice David K. Overstreet, U.S. District Chief Judge Staci M. Yandle of the Southern District of Illinois, Perry Browder, president of the Illinois State Bar Association, and Dr. Amir Pasha, president of the American College of Legal Medicine and an assistant professor of medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Phoenix, Arizona. The law school is also holding its first Alumni Weekend from Thursday, November 12, through Saturday, November 14, timed to coincide with the competition. The weekend was created partly because many volunteer attorneys who judge early rounds are SIU Simmons graduates, and it includes an open house, a welcome reception, an alumni luncheon and a Saluki football game.

Articles.Title: SIU’s Health Law Moot Court Looks at AI, Also Honors Event’s ‘Pillars’ - Illinois State Bar Association

stories.Headline: Databricks' new Genie tool is the latest sign of the AI industry's full court press for knowledge workers
stories.Summary:
Databricks, a San Francisco data and AI company, announced on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, a second generation of its Genie assistant that operates as an always-on, autonomous agent for enterprise work. Users can give Genie a goal, and it takes ownership of the work, delegates to subagents, tracks progress, follows up on missing inputs, and reaches out when a person needs to make a decision. A new priority inbox highlights items needing attention, and Genie emails users when they are away. The launch came a day after Anthropic released its own set of AI productivity tools aimed at corporate users. Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi said the agents run in the background at all times.

The new Genie is grounded in Genie Ontology, which captures a company's horizontal context, including definitions, metrics, people and processes, and keeps it current as the business changes. Genie Search expands to more than 100 enterprise data sources, including Google Drive, Jira and Confluence, and indexes content in place without moving or copying it. Genie runs within a company's existing Databricks environment and is governed by Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway, so every action stays within existing controls. Genie now runs in autonomous mode on its own compute, and every action is fully auditable. Ontology Manager, a new feature, lets teams manage and govern business context.

Ghodsi, who co-founded and leads Databricks, said Genie has made him a "10x more productive CEO" and that he uses it every hour of the day. He said it can work because it knows how the company operates, including what counts as revenue and which numbers are official. Ghodsi also said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is an amazing CEO and should remain in that role after the revelation of Huang's extramarital affair with a woman U.S. officials believe to be a spy for China. Ghodsi said he thinks the industry will weather the storm. Databricks, still privately held, raised $5 billion at a $190 billion valuation in August.

The industry is pushing harder into corporate work because AI has transformed software programming but remains experimental in other business functions where returns are less clear. Anthropic's prospectus for its initial public offering said the work of knowledge workers represented more than $40 trillion in economic value globally in 2025. Anthropic's IPO, expected the following week, could value the company at $1.4 trillion, and many in the industry are watching it closely. Anthropic's tools include a spreadsheet application that competes with Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets, and a feature that lets Claude join video calls. Some believe recent advances in AI agents and model capabilities may let the technology capture a broader part of the market.

Articles.Title: Databricks' new Genie tool is the latest sign of the AI industry's full court press for knowledge workers

stories.Headline: Google warned school districts about disabling AI mode for its search engine. Some Chicagoans replied with protest.
stories.Summary:
Google warned school districts this month that schools which disable AI features would not be able to use its search engine, because AI is so embedded in the technology. Protests broke out Wednesday, November 11, 2026, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and in Chicago, where the district had recently blocked student access to generative AI tools. About 30 people gathered outside Google's office in Chicago's West Loop, where most were parents and educators, along with some students. The demonstrators shouted chants including "Hey Google, nice try," and some held signs and spoke against the company's AI tools. The protest reflects a wider dispute over how much tech companies should be involved in public education.

Chicago Public Schools said in a statement that it was "actively exploring all options to independently suppress" the AI overview shown at the top of Google searches. If the district cannot get search without that feature, a spokesperson said, it will "look to other search solutions." Reese Mackey, a 16-year-old junior at Kenwood Academy High School, said students are owed lessons from teachers rather than from a bot. Cassie Creswell, executive director of Illinois Families for Public Schools, which led the Chicago rally, said schools should reassess whether to use Google at all. A Google spokesperson said the company is piloting its "Guided Learning" feature, which uses AI to walk students through problems step by step rather than giving quick answers.

Concerns about students' AI use and screen time have grown under the Trump administration, which has been largely friendly with the AI industry. New York City, under Mayor Zohran Mamdani, banned student-facing AI, including chatbots, from preschool through eighth grade just before this school year began. At the end of October, Chalkbeat obtained a list of nearly 40 products the city's Education Department flagged for AI usage, including Grammarly and Kahoot. Chicago has approved at least three generative AI tools, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Gemini Notebook, after contracts barred the companies from using student data to train their models. The district also backtracked on plans to roll out Google Gemini in high schools for 2026-2027 after community pushback.

Illinois Families for Public Schools wants Chicago to impose a three-year moratorium on generative AI in schools, and it urged school board candidates to sign its pledge in the recent election. About half of the incoming Chicago Board of Education members, including President-elect Jessica Biggs, signed on. Michilla Blaise, the District 5b board member who was reelected, said she believes AI is creating larger learning gaps in communities on Chicago's West Side. The pledge also calls for a chief privacy officer to protect student data, limits on screen time across all grade levels, and a ban on collecting biometric data such as face scans and fingerprints. Creswell said she hopes officials elected in the midterms will answer to their constituents rather than the tech industry.

It is unclear whether Chicago Public Schools can turn off Google's AI features while still providing access to the search engine, since the district has not yet set a response. The articles do not say which alternative search solutions the district would adopt. They also do not say whether Google will change its position, or whether the Cambridge protest led to any action. Whether the newly elected school board will adopt the moratorium or other pledge measures is not stated. How the Democratic midterm wins will affect AI policy in education is also left open.

Articles.Title: Google warned school districts about disabling AI mode for its search engine. Some Chicagoans replied with protest. - Chalkbeat

stories.Headline: West Virginia lawmaker seeks to strengthen state police investigations into AI-generated crimes involving children
stories.Summary:
Sen. Vince Deeds, a Republican from Greenbrier County, said he will introduce legislation in January to expand the West Virginia State Police's ability to investigate tips about the production, possession and financial extortion of child sexual abuse material. The announcement came during an interim meeting of the Joint Judiciary Committee in Charleston on a Tuesday, as reported on November 11, 2026. Deeds described the state police as the front line in these cases and said the agency needs additional resources to keep up. He framed the bill as a way to supplement law enforcement work through legislation. Sgt.

Rachel Blankenship, director of the State Police Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, told lawmakers that tips have grown faster than the agency's capacity to respond. So far this year the task force has received just under 2,300 tips from internet service providers and child welfare agencies, handled by 15 troopers and 50 affiliates in counties and cities. She also reported more than 1,700 screened-out child protective services referrals this year, up from 1,382 last year, meaning more tips are being routed to agencies that coordinate with her task force. Blankenship said the main focus of her testimony was the need to address AI-generated child sexual abuse material through law. She noted that West Virginia defined "computer-generated pornography" in its sexually explicit conduct statute in 2025.

Blankenship described a pattern in which offenders take existing photos of people, feed them into AI platforms and generate abusive images. According to her, Meta and Google have been reliable in reporting, but newer messaging providers that emphasize anonymity have become a hotbed for self-produced material by teenagers, along with financial sextortion and sadistic online exploitation. Deeds said lawmakers have had to update the criminal code repeatedly over the past decade as the crimes changed, and he said artificial intelligence is now being used to alter images and extort children who may feel unable to report. Separately, Attorney General JB McCuskey announced that his office is seeking legal action against Snapchat under the West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act, citing the rise of online exploitation.

Articles.Title: West Virginia lawmaker seeks to strengthen state police investigations into AI-generated crimes involving children - WBOY.com

stories.Headline: The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models
stories.Summary:
This is a breaking-story-style request with a rule I cannot fully satisfy from the articles: they describe a technical guide and do not report an event with who did what and when beyond a publication date, so I will write what is known in two paragraphs and end with the required sentence. Hugging Face published an update on November 12, 2026, titled "The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models," written by Suvaditya Mukherjee, Merve and Pedro Cuenca. The post provides fine-tuning scripts and containers for TRELLIS.2, a 3D generation model, that can run locally or on Hugging Face Jobs. The authors say users can run the scripts with a few arguments if their dataset is on the Hugging Face Hub.

The guide also explains how the script works and includes a repository for users who want to modify the code. The guide aims to adapt TRELLIS.2 to a specific object category using the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset. The experiment uses a subset of 188 footwear objects from the 1,030 in GSO. In initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct but had incorrect soles.

The authors add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT, and freeze the texture flow DiT. The configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters, using rank 8 adapters in one stage and rank 16 in the other. Preprocessing renders 16 views of each object with Blender, and for the 188 objects the full run took approximately one hour on an a100-large job. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

stories.Headline: Kenya’s AI Bill 2026: Key Things to Know After Rejection By Senate ICT Committee
stories.Summary:
Kenya's first dedicated artificial intelligence bill has stalled after the Senate's Information, Communication and Technology Committee asked the Senate not to proceed with the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026. The committee, chaired by Trans Nzoia Senator Allan Chesang, said the bill's penalties did not suit a sector still finding its footing. The bill was sponsored by nominated Senator Karen Nyamu in early 2026. The committee also warned that the law, if passed, could drive investors and local developers away and slow the growth of Kenya's digital ecosystem, often called the Silicon Savannah.

The bill had offered several potential gains, chief among them legal clarity for developers, investors and users. It would have created an Office of the AI Commissioner and an Advisory Committee, and it would have introduced tiered risk management, compliance auditing and testing sandboxes. Existing laws such as the Data Protection Act, 2019 and the cybercrime laws were not designed for AI-specific risks like algorithmic bias and deepfakes. Supporters argued that defined liability and transparency duties would have made developers and deployers accountable. Rejecting the bill leaves those questions unanswered for now.

The committee's objection centred on penalties and obligations that it considered too harsh for a young sector, a concern the articles say a poorly calibrated law could turn into a real burden. Nyamu sponsored the bill, but the articles do not record a response from her to the committee's position. The committee's recommendation is the reason cited for halting the process. Kenya's digital space remains governed by the Data Protection Act, 2019, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, 2018 as amended in 2025, and the Virtual Asset Service Providers Act, 2025. Taken together, those laws leave AI largely outside any specific framework.

The articles indicate that the uncertainty could affect citizens harmed by biased or opaque systems, victims of harmful deepfakes, and businesses that cannot yet tell which standards will eventually apply. Counties already using AI in service delivery would also have lacked guidance. The articles do not say when or whether a revised bill will return to the Senate. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Kenya’s AI Bill 2026: Key Things to Know After Rejection By Senate ICT Committee - Tech Labari

stories.Headline: SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI’s natural gas ambitions
stories.Summary:
SoftBank reported a $7.1 billion quarterly loss on Tuesday, and more than half of it came from losses tied to power-generating equipment. The company had paid turbine manufacturers nonrefundable deposits to secure orders, and it now considers much of that money effectively worthless. Starting about two years ago, SoftBank reportedly placed deposits on more than 13 gigawatts of turbines, almost 50% more than it needed. The loss on the misplaced bet is over $3 billion.

The company's push into natural gas was part of a larger plan led by CEO Masayoshi Son, who wanted to capture a share of the power market for AI data centers. In February, SoftBank's SB Energy subsidiary said it would spend $33 billion on a 9.2-gigawatt natural gas power plant. The articles say that the over-ordering helped SoftBank secure turbines and speed up its projects, since turbine queues now extend into the early 2030s. Peter Gardett, CEO of Noreva, told TechCrunch that SB Energy had little choice but to overbook turbines if it wanted some right away.

Gardett described the charge as the price of finding out what the turbines were actually worth. Data center operators are also learning that natural gas carries risks of its own, including winter curtailments when supplies dip and demand spikes. Brent Nelson, senior managing director of markets and strategy at Ascend Analytics, said on the Equity podcast that a grid connection is probably still the best option for most data centers, even a smaller one than they would normally request. He suggested large batteries as a cost-effective way to cover the shortfall by shaving peak loads or riding out utility requests to curtail use.

The articles suggest that operators may be reaching the same conclusion, which could slow the natural gas market's growth below what SoftBank expected. The articles do not expect SoftBank's losses to trigger a wave of cancellations among gas power plants, since AI's power demand still appears too large for that. Natural gas remains popular for now, though SoftBank may have reached the limit of what the market will bear. The articles are written by Tim De Chant, a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch.

Articles.Title: SoftBank’s billion-dollar loss may have put a cap on AI’s natural gas ambitions

stories.Headline: Proposed Council Bill Promotes Education Against "Negative Effects" of AI Chatbot Use
stories.Summary:
A new bill before the New York City Council would require the city's Department of Health and Mental Hygiene to educate residents about the possible mental health effects of chatbot use and to study how such use relates to mental health. Council Member Frank Morano introduced the measure, Int. No. 1049-2026, on September 10, 2026, and it was referred to the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use. The bill has not yet been given a hearing date, and it would take effect immediately upon passage.

The bill defines a chatbot as an artificial intelligence system that communicates interactively with users in natural language, generating or selecting content in response to text or voice input. Within 180 days of enactment, the Commissioner of Health and Mental Hygiene would have to launch a public awareness campaign covering risks such as psychosis, suicidal ideation, distorted decision-making, social isolation, and self-harm. The campaign would also address engagement tactics that may encourage prolonged use, along with ways to recognize overreliance and the treatment resources available. Materials tailored to people under 24, adults over 60, and veterans would be published on the department's website and reviewed each year. The Commissioner would also run a citywide survey on chatbot use and its links to mental health, with the first survey due within 180 days and repeats every three years after that.

Council Member Morano said he was alarmed by reports of people developing delusions and suicidal or violent thoughts after long conversations with AI chatbots. In an interview with the New York Post, he compared the potential public health risk to the opioid epidemic, warning that the problem could become the next major crisis facing the country. Under the bill, the Commissioner would begin submitting an annual report to the City Council Speaker and the Mayor one year after enactment. That report would summarize outreach activities, review current research, count chatbot-related mental health emergencies in the city during the prior year, and propose policy responses.

Articles.Title: Proposed Council Bill Promotes Education Against "Negative Effects" of AI Chatbot Use - CityLand

stories.Headline: The Bank of Nvidia just lost its banker — here’s where the AI trade is exposed
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia and left its board on Thursday, effective immediately, after reports of three affairs, one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, became interim CEO, and Nvidia still plans to report earnings on Tuesday. Nvidia's stock fell to its lowest level in more than a year, briefly sitting about $2 trillion below its October record before recovering to a loss of roughly 4% at the close. The selling was uneven across the AI trade. Nebius and CoreWeave, cloud companies that rent out Nvidia chips, took the heaviest losses, while Broadcom and AMD each rose more than 5%.

Analysts tie the pattern to Huang's role as a financier of the AI boom. Nvidia holds stakes in companies including Intel, SpaceX, CoreWeave, Coherent and Safe Superintelligence, bought $3 billion of Meta's stock offering, and has pledged up to $10 billion to Anthropic ahead of its IPO next week. It also holds a $30 billion stake in OpenAI and has a preliminary deal to invest as much as $100 billion more. Many of those companies buy Nvidia chips in turn. By Yahoo Finance's count, Nvidia's latest quarterly filing lists about $530 billion in commitments and guarantees, including roughly $65 billion to rent back cloud capacity and a guarantee of up to $105 billion on OpenAI's Ohio data center leases.

Liz Thomas, chief market strategist at SoFi, said these circular relationships have been a subject of discussion for most of the past year. Kress, who signed off on many of the deals as CFO, now decides how many more to make. The article describes several pressure points: the OpenAI guarantee pays out only if OpenAI defaults, a downturn that sank OpenAI would likely also hit Nvidia's sales, and Nvidia's receivables reached $63 billion last quarter with collection times rising to about 60 days from 45. The value of Nvidia's largest public stock holdings has also fallen by more than $20 billion since June, led by Intel. Nvidia's balance sheet offsets some of this, with about $99 billion in cash and securities against $33 billion of debt at the end of July.

The article notes that money for the AI build-out was already getting harder to find, since CoreWeave's chief executive said the company won't borrow without collateral at current rates. Savita Subramanian of BofA said large tech companies are now issuing more stock than they buy back. Nvidia's earnings report on Tuesday will show whether Kress stands behind the guidance and commitments and whether customers are paying on time. Thomas framed the question for the coming week as whether the market can survive without positive results from Nvidia.

Articles.Title: The Bank of Nvidia just lost its banker — here’s where the AI trade is exposed

stories.Headline: New York Opens Registration for Frontier AI Labs Ahead of RAISE Act
stories.Summary:
New York has opened a registration portal for large frontier AI developers, including Anthropic and OpenAI, which must sign up by January 1, 2027. The move comes as the state prepares to enforce the RAISE Act, one of the country's most significant AI safety laws. The law takes effect at the start of next year and applies to frontier developers with more than $500 million in annual revenue. Companies covered by it will need to publish safety frameworks on their websites and release public transparency reports for their models.

The law also requires those developers to report critical safety incidents within 72 hours. Oversight will fall to the newly formed Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust, known as DIGIT. Penalties can reach $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for later ones. The state can also take enforcement action against companies that fail to register, though a spokesperson declined to give details on how that would work.

Governor Kathy Hochul spoke at a press briefing on Tuesday and criticized technology leaders who present AI as inevitable and treat collateral damage as acceptable in the race to win. She said New York is building a national model for sensible AI regulation that puts communities and people ahead of corporations and powerful technology. Hochul also opened the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, a center first announced in January with $55 million in donations and capital. The center will independently evaluate the safety, security and operation of advanced AI systems and help DIGIT review companies' safety frameworks.

The RAISE Act builds on existing state rules. Last year New York began enforcing a law requiring AI companion operators to remind users they are talking to a bot and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm. In October Hochul signed a separate chatbot safety law for minors, which takes effect on June 1, 2027. Other states have passed similar measures, including California's SB 53, in force since January, and Illinois' SB 315, which takes effect at the start of 2027.

Articles.Title: New York Opens Registration for Frontier AI Labs Ahead of RAISE Act - AI Insider

stories.Headline: Chinese banks have been using artificial intelligence (AI) for their work in earnest, from simple ta..
stories.Summary:
Chinese banks have been putting artificial intelligence to work in earnest, moving from simple task automation toward systems that accelerate research and handle complex jobs. According to a report by the Chinese outlet Caixin on the 11th, Jiangsu Bank replaced 1.2 million cumulative business hours through AI-related applications.
