Articles.Title: AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

stories.Headline: SoftBank Group (TSE:9984) Lands Malaysia AI Deal, But Is The Valuation Opportunity Real
stories.Summary:
SoftBank Group (TSE:9984) has agreed with Grab and Petroleum Sarawak Berhad to deploy an initial US$1.85 billion of seed capital into AI infrastructure projects across Malaysia. The announcement was reported in an article published on November 11, 2026. The share price has fallen 33.57% over the past 30 days and 30.85% over the past 90 days. The one-year total shareholder return is down 29.46%, although the three-year and five-year returns remain strongly positive. Recent headlines about a ¥7.1 billion quarterly loss tied to AI infrastructure spending, revised US data center plans and blocked robotics deals have weighed on sentiment.

Simply Wall St's analyst consensus narrative puts SoftBank Group's fair value at ¥7,782.47, compared with a last close of ¥3,855. That analysis uses a 5.0% discount rate and cites SB Energy's planned Nasdaq listing, backed by roughly 8.8 GW of contracted AI data center capacity. The same narrative describes an estimated US$430 billion lease revenue backlog still to be realized. It also covers a planned multi-gigawatt AI data center build-out in France, including an initial €45 billion investment to deliver 3.1 GW of capacity by 2031. Simply Wall St's own discounted cash flow model, by contrast, gives a fair value of ¥2,366.65.

The article was produced with AI automation by Simply Wall St, which states that it has no position in any stocks mentioned. Simply Wall St says the piece is general in nature, is not financial advice and does not factor in the latest price-sensitive announcements. The article describes SoftBank Group's sentiment as clearly split between investors. It also says the stock's 30-plus percent monthly slide could signal real cracks in the business or a sharp swing in mood.

The article notes that its fair value estimates depend on SoftBank Group's AI and infrastructure pipeline, and it names higher funding costs and delayed exits such as OpenAI and SB Energy as risks. The article itself records that 23 investors see the stock as 50% undervalued. It also lists related Simply Wall St coverage, including a ¥1 trillion bond sale. The article does not say how the Malaysia seed capital will be divided among the three partners, or when the projects will begin.

stories.Headline: Howard Marks' Latest Memo: Who Can Actually Profit From AI Investments?
stories.Summary:
Howard Marks, co-founder of Oaktree Capital, released an investment memo titled "A Layman Thinks About AI" on November 11, 2026. The memo followed "Is It a Bubble?", which Marks had updated in December 2025, and it again took up AI investing. This time he focused on the sales volume and price of computing power. He asked whether the value AI creates for users could support trillions of dollars in infrastructure investment. He also asked which companies would be able to make profits from it.

In December 2025, Marks used railways and the internet to show that speculation can build infrastructure early and speed up the spread of technology. He warned that the first investors who put in capital may lose money even when the data centers prove useful. In February 2026, in "AI Hurtles Ahead," he argued that the technical potential of AI is more likely to be underestimated. He kept his earlier advice to participate moderately, select targets carefully and invest prudently. In his latest memo, Marks split the bubble question into three judgments about the technology.

Those three judgments concern what the technology itself can achieve, whether enterprise capital spending will earn sufficient returns, and whether the prices investors pay for stocks and bonds are reasonable. Marks still believes AI will transform enterprises, the economy and daily life. He argues that no judgment on capital spending or security prices can be made until investors understand AI's use cases, profit attribution and infrastructure returns. If several models perform similarly on the same task, suppliers may be forced to cut prices, leaving more of the efficiency gains with users. Marks also pointed to debt across the whole market, not just individual deals.

In December he questioned whether the narrow spread on 30-year bonds issued by cloud vendors could compensate for long-term technical uncertainty. In November he cited Goldman Sachs data showing that global AI-related debt issuance in 2026 had approached $600 billion by the memo's release. About $400 billion of that had entered the US investment-grade bond market, more than one-fifth of the market's new supply for the year. Marks questioned whether cloud vendors could keep their credit ratings as they keep borrowing. He also asked whether the AI industry's financing needs would raise capital costs for other borrowers.

The memo also changed how he views investment portfolios. An equity stake in a frontier model company and a data center loan backed by a long-term lease, he noted, call for different judgments. The equity depends on technology, competition, pricing and valuation, while the loan depends on tenant credit, contract terms, power supply and residual asset value. Yet a tech stock, a data center loan and an investment-grade corporate bond may all depend on growth in computing power demand. In that case, holding different assets could mean taking on the same type of risk.

At the end of the memo, Marks poses questions for investors to answer themselves. He asks how many assumptions must hold at once for a return to be reasonable, and what the maximum loss would be if the core assumption is wrong. He also asks how much optimism the current price already reflects, and whether the investment will diversify the portfolio or amplify existing risk. Marks writes that the goal is to pose the right questions rather than give direct answers, and he has long stressed knowing what one does not know.

The articles do not report whether any of these questions has been answered. The articles leave open whether AI will create enough value to justify trillions of dollars in investment, and which companies will earn returns on it. They also do not say whether cloud vendors' debt will affect their credit ratings or raise borrowing costs for others. Marks' memo ends with questions rather than conclusions, so the articles offer no forecast of the outcome.

Articles.Title: Howard Marks' Latest Memo: Who Can Actually Profit From AI Investments? - 36Kr

stories.Headline: Peru's banks say AI agents can now do the work once assigned to junior analysts
stories.Summary:
Peru's banks say AI agents can now do the entry-level analyst work once assigned to junior staff. Executives at Peru's largest banks made the warning at the FELABAN 60th Annual Assembly in Lima, held from November 3 to 6, 2026. Interbank VP Claudio Querol said AI agents can build Excel models and assemble PowerPoint decks in seconds without a salary. The warning came from the summit that Latin Times describes as Latin America's most consequential financial gathering. Peru's banking sector is now restructuring the entry point into professional life, and recent graduates are absorbing the first impact.

Credicorp, Peru's largest financial holding company, has more than 90% of its workforce using AI tools, with over 100 active use cases in production. Interbank signed a direct enterprise agreement with Anthropic in August 2026 to integrate generative and agentic AI into its operations. Interbank became the first Peruvian bank to establish that kind of relationship with a frontier AI developer. The bank bypassed the cloud marketplaces that most regional banks rely on. A Stanford Digital Economy Lab study found a 13% employment decline among workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed roles.

Querol, who leads Data, Analytics and AI at Interbank, said organizations will likely move away from large pools of junior staff. He framed the shift as a structural rethinking of how banks are organized rather than simply a productivity upgrade. Benjamin Chavez, head of data and AI at BBVA Peru, said many junior tasks can today be done by an agent in seconds. Chavez said that development forces banks to redesign the learning model. Credicorp, parent of BCP, has instead emphasized reskilling as its strategic response to automation's advance.

Rafael Lemor, AI lead at Credicorp, described the company's approach as building corporate intelligence that automates, learns, collaborates and decides with ethical judgment. Junior analyst classes at some banking institutions have shrunk by as much as two-thirds in certain areas. Firms are shifting hiring toward AI-skilled talent drawn from recent graduate pools. In Mexico, entry-level job growth slowed from 9% to below 3% annually between 2021 and 2025, according to IMCO. The International Labor Organization estimates that up to 5.6 million young people worldwide could become unemployed under an unfavorable automation scenario.

PwC's AI Jobs Barometer 2026 found that conventional entry-level vacancies have declined while AI-integrated positions grew 35% since 2019. The same barometer found that more than one in three young workers globally hold jobs with medium to high exposure to AI-driven task change. Some 72% of Peruvians have already interacted with AI-powered financial services, according to a 2026 Experian Peru study. A Stanford analysis using ADP payroll records documented steepest effects in customer service and software development. Executives at FELABAN largely left open whether companies will create enough new entry roles built around AI oversight and coordination.

The articles do not say whether companies will create enough new entry points to absorb the young professionals being squeezed out. They also do not say how Peru's banks will address shortages of experienced leaders a decade from now. The articles note that banks acknowledge this risk in private but rarely address it in hiring strategies. Interbank, BBVA Peru and Credicorp have not announced specific figures for future junior hiring in the articles. The articles leave open how quickly the restructuring will proceed across Peru's banking sector.

Articles.Title: Peru's banks say AI agents can now do the work once assigned to junior analysts

stories.Headline: CoreWeave turns to customer prepayments, shorter contracts to fund AI growth
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, a company that rents out the computing power behind AI, disclosed in its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday that it is changing how it pays for its growth. The neocloud said it is asking customers to pay up front more often, borrowing against specific contracts, and pursuing short-term deals that can carry higher prices. The company reported $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% from a year earlier, but it also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in quarterly interest expense. CEO Michael Intrator told analysts on the earnings call that the company will not use the unsecured debt market at current yields.

Instead, CoreWeave plans to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing funds as needed to build infrastructure for a backlog of $132.5 billion. The company expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, including more than $3 billion tied to signing new contracts for capacity it has already built. Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on large Microsoft prepayments, which suggests the industry is moving toward having big technology customers pay for buildouts. The approach eases immediate borrowing needs, but it also commits CoreWeave to providing services at prices that may look less attractive later if demand changes.

Intrator said prices rose about 25% in July and another 10% later in the quarter, and that prices were still climbing in a way that more than offsets cost increases. He also said the company is allocating more capacity to short-term deals where pricing justifies it, selling at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for four- and five-year contracts on new infrastructure is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt. In August, CoreWeave closed a $2.6 billion loan called DDTL 5.5, its first built specifically for shorter-term customer contracts, which lets it borrow in installments. The article notes that lenders tend to favor longer contracts because they offer more predictable cash flow, so short-term deals involve a tradeoff.

Wall Street responded positively to the earnings, but bond investors have been more cautious, with yields on some of CoreWeave's bonds rising above 15% last month. That reaction suggests concern about the debt needed to build data centers before those investments produce returns. The article describes CoreWeave's strategy as a way to expand without relying on unsecured debt, one that could boost profits while adding risk around contract renewals and pricing. It also shows how much the AI infrastructure boom depends on demand that has yet to be proven over time. TechCrunch said it had reached out to CoreWeave for more information about its loan facility.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave turns to customer prepayments, shorter contracts to fund AI growth

stories.Headline: From AI ambition to business impact
stories.Summary:
Microsoft's Frontier Company, a unit led by Rodrigo Kede Lima, published a blog post on November 12, 2026, arguing that businesses now need to move from AI that impresses to AI that changes how they operate. The company says it has engaged on nearly 500 projects with more than 200 customers across 28 countries, including 3M, BMW, Mastercard, Unilever and Siemens. It describes working side by side with customers through its Forward Deployed Engineering teams. Most customers with completed initial projects have returned for further work, which the post says has produced hundreds of follow-on projects.

The post says the technology is ready and that what slows AI adoption is the surrounding work of finding the highest-value uses, building trust and governance, redesigning operating models, and helping people adapt. It offers four guiding principles: begin with value, redesign the process rather than the task, build in fast cycles with customer teams, and put security, governance and cost management in place from the start. Several examples are given: Unilever is using a digital twin at its Pondicherry factory to anticipate problems, 3M is building an AI agent workflow to automate parts of customer order management, and Northern Trust cut data preparation time for onboarding by 83%, from about two and a half weeks to three days. KT says its AIO-Net platform now detects network issues in two to three minutes, down from more than ten, and Saint-Gobain used Microsoft Discovery to process 62,000 patents and 44,000 research abstracts.

Kede Lima and the company frame these efforts as a response to a gap between AI ambition and results. The post cites IDC research, sponsored by Microsoft, finding that 66% of organizations report substantial or transformative results from AI, yet only 48% are scaling or seeing consistent value across the business. The same research found that 71% expect AI spending to rise by at least 10% over the next year. The post says Microsoft Frontier Company was deliberately built to be flat and fast, with a single front door for customers, and that the company is adjusting its own approach as it goes. It concludes that success should be judged by whether customers can run, govern and improve their own AI systems after the engagements end.

Articles.Title: From AI ambition to business impact

stories.Headline: Micron (MU) Has Next Year’s High-Bandwidth Memory Mostly Sold. Can That Anchor a Decade-Long Case?
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, the S&P 500 fell 4.36%, its worst day since the April 2025 tariff crash, wiping out roughly $3 trillion in value across its companies. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52% into a correction, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 12%, its worst day since 2020. The slide followed an October in which the S&P 500 technology sector lost 6.8%, its biggest monthly drop since March 2025. Defensive groups such as consumer staples, by contrast, had a record month. Growth stocks tend to feel such swings first because their prices rest on faster expected sales and earnings growth.

Investors are questioning how companies will pay for their large artificial intelligence budgets and whether those spending plans will pay off. The midterm election results raised a second concern, as investors wondered whether data center construction could slow if new rules follow. October's jobs report showed payrolls up 165,000, against the 65,000 economists expected. Traders now put the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December above 75%. Edward Jones senior global strategist Angelo Kourkafas called the report a "blowout jobs report."

Micron Technology, listed on the NASDAQ as MU, ranks 10th on one published list of the 10 best growth stocks to buy for the next decade. Gavin Baker, who runs Atreides Management, has argued that the memory chip shortage will last and that Micron looks inexpensive for what it earns. Philippe Laffont's Coatue Management added nearly three million shares in a single quarter. David Tepper's Appaloosa tripled its stake late last year before trimming some of it. Chief Executive Officer Sanjay Mehrotra said the company has agreements covering the vast majority of its calendar 2027 high-bandwidth memory supply.

Micron reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, up 379% from a year earlier, and full-year revenue of $133.19 billion. Data center revenue rose fourfold, and gross margin and earnings per share also set records. Mehrotra said the supply agreements are priced significantly higher than a year earlier, and he expects an even stronger fiscal 2027. Customers have agreed to buy most of the high-bandwidth memory Micron plans to supply next year before it has been made. The company has a market capitalization of $825.89 billion and 184 hedge fund holders as of Q2 2026.

Insider Monkey, the publisher of the article, said it believes certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and less downside risk than Micron. The article describes growth stocks generally as companies expected to grow sales and earnings faster than the market average, often reinvesting profits rather than paying dividends. It notes that such stocks often carry high price-to-earnings ratios, leaving little room for disappointment. Investors holding Micron through a downturn are described as needing to consider which companies can keep compounding through several more months like this one.

The articles leave open whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates in December, and whether the midterm results will slow data center construction and AI spending. They also do not say whether Micron's supply agreements will hold up or how its fiscal 2027 results will compare with Mehrotra's expectations. The sources do not state whether the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index or the Nasdaq will recover from their November declines. Whether Micron can justify a decade-long case, as the headline asks, is not settled by the reporting.

Articles.Title: Micron (MU) Has Next Year’s High-Bandwidth Memory Mostly Sold. Can That Anchor a Decade-Long Case? - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: Doosan Electronics Revenue Tops 800 Billion Won for First Time on AI Demand
stories.Summary:
Doosan's Electronics Business Group reported record third-quarter revenue of 802 billion won, the first time its quarterly sales have topped 800 billion won. The company announced the results on November 9, 2026, showing an 82.4% gain from a year earlier and an 18.6% rise from the previous quarter. The growth came mainly from copper-clad laminates, a material used in AI accelerators, memory and optical modules. The division has now posted record revenue for four straight quarters, and its results beat analyst estimates of roughly 700 billion to 740 billion won.

Doosan has said it will expand capacity sharply to meet demand. It announced in April a roughly 180 billion won investment in a new laminate plant in Thailand, then in September approved about 970 billion won more for South Korea and China. Of that, about 420 billion won will go to optical-module laminate lines in South Korea, and about 550 billion won to facilities in China for AI accelerator and network switch materials. If the plans proceed, capacity should reach about 2.1 times its September 2026 level by the end of 2028 and as much as 2.7 times by the end of 2029. The company did not disclose the division's profit, but analysts estimate operating profit of about 235 billion won.

Doosan's standalone businesses, which include the Electronics group, DDI and Doota Mall, reported third-quarter revenue of 892.2 billion won and operating profit of 237.9 billion won. Those figures rose 70.2% and 119.6% from a year earlier, respectively. The company projects fourth-quarter revenue of 814.6 billion won for the Electronics group and full-year revenue of 2.91 trillion won, a 55.1% annual increase. Consolidated third-quarter revenue reached 5.4269 trillion won, and the board approved a quarterly dividend of 1,000 won per share, with a record date of November 24 and payment on December 9.

Articles.Title: Doosan Electronics Revenue Tops 800 Billion Won for First Time on AI Demand - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: NAVER Secures 2 Trillion Won in AI Factory Compute Deals
stories.Summary:
NAVER said on November 12, 2026, during its third-quarter earnings conference call, that it had secured computing service supply contracts worth about 2 trillion won ($1.4 billion) for its AI factory business. The company is pursuing the business with Brookfield and Nvidia. Revenue is set to begin when the service launches in the first half of next year. NAVER also plans to expand the business by pursuing additional contracts with global AI firms. The announcement was reported by Seoul Economic Daily.

The contracts were signed with an AI inference company, according to CEO Choi Soo-yeon. NAVER completed third-party allotment share offerings to both Brookfield Computing and Nvidia, which the CEO said minimized the initial capital burden. The company plans to pursue medium- to long-term contracts with large clients while broadening its customer base. The stated aim is to reduce dependence on any single customer while securing stable revenue and profitability. The CEO said the contracts secured so far exceed the volume initially targeted.

Choi said NAVER has secured infrastructure with enough power and liquid-cooled data centers to supply Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin GPUs on time. She said competition for those chips is intensifying and only a limited number of sites can accommodate them. The company is pursuing Asia's largest order to offer the Vera Rubin platform ahead of competitors. The CEO also said NAVER is negotiating prices for adopting the latest GPUs and is in discussions with multiple other customers.

Choi said NAVER has the operational capability to commercialize services quickly once GPU equipment arrives. She said this would bring forward monetization and secure high utilization rates and profitability. The CEO added that the company will generate meaningful revenue and results in the AI factory business. The article does not report independent assessments of the deals from investors, analysts or other parties. It also does not name the AI inference company or the global AI firms NAVER is pursuing.

NAVER's stock code is 035420, according to the article. The article notes that Choi said the customer secured this time is highly likely to lead to additional contracts as AI models expand in scale. The article does not state the contract durations, the total value of the medium- to long-term contracts, or the terms of the Brookfield and Nvidia share offerings. It also does not state the number of GPUs involved or when the additional contracts might be signed.

Articles.Title: NAVER Secures 2 Trillion Won in AI Factory Compute Deals - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI slump not seen affecting Bank of Japan’s rate-rise plan
stories.Summary:
The Bank of Japan is expected to keep raising interest rates at roughly one hike every three months, according to some analysts, despite growing uncertainty over artificial intelligence and data center investment. The Japan Times reported the story on November 12, 2026, with economist Soichiro Tateishi of the Japan Research Institute saying the effect on the central bank's pace of hikes would not be significant. The article ties the uncertainty to the Democratic Party's strong win in the U.S. midterm elections earlier that month. Concern has grown that data center construction could slow, since many candidates pledged stricter rules for such projects.

Tateishi's view is that a slowdown in the AI sector would not change the central bank's timing much. The Bank of Japan itself argues that AI is only one of several factors pushing up inflation in Japan. That position means the bank's plan to keep tightening policy is not expected to bend to developments in one technology sector. The reporting does not give a new rate figure or a specific date for the next move. What it does establish is that the policy path rests on a broader inflation picture than AI alone.

The article is written by staff writer Kazuaki Nagata and attributes the bank's position to the bank's own arguments, not to new policy statements. Tateishi is quoted directly, while the bank's view is presented as its stance on inflation drivers. The piece is brief and does not describe any formal decision by the bank in the coming weeks. It also does not quantify how large the expected slowdown in data center investment might be. Readers are left with the analysts' expectation that rate increases will continue on their current schedule.

Articles.Title: AI slump not seen affecting Bank of Japan’s rate-rise plan

stories.Headline: South Korea's Samsung Expands Chungcheong Region Investment to approximately $108 Billion for HBM, OLED, Battery Hubs
stories.Summary:
Samsung Group said on the 12th that it is raising its investment in South Korea's Chungcheong region from 140 trillion won to 144 trillion won, roughly $108 billion. The announcement came at a groundbreaking ceremony for the Chungcheong region megaproject at Samsung Electronics' Onyang campus in Asan, South Chungcheong Province. The plan covers production bases for high-bandwidth memory, organic light-emitting diodes, AI server package substrates and next-generation batteries. The increase is 4 trillion won over the July plan, and several major plants have moved up their start dates.

Four affiliates are taking part, each with its own share of the total. Samsung Electronics will invest 60 trillion won, about $45 billion, for HBM production at its Asan and Cheonan sites. Samsung Display will put in 67 trillion won, about $50.2 billion, with the largest share going to its A7 advanced OLED line in Asan. Samsung Electro-Mechanics will commit 8 trillion won, about $6.0 billion, to a Sejong plant for AI server package substrates, and Samsung SDI will invest 9 trillion won, about $6.7 billion, in a next-generation battery mother factory in Cheonan. Operations are targeted for June 2028 at Onyang Line 5, September 2028 at the Sejong plant and the second half of 2029 at the A7 line.

Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong spoke at the ceremony and described the site's shift from simple chip assembly and inspection to a base for HBM, which he called the heart of AI semiconductors. He said the megaproject is a historic challenge to reshape South Korea's future and called for the central government, local governments and companies to pool their efforts. Jun Young-hyun, the vice chairman who heads Samsung Electronics' DS Division, credited active support from national and local government for the speed of construction. Samsung Display CEO Lee Cheong and Samsung Electro-Mechanics CEO Jang Duck-hyun also made statements about their projects and their goals for the Korean display and AI industries.

The company says the strategy responds to surging AI chip demand and aims to gather back-end packaging, materials and components in one region. The article notes that as front-end miniaturization nears its limits, packaging now shapes chip performance, and that linking HBM, substrates and batteries in one place should speed supply chain response. It also warns that compressed construction timelines and overlapping investments by each affiliate could raise pressure on funding, equipment and personnel. Samsung plans to press ahead with similar megaprojects in the Honam and Yeongnam regions and the Seoul metropolitan area semiconductor cluster.

Articles.Title: South Korea's Samsung Expands Chungcheong Region Investment to approximately $108 Billion for HBM, OLED, Battery Hubs - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Billionaire venture capitalist Vinod Khosla says judge AI by usage, not stock prices
stories.Summary:
Billionaire venture capitalist Vinod Khosla said on Tuesday that AI should be judged by actual usage rather than by stock price moves, speaking on Yahoo Finance's Deirdre Bosa Live. The remarks came as Wall Street questioned whether AI is a bubble, with most of the worry focused on who is paying for the build-out. Khosla, a Sun Microsystems co-founder and early backer of OpenAI, measures usage in tokens, the chunks of text AI models process. The article presents his view as the key number to watch rather than the market's mood swings.

Combined free cash flow for Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle fell to about negative $31 billion in the third quarter, according to Goldman Sachs. That compares with positive $37 billion to $62 billion a quarter through 2025. OpenAI's quarterly revenue jumped nearly 50% to $10 billion. Much of Big Tech's cash goes into computing power that AI labs rent to run their chatbots. The article also notes that the share of Americans online rose from about 43% in 2000 to 59% in 2002, even as the Nasdaq Composite lost 78%.

Khosla's position is that usage has been real while the risk lies in overbuilding. The article says telecoms spent more than $500 billion laying fiber, and with 85% of it unused, bandwidth costs fell 90%, according to research by Kai Wu of Sparkline Capital. Wu also says early AI adopters are more evenly spread across sectors than infrastructure stocks. John Chambers, who ran Cisco through the dot-com boom and bust, told Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed this month that he expects major train wrecks this time too.

Corning fell 99% from 2000 to 2002 and did not top its dot-com high until February, a month after it signed a deal worth up to $6 billion to supply fiber for Meta's AI data centers. The article says the stock more than doubled by late June and has since given back more than half. Alphabet, Meta, and Netflix, none of which was public when the Nasdaq peaked, have added more than $5 trillion in market value since their first trades. Cisco is worth about $174 billion less than at its 2000 peak, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.

OpenAI cut its Luna model's price 80% after launch, and CFO Sarah Friar said use rose almost 10 times. Khosla said there will be a silicon shortage for a couple of years, while Wu noted that chips wear out over years, not decades. The article leaves open whether the winners will treat AI as a cheap ingredient as bandwidth became. It also does not say whether the spending by these five companies will be recovered.

Articles.Title: Billionaire venture capitalist Vinod Khosla says judge AI by usage, not stock prices

stories.Headline: Anthropic agrees to strict AI privacy rules in schools
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company, has agreed to a set of strict privacy rules for schools that use its tools, according to a report published November 11, 2026, by District Administration. The standards apply automatically to schools that use Claude for Teachers, the article says. They ban AI providers from training their models on data belonging to students and staff. The agreement was reached with the American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers, the two unions named in the report.

The article gives no further figures, dates for when the rules take effect, or penalties for violations, so those details cannot be reported here. What the report does establish is the core change: schools using the product are protected from having student and staff information used to train the company's models. The rules cover the schools that use Claude for Teachers rather than all AI tools in education. Beyond that, the report offers only the headline terms of the deal.

The article names Anthropic and the two teachers' unions as the parties to the agreement, and it does not include direct statements from any of them. Micah Ward is listed as the reporter. The piece appears alongside related coverage on AI in schools, including a separate story about Google restricting its search engine in schools that ban AI, but those stories are not part of this agreement. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Anthropic agrees to strict AI privacy rules in schools - District Administration

stories.Headline: SoftBank Takes $7 Billion Hit on US AI Data Centre Investme
stories.Summary:
SoftBank, the Japanese investment group, has reported billions of dollars in losses after changing its plans for US AI data centre infrastructure, according to Analytics India Magazine. The company had paid suppliers in advance and reserved manufacturing capacity to secure power generation equipment for its planned data centres. Between 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, those advance payments reached $9.5 billion. As its data centre plans evolved, SoftBank changed its equipment needs, leaving some already-paid-for equipment unused.

The company has written off $3.7 billion tied to that unused equipment and to changes in purchase agreements. It also reported a separate loss of ¥203.8 billion, around $1.3 billion, linked to warrants granted to OpenAI through its data centre business, Energy Global. Those warrants let OpenAI buy shares in Energy Global, so as the business grew in value, SoftBank's cost rose. Energy Global's valuation has increased mainly because its data centre business has expanded. SoftBank also recorded ¥136 billion, around $900 million, in additional employee and director compensation expenses linked to that increase in value.

SoftBank's leadership reported the losses, and the company clarified that the write-offs do not affect its PORTS-Pike power generation project, which is part of its broader US data centre expansion. The article describes the losses as a sign of how expensive it is to build AI infrastructure, since companies must also secure reliable power supplies to keep facilities running. It adds that SoftBank's task now is to ensure its investments in power generation and data centre infrastructure produce business returns. The article does not say what further steps the company will take or how the markets have reacted.

Articles.Title: SoftBank Takes $7 Billion Hit on US AI Data Centre Investme - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips
stories.Summary:
Fractile, a British startup building AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C round backed by Britain's Sovereign AI Fund, announced on November 11, 2026. The company said the investment aims to ensure the United Kingdom has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy. The round was led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Redpoint. Fractile is now one of the best-funded players in the race to build purpose-built AI chips, alongside Axelera, Etched and OLIX.

The funding matters because these chips are one way to lower the cost of inference, which means running increasingly demanding AI models in production. Fractile is pursuing a full-stack approach that pairs its hardware with a machine learning compiler meant to speed up how large language models run on its chips. The company describes itself as a frontier AI company, and the British government said the valuation was over £5 billion, a figure that could be around $7 billion according to reports from the Financial Times and a Reuters source. After a pivot, its design stacks DRAM, the most common type of memory, directly on top of each chip in a way the company hopes will avoid the usual tradeoff between memory and capacity. That tradeoff has grown more painful with agentic AI, where companies want long chains of tasks run on large models without losing speed.

Fractile's chief executive, Walter Goodwin, wrote in a LinkedIn post that the company still has a lot of work ahead. He said the new funding will let the startup ship its first chips and systems next year. The British government has framed the investment as a step toward a stronger national role in AI hardware. The company's leadership has presented the round as the next phase of that effort rather than a finished milestone.

Fractile's progress will now depend on whether it delivers working chips and systems next year as planned. The articles do not say how the chips will perform against competitors or when they will reach customers. Fractile's approach to memory is still unproven in production, and the available reporting does not describe any customers or orders. For now, the round gives the company resources to attempt that delivery.

Articles.Title: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips

stories.Headline: T-Robotics, KAIST Manufacturing Physical AI Research Institute Sign MOU to Strengthen Commercialization Cooperation
stories.Summary:
T-Robotics, a robot manufacturer, announced on November 13 that it had signed a memorandum of understanding with the Manufacturing Physical AI Research Institute at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST). The agreement is meant to advance the development and commercialization of the physical artificial intelligence industry. Both sides plan to build a framework for cooperation on standardization in the sector. They also intend to pursue commercialization and expansion into global markets based on technology demonstrations.

The partners aim to bring physical AI technologies into use at industrial sites and to revitalize the domestic ecosystem for related industries. T-Robotics had already taken part in the KAIROS project, a physical AI manufacturing demonstration platform led by KAIST. The company is now testing whether its own humanoid robot, TR-WORKS, and its autonomous mobile robots can be applied on site for manufacturing and logistics automation. The articles do not say what milestones or timelines the new agreement sets.

T-Robotics has built its business on vacuum robots used in display manufacturing and is now expanding into autonomous mobile robots and smart factory systems. It is also developing next-generation robots, including humanoids, along with technologies for robot mobility, task execution, and manufacturing process automation. The company says it wants to meet automation demand across a range of industrial sites. A company official said the agreement will widen existing cooperation with KAIST and help define concrete chances to demonstrate and commercialize physical AI. The official added that combining robot manufacturing with physical AI should improve the technology's fit at industrial sites and strengthen the company's competitiveness abroad.

Articles.Title: T-Robotics, KAIST Manufacturing Physical AI Research Institute Sign MOU to Strengthen Commercialization Cooperation - 아시아경제

stories.Headline: Complete Defense Solutions Shares Video on the Services Ai Arsenals Plans to Offer Defense Manufacturers
stories.Summary:
Complete Financial Solutions, Inc. (OTCID: CFSU) directed its shareholders on November 2, 2026, to a new video from Ai Arsenals, Inc. (AiA), explaining the company's plans for secured AI compute and defense manufacturing services. The video was released by Complete Defense Solutions (CDS), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, and was published in Las Vegas, Nevada. The announcement follows an October 6, 2026 disclosure that CDS had entered into a Binding Letter of Intent with AiA. The video is intended to help shareholders understand the business and service offerings that Ai Arsenals plans to provide.

Under the Binding Letter of Intent, CDS would acquire newly issued AiA Series A Preferred Stock intended to equal 9% of AiA's total valuation at the time the proposed transaction is completed. In exchange, the Company would issue its Series A Defense Preferred Stock, an arrangement referred to as the Exchange. The Exchange has not closed and remains subject to a 90-day due diligence period that began on October 4, 2026. The Exchange Amount has not been fixed and is to be agreed in writing at or before closing. There is no definitive agreement for AiA to provide services to CDS or to any company CDS may acquire, and CDS has not acquired any such company.

Ken Tapp, a Director of Complete Defense Solutions, said that while the transaction is pending, CDS and AiA are working to align CDS's defense acquisition strategy with AiA's advanced manufacturing and energy solutions. Tapp said defense manufacturers need secured AI compute and AI-ready manufacturing facilities at sovereign secured locations, and that Ai Arsenals is working to build them. Jeff Gabrelcik, Chief Executive Officer of Complete Financial Solutions, said the Company is now describing what it intends to acquire, a shared foundation of sovereign AI and manufacturing solutions. Gabrelcik said such a foundation is difficult for a single defense manufacturer to build on its own.

The release is aimed at shareholders of the Company and at executives of U.S. defense manufacturers, whom Tapp addressed directly in a video titled "A Message to America's Defense Manufacturers." The companies state that they will continue to provide educational media to shareholders, though non-disclosure agreements limit the information that can be made public. The Company is a U.S.-based holding company focused on defense, aerospace, space, advanced technology and manufacturing, and CDS describes itself as a management holding company connecting institutional capital with military technology and AI-driven defense manufacturing. Ai Arsenals describes itself as an early-stage sovereign secure AI and defense manufacturing company with a limited operating history and no revenue. In June 2026, the White House issued National Security Presidential Memorandum 11 (NSPM-11), which changes how the Department of War, the Intelligence Community and other national security agencies acquire and use artificial intelligence.

The release states that the facilities, secured AI compute, power infrastructure and AI tools described by Ai Arsenals are plans rather than current operations, and that AiA's ability to finance and accredit them is not assured. It also notes that the availability and timing of power technologies, including micro-reactors and small modular reactors, are uncertain, and that zoning approvals and substantial funding may be required. The release says Company shareholders could face dilution from the issuance of Series A Defense Preferred Stock, and that AiA's stock has no public market and an uncertain value. The information about Ai Arsenals was provided by AiA and has not been independently verified by the Company. The articles leave open whether the Exchange will close, whether the Exchange Amount will be agreed, whether CDS will acquire any defense manufacturer, and whether any such company will use AiA's services.

Articles.Title: Complete Defense Solutions Shares Video on the Services Ai Arsenals Plans to Offer Defense Manufacturers - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: How Conversational AI Is Moving Hotel Linen Management From Reactive to Proactive
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion piece by Mike Rispoli, VP of Product Management at Laundris, published on hospitalitynet.org on November 11, 2026. It argues that hotel linen management is moving from a reactive model to a proactive one through conversational AI. Rispoli describes how operators can use AI, combined with real-time RFID inventory data and historical usage patterns, to see shortages and loss patterns before they become costly. The article presents this as a shift in how hotels run their operations. Traditionally, linen management has depended on manual counts, often performed at the end of a shift, when staff are rushing.

Rispoli writes that these counts can be inaccurate, because stacks may be estimated rather than counted and carts or closets may be missed. Uncertain numbers lead operators either to over-order to avoid shortages or to place emergency orders after discovering a shortfall too late. Employees also spend hours searching for linen and recounting inventory. Rispoli says that without knowing where linen is going, replacement costs can keep rising unexplained. RFID improved the picture by tracking individual items automatically and producing a more accurate view of inventory within seconds.

Dashboards still require users to know which report to open, which filters to apply and what the data means. Rispoli argues that conversational AI removes this translation step by letting an operator ask questions in plain language and receive an answer based on inventory data. He describes the Laundris Assistant as one such tool, working with inventory data already captured in the Laundris platform. Operators can ask about stock, locations, loss trends and inventory needs, and can generate tailored reports and charts. Rispoli says the benefits reach housekeeping managers, purchasing decisions and loss control.

Operators could identify a coming shortage or an unusual loss pattern before it becomes expensive, and could order based on actual usage rather than buying extra as insurance. Staff would spend less time searching for linen and more time servicing rooms. Rispoli also notes that the Laundris Assistant lets operators get granular information without filtering through dashboards or waiting on a support ticket. He describes Laundris as a company that helps hotels improve efficiency, optimize inventory and reduce linen loss through RFID tracking and AI analytics. The article's background is largely the author's account of how linen management has developed, from manual counting on clipboards and in spreadsheets to RFID tracking and now conversational AI.

Rispoli presents the change as an evolution in operational technology rather than a response to a specific event. He identifies himself as VP of Product Management at Laundris, a company he describes as modernizing commercial laundry and linen services for the hospitality industry. The article does not report any adoption figures, cost savings or independent evaluation of the Laundris Assistant. It does not say how widely hotels currently use conversational AI for linen management or how the tool performs against alternatives. More to follow.

Articles.Title: How Conversational AI Is Moving Hotel Linen Management From Reactive to Proactive

stories.Headline: What this S’pore bank weighs in tailoring its AI tools across Asean
stories.Summary:
UOB, Singapore's third-largest lender, is shaping how it rolls out artificial intelligence across Asean, where a tool that suits a customer in Singapore may not suit one in Indonesia. The bank says differing regulations, customer needs and levels of digital maturity shape how its AI solutions are designed, deployed and governed in each market. Lawrence Goh, head of Group Technology and Operations at UOB, said that Indonesia requires customer-facing AI applications that handle personal data to be hosted onshore. The bank runs a standardised central platform and adapts deployment to local rules.

Markets with rich financial data, such as Singapore, can support AI-powered credit assessments. The bank's example is B-Score 2.0, an AI-enabled tool for its Commercial Banking Portfolio launched in August 2025, which draws on more than 3,000 data points to flag early signs of borrower distress among business accounts in Singapore. A regional rollout of the tool is in progress. UOB aims to become the "No. 1 trade bank in Asean" and help businesses trade across borders. Operating income from the Asean-4 markets of Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam grew 5 per cent year on year in the financial year ended December 31, 2025, and those markets contributed 28.5 per cent of operating income, second only to Singapore's more than half share.

Goh said the bank is building its technology on trust, control and reliability, so it can use regional scale where suitable, localise where needed and scale AI responsibly. Any technology it deploys must answer questions about whether the data is trustworthy, whether the party interacting with the bank is authentic, what it is authorised to do, and whether it can operate securely and consistently at scale. These questions matter more as UOB expands its use of agentic AI, in which AI agents act on behalf of people. Goh expects organisations to move from experimentation to enterprise-scale deployment of agentic AI over the next two to five years.

Trust is a concern for customers as well. UOB's Asean Consumer Sentiment Study 2026, which surveyed 5,000 consumers in Singapore and the Asean-4 markets in June 2026, found that 62 per cent trust AI-powered tools to act in their best interest on financial decisions, 14 percentage points below the 76 per cent who trust their primary bank to do so. Goh said AI may change how banking is delivered but not what customers value most, namely confidence that their money is safe, that their interests are protected and that someone remains accountable. He argued that the institutions that succeed will be those that use AI to strengthen that confidence. The article was produced in partnership with the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Global Finance & Technology Network.

Articles.Title: What this S’pore bank weighs in tailoring its AI tools across Asean - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Mercedes Lawyer Joins AI Native Compound Law
stories.Summary:
Compound Law, an AI-native law firm based in Berlin, has hired Marc Schuba, a former White & Case lawyer who most recently served as Legal Counsel at Mercedes-Benz, and Philipp Brandt, a business lawyer with more than 20 years of experience, who joins as a partner. The firm was co-founded by the former General Counsel of Zenjob, Julian Jantze, who is now its Chief Legal Officer. The article reports the hires on November 11, 2026. The move is notable because it involves an experienced in-house lawyer from a major corporation joining a firm built around a model that avoids the billable hour and puts AI at the centre of its work. The firm runs on two linked companies: a regulated law firm that advises clients and is responsible for the legal work, and a technology company that builds Compound OS, its AI platform.

Compound OS uses AI agents to prepare research, carry out analysis and draft documents, after which a lawyer reviews every result and is accountable for the final output to the client. Work is billed at fixed prices agreed up front rather than at hourly rates. The new hires will cover IT and AI law, data protection and intellectual property. The firm's focus is Germany and the EU, where, according to the article, the top 100 German law firms billed more than €10bn last year, and it plans to extend into further markets as it grows. Schuba told the publication that the traditional law firm model is out of date because it sells the same judgment repeatedly by the hour.

He argued that good legal judgment can be captured, refined and applied at scale, so that the firm codifies it once, lets its agents apply it, and improves it with each matter, which he said makes competitive fixed pricing possible. Jantze said that both new partners have long built their own software and online tools, and that clients with questions on software contracts, the EU AI Act, trademarks or a crisis will be routed directly to a partner with years of experience in the field. The article places the hires within a wider pattern in which experienced lawyers leave traditional firms to work in firms that do not bill by the hour, and it notes that these so-called NewMod firms are increasingly taking on complex, high-value work rather than only startup contracts or bulk review. The author suggests that large commercial firms are still using AI within a billing model that often works against its wider adoption, and expects more AI-native firms to appear. The article does not say what further steps Compound Law will take or when it will enter new markets.

Articles.Title: Mercedes Lawyer Joins AI Native Compound Law - Artificial Lawyer

stories.Headline: OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI
stories.Summary:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released a new guide on November 4 called the "OCC Supervisory Framework on Bank Use of Super Intelligence," which is meant to help its examiners review how banks use artificial intelligence. The guide focuses on generative AI, which creates text and other content, and agentic AI, which can act without a person stepping in each time. The agency used the term super intelligence because the executive branch adopted it in place of artificial intelligence, following a September 29 executive order signed by President Donald Trump. Some AI tools now handle credit decisions, customer service and fraud detection, which prompted the agency to set out how examiners should check them. The article frames the release as a response to the growing amount of work banks are handing to these systems.

The guide does not create new rules for banks, according to an analysis from the law firm Ballard Spahr, and it works as a resource for examiners instead. Banks will not treat AI as a separate risk category, and examiners will instead look at how AI changes risks banks already manage, including fraud, privacy, cybersecurity and work with outside vendors. The OCC built the guide around six areas, asking what an AI system is allowed to do, what happens when it makes a mistake, what guardrails exist, who is watching, how a bank recovers from failure, and whether safety checks keep working over time. The guide also ties risk to how much freedom a system has, and it lays out four risk levels, with autonomous payment bots and instant credit decisions at the top and internal tools that never touch customer data at the bottom. The OCC warned that a person who simply clicks approve does not provide real oversight, and reviewers need the skills, facts and power to reject or stop what the AI does.

The OCC's position is that banks remain responsible for their AI systems, and a bank is still on the hook if its AI breaks the law, the analysis said. The agency pointed to customer harm from chatbots that give wrong answers about fees, interest rates or account balances, which could lead to legal trouble. Because many banks buy their AI from outside companies, vendors face extra scrutiny, and the guide asks whether contracts spell out who pays when an AI tool causes harm. It also asks whether vendors must warn banks before changing how their AI works, since a vendor could add new AI features to an old product without the bank noticing the new risks. In a bulletin released with the guide, the OCC said the document sets no binding standards and banks are not expected to use it to grade their own AI programs.

Even without binding force, the analysis said banks should not ignore the guide, which offers a clear preview of what examiners may ask in future bank exams. Banks are encouraged to study it and check whether current risk and compliance programs already cover the issues the OCC raised. Institutions that find gaps now may have an easier time when examiners arrive, the analysis suggested. The article does not say whether the OCC plans further guidance or enforcement actions tied to AI, so those details remain unclear.

Articles.Title: OCC Gives Bank Examiners a New Playbook for Reviewing AI - PYMNTS.com

stories.Headline: Slow and steady characterizes nation’s rational AI buildout
stories.Summary:
The recent swings in US chip stocks, driven by midterm-election worries over data-center regulation, were highlighted in a China Daily commentary published on November 10, 2026. The piece argues that such volatility shows how dependent the American AI buildout has become on a policy and regulatory landscape that could shift quickly. It contrasts this with China's approach, which it describes as demand-driven, self-reliant and coordinated with the power grid. The commentary presents this as a structural difference rather than a boast of superiority.

The piece points to several figures to support its case. Wang Weiming, chief engineer of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, said that in the first three quarters of 2026, computing power driven by domestic AI chips and large language models grew more compatible, with more than 1,000 application scenarios taking shape across 20 industries, including steel, automobiles and pharmaceuticals. Xie Cun, an MIIT spokesman, said China's intelligent computing capacity reached 2,592 EFLOPS by the end of September, up 146 percent year on year. Jiang Yi, a spokesman for the National Development and Reform Commission, said estimates put new direct investment in computing network construction during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30) at 4 trillion yuan, or about $599.59 billion, with enterprises as the main investors.

The commentary credits several policies for this approach. It describes the "East Data, West Computing" initiative, which links computing demand in eastern China with resources in the western regions. It also cites the separation of industrial and residential electricity pricing, which it says keeps the cost of the buildout from falling on ordinary households. By contrast, the piece describes US data centers competing with homeowners for water in drought-stricken states, pushing up household power bills, and facing projects halted by litigation and protests.

The commentary is not uncritical of China's own path. It warns that rapid growth in computing capacity can invite overheating, and it urges building what is needed, where it is needed, with chips, power and users in place. It frames China's patient, long-term planning as a strategic advantage that must be protected from the temptation to overreach. The article carries no reported reaction from US officials or industry groups, and it does not describe any specific next steps beyond calling for steady and deliberate growth.

Articles.Title: Slow and steady characterizes nation’s rational AI buildout - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: U.S. stocks rebound as CoreWeave reignites AI rally
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks rebounded on Wednesday, November 11, as a strong quarterly report from CoreWeave revived confidence in spending on artificial intelligence. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 254.6 points, or 0.49 percent, to close at 52,486.49 in New York. The S&P 500 gained 98.45 points, or 1.31 percent, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 400.31 points, or 1.6 percent. CoreWeave, a company described as a neocloud business, soared 24.71 percent after reporting third-quarter revenue of 3.66 billion dollars. That figure was up 168 percent from a year earlier, and the company also raised its outlook for the full year.

The S&P 500 finished at 7,619.38, and the Nasdaq Composite ended at 25,466.19. Ten of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended higher, with technology leading by adding 2.71 percent, followed by energy, up 1.83 percent. Consumer discretionary was the only sector to fall, edging down 0.36 percent. CoreWeave raised its full-year revenue forecast to between 13 billion and 13.3 billion dollars, up from a prior target of 12 billion to 13 billion dollars. West Texas Intermediate crude settled at 86.53 U.S. dollars a barrel, up 0.57 percent, after rising from two-month lows.

CoreWeave chief executive Michael Intrator said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday that demand for compute is growing faster than the capacity to deliver the infrastructure. He added that this is echoed by expanding margins on each additional contract, and he credited strong demand for AI compute capacity. Kevin Rippey, a technology analyst at Evercore ISI, said sentiment around the frontier is the core driver of the AI trade set. Rippey said the market gets through this event, and that looking out into December one can draw quite a bullish construct. Baird analyst Tristan Gerra cut his rating on Nvidia to neutral, citing uncertainties over U.S. government action, investigations, and the tenure of its chief executive.

Nvidia rose 2.87 percent in the Xinhua account, recovering part of its two-day slide even after the Baird downgrade, and Yahoo Finance put the gain at roughly 4 percent. Micron Technology and SanDisk both jumped over 11 percent, with significant gains also in Advanced Micro Devices, Intel and Broadcom. Yahoo Finance reported that AMD and Broadcom rose over 5 percent, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing rose 4 percent and ASML gained 3 percent. Oil moved higher as doubts grew over a diplomatic settlement with Iran, after Tehran said it would not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country. Fresh attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz also kept shipping risks in focus.

Nvidia shares rose for the first time since chief executive Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, according to Yahoo Finance. A company board investigation, increased scrutiny from lawmakers, and questions over whether restricted semiconductors were diverted to China have weighed on the stock. Even with the bounce, Nvidia is down about 14 percent in November and has lost about 700 billion dollars in market value. Earlier in the week, CoreWeave had risen 5 percent on Monday as AI stocks bounced back from a selloff the previous week. A Yahoo Finance analysis said CoreWeave guided to third-quarter interest expense of 860 million to 940 million dollars, and that total debt, leases included, had climbed to 51.6 billion dollars at June 30.

The U.S. bond market was closed on Wednesday for Veterans Day, so there was no trading in Treasuries a day after the benchmark 10-year yield topped 5 percent on hotter-than-expected inflation data. Traders still see a December rate hike as near-certain, with the odds of a quarter-point move at about 90 percent, according to CME FedWatch. Investors next turn to weekly jobless claims and Nebius earnings on Thursday. Baird said it would stay neutral on Nvidia until the upcoming congressional hearing and the U.S. government investigations reach their conclusions. The articles do not say when the hearing will be held or how long the investigations will last, and they leave open whether the rally will last.
