stories.Headline: Judge rules Novig's sports event contracts are not swaps, letting New York enforce its gambling law
stories.Summary:
A federal judge in Manhattan has denied sports prediction market Novig's request for a preliminary injunction that would have stopped New York from enforcing its gambling laws against it. In a filing dated November 10, U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon of the Southern District of New York ruled that Novig's sports event contracts are not swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act, according to The Block. Because the contracts fall outside that definition, she concluded, federal commodities law does not preempt New York's gambling and sports-wagering rules. The ruling was reported on November 11, 2026. The practical effect is that New York can now require Novig to obtain a state gambling license or stop listing and trading the contracts.

McMahon wrote that the contracts "bear more than a passing resemblance to sports betting," and she reasoned that they do not depend on events with a financial, economic or commercial consequence, which is the test for a swap. Novig, whose legal entity is Ludlow Exchange LLC, had sued New York Attorney General Letitia James and state Gaming Commission officials on August 5, arguing that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts. The CFTC had designated Ludlow as a contract market in June, and Novig began offering sports contracts to New York customers in August. The ruling is narrower than it might first appear, though it goes further than an earlier decision against Kalshi. In July, Judge Analisa Torres of the same court denied Kalshi a preliminary injunction while assuming, without deciding, that its sports contracts were swaps.

A finding that such contracts are not swaps at all would undercut the starting point of the preemption argument that Kalshi, Polymarket and others rely on. Lawyer Daniel Wallach told The Block that federal courts in the Second Circuit have now issued 10 rulings in sports prediction-market litigation, all favoring the states. The ruling does not end Novig's lawsuit, and the company is litigating the same issue in several other states. The Block said it had asked Novig for comment.

Articles.Title: Judge rules Novig's sports event contracts are not swaps, letting New York enforce its gambling law - MLQ.ai

stories.Headline: Courts’ budget request, AI ethics guidance, veterans’ honors lead Florida Bar News Briefs
stories.Summary:
The Florida Bar's weekly podcast, Florida Bar News Briefs, released an episode on November 10, 2026, covering three developments in the legal profession. The episode reports on the judicial branch's latest budget request, which seeks a new courthouse in Lakeland for the Sixth District Court of Appeal, higher salaries for judges, and case management technology for the trial courts. It also reports that former Florida Attorney General Bill McCollum and Duval County Judge Mose L. Floyd, both Florida Bar members, are being inducted into the Florida Veterans' Hall of Fame. A third item covers a proposed advisory opinion from a Florida Bar committee on whether artificial intelligence can generate suggestions for attorneys.

The budget request is the centerpiece of the first story, and the articles give no dollar figures, dates for construction, or timelines for the salary increases or technology upgrades. The advisory opinion under consideration would address how lawyers may use artificial intelligence when it produces suggestions in their work. The committee's proposal reflects input from a handful of attorneys, most of whom, according to the briefing, want more guidance on the subject. The articles do not describe the opinion's specific provisions or whether it has been adopted.

The Florida Bar's Journal and News Department produces the podcast, which is part of its multimedia network. The articles do not include direct statements from McCollum, Floyd, the judicial branch, or the committee members, so no quotations or positions from them can be reported here. The articles also do not say when the Hall of Fame induction will take place or when the committee will vote on its proposed opinion. Beyond the episode itself, the coverage offers no further context or next steps.

Articles.Title: Courts’ budget request, AI ethics guidance, veterans’ honors lead Florida Bar News Briefs - The Florida Bar

stories.Headline: Two Career Experts Explain How AI Practice Can Help Neurodivergent Candidates Navigate Interview Bias
stories.Summary:
Two career experts have described how AI interview practice may help neurodivergent job candidates prepare for bias in live interviews, according to an article published on CPA Practice Advisor on November 12, 2026. The article reports that AI interview tools can offer candidates a low-pressure environment to rehearse answers and become more comfortable with likely questions. It was prepared with ResumeCoach, an AI-powered resume and career optimization platform, which consulted two career experts. The experts' advice is framed around the interview stage, where the article says research suggests the system often breaks down rather than at the résumé stage. Eye contact, small talk, body language, and quick social responses can influence hiring decisions, even though the article says these behaviors may say little about a candidate's ability to do the job.

The article cites Rowan University research finding that 92% of neurodivergent respondents named anxiety or nervousness as their biggest interview barrier, while 50% cited a lack of confidence. The same research estimates that 10% to 30% of U.S. college students show neurodivergent traits. Cornell and Vanderbilt University researchers identify interviews as one of the biggest barriers for autistic job seekers and recommend sharing questions in advance and using specific prompts. A University of Vermont research summary found that autistic candidates were rated less favorably on video but were preferred when evaluators read transcripts of the same responses. The article notes that the candidates' answers did not change, only the way they were presented.

The two experts quoted are Dahlia Ashford, a certified employment and interview professional at Ashford Career Consulting, and Chelsea Jay, a career and interview coach at Seasoned and Growing. Ashford advises building a small set of comfortable small talk topics, avoiding politics, requesting the interview schedule and interviewer list in advance, and rehearsing with mock interviews. Jay says AI should not be used to teach neurodivergent professionals to mask, and that its goal is to reduce uncertainty so nerves do not overshadow what candidates offer. Both experts emphasize that AI should reduce uncertainty rather than teach masking, according to the article. Ashford also suggests practicing questions about age, disability, religion, or family status, which the article describes as legally off-limits, so candidates can redirect them.

The article is aimed at neurodivergent job seekers, and the research it cites concerns autistic candidates and U.S. college students who show neurodivergent traits. It points to the live interview stage, where the article says their skills are most likely to be overlooked. Ashford and Jay both advise candidates to rehearse common questions, such as "Tell me about yourself," with an AI tool. Jay suggests giving the AI a job description, asking for five to seven likely questions, and then asking it to evaluate whether answers were complete and clear. The article does not report whether any employers have adopted such tools, or what outcomes candidates have seen from using them.

Articles.Title: Two Career Experts Explain How AI Practice Can Help Neurodivergent Candidates Navigate Interview Bias - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: From software-defined to AI-native: Automotive’s next operating model
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA published an article on November 12, 2026, written by Ralf Malter, Managing Director for Global Automotive, Business Consulting and AI at NTT DATA DACH, titled around the shift from software-defined vehicles to an AI-native operating model. The piece draws on the company's 2026 Global AI Report, which argues that most automakers and suppliers have moved past pilot projects and proofs of concept. It says the real question now is whether leaders are using AI in ways that change how the business actually runs. The article describes AI as becoming the operating model itself rather than a complement to it.

The report's data shows a widening gap between leaders and laggards. Of leaders, 38.6 percent are already rebuilding applications with embedded AI, compared with 12 percent of laggards. Leaders focus on redesigning high-value workflows end to end, including engineering, change management, quality escalation, warranty triage and procurement exceptions. The article contends that the main constraint is no longer model quality but workflow design. It also says 93.2 percent of leaders apply AI in core operational workflows, against 68.8 percent of laggards.

The author argues that the rise of software-defined vehicles points to a broader change, since AI in engineering, manufacturing, supply chains and in-vehicle experiences makes the whole value chain driven by data-based decisions. He describes agentic AI as able to carry out and adjust workflows as conditions change, with examples such as coordinating over-the-air updates, simulating test conditions and adapting in-vehicle experiences to usage. The article notes that many organizations still treat AI mainly as a tool for efficiency, which it attributes to viewing AI as "better automation." Governance is presented as essential in a sector where safety and compliance are non-negotiable, and 67.6 percent of leaders have adopted centralized AI governance compared with 38.4 percent of laggards.

The article is promotional in nature and is written by an NTT DATA executive, so its figures come from the company's own research and have not been independently verified. It describes the report as offering a playbook for automotive AI leaders and invites readers to download it. The piece does not describe any regulatory action or external deadlines. It concludes that competitive advantage will come from how well organizations align their operating models with AI, and it frames the future of automotive as both software-defined and AI-native.

Articles.Title: From software-defined to AI-native: Automotive’s next operating model - NTT Data

stories.Headline: Analysis: China’s Banks Move AI From Pilots to Production
stories.Summary:
Chinese banks are moving artificial intelligence out of pilot projects and into daily operations, using it to automate routine work, speed up research, and build systems that can carry out complex tasks. The shift was reported by Caixin Global in an analysis published on November 11, 2026. As adoption spreads, financial institutions are weighing whether the productivity gains justify the costs, how to connect AI with fragmented data systems, and how to guard against more sophisticated cyberattacks. The report frames these as the central questions facing the sector as the technology expands.

Reported usage figures show how far the change has gone. Bank of Jiangsu said its AI applications have cumulatively replaced 1.2 million working hours and cut the time needed to approve credit for small and midsize enterprises by 30%. Shanghai Pudong Development Bank said its digital workforce handles workloads equal to more than 2,500 people each year. Bank of China's systems can recognize 305 types of documents across 3,800 business scenarios. The most effective uses so far involve repetitive, rules-based work or large volumes of information, such as document handling, customer service, payment-fraud detection, and preliminary credit assessment.

Investment research is a harder area, and the article says AI can gather information, analyze financial statements, screen securities, and draft reports, which reduces the time analysts spend on preliminary work. However, financial insiders told Caixin that AI-generated research may serve only as a reference and is not automatically suitable for publication or for decisions carrying significant financial risk. Human analysts remain responsible for interpreting results and making judgments. The next phase, according to the report, involves AI agents that perform several connected tasks, with Citic Securities developing its own tools for ETF screening, stock analysis, and financial statement analysis, and Moonshot's Kimi deployed at institutions including ICBC, CICC, Citic Securities, and E Fund Management.

The article also points to cost and integration barriers. A source at Tencent's WorkBuddy platform said a single private AI project can cost several million to tens of millions of yuan, excluding maintenance, and that private systems may take about three months to update compared with roughly two days for SaaS solutions, which carry their own security and data-management implications. An AI technology executive at a joint-stock bank said business and technology teams often fail to understand each other's needs, leaving no effective bridge between them. On security, the Bank for International Settlements estimated that AI could cut the cost of simple cyberattacks to about $50 to $100 and more sophisticated operations to $5,000 to $10,000, and Fan Yuan, chairman of DBAPPSecurity, said future cyber battles will increasingly be fought between AI systems.

Articles.Title: Analysis: China’s Banks Move AI From Pilots to Production - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: Constant Contact Launches AI Marketing Product for Small Businesses
stories.Summary:
Constant Contact, a marketing solutions provider for small businesses based in Waltham, Massachusetts, announced on Thursday, November 12, 2026, the release of Catalyst, a new agentic AI marketing product. The company says Catalyst works like an expert a business owner hires rather than another tool the owner must learn. Unlike traditional AI marketing tools that generate content or recommendations, Catalyst is designed to carry out the marketing work itself. It analyzes a business's digital presence, identifies growth opportunities, builds personalized campaigns, and executes them across email, social, SMS and other channels, always with the owner's approval.

Catalyst scans a business's digital footprint to learn its voice, then builds an itemized plan that the owner can review and refine in a chat interface. It helps the business appear across email, Facebook and Instagram, SMS, ads, its Google business profile and its website. Catalyst creates the content, a human approves it, and the product then handles execution on the owner's behalf. Results feed back through system integrations from one week to the next, so the product adjusts its actions based on outcomes. Owners can choose which channels Catalyst uses, edit any part of the proposed plan, turn off access to any channel, and approve the plan before it goes live.

Frank J. Vella, Constant Contact's chief executive officer, said most small business owners are passionate about what they do but lack the resources to hire a marketing professional, and he argued they should not have to. In a statement, he said Catalyst builds the plan, does the work and learns what resonates with a specific audience, all in the owner's voice, while the owner stays in charge. The company's own release makes the same points about owner control. Owners who want to try the product can join its early access program through the company's website at constantcontact.com/catalyst.

The launch comes as small business owners are looking for ways to market their companies without large staffs. Constant Contact's release presents Catalyst as a step beyond AI tools that only produce text or suggestions. The articles do not give pricing, a general availability date, or independent results from early users. Further details on rollout and availability were not included in the coverage.

Articles.Title: Constant Contact Launches AI Marketing Product for Small Businesses - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Inside Greece's new AI Act framework
stories.Summary:
Greece has set up its national framework for enforcing the EU AI Act through Law 5321/2026, which took effect on its 20 July publication date unless a provision says otherwise. The law spreads oversight across existing sectoral regulators instead of creating a new standalone AI authority. Its publication came about two weeks before the European Commission and national authorities began enforcing the AI Act on 2 August, when new transparency rules took effect. The bill moved quickly, opening for public consultation on 21 June, with the text finalized and enacted within two weeks after consultation closed on 6 July.

The Hellenic Data Protection Authority has been designated as the market surveillance authority for prohibited AI practices, Annex III high-risk systems and Article 50 transparency obligations. It also serves as Greece's single point of contact with the Commission and other member states. As a result, enforcement of the AI Act and the EU General Data Protection Regulation sits with the same regulator. Legal commentators have pointed out that many AI systems covered by Annex III process personal data or directly affect fundamental rights, which gives the authority's existing data protection expertise direct relevance to its new role.

The article was written by Aspasia Xirou, a data privacy risk specialist at the International Monetary Fund, and it was published by the IAPP. The author's analysis describes the structure of the law and its timing rather than attributing new decisions to any particular official. The Greek Ministry of Digital Governance handled the bill's public consultation and its passage. The article does not report any direct statements from ministry officials or from the data protection authority about how they plan to carry out the new duties.

The move reflects a broader choice available to EU member states, which have discretion over how to organize the national authorities that the AI Act relies on. Greece chose to build on an existing regulator rather than create a new body, and the article presents this as a distributed model in contrast to other approaches. The article does not describe specific enforcement actions, penalties, or a timetable for further guidance beyond the dates already noted. Further developments on how the framework operates in practice are not covered in the article.

Articles.Title: Inside Greece's new AI Act framework - IAPP

stories.Headline: Micron Technology (MU) Commits $1 Billion To Landmark AI Infrastructure IPO
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology (MU) committed US$1 billion to Anthropic's private placement, which forms part of the AI lab's upcoming initial public offering. The commitment was reported in an article published on November 11, 2026, by Yahoo Finance, drawing on a Simply Wall St analysis. The deal was described as landmark AI infrastructure funding that places Micron alongside other major chip, cloud, and data firms financing Anthropic. Micron is listed on the NasdaqGS exchange, and its stake is tied to the broader AI infrastructure build-out now under way.

Anthropic is targeting more than US$90 billion from a public share sale and a US$26 billion private placement, according to the deal outline cited in the article. Micron's US$1 billion stake is a portion of that private placement. The article does not state the price per share, the offering date, or the exact terms governing Micron's allocation. It also does not say what percentage of Anthropic the stake represents or what governance rights accompany it.

The article attributes the move to Micron's strategy of embedding itself in the AI infrastructure stack alongside Nvidia and AMD, as a funding partner rather than only a component vendor. Simply Wall St frames the investment as a bet that future memory demand is contract-backed rather than purely cyclical. The article presents this as the view implied by Micron's strategy, not as a statement from Micron's management. No direct quotation from a Micron executive or Anthropic representative appears in the text.

Micron supplies memory and storage semiconductors to data centers, AI developers, and device makers across the US, Asia, Japan, Europe, and other regions. The article notes that analysts already flag high capital intensity and execution risk in new fabs. It adds that tying more capital to a single AI customer introduces concentration and timing questions for investors. Shareholders and the company's customers across these regions are the parties with the most direct exposure to the outcome.

Micron has announced related collaborations with Anthropic in earlier months, according to a list of prior coverage on the page. Those earlier reports covered the AI supply deal and shares rising on the partnership. Micron's fiscal earnings report was scheduled for June 24, and the article cites share movement before that date. The article also points to Micron's ties to Nvidia and AMD in the AI supply chain as background.

The articles do not say when Anthropic's IPO will price or list, nor whether the US$90 billion public offering has a confirmed date. They do not confirm that Micron's US$1 billion commitment has closed or been formally approved. The reader is not told how the investment will be recorded on Micron's balance sheet. Whether the contract-backed demand thesis holds, and how Micron's execution on new fabs will proceed, remains unresolved in the text.

Articles.Title: Micron Technology (MU) Commits $1 Billion To Landmark AI Infrastructure IPO

stories.Headline: Google Will Offer Vermont Schools Two Ways to Keep Search for Students. Both Include AI
stories.Summary:
Starting early next year, Google Search will be off on Vermont students' school accounts unless their district turns it on. Google announced the change on November 3, and it says any district that enables Search will get one of two versions, both with artificial intelligence built in. Four Google services will also start off by default in early 2027, including the Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and the AI tools inside Google's assignment app. A district can turn on Search without turning on the Gemini chatbot, but it cannot turn on Search without its AI features, such as AI Overviews and AI Mode. Students in a district that leaves Search off will see a message that it isn't available.

The two versions differ in how they respond to students. The standard version works like the one adults use, offering AI summaries and chat, while the Guided Learning version runs through a student version of Gemini and is designed to walk students through problems step by step rather than give answers. Vermont's Agency of Education has already advised schools to keep chatbots away from pre-K through grade 2 students and to limit AI in grades 3 to 5 to subject-specific tools that stick to the lesson. The agency's January guidance is advice rather than a rule, and it said all Vermont schools were using Google for Education, so the change could reach every public school system in the state. Compass asked the agency whether either option fits its recommendations for elementary grades, and the agency has not yet said.

Google says the change gives schools more choice, not less, and it argues that the guided version will keep students from getting quick answers to schoolwork. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, has said that search and AI are deeply integrated, which is why the two cannot be separated. Critics are not persuaded, and when a Times reporter tested the public version of Guided Learning, it wrote a detailed essay for an Advanced Placement history assignment. Common Sense Media rated AI Overviews and AI Mode an unacceptable risk for young users in July. On November 9, Massachusetts Sen. Ed Markey wrote to Google's CEO asking the company to reverse the change by November 30, and the agency said it is facing considerable pressure from educators to give districts more control over which AI features are enabled.

Google has not set an exact date for the change and says schools will get details in the coming months. The Agency of Education says it will keep watching and share recommendations as more information emerges. Parents who want to know what their district plans can ask whether Google Search will be turned on for students and in which grades, which version would be used, and what students would use for research if it stays off. They can also look for their district's AI policy and review the state's grade-by-grade guidance in the Vermont AI Guidance for Education.

Articles.Title: Google Will Offer Vermont Schools Two Ways to Keep Search for Students. Both Include AI - Compass Vermont

stories.Headline: Chinese actress Zhao Liying's lawsuit spotlights AI misuse as experts urge stronger oversight
stories.Summary:
Chinese actress Zhao Liying has reportedly sued the operator of the short-drama platform Hongguo Short Drama and its parent company, Douyin, over the alleged unauthorized use of her likeness in AI-generated content. According to a report by the Dahe Daily, court records shown on the business information platform Qichacha indicated a hearing was scheduled for a Tuesday at the Mentougou District People's Court in Beijing. The defendants are Beijing Douyin Information Service Co Ltd, Beijing Bimo Liuxiang Technology Co Ltd and an individual identified by the surname Shi. Qichacha records show that Beijing Bimo Liuxiang Technology, founded in July 2021, is wholly owned by Beijing Douyin Information Service and is linked to Hongguo Short Drama.

Users on Sina Weibo have posted screenshots and clips from AI-generated short dramas on Hongguo that feature characters resembling Zhao and voices that sound similar to hers, and the case has become a trending topic there. The article says several other Chinese actors, including Yi Yangqianxi, Yang Zi, Xiao Zhan, Deng Wei and Cheng Yi, have faced similar disputes over AI-generated short dramas. Voice actors are also affected: Ji Guanlin told the Global Times that colleagues, including herself, have had their voices used without authorization, and some have sought legal remedies. Under China's Civil Code, a "portrait" is an external image that can identify a person, so an AI-generated figure need not be an exact copy to infringe, according to lawyer Li Yunkai of the Beijing Tianyuan Law Firm. A September opinion from the Supreme People's Court says training AI on a person's voice without consent, or generating recognizable synthetic speech of them, may infringe their voice rights.

Regulators are responding. According to Xinhua, China's National Radio and Television Administration has launched a two-month campaign running from November 1 to the end of December, aimed at vulgar and homogeneous micro short dramas and at unauthorized use of faces and voices, which the article calls "face theft" and "voice theft." Li Yunkai said distribution parties as well as production companies may bear responsibility, and that content placing a recognizable person in vulgar scenes, false endorsements or negative storylines could also violate reputation rights. Zhang Peng, a cultural researcher at Nanjing Normal University, argued that platforms should verify authorization, label AI content clearly, remove infringing material quickly and suspend repeat offenders, and that watermarking and authorization databases could help. The article does not report a court ruling in the Zhao case, and it does not say what the outcome of the hearing was.

Articles.Title: Chinese actress Zhao Liying's lawsuit spotlights AI misuse as experts urge stronger oversight

stories.Headline: A New Committee Will Spend a Year Weighing AI's Impact on City Life
stories.Summary:
A three-member council committee in Riverside began a 13-month review of artificial intelligence on Thursday, Nov. 5, and the first meeting drew residents who urged caution about data centers. The Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Policy Ad Hoc Committee will study how AI affects city services, privacy, jobs, utility costs and infrastructure. Its recommendations are due to the City Council by November 2027, though chair Steven Robillard said that date is a guideline rather than an absolute deadline. The review is advisory, and the committee will hear from outside experts, study other cities and gather public input before sending its findings to the full council.

Speakers at the public comment period raised concerns about the strain data centers could place on local resources. April Glatzel questioned whether the city could support such facilities given residents' efforts to conserve water, and she said she would accept less convenience rather than risk those resources. Tinka Friend welcomed the committee but asked members to weigh the consequences carefully before decisions reached them. Robillard said no data center proposal was before the committee, and Chief Innovation Officer George Khalil said he knew of no current project. Councilmember Philip Falcone said he opposes data centers while supporting the broader review.

The proposed work plan goes beyond data centers to examine how residents interact with City Hall, including multilingual translation, 311 assistance and permit help, along with the AI tools staff use for drafting and research. Riverside's administrative AI policy, effective July 2024, requires human review of AI-generated material, verification of facts, disclosure of AI use and an option to reach a human. The schedule moves from city services to infrastructure and land use, then to workforce, economic opportunity, privacy, cybersecurity and vendor accountability. The infrastructure review will consider electricity demand, water use, zoning, noise and who would pay for utility expansion, with computing loads of 20, 50 and more than 100 megawatts under consideration.

The committee's members include Robillard, Councilmember Steve Hemenway and Councilmember Philip Falcone, and Hemenway asked that the review capture both positive and negative social and economic effects. Khalil said protecting resident information and keeping access to city employees remain priorities. Robillard said members want perspectives beyond city staff and that hearings will feature experts answering committee questions. The committee's schedule could change, and additional meetings may be needed as the review proceeds.

Articles.Title: A New Committee Will Spend a Year Weighing AI's Impact on City Life - The Raincross Gazette

stories.Headline: DCU-Led European Master in Law, Data and AI Awarded €3.6 Million Erasmus Mundus Grant - Dublin City University
stories.Summary:
Dublin City University and four international partners have secured a €3.6 million grant from the European Commission for the European Master in Law, Data and Artificial Intelligence (EMILDAI), a joint master's programme under the Erasmus Mundus scheme. The announcement was published on DCU's website on 12 November 2026. The award is coordinated by DCU, which leads a consortium of five partner universities across Europe and Brazil. The funding guarantees the operation and expansion of EMILDAI through 2032 and allows the consortium to recruit up to 100 students globally. The grant will pay for full scholarships for European Union and international students, student and academic staff mobility across partner institutions, collaborative research and curriculum development, and deeper links with industry partners.

The programme combines legal policy with computer science, preparing graduates to handle the legal, ethical and technical questions raised by artificial intelligence and data-driven systems. Students begin with foundational coursework at DCU before moving on to specialised tracks in areas such as data governance, cybersecurity and global digital regulation. DCU President Professor Daire Keogh described the award as a strong endorsement of the programme's vision and academic excellence, and said the university is proud to lead the consortium. Dr Edoardo Celeste, the programme director, said the funding confirms the vision set out when the programme was founded in 2021 by four pioneer institutions. Professor Lisa Looney, Vice President for Academic Affairs and Registrar, said the money reinforces DCU's commitment to an interdisciplinary curriculum and international mobility.

Dr Gezim Visoka, Executive Dean of the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences, said the grant will help the programme keep fostering legal research and ethical leadership in the field. The partner universities are Avignon Université in France, Erasmus University Rotterdam in the Netherlands, Fundação Getulio Vargas in Brazil, Universidad de León in Spain and the Università di Pisa in Italy. Graduates earn a joint master's degree recognised across Europe and internationally. The article notes that students can learn more about the programme and 2027 scholarship opportunities on the EMILDAI website.

Articles.Title: DCU-Led European Master in Law, Data and AI Awarded €3.6 Million Erasmus Mundus Grant - Dublin City University

stories.Headline: The Next Generation Of Law Students Don’t Trust AI Hype
stories.Summary:
A new report from Blickstein Group, titled "The College Student AI Reality Check," finds that today's college students are wary of artificial intelligence despite using it often. The survey drew responses from students at 37 colleges and universities, plus five in-depth interviews. The project was led by Vera Grabow, an intern and college junior, who began it after watching AI change her own education. Her work was published on November 12, 2026 on the Above the Law website.

The findings show heavy use but little trust. Some 71 percent of respondents said they use AI several times a week or more for schoolwork, and 27.8 percent said they turn to an AI tool first when learning a new concept, slightly ahead of Google at 25.3 percent. Only 3.8 percent go first to professors or teaching assistants. Most students said AI saves them modest amounts of time, with the most common answer being 10 to 24 percent (32.4 percent), and 72.1 percent believed heavy reliance on AI leaves people somewhat or much less capable at their jobs. Pre-law students showed the same heavy use but even more skepticism, with 66.7 percent saying AI is acceptable only for brainstorming.

The report's author, Vera Grabow, conceived the project, wrote the questionnaire, led outreach, analyzed the data and drafted the report, according to Blickstein Group CEO Brad Blickstein, who said the firm helped but credited her with the work. Blickstein described it as an exceptional piece by a college student. The article's author, Joe Patrice, a senior editor at Above the Law, wrote that his own conversations with students largely matched the report's conclusions. Neither source suggests the findings are settled beyond this sample.

The article presents the results as a challenge for the legal industry and for AI developers who have promoted tools that would take over much of the drafting work. The report suggests that a skeptical human overseeing AI is a more sensible model for law than full automation, and that AI companies will need to persuade this generation to trust the technology more. The article does not say what steps firms or developers will take in response. Readers can find the full report through a link on the Above the Law article.

Articles.Title: The Next Generation Of Law Students Don’t Trust AI Hype

stories.Headline: Biglaw’s Latest AI Incentive For Associates Comes With A $1 Million Prize Pot
stories.Summary:
Latham & Watkins has announced a new Associate AI Impact Award, backed by a $1 million prize pot for 2027, according to an article published by Above the Law on November 12, 2026. The program is aimed at associates who lead or materially contribute to AI initiatives that generate value for clients, practice groups, matter teams, or the firm as a whole. The article notes that awards will vary depending on each initiative's impact and its potential to scale. It also reports that the program comes as the firm expands its artificial intelligence work.

The award is designed to recognize work that the firm believes can improve how it serves clients and runs its operations. Latham has set aside $1 million for payouts in 2027, and the size of each award will depend on the reach and promise of the initiative behind it. The article does not describe specific eligibility criteria, application steps, or how many awards will be given. It does state that the money is meant to reward associates who turn AI ideas into practical results. Because the program ties rewards to impact, the firm appears to be using financial incentives to encourage lawyers to experiment with the technology.

Michael Rubin, global chair of Latham's AI practice and chair of its AI strategy committee, commented on the program. He said that associates bring firsthand insight into where AI can make a meaningful difference. He added that the award is meant to foster that ingenuity and to identify and scale the ideas most likely to create value for clients and the firm. The article presents these remarks as the firm's rationale for the program, and Rubin's role places him at the center of its AI strategy.

The program follows several recent moves by the firm to expand its AI capabilities. According to the article, Latham recently partnered with Harvey on a tool for investment funds. It also invested in Nvidia-powered servers that let the firm run and customize AI models in-house. The article does not say what the firm plans to announce next or how the 2027 awards will be judged in detail. Those details, along with the first recipients, would likely come in later reporting.

Articles.Title: Biglaw’s Latest AI Incentive For Associates Comes With A $1 Million Prize Pot

stories.Headline: Hillsborough County commissioners delay vote on AI data center moratorium
stories.Summary:
Hillsborough County commissioners have postponed their vote on a proposed moratorium on new artificial intelligence data center development, and no new date has been set. The delay came at the county's November 10, 2026 meeting, where commissioners chose to wait until two newly elected members are sworn in. Reporter Amelia Yean covered the postponement for WMNF, which posted her story on November 11, 2026. The swearing-in ceremony for the two new commissioners is scheduled for the following Tuesday at 6:30 p.m. The vote on the moratorium itself was unanimous when it was taken up, though the final vote has now been pushed back.

The proposed moratorium would halt any new data center proposals for one year. During that time, the county would study the possible effects of such facilities on its infrastructure, noise levels, water supplies, and energy use. Adam Gormly, director of the county's Development Services Department, said the new members need time to understand the legal and planning implications of the measure. He also told residents that the delay does not open the door to any data center approvals in the meantime. According to the report, there are currently no pending applications for data center projects in the county.

Gormly's remarks were the main official explanation given for the postponement, and the article does not describe any objection from the other commissioners or from the public. The commissioners who will take part in the eventual vote are those who will be sworn in next week, along with the current board. The article does not say when the rescheduled vote will happen, only that the timing is unclear. The county is moving forward with the review even as the vote is pending, and the study period would begin once the moratorium is approved.

The county's action comes at the same time as a similar effort in Tampa. The article notes that the Tampa City Council is considering its own moratorium on data center proposals. The report does not say whether the two governments are coordinating their efforts. Based on the information available, the next step is the rescheduled vote on the Hillsborough County moratorium, which will follow the swearing-in of the two new commissioners.

Articles.Title: Hillsborough County commissioners delay vote on AI data center moratorium - WMNF

stories.Headline: Sen. Elizabeth Warren Said to Take Senate Banking Gavel in January, Push Tougher Crypto, AI Rules
stories.Summary:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, is said to be set to take over as chair of the Senate Banking Committee in January. According to reporting cited in the articles, she plans to pursue tighter oversight of financial and technology companies, including rules for cryptocurrencies and prediction markets. Cointelegraph reported on November 9 that she also intends to tighten export controls on artificial intelligence chips sent to China. The report frames this as part of a broader push to strengthen scrutiny of Wall Street firms and major technology companies.

Her financial and housing priorities are also outlined in the coverage. They include a cap on credit-card interest rates, an expansion of the affordable housing supply and a reduction in consumer debt. Crypto businesses tied to President Donald Trump's family are expected to be a key focus of her oversight. The articles describe these as areas where she would seek to use committee authority, though they do not spell out the specific bills or steps she would take.

Those points, however, rest on reports that have not been fully confirmed. The articles state that her assumption of the chairmanship has not been separately verified, and neither has the timeline for any specific legislative effort. The coverage is based on a November 9, 2026 report, and the articles do not describe any formal announcement from Warren or the committee. Readers should treat the plans as reported intentions rather than settled policy.

stories.Headline: Colorado Joins Other State AI Leaders in Regulating the Use of AI in Psychotherapy Services - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
Colorado has enacted HB 26-1195, a law regulating the use of artificial intelligence in psychotherapy services, which went into effect on August 12, 2026. The law was enacted alongside two other Colorado AI healthcare laws this year, SB 26-189 and HB 26-1139. The article describes the law as establishing new restrictions for Colorado psychotherapy providers who want to use AI in their practices. It was published on November 12, 2026, by the National Law Review, and it was written by lawyers from Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton LLP. The authors are Carolyn V. Metnick and Madeline Cunnion.

Under the law, AI may be used for administrative support, such as scheduling, billing, insurance claims, and general therapy communications. It may also be used for supplementary support, such as maintaining client records, analyzing progress data, organizing referrals, and collecting intake questionnaires. In either case, the licensed provider must keep responsibility for reviewing all AI output. The law bars AI from recording or transcribing therapy sessions unless the client is told in advance, told the specific purpose, and gives written consent. It also bars AI from therapeutic communication with clients without real-time interaction among provider, AI, and client, and from generating treatment plans or recommendations without provider approval.

The article does not name a legislator or state official who sponsored or signed the law, so the responsible parties are described only through the law itself. The authors of the article are the only named people who comment, and they state that Colorado's framework shares common elements with other states' rules. They advise providers to confirm written, revocable consent workflows, update intake materials, audit AI tools against the statute's categories, and review marketing claims. The authors also say that flexible compliance programs are needed in a still-developing field.

Several groups are affected by the law. Psychotherapy providers in Colorado must follow its consent, review, and disclosure requirements, and any person or company offering AI tools cannot suggest that the AI's output equals licensed psychotherapy services. Clients of psychotherapy providers gain the right to written notice and consent before AI records their sessions. Organizations deploying AI in mental health across several states face what the authors call a patchwork of differing state rules.

The article explains that Colorado's 2024 Artificial Intelligence Act made it an early leader in AI regulation. It notes that HB 26-1195's core provisions resemble legislation Illinois enacted last year, and that Tennessee, Nevada, and Vermont have adopted advertising and marketing restrictions, some resembling Colorado's. The article also says that SB 26-189 repealed and replaced much of Colorado's landmark AI Act. The law's text sits in the article's footnotes, with the sections cited for each provision.

The article does not say how the law will be enforced or what penalties apply to violations. It also does not say whether other states will adopt rules resembling Colorado's, or how courts or regulators will interpret terms such as "administrative support" and "supplementary support." It leaves open how the Colorado Consumer Protection Act's advertising provision will be applied in practice. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Colorado Joins Other State AI Leaders in Regulating the Use of AI in Psychotherapy Services - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: AI Can Review Your Contracts, but Should It Negotiate Them?
stories.Summary:
Raman Rai, an AI deployment and adoption adviser who has worked on large-scale implementations, spoke at Law.com's General Counsel Conference East about the rush by companies to adopt artificial intelligence. According to the article dated November 12, 2026, he told general counsel that many firms are spending heavily on AI without first deciding which problems the technology should solve. The piece frames this as the core risk facing corporate legal departments under growing pressure to adopt AI. Rai's warning centers less on picking the wrong tool than on letting AI make decisions that call for a lawyer's judgment. The article's headline asks whether AI that can review contracts should also be trusted to negotiate them.

The article is reported by Trudy Knockless and carries no further detail on specific tools, rules, or contract terms. It gives no figures, dates for any new requirements, or formal changes to how legal departments must operate. What it does set out is a general distinction between using AI for review and handing it negotiation tasks that depend on legal judgment. Readers should understand this as the adviser's framing of the issue rather than a described policy or mandate.

The reporting does not indicate that any company has yet made such a change. Rai is the person responsible for the views expressed, and the article attributes his remarks to his work in AI deployment and adoption, including a role connected to UN Women UK. The article reports his concern in paraphrase: companies are investing heavily without always settling on the problems AI should address, and the greater danger lies in delegating judgment-heavy decisions to the technology. The piece does not include direct statements from other executives or from the legal departments themselves on this specific point.

The attribution is limited to what Rai told the conference audience. The article sits within a wider conversation in the same publication, including a related piece on Harvey Forum Chicago where general counsel discussed rising expectations for AI use. Those pieces suggest that in-house lawyers are increasingly expected to exhaust AI options before sending work to outside counsel. The articles provided do not describe what happens next for the specific question of AI negotiating contracts.

Articles.Title: AI Can Review Your Contracts, but Should It Negotiate Them?

stories.Headline: New Bedford Slams the Door on AI Data Centers as Power, Water, Neighborhood Fears Force Citywide Freeze
stories.Summary:
The two articles supplied do not mention New Bedford, a citywide freeze, or any local ban on AI data centers, so the headline's claim cannot be supported from them. What they do describe is a set of events in Finland, Texas, California, Virginia and the United States Senate. This story reports those events, which the articles tie together around who controls land, water and electricity for AI. The first article was published on 9 November 2026, and the second on 11 November 2026.

In Finland, reports describe the clearing of hundreds of thousands of trees for Google data-center sites in the towns of Muhos and Otanmäki. The country's Licensing and Supervision Authority then ordered a halt to environmentally significant preparatory work while environmental assessments are carried out. In the United States, the Senate this week advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, which eases permitting for energy projects. Those projects include data centers, pipelines, power plants and highways. Twenty-two Senate Democrats joined Republicans to advance the bill, so the Senate will hold a final vote next week.

To speed these projects, the bill would cut the public comment period from 90 days to just 30 days. It would also scale back the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act, according to the article. It requires new data centers of 20 megawatts or more to pay the full cost of the infrastructure built to serve them. An independent study cited by the article claims it would cut residential electricity bills by $50 to $78 per year by 2040. Initial modeling found that average annual costs of the electricity system would fall by 3.5% to 7%, saving $350 billion through 2050, and about $55 billion could be collected from data centers over 10 years.

On the Finnish clearing, Google disputes calling it illegal and says it acted in line with Finnish forestry requirements. Senator John Hickenlooper, a Colorado Democrat, said the bill is not perfect and that work should continue with Tribal Nations and environmental groups to strengthen it. He argued that the bill offers a golden opportunity to keep a promise to voters to make energy more affordable. He voted to advance it on Monday despite having repeatedly criticized the Trump administration for attacks on public lands, including the planned rescission of the Roadless Rule. The bill was drafted by four senators, two Democrats and two Republicans, including Republican Senator Mike Lee of Utah.

Kara Matsumoto, the senior policy director at CLF, said the group will keep fighting what she called corporate greed because most Americans want more nature protected, not less. Environmental groups and opposing Democrats argue that the bill opens the door to the sale of public lands. Hundreds of local and national organizations are urging Congress not to pass it as written, and Representative Jared Huffman of California attended a protest against it in Washington on Monday. Meg Slattery, a staff scientist at the nonprofit EarthJustice, warned that booming demand from the data center industry could simply absorb any extra power that comes online. Critics also say the bill would reduce state, local and Tribal government participation, and would let the Bureau of Land Management replace written comment opportunities with public meetings.

The first article says data centers are causing conflicts across the United States and Europe over electricity, water, land, noise, public subsidies and local consent. It notes that the OECD says AI infrastructure consumes water directly for cooling and indirectly through electricity generation. In many American communities, developers have used nondisclosure agreements, limited public reporting and opaque ownership structures, and residents in rural Utah, Idaho and Georgia have raised worries about water pressure and noise. California has enacted laws requiring reporting on energy consumption and efficiency, along with disclosure of water use and land-use impacts. Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered a pause on approvals for data centers seeking grid interconnection while agencies audit projected demand, and Virginia issued a 2026 executive order on data-center accountability.

If the Senate passes the bill next week, it must still move through the House before reaching President Trump's desk. Many Democrats, including Representative Huffman, are demanding that their party wait until they take control of Congress in January and then deliver a better bill. That Democratic leadership takes over after historic wins in last week's midterm elections, and the articles describe the bill as the first major test the party faces. The articles leave open whether the final Senate vote will succeed and whether the House will accept the bill as written. They also leave open whether the Finnish assessments will allow Google's work to resume, and they report no outcome from the Aarhus Convention complaint filed by Lighthouse Reports against the European Commission.

Articles.Title: Senate Votes to Weaken Public Land Protections, Boost AI Data Centers - GearJunkie
