stories.Headline: U.S. Stocks Gain After CoreWeave Update Eases Some AI Concerns
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, a neocloud provider of computing capacity for artificial intelligence, saw its shares climb in premarket trading on Wednesday after it reported quarterly results that beat analyst estimates and raised its outlook for the year. The company said in a Tuesday statement that revenue jumped 168% to $3.7 billion in the third quarter, the three months ending September 30. Chief Executive Michael Intrator called the period a "breakout quarter," crediting growth to several funding sources, including financing backed by customer contracts and roughly $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits. By 5:08 a.m. ET, the stock was about 10.8% higher, with fellow neoclouds Nebius and IREN also rising.

The updated guidance calls for adjusted operating income of $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion on revenue of $13 billion to $13.3 billion for 2026. Analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha had expected $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income, and analysts polled by LSEG had projected $12.86 billion in revenue for the year. The results come after neoclouds, including CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, drew scrutiny earlier this month as investors questioned whether the AI trade could be sustained. CoreWeave drew particular alarm when the spreads on its credit default swaps widened past 11%, a level generally viewed as distressed, meaning investors were paying more for protection against a default.

Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank told CNBC that CoreWeave had done well to ease financing worries by moving away from unsecured bond financing. Blank said the stock might have reached its bottom, while adding that the shares had been beaten down enough that he saw more potential upside than downside. CoreWeave's CEO was scheduled to appear on CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" at 9:50 a.m. ET to discuss the earnings.

stories.Headline: Google unveils Gemini Robotics 2.5 with 96% success rate in tasks
stories.Summary:
Google has launched Gemini Robotics 2.5, an AI model meant to improve how quickly and precisely robots learn and perform tasks. The company announced the model, which it calls its most capable vision-language-action model to date, on November 10, 2026. Google DeepMind's Carolina Parada, who leads the company's robotics work, introduced it in a post on the company's website. Its tests were run with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz, where humanoid robots sorted automotive parts successfully. The announcement came in reports published on November 9 and 12, 2026.

The model increases the number of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it learns them. Google tested Gemini Robotics 2.5 across more than 200 distinct tasks, such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box and pipetting a liquid. Compared with previous baselines, it achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the task, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster. The model natively works with several robot types, including Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid with a five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand, and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered grippers. Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out to Google's robotics partners.

Google is responsible for the model, and Carolina Parada described it as a step toward robots that can work in less structured settings. The company said the model improves dexterity, reliability and safety, helping robots leave the lab for everyday environments. Google also said Gemini 4 Argon, its frontier model, helped accelerate the robotics research behind the release. The company framed the work as progress toward physical artificial general intelligence. Google also said it is releasing the ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark as an open-source tool for testing robots against unsafe instructions.

Apptronik's co-founder and CEO, Jeff Cardenas, said the models improved dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training. He said they carried over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off. The pilot ran on active automotive production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. Factory technicians are affected because the robots take over repetitive kitting work, freeing them to focus on complex build tasks. Monotonous parts sorting is the work the robots were built to relieve, and the companies said it can help keep assembly lines moving.

Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz tested the model in a proof-of-concept on the production lines. In that pilot, Apollo 2 autonomously sorted metal automotive brackets from bulk bins into trays in the order each vehicle needed. The system pairs Gemini Robotics ER, which tracks the workflow, with the Gemini Robotics 2.5 actions model, which controls the hands and arms. Google said its safety features let robots steer around hazards in real time, improving safe task completion by 33% around obstacles and 43% around nearby people. The company reported that its Argon model achieved 99.5% jailbreak resistance, compared with 82% for its previous baseline.

Google presented the release as an advance in dexterity, reliability and safety for robots working alongside people. The company described earlier work, including Gemini Robotics 2 in July 2026, which brought whole-body intelligence to robots. The Gemini Robotics 1.5 model, introduced in September 2025, brought AI agents into the physical world. The first Gemini Robotics model appeared in March 2025 and brought AI into the physical world. Google's releases in this line have built on one another over roughly two years.

Google has not said when Gemini Robotics 2.5 will be generally available beyond its robotics partners. The articles also do not say how many factories or robot fleets will adopt the model. They give no detail on the outcome of the ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark beyond Argon's score. Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz have described the pilot as promising progress toward widespread industrial use, but the articles do not say when that might happen.

stories.Headline: Ten things I've been told about artificial intelligence by San Francisco's AI warriors
stories.Summary:
The articles do not describe a single event, law or policy change, so the story they support is a feature about how AI safety experts and religious leaders in San Francisco are talking about the technology. The first piece, published on November 12, 2026 by the Australian Financial Review, reports on a three-day AI study tour in San Francisco during which a reporter met with frontier AI labs, former AI employees and AI safety experts. The reporter says so many alarming things were said during the trip that it became almost easy to grow numb to them. One example offered was the idea of a rogue AI agent defecting to a foreign power and trying to corrupt other agents, which some safety experts consider a plausible concern rather than a fringe one.

The second piece, from The Free Press and dated November 10, 2026, is an essay by Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone of San Francisco. He writes that the city hosts some of the world's most powerful AI systems and that their developers are making decisions that will shape how billions of people live. He says several of these developers have expressed concern about the dangers of their work and have turned to the Catholic Church for moral guidance, including people who are Catholic, people of other faiths and people with no religion. Many of them have read Magnifica Humanitas, the first encyclical of Pope Leo XIV, released in the spring, which addresses how to safeguard the human person in the age of AI. The archbishop argues that whether AI serves humanity will depend less on the brilliance of its builders than on their virtue.

Both pieces share a theme: that the people closest to AI development see serious risks and that technical expertise alone may not answer how the technology should be used. The archbishop draws a comparison to the industrial revolution, recalling how Pope Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical Rerum Novarum responded to workers left vulnerable by factories and railroads. The archbishop's essay frames the Church as a possible source of guidance for this new period of change. The articles do not describe any formal rules, regulations or commitments that have resulted from these conversations, and they do not say what will happen next.

stories.Headline: SpaceXSI's Grok Build AI agent exposed sensitive data
stories.Summary:
Security researchers at Claroc found that Grok Build, an AI coding agent from SpaceXSI, was leaking confidential data from thousands of applications built on the platform. The exposure came from insecure default sharing settings, and the researchers reported it to SpaceXSI on November 8, 2026. Claroc's findings were published on November 12, 2026, in reporting by TechGig and Ars Technica. Researchers identified 43,601 addresses ending in grok.me that were visible through passive DNS services. Passive DNS services collect and index domain names seen in DNS traffic, which made these addresses discoverable.

Of those 43,601 addresses, 35,578, or 94.7 per cent, could be accessed without any authentication, according to TechGig. Claroc said the default privacy option for publishing apps was "Anyone with the link," which was pre-selected for users. Ars Technica reported that Grok Build's randomized URLs were structured so the random words sat to the left of grok.me, letting passive DNS searches enumerate them. Claroc said Google's approach places the randomness to the right of the domain, which would have kept the links invisible to such searches. Claroc said that Grok Build's links were set to "Anyone with the link" by default, and users could change the setting to "invited users" or "only you."

Claroc reported that about one in ten apps held sensitive internal business information, and 2 per cent exposed data serious enough for a high or critical severity rating. The exposed material included a hospital employee directory with more than 3,500 names and an intensive care briefing with patient information. A trucking company's recruitment database listing more than 1,000 individuals was also exposed. An employee timesheet's downloadable code contained 18 accounts with plaintext passwords, including administrator credentials. Ars Technica added that a Peruvian construction company's dashboard held 3,784 worker medical exams, and that a Tesla service-center scorecard named 22 technicians.

SpaceXSI itself was among the affected parties, and Claroc found 24 of its apps exposing an onboarding plan, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, and advertising proposals. Claroc said SpaceXSI did not respond to its initial notice, so a Claroc official tagged Elon Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer on X. Ars Technica reported that SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending questions about the article. A Cursor representative, which SpaceXSI recently acquired, said that Grok Build apps are "private by default" and that competing coding agents also offer shareable links. Claroc's tests contradicted that statement, showing that Grok Build required users to change the default setting to one of the two more restrictive options.

The problem traces to how Grok Build placed the random portion of its links, which is a design decision that undermined the access protection the randomization was meant to provide. Ars Technica reported that Muse, a Meta agent, had also suspended a link-sharing feature after it was found leaking sensitive data. According to Ars Technica, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini place their secret randomness in the URL path, so DNS does not expose it. Claroc said it was working to notify other affected app creators, and Asaf Aprozper, Claroc's co-founder and CTO, said he was contacting companies directly. Ars Technica noted that a luxury cruise company's security team began containing the exposure after Claroc shared its findings.

Several questions remain open in the reporting. The Cursor representative did not respond to follow-up questions about whether SpaceXSI intentionally exposed its internal information. Ars Technica reported that SpaceXSI also did not say why it removed the data after Ars asked about it, or whether it planned to notify customers whose information was exposed. The articles do not say how many of the affected organizations will be contacted or what remedies they will receive. Ars Technica advised Grok Build users to choose the "invite others" option unless they intend to make an app widely available.

stories.Headline: Silicon Valley's herd mentality in cozying up to Trump backfired as Democrats may seek retribution, China closes the AI gap, and anti-Big Tech sentiment grows (Nick Clegg/The Atlantic)
stories.Summary:
Silicon Valley's tech leaders moved to align themselves with Donald Trump in the period after he won reelection in 2024, and Nick Clegg, a former deputy prime minister of the United Kingdom and former president of global affairs at Meta, argues in The Atlantic that the move has backfired. The article was published on November 11, 2026, after MAGA suffered significant losses in the midterm elections. Clegg frames his piece as a critique of a herd mentality in the Valley rather than of individual leaders, and he says the approach has been a near-total failure measured against its own stated goals. The article notes that the tech leaders gave three main reasons at the time, including helping the United States win its AI competition with China.

Clegg writes that over the past 18 months China has been closing the gap with the United States on model performance and chip development, and in some respects has outpaced America. He says public attitudes toward AI in the U.S. are now more negative than under President Biden and worse than almost anywhere else on the planet. The Trump administration has helped some tech firms in their fights with European Union enforcement decisions, Clegg acknowledges, with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick named as an ally. Yet anti-Big Tech sentiment is higher in many parts of the world, and economies including Canada, India, Germany and Brazil are seeking to depend less on what Silicon Valley produces.

Clegg points to several reasons he believes the miscalculation occurred, and he attributes them to the leaders themselves rather than to outside forces. He describes a fear of missing out after Elon Musk spent Election Night 2024 at Mar-a-Lago, which pushed others to follow. He also describes a desire for payback against traditional media, academia and cultural elites, along with what he calls a misunderstanding of politics among wealthy people who assume it is easy. Clegg further says that tech leaders read Trump's narrow popular-vote win as a mandate and assumed the political pendulum would never swing back. He identifies venture capitalists such as Marc Andreessen and David Sacks as influential in the culture wars and in pro-crypto campaigns in the 2024 cycle.

Clegg cites the background of the Biden administration's clumsy treatment of tech leaders and a conservative sense of being unwelcome in the Valley's liberal milieu. He also draws a comparison to Brexit, where a narrow referendum majority was used to justify a hard-line approach, and he notes that a significant majority of Britons now consider it a mistake. He writes that many U.S. voters dislike the cliquishness and extremism of the second Trump administration and see the government's close relationship with the Valley as part of the problem. Clegg says he announced his departure from Meta a few days before Trump's 2025 inauguration. He also says he now works in venture capital himself.

Clegg warns that Democrats now have every incentive to make life uncomfortable for Trump-supporting tech leaders, which he says could lead to a cycle of retribution that would harm Silicon Valley, innovation and Democrats too. He urges major technology companies to stay out of party politics and to maintain open, productive relationships with whoever holds power. He concludes that tech leaders should stop picking political winners and losers. The article does not describe any further scheduled steps or formal responses from the leaders named.

stories.Headline: Fibocom Showcases Robotic Mower, AI Device and Wireless Connectivity Solutions at electronica 2026
stories.Summary:
Fibocom, a Chinese wireless communication module company, showcased its connectivity, AI and robotics technologies at electronica 2026 in Munich, Germany, with a press release dated November 12, 2026. The company offers OEMs options ranging from wireless modules and PCBA designs to application-specific algorithms and system integration support. Its robotic mower portfolio covers three sensing and navigation architectures, which the company presented as options for different design needs. Fibocom's exhibits also included an AI companion solution and board-level wireless products for broadband, portable and IoT applications. The company's showcase framed these products as ways for manufacturers to build devices across consumer, industrial and connectivity markets.

The first robotic mower architecture is a lightweight monocular-vision solution without LiDAR or RTK, designed for cost-optimized products. The second combines monocular vision with 3D LiDAR for complex, obstacle-rich gardens, while the third pairs stereo vision with RTK for depth perception and high-precision positioning across larger lawns. Beyond sensor selection, Fibocom provides core hardware, proprietary perception and navigation algorithms, and system integration support to help manufacturers build on existing solution architectures. The AI companion solution combines the MagiCore core unit, AI Cloud, app, IP Agent customization, and connectivity and AI token services. Fibocom also supports complete device customization and delivery, and its 5G CPE and outdoor unit PCBA solutions are shown alongside MiFi and Dongle designs.

Fibocom states that its robotic mower and AI companion offerings rely on its own hardware, algorithms and services. The company says it is China's first wireless communication module company listed on both the A-share and H-share markets, founded in 1999. Fibocom describes wireless communication and artificial intelligence as its core technologies, providing integrated hardware and software solutions for industry applications. Its one-stop solutions include cellular communication, AI, automotive and GNSS modules, along with AI toolchains, AI Agent, global connectivity and cloud services. The company says these products support digital intelligence upgrades in robotics, consumer electronics, low-altitude economy, intelligent transportation, smart retail and smart energy.

The press release presents these offerings as serving OEMs and device makers that want to accelerate product development. The press release names customers and applications that Fibocom says are affected by its products. A zodiac-themed AI companion toy called AiMOON, developed by a customer using MagiCore, demonstrates integration into character-based consumer products. Customer devices on display cover applications in asset tracking, industrial monitoring and remote health monitoring. An AI smart pet collar combines Fibocom cellular connectivity with pet tracking, activity monitoring and AI-based pet vocalization recognition.

The robotics showcase also featured development kits and stereo camera hardware from D-Robotics. Fibocom's component portfolio includes LE270 and LE271 LTE Cat.1 bis modules, the low-power IoT module MQ771, and the MGB GNSS series. A separate BusinessKorea article, dated November 11, 2026, reports that Doosan Corp. also participated in electronica 2026, held in Munich, Germany, from November 10 to 13. The exhibition involves about 3,500 companies from around 60 countries, and the Semicon Europa semiconductor trade show was held at the same time. Doosan Corp. showed electronic materials for AI data centers, semiconductor packaging, automotive electronics, and 5G and 6G communications.

Its centerpiece was high-end copper clad laminate for AI accelerators and optical modules, which the company says has low dielectric constant and low dielectric loss properties. Doosan also introduced Patterned Flat Cable for electric vehicle battery systems, which it says can reduce weight and volume by more than 80% compared with conventional wiring harnesses. The company said it can produce 2.5-meter PFC through a roll-to-roll process it developed for the first time in the world. The Doosan article says the company has led the localization of CCL since 1974 and now supplies global AI semiconductor companies. To meet rising demand, Doosan is expanding domestic production lines and building new production bases in Thailand and China.

An official said the company will reflect market trends and customer requirements from the exhibition in product development. The article describes Doosan's European participation as an opportunity to establish its position in the European market. The Fibocom release does not state any follow-up plans beyond offering integration support and customized development for its customers. Neither article gives pricing, sales volumes or timelines for commercial availability of the products shown.

stories.Headline: How AI Diagnosed a Medical Mystery My Doctors Missed for Decades
stories.Summary:
The articles do not describe a single medical mystery diagnosed by AI, so the headline's story cannot be confirmed from them. What they contain is a Becker's Clinical Leadership interview, republished on the Cedars-Sinai website on November 10, 2026, with Yaron Elad, MD, the chief medical informatics officer at Cedars-Sinai and a cardiologist. In it, Elad discusses how patients increasingly bring AI-generated diagnoses, treatment ideas and questions into appointments. The remaining items on the page are unrelated Cedars-Sinai news about other physicians and topics. Elad said patients tend to trust AI more than they trusted ordinary internet searches, because AI tools usually draw on stronger, cited sources while search results can lead people to information that is not evidence-based.

Some patients arrive with printouts of their AI queries, and others bring a list of questions the tool generated. He said his bigger concern is accuracy, since physicians are trained to spot flawed AI output but patients may not be able to tell when advice is inappropriate or wrong. He encourages patients to share their AI findings with their doctors. Elad also raised the issue of patients using personal AI to record visits, which California law permits only with a doctor's consent. He said he personally would not object, but warned that AI-generated notes often contain errors that a physician should review.

He said that without a doctor's review, a patient may be relying on a record that misunderstands or misconstrues what was said. The articles do not describe any regulatory change or new policy beyond these general observations. The articles offer no account of a patient whose condition went undiagnosed for decades, no name of such a patient, and no description of any AI diagnosis of that kind. They also do not say what, if anything, will follow from these trends. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
stories.Summary:
Oura, the smart ring maker and health intelligence platform, has agreed to acquire the artificial intelligence health company Counsel Health. The deal was announced on November 10, 2026, in a news release issued on a Tuesday. It is an all-cash transaction worth $625 million, according to reporting on the announcement. Counsel runs a primary care platform built around AI, which pairs conversational medical AI with access to licensed, board-certified physicians. The deal follows Oura's recent postponement of its initial public offering.

Under the agreement, Oura will pay $625 million in cash, and the acquisition is expected to close before the end of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and purchase price adjustments. Approximately 70 Counsel employees will join Oura after the transaction. Counsel co-founder and CEO Dr. Muthu Alagappan will become Oura's chief clinical AI officer. Counsel currently has approximately 50 on-demand physicians supporting its services, and it will keep serving enterprise partners, including health plans, healthcare systems, employers and consumer health organizations. The companies plan to build their combined platform across three areas, preventive care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care, the last covering reproductive health, aging and cardiometabolic conditions.

Oura chief executive Tom Hale said members can now act on what they learn about their physiology, with services ranging from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care and referrals. He described the goal as a new model of care that is more immediate, personalized and proactive. Hale called the deal a major step toward the promise of a 24-7 doctor in your pocket. The company's release said Counsel was founded and built by physicians and AI researchers, and that it combines medical AI with in-house physicians. Oura said members can start from an Oura insight or chat directly with Counsel's medical AI, and conversations can escalate to a board-certified Counsel physician within minutes.

Alagappan explained, in the acquisition announcement, that the partnership is meant to connect continuous health information with clinical expertise. Counsel has stressed that wearable data gives physicians extra context about patients' health patterns between appointments. Oura members are the people most directly affected, since they could gain a closer link between personal health monitoring and medical help. Counsel's enterprise customers are also affected, because those services will remain available to organizations whose members do not own an Oura Ring. The articles caution that wearable measurements do not independently establish medical diagnoses, and that clinical assessments and laboratory testing may still be needed depending on a patient's condition.

The deal builds on an existing partnership that brought Counsel's medical AI service into the Oura app in June 2026, as TechCrunch reported. The Verge reported on November 10 that the acquisition follows that earlier integration of the chatbot. Oura disclosed preliminary fiscal 2026 revenue of approximately $1.75 billion, a 92% increase over the previous fiscal year, along with fourth-quarter revenue of $533 million. That quarter ended September 30, 2026, and revenue rose 153% year over year, with adjusted EBITDA of $87 million, a 16% margin. Oura has more than six million members and was valued at approximately $11 billion after a late-stage funding round in 2025.

The IPO had been scheduled for the final week of September but was postponed despite strong demand, citing market uncertainty. Hale said at the time that the company has the luxury of choosing its moment and aims to deliver an extraordinary IPO for employees and investors. After the deal closes, Counsel's roughly 70 employees will join Oura, and Alagappan will take his new role. The companies are expected to share more as the acquisition progresses and their platforms are integrated. The articles leave open the full availability and pricing of future healthcare features, and they give no new date for the IPO.

stories.Headline: ST Unveils Industrial MCU With AI Accelerator
stories.Summary:
STMicroelectronics unveiled the STM32H7P industrial microcontroller on November 10, 2026, featuring hardware accelerators for digital signal processing and artificial intelligence workloads. Separately, Knewbots, a ThunderSoft subsidiary, and the Beijing Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center jointly unveiled a full-stack industrial embodied AI platform for logistics on the opening day of CeMAT ASIA 2026. The MCU combines a 520MHz Arm Cortex-M7 processor with a hardware signal processor and a neural processing unit. The platform operates on a "single-brain, multi-machine" architecture that integrates several robot forms to bridge warehousing and the production line. The companies signed their strategic partnership in January 2026 and have since shown their robot cluster collaboration at several major events.

The STM32H7P supports up to 2MB of embedded flash memory and integrates analog-to-digital converters, digital-to-analog converters and timers. Its signal processor can reduce processing time by up to 80% compared with conventional CPU-based software, while its neural processor delivers up to 85 giga operations per second. ST says AI inference for arc fault detection in solar systems runs 40 times faster than software-based processing. The MCU is designed to operate at temperatures up to 125 degrees Celsius. In the platform, Beijing Humanoid's "Huisikaiwu" supplies embodied large models and whole-body motion control, while Xiaowu's industrial platform coordinates multi-vehicle operations in real time.

ST is supplying samples to original equipment manufacturers, with mass production scheduled to begin in January 2027. Pricing for the LQFP100 package with 1MB of flash starts at $4.43 per unit for orders of 10,000 units. The Knewbots platform links three robot types under one scheduling system: Beijing Humanoid's "Tianyi" series for precision tasks, an FMR forklift for pallet transport, and under-ride AMRs for moving racks and totes. The two companies plan to deliver lightweight, mass-producible robotic cluster solutions for automotive manufacturing, high-end equipment and smart factories. The solution targets sectors including automotive, smart logistics, semiconductors, and 3C electronics and home appliances.

ST's announcement names the company as the party responsible for the STM32H7P, and its statements describe the MCU's performance and intended industrial uses such as digital power, motor control and condition monitoring. The Knewbots and Beijing Humanoid announcement describes the platform as addressing labor-intensive bottlenecks, such as end-of-line material delivery, shelf-to-station transfers, unsorted picking and automated loading. The articles attribute the platform's launch to Knewbots and the Beijing Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center together. The articles do not give direct quotations from any executive of either company.

The MCU is aimed at industrial equipment makers, and the articles say it is being sampled to original equipment manufacturers. The logistics platform is aimed at automotive, smart logistics, semiconductor and 3C electronics and home appliance manufacturers, which the articles say face labor-intensive material handling. Workers in these facilities would be affected by the automation of material flow described in the articles. The articles do not report any reaction from customers, workers or competitors to either announcement.

The articles report that ST's industrial MCU line is built around digital signal processing and AI acceleration for motor and power applications. They also report that Knewbots is a subsidiary of ThunderSoft and lists its main products as intelligent cockpit, driving and automated testing systems. The Beijing Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center's platform builds on its general "Huisikaiwu" system. The two companies had demonstrated their cluster collaboration at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, the World Humanoid Robot Games and the World Robot Conference before this launch.

Mass production of the STM32H7P is scheduled for January 2027, and the articles give no timeline beyond that. The Knewbots and Beijing Humanoid partners plan to deliver mass-producible cluster solutions, but the articles give no date for this. The articles do not say how many units either product will ship, which customers have committed to either one, or what the logistics platform will cost. The articles also leave open whether the two companies' plans will reach the scale they describe.

stories.Headline: UK GDP growth hits 0.7 per cent in third quarter on AI boost
stories.Summary:
The UK economy grew by 0.7 per cent in the third quarter, its fastest pace in more than two years, according to figures published by the Office for National Statistics. Investment in artificial intelligence was among the factors behind the increase, which was in line with City economists' estimates and above the Bank of England's 0.4 per cent forecast. It was the strongest quarter for output since the first three months of 2024. Excluding the pandemic, the figures put the economy at its highest level of performance since 2017. The ONS said monthly output rose by 0.2 per cent in September, ahead of a projection of no growth.

Growth was again led by services, which make up nearly three-quarters of the economy, with IT and communications the largest contributor. The ONS pointed to evidence that many businesses reporting the largest turnover increases in computer programming were involved in artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Production output, including manufacturing, rose by 0.1 per cent in the quarter, while construction output fell by 0.7 per cent. Household expenditure rose by 0.6 per cent as consumers drew on their savings, and business investment increased by 0.35 per cent. Government spending increased by 0.2 per cent between June and September.

Chancellor John Healey said the UK is showing standout resilience and that the economy is growing at its fastest rate in almost ten years, outside the pandemic. Sandra Horsfield, an economist at Investec, said that while the UK is not prominently involved in AI chip production, AI-related services appear to be playing an increasing role. Horsfield calculated that 0.2 percentage points of the 0.7 per cent quarterly growth can be attributed to AI. Analysts said the rise in business investment may also be linked to the rollout of AI technology. The Bank of England, which raised the base rate to 4 per cent on 5 November, is the institution whose forecast the figures exceeded.

Research published this week found that Yorkshire has the lowest AI adoption rate among SMEs of any UK region, showing that adoption remains uneven across the country. Consumers and businesses are the groups most directly affected by the rising energy bills and higher inflation that economists expect to slow growth. Economists expect growth to slow in the final three months of the year as those pressures reduce consumers' spending power. Inflation stands at 3.6 per cent and unemployment has dipped to 4.7 per cent, according to the latest official figures. The stronger than expected figures make a further rise in interest rates more likely in the coming months, economists said.

The Bank of England raised the base rate to 4 per cent on 5 November, its first increase in three years. The increase followed months of speculation that an oil price shock from the Middle East war could force a rate rise. Separately, PhysicsWallah, an edtech firm, reported that AI now writes 90 per cent of its code. The ONS's full breakdown is set out in its first quarterly estimate of GDP for July to September. The inflation and unemployment figures are due to be updated next week.

stories.Headline: Airbnb and Travel Stocks Fall as OpenAI Acquisition Raises New AI Threat
stories.Summary:
Shares of major online travel agencies fell on Tuesday, November 10, after OpenAI acquired Odessia, an automated travel platform, according to a report cited by PYMNTS. The deal prompted investor concern about possible disruption to established booking sites, and Expedia Group dropped nearly 4 percent, Tripadvisor fell more than 3 percent and Booking Holdings slipped more than 2 percent. Unlike traditional aggregators that send users to third-party sites to finish a purchase, Odessia handles trip planning, fare comparison and reservations inside a conversational interface. The platform was built on OpenAI's GPT 5.5 and Codex models and processed about $60 million in travel volume during its first year.

Odessia's founder, Francis Davidson, confirmed the acquisition on LinkedIn and said he will join OpenAI to lead its travel technology work. Davidson previously founded the hospitality company Sonder, which grew to $600 million in revenue, and he launched Odessia in late 2025 with funding from the venture firm Sequoia, individual angel investors and commercial travel partners. In his announcement he said he believed Odessia had built the best AI travel agent on the market. He also said tens of thousands of early adopters used the platform to plan more than $60 million of travel over the past summer. The articles present these statements as his own claims.

The article ties the selloff to growing competition as conversational software shifts toward autonomous commerce, with platforms moving from search assistants to agents that complete multi-step bookings. PYMNTS Intelligence research found that nearly 25 percent of consumers feel comfortable letting artificial intelligence plan their travel itineraries. Established intermediaries such as Booking Holdings and Kayak have been adding conversational tools and native checkout to protect their transaction volumes. Analysts quoted in the piece warn that well-funded AI developers entering direct booking could bypass legacy web portals and change how consumers find, compare and pay for travel. The articles do not report any regulatory response or further steps by the companies involved.

stories.Headline: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
stories.Summary:
Google has launched Gemini-powered smartglasses that are available for preorder starting at $395, with a privacy-focused pitch. The first glasses were made in a collaboration between Google, Samsung, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, and preorders opened on November 12, 2026. Warby Parker is offering three frames called Alden, Reid and Wren, while Gentle Monster has six styles that start at $449. Google says the devices are designed to address concerns about privacy that have dogged smartglasses since the Google Glass era.

The frames weigh about 41 grams before lenses are added, and the final pricing will depend on lens choice. The glasses have no screens, and users can interact with Gemini by voice or by activating a 12 MP wide-angle camera. Gentle Monster's styles come in dark red, pink, gray and yellow, with clear, tinted, blue or brown lenses. The devices are set to ship and appear on store shelves on December 10. At launch they work with iPhones from the 13 Pro onward, and with Pixel 7 or newer or Samsung Galaxy S or Z series devices running One UI 9 or later.

Google says it has built features to limit misuse of the glasses and to protect people around the wearer. A recording light stays on whenever the camera is active, and the glasses refuse to activate the camera if that light is covered or altered. The glasses also have a physical off switch. Google's terms of use require users to agree not to record people without consent or in sensitive areas, and Google may remotely disable the glasses if those rules are broken. The company says it will not allow Play Store apps to live stream video from the glasses, and it will not permit real-time facial recognition.

Reviewers and the article's author point out that Gemini is not always reliable, and that without a screen it may be harder to verify its output. Privacy concerns are central to the launch, since the glasses automatically redact faces before sending video to Google for processing. Google says images and videos captured by the glasses will not be saved in Gemini history or used to train AI models or target ads. Data on the glasses is encrypted in transit to the cloud but is not encrypted on Google's servers. Those affected include people around the wearer, whom the glasses are designed not to record without consent.

The same week, Google Cloud introduced a separate agentic AI solution called Gemini for healthcare, announced in a press release on Tuesday, November 10. The solution is built on the universal Gemini agent and aims to unify clinical, operational and administrative systems used in healthcare delivery and health plan operations. It brings together information from electronic health records, billing platforms, clinical guidelines and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services datasets. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said the challenge in healthcare is making data actionable across a highly regulated ecosystem.

Google's smartglasses will support Gemini Guided Vision, which provides conversational audio descriptions for people who are visually impaired. The glasses also let users ask for recommendations or have an event poster added to their calendar. The American Hospital Association estimated that administrative costs account for 25% to 35% of total healthcare spending in the United States. Clinicians spend more than a full day each week on documentation and administrative requirements, according to the release. Superscript CEO Rahul Naidoo said medical providers face a 20% to 40% patient default rate on bills.

Articles leave open how Google's smartglasses will be priced once lenses are included, and the Ars Technica article notes the final figure will depend on lens choice. Google has not yet named the Gentle Monster styles beyond their colors. The sources also do not say when Private AI Compute will come to glasses, or when Samsung Galaxy devices outside the S and Z series will be supported. Whether the Gemini for healthcare solution will be deployed by any particular provider is not stated in the articles.

stories.Headline: China’s graft crackdown sends drugmakers to doctors’ AI apps
stories.Summary:
Drugmakers in China are turning to a new wave of AI assistants built for doctors, after a sweeping graft crackdown made traditional outreach to physicians harder. Companies such as Alibaba Health and JD Health have brought out tools similar to OpenEvidence in 2026, and the article says drugmakers are exploring marketing with app makers or customising platforms for specific diseases. The shift followed stricter measures issued in the summer that govern pharma employees who provide product information to doctors and hospitals. Doctors' use of these tools has grown quickly, rising to 93% of the hundreds surveyed by Alibaba Health, up from around 70% a year earlier.

Alibaba Health is considering a model in which promoted medical research and clinical evidence would appear alongside AI-generated answers on its Hydrion app. Chief technology officer Wang Xiangzhi said the company has not yet begun working with drugmakers on this, though domestic and foreign firms showed strong interest. He argued that if doctors gather on one platform, marketing budgets would move online. PICA Health has built JD Health's Zhiyi assistant into its app, offering drugmakers digital academic promotion and physician education services. Research firm Frost & Sullivan estimates that enterprise spending on digital health marketing in China will grow at a compound annual rate of 27.5% from 2027 to 2030, reaching 274.4 billion yuan (S$53 billion).

The article reports that the China Pharmaceutical Innovation and Research Development Association declined to comment, while Roche said it explores third-party medical AI tools for direct marketing to doctors and hospitals. Bayer said it monitors developments in technology that could help it engage healthcare professionals in a compliant manner. Null Hypothesis CEO Gu Fei said major Chinese and foreign drugmakers had licensed its KnowS tool to build disease-focused academic platforms for physicians, though he declined to name them. The article also cites drugmakers Zhejiang Xianju Pharmaceutical and Xian Shijishengkang Pharmaceutical, which said the rules and hospital visit limits hurt sales. The reporting does not say how regulators will treat promoted content on these platforms.

stories.Headline: KORA Systems Develops AI OS With Qualcomm
stories.Summary:
KORA Systems, a Silicon Valley startup formerly known as Playtron, has been developing an AI-centric desktop operating system with Qualcomm, officially announced on November 10 local time. The company plans to release the Linux-based OS in the second half of 2027, with a mobile version to follow. CEO Curt McMaster told THE ELEC in an interview published on November 13, 2026. The system is optimized for Qualcomm's Snapdragon X2 Elite platform, though it also supports Intel and AMD processors.

The OS is designed so that AI agents are built directly into the system rather than added on top, as with Windows and macOS. AI coordinates the central processing unit, graphics processing unit and neural processing unit, and can access system resources such as files. The Snapdragon X2 Elite can run a 26-billion-parameter large language model entirely on-device, alongside speech recognition and conversion models. Users can choose AI models from different providers, and the Neural Workspace feature separates the data AI agents can reach for each project. KORA also supports Windows PC games and applications, including Steam and Epic titles through a feature called GameFrame.

McMaster is a co-founder of Cyanogen, an Android-based operating system company. The partnership began at Qualcomm's Snapdragon Summit last year, when HUMAIN CEO Tareq Amin unveiled plans for an enterprise AI OS on the same chip. HUMAIN, a Saudi Arabian AI company, lacked its own underlying operating system, so McMaster reached out first. That led to joint development of HUMAIN OS, which shares its architecture with KORA. KORA changed its name from Playtron in July 2025 after shifting its focus to AI-centric OS development.

The company's developer and creator users are the intended audience for KORA, while HUMAIN OS targets enterprises. KORA incorporates technology from GameOS, a Linux-based system developed during the Playtron era. Its Importer feature is in development to help users install Windows applications and games, and Android applications are expected to run through emulation. On Arm-based platforms such as the Snapdragon X2 Elite, an additional layer translates x86-64 instructions. The articles do not say how well these translation layers perform.

The second article reports that the U.K. Ministry of Defence announced on Tuesday a £90 million investment, about $120 million, in a network of drones, sensors and AI systems for the Royal Navy in the North Atlantic. Called Atlantic Net, the network is meant to protect undersea cables and energy networks from Russian submarines. U.K. company Ocean Infinity Solutions was selected to provide it. Atlantic Net is the first phase of the Royal Navy's Atlantic Bastion program, a plan to build a hybrid naval force to hunt and track enemy submarines.

Atlantic Net will bring together maritime systems, underwater sensing, communications, remote operations and data services into a single capability directed by the Royal Navy. The Royal Navy will receive autonomous systems across the North Atlantic, including advanced sensors to detect Russian submarines and illegal activity, and uncrewed systems that can patrol underwater. The goal is a single surveillance service giving submarine-hunting warships and Astute-class attack submarines earlier warning of threats. The ministry did not disclose an expected date of entry into service.

Luke Pollard, U.K. Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said the investment gives the Royal Navy new technology to find threats earlier and protect critical infrastructure. Ocean Infinity, named Commercial Mission Partner for Atlantic Net, said it has used robotics at sea for more than a decade. Joe Robinson, president of Solutions at Ocean Infinity, said the program moves naval capability beyond heavily crewed fleets. Atlantic Net is intended to work alongside NATO and Joint Expeditionary Force allies to strengthen protection against sabotage and hostile activity.

Ocean Infinity operates a 14-ship fleet of Armada-class ships, which are minimally crewed and carry underwater robotic systems. The company has searched for the Argentine submarine ARA San Juan in 2018, the battleship USS Nevada off Hawaii in 2020 and the destroyer USS Stewart off California in 2024. Its searches for Malaysian airliner MH370 in the Indian Ocean, in 2018 and this year, were less successful. The articles also note that NATO began its anti-submarine exercise Dynamic Merlin 26 in the Baltic Sea off Sweden on Monday.

stories.Headline: Carrier delivers consistent, human-centered employee support with Microsoft 365 Copilot
stories.Summary:
Carrier Global Corporation has deployed a Microsoft 365 Copilot agent called Here for You to help its 200-plus Global People Services advisors deliver consistent, human-centered employee support across regions. The Microsoft customer story was published on November 11, 2026, and describes how the agent has become one of Carrier's most actively used. Advisors serve employees across Asia, Europe, and the Americas, and before the agent existed they sometimes asked managers to review unclear or sensitive responses. The agent gives advisors on-demand guidance for clearer and more consistent interactions across regions and languages. Carrier's stated aim is to be "more tech and more human," so automation handles routine HR transactions while advisors focus on empathy and judgment.

Carrier first defined Here for You as a service model that guides advisors through four stages of an interaction: connecting personally, confirming the employee's need, owning the resolution and next steps, and closing with clarity. Carrier built the agent with Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Copilot Studio, grounding it in Here for You materials, standard operating procedures, and process knowledge stored in Microsoft SharePoint. Employee requests arrive in ServiceNow, and an advisor opens the agent in Microsoft 365 to enter details or a draft response and request a structured reply, a tone check, or process information. The advisor then reviews and validates the output, adapts it to the employee's circumstances, and returns the response through ServiceNow. Carrier is working toward merging the agent directly into ServiceNow, but that interoperability is not yet complete.

Magda Warda, Executive Director of Global People Services at Carrier, said the team had an opportunity to improve response time, accuracy, and clarity, and that the tool made human interactions better rather than replacing them. Cheryl Rearick, Vice President of Talent and Employee Experience at Carrier, said the goal was to turn employee support into moments of connection by pairing technology with human empathy. Shraddha Lama, Manager of Global People Services at Carrier, described Copilot as a force multiplier that gives advisors relevant, contextual guidance in seconds. Carrier applied internal privacy, security, access, and Copilot Studio governance controls, and advisors remain accountable for each employee interaction. Warda said Carrier's digital and AI teams identified the agent as one of the company's most actively used.

The employees served by Global People Services are the primary beneficiaries described in the story. Advisors supporting employees in Japan and China reported clearer local-language responses, and advisors who once asked colleagues to review messages can now respond confidently on their own. The agent creates consistency without forcing every advisor into an identical voice, according to the article. Warda said the company is tracking whether customer satisfaction is rising and whether employees feel better treated, rather than measuring usage alone. Carrier Global Corporation is listed with more than 10,000 employees, based in the United States, in the Industrials and Manufacturing industry.

A separate GlobeNewswire release dated November 10, 2026, from eSoftware Associates (ESW), a U.S.-based Microsoft partner founded in 2006, urges manufacturers expanding Microsoft 365 Copilot to review superseded drawings and supplier permissions. The release cites the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report, which tied third parties to 61% of manufacturing breaches and internal data compromise to 81% of them. ESW recommends five steps: marking the approved drawing, retaining older revisions under access rules, limiting discovery during governance reviews, reviewing supplier and partner permissions, and reviewing access at project close-out. ESW says it has served more than 1,500 organizations. Russell Kommer, founder and CEO of eSoftware Associates, said staff need to know whether a drawing is the approved revision and that older file access should reflect legitimate need.

The Carrier article does not say how many employees the agent has served or what satisfaction results Carrier has measured. It also does not give a timeline for completing the ServiceNow integration. The ESW release notes that its quotation from Kommer is marked as a draft pending his approval. The articles do not report whether any manufacturer has adopted the ESW steps or what follow-up Carrier plans beyond continued exploration of AI across the business.

stories.Headline: Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer
stories.Summary:
An AI-assisted attack against an unnamed US retailer was detailed by Symantec on November 12, 2026, after the attack occurred in September. The threat actor's hand-typed commands were repeatedly blocked by security software, so the attacker switched to what appeared to be AI-generated commands. These commands broke through the retailer's defenses rapidly, and the attacker harvested credentials and achieved lateral movement within minutes. Symantec said it did not identify the initial access vector, focusing instead on the timeline gleaned from its post-incident investigation. The firm said the incident is one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks it has investigated since May, with activity heavily concentrated around September.

The attacker first worked by hand, which investigators determined from artifacts such as typing errors, and every staged payload was terminated by security software. When the attacker tried again the next day, the tactics changed, and for almost two hours the attackers submitted long, error-free PowerShell scripts with labelled output sections. Roughly 10 minutes after querying the victim's SolarWinds Orion monitoring software, the attackers moved laterally to a second server. During the second stage, the threat actor gained initial access to a Web server and stole credentials from configuration files tied to SolarWinds Orion. No vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required in the incident.

Symantec's blog post hypothesizes that the attackers were likely financially motivated, since they searched point-of-sale scripts for passwords. Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard activity. Investigators concluded the activity was more consistent with an operator relaying output to an AI tool than with an autonomous agent. Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, said the incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. He called it a game-changer for attackers and said defenders can potentially leverage the retry pattern, which can be treated as a high-priority alert.

Separately, in Korea, the National Center for Digital Sexual Crime Response uses AI to detect suspected child sexual exploitation material and speed up takedown requests. The center's system collects posts around the clock using about 220 keywords and analyzes text and images together. It presents its assessment to staff for review, and once a staffer approves a report, the system prepares the information the relevant platform or authority requires. Director Kim Mi-soon said the system handles most of the process automatically, and that AI is also detecting deepfakes that are hard to identify with the naked eye. Images are now blurred by default to protect staff from repeated exposure to disturbing material.

Officials say AI adoption raised the average number of cases processed per worker each day from 20.8 in 2025 to 202.1, a roughly 9.7-fold rise. Between April and September this year, the center processed 96,210 cases, more than twice the 45,438 processed in all of 2025. The center supported 10,637 victims in 2025, up from 4,973 in 2020, and teenagers and people in their 20s made up 77.6 percent of those supported last year. Among websites whose server locations the center could identify, at least 95.5 percent were hosted overseas, complicating enforcement. The center said 28.5 percent of its takedown requests went unfulfilled in 2025.

Park Kwang-soo, head of the Women's Human Rights Institute of Korea, which oversees the center, credited the technological gains to the expertise and dedication of staff. Park said victim support must begin and end with people, whatever technology is used. Officials said technical improvements must be accompanied by international cooperation, stronger platform accountability, and efforts to disrupt the revenue sustaining illegal sites. Kim said the center plans to expand coverage from 14 platforms to 139 by 2027, and is developing an AI chatbot to send vulnerable young people information about support services. The articles do not say whether the US retailer was ever identified, and they do not state how the grooming detection technology will work in practice.

stories.Headline: Data.co Launches Private AI Platform and Data Marketplace Featuring 91 Datasets From 25 Providers
stories.Summary:
Data.co launched its enterprise data and artificial intelligence platform from Seattle, Washington, United States, on November 12, 2026, according to a press release. The platform combines private AI infrastructure, enterprise governance and a marketplace of public and licensed datasets. It opens with three offerings: Data.co Control, the Data.co Marketplace and app.data.co, a centralized access point. The company says the platform addresses two challenges facing enterprise AI adoption: keeping sensitive data under control and simplifying access to reliable external information.

Data.co Control lets organizations run and govern AI inside their own infrastructure, with support for on-premises, private cloud, hybrid and fully air-gapped deployments. The product includes a customer-local runtime, private language model infrastructure using vLLM and Ollama, and deterministic policy enforcement for users, models and AI agents. It also offers permission-aware connectors, AI agent governance and exportable audit records for compliance reviews. The Data.co Marketplace provides 91 datasets from 25 providers, accessible through a query console, a REST API at api.data.co/v1 and an MCP server. Each record carries source attribution, licensing information and a retrieval timestamp.

Nate Nead, chief executive of Data.co, said companies are adopting AI quickly but face problems with sensitive data leaving their infrastructure and with weak access to trusted external data. Timothy Carter, chief revenue officer, said the company is creating a unified access layer so customers do not have to build many separate connections. Samuel Edwards, chief marketing officer, said AI is only as useful as the information it can reliably access. Data.co is a division of Nead, LLC and DEV.co, and the press release names Edwards as the contact.

The company says Data.co Control is designed for financial services, healthcare, legal services and manufacturing, among other industries. The marketplace draws on sources including SEC EDGAR, FDIC BankFind, GLEIF, UK Companies House, the CFTC and the CFPB. It also includes economic data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, Energy Information Administration, Federal Reserve Board, U.S. Treasury, World Bank and U.S. Census Bureau. Government sources include USAspending, the Federal Register, the Federal Election Commission and Senate lobbying disclosures. Healthcare and safety sources include openFDA, CMS NPPES, the CPSC, NHTSA and EPA ECHO, while IRS and OpenAlex data cover nonprofits and research.

The press release says the marketplace applies source-specific licensing controls and restricts personal data in corporate, political and regulatory records. Through its LAW.co integration, the platform offers U.S. court opinions, AI-generated case summaries and citation relationships. Data.co says it manages upstream provider connections through standardized contracts that enforce query validation, rate limits, caching and licensing restrictions. The company describes the platform as built for an AI economy that depends on trusted data, as agents move toward autonomous research and task execution. Data.co frames its approach as keeping every dataset's origin documented and every response traceable.

The launch was announced in a press release distributed through Plentisoft and published by The Manila Times. The articles do not report pricing, customer names, adoption figures or the timeline for further rollouts. They also do not say how many datasets will be added beyond the launch catalog. Nor do they give details on how the company's licensing terms will be enforced with each of the 25 providers over time.

stories.Headline: Meta AI Cheat Sheet: Features, Pricing, and How to Use It
stories.Summary:
Meta released Muse Ember on November 9, 2026, a small AI model built for large-scale, repetitive tasks run by AI agents. The model is aimed at businesses and developers who want to automate coding, document processing, and data extraction at a lower cost. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna. Ember is the smallest model in Meta's Muse family and is meant to work alongside larger models rather than replace them.

Muse Ember supports text, images, audio, and video, and it has a context window of 1 million tokens. It can produce up to 512,000 output tokens, allowing it to handle large documents, screenshots, charts, and recordings. The model is priced at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. It was trained with Muse Wonder Full, which Meta describes as the first model of its kind released by the company. Meta Superintelligence Labs lead Alexandr Wang confirmed that development.

Meta said the division of labor between its models is that larger models plan while Ember handles the volume of execution. Meta published benchmark results with Artificial Analysis on November 9, 2026. Ember scored 40.9% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, ahead of Claude Haiku 5.5 at 39.2% and GPT-6 Luna at 16.4%. Ember also scored 36 on the Artificial Analysis Index, matching Claude Haiku 5.5 and beating GPT-6 Luna's 28.

Ember did not lead every benchmark. Claude Haiku 5.5 scored higher on FrontierCode 2.0-AA, and the articles do not give further details of that comparison in the excerpt provided. The articles say the model is intended for businesses and developers running repetitive agentic workflows. The excerpts do not state how many organizations have adopted the model so far.

Meta's consumer assistant, Meta AI, is available for free on web, iOS, Android, Mac beta, and compatible smart glasses, with paid Meta One plans starting at $7.99 per month in the US. Meta AI uses the Muse Spark model family for its conversations, and Muse Image generates pictures from text prompts. Meta says its privacy controls affect how interactions are used for personalization and advertising in supported regions. The articles do not say how the Muse Ember pricing compares with Meta AI subscription costs.

stories.Headline: Nitrogen Brings Its AI-Powered Advisor Platform to Claude and ChatGPT, Expands Nucleus Capabilities
stories.Summary:
The headline says Nitrogen is bringing its advisor platform to Claude and ChatGPT and expanding its Nucleus capabilities, but the two articles supplied never mention Nitrogen or Nucleus. What they cover is the arrival of personal finance features in Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT, so this account sticks to that. Anthropic introduced Personal Finance as a dedicated feature within Claude on November 5, 2026, and OpenAI had introduced its Finances feature in ChatGPT on May 15, 2026. Both tools let users link bank accounts through Plaid and review spending, investments and savings goals through a conversational interface. Both reportedly give a read-only view of linked accounts, so neither chatbot can move money or change account details.

Claude Personal Finance connects supported bank accounts, credit cards, loans and investment accounts through Plaid, and it began rolling out in beta to Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers in the United States. It works across Claude's web, desktop and mobile applications, though access is being introduced gradually. Anthropic says Claude can see bank names, account names, account types, the last four digits of an account number, balances, credit limits and transaction history. Mint reports that history as up to 2 years, while iTech Post puts it at 24 months. Compatible institutions mentioned include Bank of America, Capital One and Chase, and Claude can build dashboards and flag unusual charges, duplicate transactions and rising bills.

Anthropic is the company behind Claude Personal Finance, and it says conversations inside the Personal Finance hub are not used to train its models by default. The company also says removing a bank account means Claude can no longer use that previously shared financial data. Anthropic has also stated that Claude Personal Finance carries no advertisements or product suggestions, and the company does not offer its own credit cards, loans or savings accounts. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, applies the user's existing ChatGPT data controls to conversations about connected financial accounts. OpenAI says financial account data is removed from its systems within 30 days of a user disconnecting the account.

The Mint article notes that ChatGPT's data controls leave model improvement switched on by default, so users must open Settings and turn off the option called Improve the model for everyone. iTech Post adds that Anthropic's no-training promise covers only the Personal Finance hub, while conversations outside it remain under the user's regular privacy settings. Mint says neither tool is meant to replace a professional financial advisor, and iTech Post says they are not substitutes for banking applications either. iTech Post warns that AI responses can contain errors and that balances may not reflect the latest transactions. Users are advised to check figures against official statements and to consult qualified professionals for important decisions.

On the background, Mint says OpenAI began testing advertisements on selected lower-priced ChatGPT plans in January 2026, while no clear advertising policy has been given for the Finances feature. OpenAI's feature has grown since its May launch, and it now includes weekly financial insights, credit monitoring, stock watchlists, voice support and manual account entry. iTech Post says ChatGPT can reach balances, transactions, investments, liabilities and subscriptions, and can help with expense organization, budgeting and savings planning. Mint describes Anthropic's approach as a deliberate disconnect from promoting finance products. The Mint piece was published on November 9, 2026, and the iTech Post piece followed a day later.

Looking ahead, Mint reports that OpenAI is aiming to widen ChatGPT's financial abilities through a tie-up with Intuit. The partnership is expected to bring more help with credit card applications and tax questions, among other services. Anthropic, for its part, is aiming to partner with banks, wealth managers and other financial services firms to improve Claude Personal Finance. Mint says both tools currently offer more or less the same tracking options, and that Claude's default privacy stance may appeal to users wary of how their financial data is used. The articles leave open when Claude's rollout will reach all eligible users, and neither mentions Nitrogen or Nucleus.

stories.Headline: I'm making LLMs work on small and old devices
stories.Summary:
A developer working under the name hyperionaidev has published smolmaxxing, a GitHub project that aims to run the largest possible language models on the smallest hardware, such as TV boxes, old tablets, single-board computers and routers. The repository was posted on November 12, 2026, and it reports measured results from two devices so far. One is a Xiaomi TV Box S (3rd Gen) with an Amlogic S7D chip, 1.9 GB of RAM (about 1 GB usable) and Android 14 without root access. The other is a jailbroken 2013 iPad Air running iOS 12.5.7 with 1 GB of RAM (about 700 MB usable).

On the TV box, the everyday model is Qwen3.5-2B, which runs at 7.7 tokens per second, while the 1-bit Bonsai-1.7B reaches 24 to 26 tokens per second. The largest model tested is Ling-mini-2.0 with 16 billion parameters, running at 5.1 tokens per second on the TV box and 2.6 to 4.5 tokens per second on the iPad. The project says both devices run 8B and 16B mixture-of-experts models on about 1 GB of RAM by keeping only part of each model in memory and reading the rest from flash storage as needed. The author states that phones, single-board computers and routers are planned, and that the techniques need only basic NEON instructions for the 1-bit kernel and work on any Linux or Android device with more model than RAM.

The work is a set of patches to the llama.cpp project, and the author describes several methods: kernels built for specific chips, a "headless" mode on the TV that stops the launcher and Google services while a model runs, and an expert pager that keeps popular experts in RAM while loading others from flash on demand. The repository is maintained by hyperionaidev and is released under the MIT license, with model weights carrying their own licenses. Its documentation includes setup guides for the TV box and the iPad, a lessons file and a lab notebook covering 160 experiments, including failures. The page shows 322 stars and 11 forks at the time it was captured, and the articles do not say what further development or timeline the author has planned beyond the devices already listed.

stories.Headline: Siri AI Coming to Older Apple TV 4K Models in tvOS 27.2.1
stories.Summary:
Apple plans to bring Siri AI to older Apple TV 4K models through an upcoming tvOS 27.2.1 update, according to a support document that lists the requirements for Siri AI across its products. The document says tvOS 27.2.1 supports Siri AI on the Apple TV 4K (2nd generation and later), but that software has not been released yet. Apple appears to have a special Siri AI build of tvOS 27.2 for the 4th-generation Apple TV 4K, which ships with tvOS 27.0 and prompts users to update during setup. MacRumors' Juli Clover reported the news on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and said reviewers had tested Siri AI on review units. Separately, leaker Aaron Perris revealed a new Mac app called Harbor on November 10, 2026, which is designed to run open-weight AI models locally.

Siri AI on the Apple TV requires a nearby paired Siri AI-enabled device, such as an iPhone 15 Pro or later, to function. The latest Apple TV costs $299, features an A19 chip, and comes with an updated Siri Remote that includes a Find My speaker and Precision Finding support. The 4th-generation Apple TV 4K is equipped with 8GB of RAM, according to Xcode 27.2, which Apple released on October 29, 2026. Harbor turns a Mac into a private AI inference server, and it can connect multiple Macs over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory for larger models. Harbor is described as running on Apple silicon, with data staying on the user's hardware rather than reaching the cloud.

Apple has not publicly said when tvOS 27.2.1 will be released with Siri AI for older Apple TV 4K models. MacRumors noted the update could come as soon as Friday, November 13, 2026, the same day the new Apple TV 4K launches. The article itself does not state Apple's official position on the timing, and it does not confirm whether the feature will appear on every older model. Apple has not commented on Harbor, and the app is currently in a private preview under Apple's Claris brand. Leaker Aaron Perris posted the details about Harbor on X, and the 9to5Mac article repeated those feature claims.

Commenters on the MacRumors article raised concerns about storage, with one noting the older Apple TV has 64GB of storage and questioning whether a few gigabytes of Siri AI code would fit. Others asked whether users could turn the feature off, and one asked what Siri AI could actually do on a television, such as identifying actors on screen. Some commenters said they did not want an AI feature or a microphone on their Apple TV, and another said they had almost no space used on their 2nd-generation model. The Apple TV 4K line is affected because owners of 2nd- and 3rd-generation models will receive the feature through tvOS 27.2.1. Mac owners using Mac studio, Mac mini, and similar machines are the audience for Harbor, which 9to5Mac says Apple is positioning for local AI use.

Earlier in 2026, MacRumors reported that Apple had announced more than 25 new devices and accessories since late August, with the new Apple TV 4K and HomeView smart home hub set for release on Friday, November 13. Apple's Mac lineup has grown in popularity this year, partly because of the budget-friendly MacBook Neo and the use of Mac hardware for running AI locally. The 9to5Mac article describes Harbor as Apple's effort to lean further into local AI inference on the Mac. MacRumors also reported that the Apple Support Community is permanently closing on November 20, 2026, which is a separate matter from the Siri AI update.

It remains unclear when tvOS 27.2.1 will ship and whether Apple will confirm the schedule before the November 13 launch. The articles do not say whether Siri AI will run locally or in the cloud on older Apple TV models, a question commenters raised directly. Harbor's public launch date has not been announced, and the articles say only that a launch is likely in the weeks and months ahead. Apple has not said whether Harbor will support older Mac hardware or what its pricing will be. The articles also leave open what Siri AI will do on the television beyond search, and whether users will be able to disable it.

stories.Headline: ByteDance Is Reportedly Working On Its Own AI Agent
stories.Summary:
ByteDance is reportedly preparing its own AI agent, according to a Bloomberg report relayed by Engadget on November 11, 2026. The Chinese company is said to be readying an AI assistant that could be revealed in the coming weeks. It is meant to compete with Meta's Muse agent and to serve a similar role. The report does not say what ByteDance will call the agent or how it will work.

Muse has already drawn more than 10 million users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has predicted that it could generate more revenue per user than the company's existing family of apps. Quartz reports that Meta launched Muse in early September and that 10 million people in the U.S. downloaded it within 40 days. Buying was the most popular task, with purchases averaging more than $200. Muse is also expected to play a big part in Meta's AI glasses, and the company has previewed a standalone charm for it. It is unclear whether ByteDance plans to put its own agent into hardware.

On the ByteDance side, Bloomberg reported that cofounder Zhang Yiming recently told employees it would likely take until at least 2029 or 2030 for the company's AI efforts to catch up with the frontier companies. ByteDance has mostly been known in AI for its video generator, Seedance, whose clips went viral on social media earlier this year and drew legal scrutiny from US-based studios. ByteDance did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Engadget. Meta's chief executive has said the company would take a commission on purchases made through Muse.

An agent from the TikTok maker would likely raise fresh concerns about data privacy and how much access personal agents should get. Quartz notes that OpenAI followed Meta with its own always-on agent, Dots, a few weeks after Muse launched. Agentic web traffic roughly tripled from August to September, most of it heading to e-commerce sites, and retailers responded in different ways. Amazon blocked Muse almost immediately, while Walmart announced a system giving each agent its own profile with approval or spending limits, and JPMorgan said it would not let outside agents into customer accounts. Economist Lindsay Owens has argued that AI shopping agents should be held to a fiduciary-style standard, legally bound to work for the shopper, though no such rule is in place.
