stories.Headline: UNESCO, Bayelsa govt begin digital education, AI training for teachers
stories.Summary:
UNESCO, in partnership with the Bayelsa State Ministry of Education, has begun a three-day master trainers programme on digital pedagogy and artificial intelligence for ICT lecturers in the state. The training, reported on November 10 and 12, 2026, was opened in Yenagoa and is part of the Expand, Integrate and Strengthen Systems project. The project is funded by the European Union and implemented by UNESCO, with technical support from the Federal Ministry of Education and the Universal Basic Education Commission. The training targets 40 master trainers who will prepare 1,445 teachers to use digital technologies and AI-supported approaches in classrooms. Esther Ikenye, UNESCO Programme Assistant, spoke at the event in Yenagoa on Tuesday.

From November 16 to 21, the 40 master trainers are to train the 1,445 nominated teachers at centres in Yenagoa, Kolokuma/Opokuma and Sagbama Local Government Areas. The teachers will then continue learning through self-paced online modules after the physical sessions. The programme will equip them to use digital tools and AI in lesson planning, learner engagement, assessment and classroom management. Trainees who finish the programme can register on the online learning portal, access free modules and obtain certificates. By the end of the three days, the master trainers are expected to navigate the platform, complete quick checks and earn a certificate.

Ikenye said the project works on three fronts, supporting policies on teacher shortages and working conditions, strengthening skills of in-service and pre-service teachers, and building connections between teachers, colleagues and learners. She described Bayelsa as one of six project focal states and said the training is a clear example of the second front in action. Commissioner for Education Gentle Emelah, represented by Monday Ake, said the training aims to improve teachers' knowledge and capacity in AI and digital teaching methods. Adam Sadiq of the UBEC Innovation and Instructional Technology Department in Abuja said many children are digital natives, so teachers need these competencies.

The EISS project is designed to strengthen Nigeria's education system through better governance, teaching and learning, and it rests on the principle that teachers are the most important in-school factor in learning. Ikenye said digital tools and artificial intelligence are already part of contemporary teaching and that the project intends to support their use for the overall benefit of society. Representatives of the European Union, the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria, the Nigeria Union of Teachers and the SUBEB Teachers' Professional Development Directorate attended the opening. Ikenye told the 40 master trainers that the programme's success in Bayelsa State depends on them.

Before the training, the programme's theme was given as "Education and Youth Empowerment in Nigeria: Expand, Integrate and Strengthen Systems to Build Teachers' Capacity and Resilience." Ikenye said the programme was designed to strengthen teachers' professional competence and promote inclusive, technology-driven education. The master trainers will also support teachers through a 26-question final assessment with a 70 per cent pass mark and module ratings required for certification. They are also expected to produce a state cascade plan with targets, timelines and support arrangements. The articles do not say how many teachers will complete certification or what the cascade plan will contain.

stories.Headline: North Carolina artificial intelligence experts weigh in on our AI anxieties
stories.Summary:
The North Carolina Department of Information Technology, known as NCDIT, is seeking artificial intelligence vendors to help integrate and implement generative AI within state government agencies, according to a Spectrum News report published November 9, 2026. The state is exploring how AI could play a larger role in everything from online state services to the tools government employees use behind the scenes. Proposals from potential vendors are due November 30. The effort is meant to give agencies a simpler route to AI tools that are secure and trusted, while providing employee training and security safeguards.

The plan is built around protecting personal information, making sure people can understand how the state reaches its decisions, and keeping humans accountable when something goes wrong. State Director of Cybersecurity Laura Rodgers described AI as a tool rather than a replacement for existing services, and she said the state's approach differs from some industry practices where workers are pressed to use AI or face dismissal. NCDIT Secretary and State Chief Information Officer Nate Denny said in a statement that the aim is to deliver government services to residents better and faster and to free employees to spend more time serving the public. Rodgers argued that the deliberate, guardrails-first approach should make residents feel safe, though she said public trust will remain critical.

A separate WUNC News broadcast from November 11, 2026, approached public worry about AI from another angle. Host Jeff Tiberii, who co-hosts the station's "Due South" program, convened a panel to separate fearmongering from real anxieties and to discuss how AI is shaping society and individuals. The guests were Lee Rainie, director of the Imagining the Digital Future Center at Elon University, Emmy Martin, a technology reporter for the New York Times and a UNC alumna, and Saif Khairat, chief AI officer and vice provost for AI at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, who is also a professor in the School of Nursing. The program, which runs about 50 minutes, was published with a description noting that headlines about AI tend to frighten audiences. Taken together, the two reports show state officials promoting cautious adoption while public discussion focuses on separating real risks from exaggerated fears.

stories.Headline: AI Drives Surge in New Businesses. Why the Boom Isn’t Creating Jobs.
stories.Summary:
Barron's reported on November 12, 2026, that a surge in new businesses is being driven partly by artificial intelligence, but that this boom is not producing as many jobs as earlier ones did. The article notes that the number of new firms opening for business continues to trend upward. It adds that employers have averaged 86,000 jobs added per month this year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The piece is written by Megan Leonhardt and carries Dow Jones copyright.

Euronews reported on November 10, 2026, that Denmark is putting another 500 million Danish kroner, about €67 million, into Gefion, its AI supercomputer. The announcement, made on a Tuesday by the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark, says the money will support the machine's infrastructure and operations at the Danish Centre for AI Innovation, which runs it. The funding adds to an earlier 700 million kroner, about €93.8 million, from the state investment fund and the Novo Nordisk Foundation. Gefion launched in 2024 with 1,528 Nvidia chips and is now nearing full capacity. The article does not say how the new money will be spent or when the extra capacity will become available.

Denmark's minister for business and competitiveness, Martin Lidegaard, said in a statement that greater computing access would let Danish companies and researchers turn ideas into new solutions, companies and jobs, and would keep ownership of future technology from passing to others. Another goal, the article says, is to help public institutions and businesses use AI while keeping sensitive data under their control. Netcompany, a Danish technology firm that builds public-sector IT systems, is joining the centre's investors and will supply software for access management, monitoring and security. Christina Egelund, Denmark's minister for research, education and digitalisation, argued that Europe must do more on its own and that Denmark should help secure European technological independence.

The Euronews piece places the announcement within a wider European effort to control the infrastructure behind AI. It cites the United Kingdom's 225 million pound investment in an AI research supercomputer in 2023, and Finland's LUMI supercomputer, funded by the European Union and participating countries at a lifetime cost above €200 million. In July, the European Commission opened a call for up to seven AI gigafactories, large data centres backed by up to €10 billion in EU and national funding. The Barron's article, by contrast, focuses on the American business boom and offers no comparison to these European investments.

stories.Headline: The AI Agents Can’t Find Anyone to Help Yet
stories.Summary:
In early November 2026, Uber, DoorDash and Airbnb reported that consumers were barely using AI agents to handle everyday tasks such as bookings and orders. United Airlines separately announced that it would ban AI agents from making bookings on behalf of customers, and that announcement came earlier in the same week as the Gizmodo report. Uber's Balaji Krishnamurthy said on the rideshare company's November 4 earnings call that AI agents placed just four rides and 500 Uber Eats deliveries during the week of Halloween. Those figures came out of a combined total of 320 million rides and food deliveries that week. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said on the company's October 29 earnings call that agents had placed "maybe several hundred orders" since launching.

United cited privacy concerns, the risk of exposing sensitive data to third parties, and the potential for unintended or unwanted transactions slowing the process for everyone. The airline also said agents cannot confirm that travel bags do not contain banned substances such as explosives. United noted that allowing a bot to make that declaration on a passenger's behalf might violate rules from the Federal Aviation Administration and the Department of Transportation. Gizmodo reported that most people are simply not using these agents, so United probably had little to worry about either way. Fortune reported that Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots both launched in September, and that agents promise to handle tasks like booking trips, ordering food, and shopping online.

United's stated reasons for the ban centered on privacy, data exposure and the risk of unwanted transactions, and Gizmodo said the airline's reasoning on banned substances may conflict with federal rules. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said on the earnings call that a median customer takes 50 seconds to order an Uber and 90 seconds to order Uber Eats. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky told investors on November 5 that agents from Muse and Instinct account for a "very non-material number" of the nearly half a million bookings made daily. Chesky also said that 80% of travelers like researching their trips, which he described as part of the experience. Consumers who are not confident in agents, according to Talkdesk's Michael Klein, want to know where, how and why their credit card information will be used.

Matt Maher, founder and CEO of M7 Innovations, told Fortune that tech giants are overcomplicating simple tasks like restaurant reservations that did not need much innovation. Maher said that if someone wants something immediately, doing it yourself as a human is easier. Khosrowshahi said Uber will have discussions with third-party AI agents and sees them as another way to reach its platform, and he said every AI system company is talking to Uber about the terms of trade. Those affected include businesses that rely on the platforms, customers who are asked to share personal data with agents, and travelers who would use airline booking tools. Uber, DoorDash and Airbnb are also building their own AI features, such as Uber Eats' Cart Assistance, DoorDash's Ask DoorDash and Text DoorDash, and Airbnb's planned agent.

Uber Eats' Cart Assistance lets customers upload a handwritten grocery list or recipe screenshot, and Khosrowshahi said baskets made with it are roughly twice the average size. DoorDash's Ask DoorDash helps users build grocery lists from photos or typed requests. Airbnb plans to start rolling out its own AI agent early next year, and Chesky said it would help guests plan their entire trip on the platform. The Gizmodo article also notes that DoorDash launched a feature in September letting people text an agent to place a food order. Fortune reported that Chesky said the company is developing a custom-designed, AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for.

Uber, DoorDash and Airbnb are continuing to develop their own AI tools, and Uber says it is negotiating terms with third-party AI companies. The articles do not say when or whether United will lift its ban, nor whether the FAA or Department of Transportation will issue any ruling on AI agents making such declarations. They also do not say whether consumer usage of third-party agents will grow once trust and transparency improve. Fortune reported that Chesky expects the company's own agent to launch early next year, but the articles give no measure of its expected adoption.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Q3 profit up 50%; losses continue
stories.Summary:
OpenAI reported that its quarterly revenue rose about 50 percent to $10 billion in the third quarter, according to the Wall Street Journal, which reported the figures on Tuesday. The ChatGPT maker nonetheless continued to post steep operating losses over the same period. Documents the newspaper viewed showed the company telling investors that its adjusted operating margin improved to -109 percent from -150 percent in the prior quarter. Its operating losses, however, widened to $10.9 billion from $10.1 billion.

The disclosure matters because investors are watching the finances of AI startups closely as they weigh profitability concerns against enthusiasm for the sector. Rival Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is preparing an initial public offering that could value the startup at about $1.4 trillion. Anthropic has started a roadshow for the share sale, which is expected to set a benchmark for the industry. The Reuters report noted that the OpenAI figures underscore strong investor appetite for AI companies despite these concerns.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on the report. The Wall Street Journal was the source of the financial details, which were drawn from documents it viewed. Reuters carried the story and reported that the company had not yet replied when it published. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Siemens Raises Growth Goals as AI Boom Drives Record Orders
stories.Summary:
Siemens has raised its growth goals after a surge in orders tied to the global artificial intelligence boom, according to the company's latest report. The headline reports record orders, with the AI-driven demand behind the upgraded outlook. The articles supplied to me do not, however, contain Siemens-specific figures, dates or statements, so the details of the revised targets and order totals cannot be confirmed from them. The only article on the topic covers Thailand's economy, not Siemens.

The one piece of relevant reporting describes an investment wave linked to the AI boom in Thailand. It reports that real GDP grew 2.4 percent in the first half of 2026 and that private investment expanded 11.6 percent. Board of Investment applications in the digital sector reached THB 1.12 trillion in the same period, already above the THB 746 billion recorded for all of 2025. AMRO projects growth of 2.4 percent in both 2026 and 2027.

The Thailand analysis was written by Allen Ng and Haobin Wang of the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office and published on November 11, 2026. It argues that the gains are narrowly based, with data centers importing much of their high-value equipment and creating relatively few direct jobs. The authors recommend supplier development, wider access to cloud and AI services, and energy reforms to broaden the benefits. The articles do not say how any of this connects to Siemens' results. stories.Headline: Anthropic Joins AFT and UFT's Binding AI Safety Standard
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has signed a legally binding agreement with the American Federation of Teachers and the United Federation of Teachers to establish safety, transparency and privacy protections for its AI products used in K-12 education. The agreement was announced Tuesday, November 10, 2026, by the two unions, and it puts their AI Safety and Privacy Standard for Schools into practice. It automatically covers school districts already using Anthropic's Claude for Teachers. The agreement's 10 provisions address how AI companies handle sensitive school data, communicate with customers and account for risks associated with their technology. Anthropic is the latest company to adopt the standard, following Microsoft, which partnered with the unions in September.

Under the agreement, districts can incorporate the protections into their contracts, which gives them legal recourse if a company fails to meet its obligations. Once incorporated, the provisions become enforceable, allowing a district to seek damages or termination of the agreement for material violations that remain unresolved. Companies generally cannot use student or educator information to develop or refine AI models, apart from a limited security and safety exception, and cannot sell that data or use it to target advertisements. The restrictions cover prompts, uploaded files and generated responses, and they also apply to previously collected data even after the agreement expires. The standard requires human review of high-risk decisions involving AI, prohibits AI companions within its scope, and requires notification of confirmed or reasonably suspected data breaches within 72 hours.

Anthropic and the unions describe the agreement as a major step for AI safety in classrooms, and Anthropic's head of beneficial deployments, Elizabeth Kelly, said it builds trust with teachers, students and school systems. AFT President Randi Weingarten called it a legally binding contract that ensures algorithms can never replace human judgment, relationships or responsibility. UFT President Michael Mulgrew said the agreement continues the unions' work to keep students and their families safe and said he was heartened that Anthropic sees the value of student privacy. Microsoft committed to making the protections available to U.S. school districts beginning November 1. Parent advocates and a policy group offered differing views: psychotherapist Nicole Runyon called it a positive step, while Michael Marinaccio of the Center for Responsible Technology said such agreements are too little, too late.

The unions have argued that existing federal student privacy law, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, was not written specifically to address generative AI. Mulgrew said that ideally the federal government would step in, but since it has not, teachers unions are working to hold AI companies accountable. Claude for Teachers was released July 14 and gives teachers premium Claude tools for free. Anthropic contributed $500,000 to the AFT's National Academy for AI Instruction in July 2025, alongside $10 million from OpenAI and $12.5 million from Microsoft. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services recommended in August that districts evaluate products based on demonstrated educational benefits, but those recommendations are advisory rather than binding.

The agreement applies only to Claude for Teachers, which is designed for educators rather than students, so provisions governing students' direct use of AI do not apply. Student information entered by teachers remains protected, and any future Anthropic educational product offered directly to K-12 students would need to meet the standard. The articles do not say how or whether the protections will be enforced in practice. Anthropic, the AFT and the UFT did not respond to requests for comment from the Daily Caller News Foundation. The articles also do not say whether Anthropic plans to offer student-facing products, and they leave open how the standard will work for districts that do not adopt it.

stories.Headline: Anthropic says a key AI safety alarm has been triggered, days before its IPO
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, in an amended prospectus filed alongside the price range for its record-setting IPO, Anthropic said it has met a key safety threshold. A week earlier, the company had told would-be investors that AI speeding up its own research might "imminently" trigger this alarm. The filing says Anthropic made the determination based on what it expects from future models and its overall rate of progress, not on what it has observed from current models. The threshold sits in the company's Responsible Scaling Policy, its rulebook for adding tougher safety measures as its AI becomes more powerful.

The threshold is triggered when AI is doing enough of Anthropic's research to roughly double how fast its models improve. The policy says that pace would pack two years' worth of AI progress, at its 2018-2024 rate, into a single year. Anthropic set its IPO price range at $70 to $78 per share on Tuesday as it began its roadshow, the round of investor meetings before pricing. That values the company at as much as about $1.4 trillion, counting every share that could exist, and trading could start as soon as Nov. 19, according to reports. Nvidia and Google are each buying $10 billion of Anthropic stock at the IPO price, part of a $26 billion private placement that also includes AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and Taiwan Semiconductor.

Anthropic says crossing the threshold means more safeguards, not a shutdown, and that humans stay in charge. The filing says the company does not expect to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding. It says it is weighing policy changes to keep humans in control, and that AI has already been accelerating its research and development. Anthropic said it is still weighing what crossing the threshold means and will release further reports. The filing also warns that, as Claude speeds up work inside the company, the organization may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control.

METR, an independent nonprofit that tests AI systems, estimated last week that Anthropic's models have been improving nearly twice as fast since October 2025. In a separate review, METR called Anthropic's August argument that it was still below the threshold "overstated" and said it was "plausible" the line was crossed by mid-July. Constellation Research founder Ray Wang said ahead of a Yahoo Finance live show appearance last month that in all S-1 filings the risks are deliberately overstated. For investors, the filing's risk factors warn that after a catastrophic AI incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have the capacity to cover the damage. Amazon and Google already own big stakes in the company.

The fear behind the threshold is that AI will improve itself faster than people can check it. In 2023, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei joined other AI leaders in warning that the "risk of extinction from AI" should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. The same filing swapped in "super intelligence" for "AI" in places, citing President Trump's Sept. 29 executive order telling federal agencies to use the term. Mentions of "AI" fell by about a quarter from the Nov. 2 version, by Yahoo Finance's count, though the filing treats the terms as interchangeable. The change came two weeks after Trump criticized the Wall Street Journal on Truth Social for sticking with the phrase "artificial intelligence."

Anthropic's roadshow is now under way, and trading could begin as soon as Nov. 19, according to reports. The company has said it will release further reports on what crossing the safety threshold means for its safeguards. The articles do not say which additional safeguards Anthropic will adopt or when they would take effect. They also do not say which policy changes the company is weighing to keep humans in control, or whether the IPO timeline could shift. More to follow.

stories.Headline: GIGABYTE Expands Its Local AI Portfolio with the Launch of AI TOP AERO Powered by NVIDIA RTX SPARK™
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE announced on November 10, 2026, the launch of AI TOP AERO, a new AI desktop powered by the NVIDIA RTX Spark platform, positioned as a Personal AI Studio. The desktop combines an NVIDIA Blackwell architecture GPU, up to 128GB of unified system memory and GIGABYTE's cooling and compact chassis design. The launch expands GIGABYTE's AI PC lineup, which it says brings local AI development, content creation and gaming to personal workspaces. The company's press release was distributed through PR Newswire from Taipei. GIGABYTE says the product launches on November 10, 2026, and regional configurations, pricing and availability will be set by local GIGABYTE announcements.

The AI TOP AERO uses the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X Superchip, which integrates a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU with an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU. Configurations offer up to 128GB of LPDDR5x unified system memory and up to a 4TB PCIe Gen5 SSD for local models and creative assets. The compact chassis measures approximately one liter, and GIGABYTE integrates its cooling design to provide thermal headroom for sustained AI and creative workloads. Connectivity includes USB Type-C, 10GbE Ethernet and Wi-Fi 7 for peripherals, data transfers and network access. The desktop also supports NVIDIA PAIR (Personal AI Router), which distributes inference tasks across devices on a local network.

GIGABYTE is the company that announced AI TOP AERO, drawing on its hardware design and system integration experience. Nvidia supplies the RTX Spark platform, which the company describes as unifying NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics and unified memory in one slim Windows PC. Nvidia's Asia-Pacific director of technical marketing, Jeff Yen, spoke about the broader RTX Spark product line at a press event in Seoul on November 6. He acknowledged that RTX Spark laptops are priced at the high end of the market and cannot be considered affordable, though he said they draw demand mainly from early adopters and developers. GIGABYTE's release describes the desktop as an addition to its own lineup of AI PCs.

Developers, creators and AI users are the groups the articles identify as the intended audience for AI TOP AERO. The GIGABYTE release says users seeking local computing options want to run models, process data and test applications on their own devices for reasons of data privacy, responsiveness and usage costs. Nvidia said demand for RTX Spark has been concentrated among companies developing AI-based services and applications, and that initial supplies are limited, leaving many customers waiting. Yen said some consumers may find conventional laptops with x86 CPUs and discrete GPUs more reasonable because of the price difference, and he said there is ample room for both markets to coexist. RTX Spark laptops start at approximately 4.7 million won and reach as high as 10 million won depending on specifications.

The articles give some background on the market shift toward local AI. The GIGABYTE release says generative AI has expanded beyond conversational assistants into AI agents, content generation and workflow automation, which has increased user interest in personal AI computing. Nvidia's Yen said running 61 million tokens through the Claude Sonnet 5.5 model in the cloud costs $1,200 per month, while running the same workload on RTX Spark requires only $20 in electricity costs. Nvidia also introduced Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B, an on-device model optimized for RTX Spark, which was trained on high-performance systems and then quantized to 2-bit precision. Nvidia says the model delivers performance comparable to frontier AI models while significantly reducing memory consumption.

The articles do not say how many AI TOP AERO units will be produced, what they will cost in any region, or when they will reach customers outside the launch announcement. They also do not state how long Nvidia's supply constraints will last or whether demand will continue to grow. The GIGABYTE release points readers to local GIGABYTE announcements for regional configurations and pricing, but no such announcements are included in the articles. Whether the desktop's sustained performance matches its claims in practice is not addressed by the articles.

stories.Headline: Cequence Security and KPMG Collaborate on Joint Report Examining how Organizations can Govern and Secure Agentic AI
stories.Summary:
Cequence Security, which describes itself as the leader in application, API, and agentic AI protection, published a report on November 11, 2026, titled Agentic AI Runtime Security, Governance, and Control. The report was developed with input from KPMG in Singapore and looks at how organizations can govern and secure agentic AI. It focuses on the shift of agents from generating content to autonomously taking consequential actions. The report concentrates on governing those actions as they happen, for agents that organizations have deployed themselves. An executive brief and a full report are both available for reading or download.

The findings will be presented to senior business, technology, and policy leaders at a joint event hosted at KPMG's office in Singapore on November 19. Cequence's CQ Prime research team tracked more than a quarter million AI agent visits across five industries during one week of October 2026. About one in seven of those visits booked, bought, signed in, or managed an account for the customer. At a Tier 1 telecommunications carrier, traffic from agents that did not identify themselves grew from about 100 requests a day to as many as 32,000 within three weeks. That surge followed the launch of a major consumer AI agent, and the traffic signed in as the customer and passed multi-factor authentication.

At one online marketplace, more visits claimed to be Google-Agent than all the genuine agent visits Cequence tracked that week, and every one of them went straight to the sign-in page and failed. Cequence reads this as a sign that attackers were testing stolen passwords in bulk under a legitimate agent's name, and it stresses that Google was not involved. The report recommends giving each agent a specific job rather than open-ended authority, with a plain-language job description turned into hard limits. It also recommends a separate control outside the agent that approves, escalates, or blocks each action in real time, because harmless-looking steps can add up to something forbidden. When an action is blocked, that control should point the agent to the allowed route so the work still gets done, and success should be measured by work completed rather than actions blocked.

In a controlled study using a Cequence research prototype, agents with only logins and fixed permissions tried to act outside their job in 44% of runs. When each agent had a defined job and every action was checked against it, those attempts fell to 1%. Task completion rose from 76% to 95%, and agents used about 35% fewer tokens per run. Gerry Chng, Partner and Head of Cyber at KPMG in Singapore, said identity verification and fixed access permissions are important but may not be sufficient when an agent carries out a sequence of actions for a business or customer. He said governance should consider the agent's role, the context of each action, and the cumulative risk across an entire task, and that KPMG contributed its experience in governance, risk, regulation, and cyber security.

Shreyans Mehta, CTO and co-founder of Cequence Security, who co-authored the report, said an approval at step one should not carry into step five. He said runtime governance means checking what an agent does at every step, and telling the agent why when the answer is no, so it gets back on track instead of looking for a way around. Mehta added that it has to work the same way for an agent a customer sends as for one an organization built itself. Ameya Talwalkar, CEO and co-founder of Cequence, said AI agents are already acting for customers across the region and that boards want to know they can trust them.

He said KPMG understands how boards and regulators think about risk, while Cequence sees what agents actually do on its customers' applications and APIs every day. Talwalkar said Singapore is setting the pace on governing AI agents, which makes it the natural home for the company's Asia-Pacific business. Cequence says AI is shifting from answering questions to taking action, with agents now issuing refunds, updating records, and moving money. Cequence has established its regional headquarters in Singapore and has a regional team that includes senior leadership in Australia.

Its customers in the region include NTT DOCOMO in Japan and Philippine Airlines. The company says it has more than a decade of bot defense and API security experience and protects more than 10 billion daily API interactions and 4 billion user accounts. Its platform gives insight into user, entity, and agent behavior, takes a no-code approach, and says it delivers value in minutes rather than days or weeks. Cequence plans to build local teams in the Philippines, Singapore, and South Korea over the coming months.

The next fixed step is the November 19 event at KPMG's office in Singapore, where the report's findings will be presented to business, technology, and policy leaders. The articles do not say how many leaders will attend or whether any regulators will take part. They do not say whether the controlled study's results, which came from a research prototype, will be reproduced in live deployments. The articles also give no detail on the timetable for the new teams or on how many organizations are already using the report's recommendations.

stories.Headline: Sarvam AI Appoints Ex-Google Cloud India MD Sashikumar Sreedharan as President and CBO
stories.Summary:
Indian AI startup Sarvam AI has appointed Sashikumar Sreedharan, who until recently was Managing Director of Google Cloud India, as its President and Chief Business Officer. The announcement was reported on November 9, 2026, and he will also join the company's board of directors. Sreedharan will lead Sarvam's business across enterprises and government institutions, and will oversee its work with digital-native companies, developers and partners. His remit also covers marketing, finance, forward-deployed engineering, service delivery and commercial operations.

The articles differ slightly on his background, though both describe a long career in technology. One puts his experience at more than three decades, while another says roughly 35 years. Before Google he led Microsoft India's enterprise business as Managing Director for more than five years, and one report adds earlier stints at IBM, Wipro and Happiest Minds Technologies. Sarvam says more than 100 enterprises and government institutions are already building with its full-stack AI offering, and the hire comes as it tries to widen that base.

In a statement on his appointment, Sreedharan said India should be a maker of the intelligence the world runs on, and that joining Sarvam was a commitment to that opportunity. He said he looks forward to working with the team and customers on products that become part of how industries and governments operate. Sarvam said its next phase of growth will focus on advancing its research, developing products for global markets and scaling its operations. The company is also making enterprise ownership of AI central to its strategy, keeping enterprise data, models and agents inside organisations so they retain control over their AI systems and the value those systems create.

Sarvam was founded in 2023 by Pratyush Kumar and Vivek Raghavan, and it builds foundational AI models, computing infrastructure and enterprise applications. It is introducing new products including Sarvam 105B, Sarvam Vision 2.1, Saaras V4 and Bulbul V4 Flash. Earlier this year it raised $234 million in the first close of a $300 million Series B round, which valued the company at $1.5 billion. Investors include HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners. Sarvam also believes enterprise requirements will feed its research, with industry demands driving research and breakthroughs helping to create new industries.

stories.Headline: BigBear.ai Expands Gross Margin by 878 Bps: What Drives the Gains?
stories.Summary:
BigBear.ai reported a sharp profitability improvement in the third quarter of 2026, with its gross margin rising 878 basis points year over year to 31.2% from 22.4%. The company attributed the gain mainly to a growing contribution from its generative AI platform, which it acquired through the Ask Sage transaction in December 2025. Stronger revenue performance also helped lift results during the quarter. Quarterly revenue grew 31% year over year to $43.6 million, the company's third consecutive quarter of organic revenue growth. Gross profit climbed roughly 83% to $13.6 million from $7.4 million, signaling improving operating economics.

The generative AI platform lets government agencies and critical industries securely access advanced AI models, build agentic workflows and process sensitive information in secure environments. Adoption across federal agencies, including the FBI, NASA, the U.S. Coast Guard and the Department of Energy, supports its expansion. The company secured more than 25 contracts worth over $225 million in value since the second quarter. Its backlog rose 22% sequentially to $330 million, improving visibility into future revenue. Management also raised its 2026 revenue guidance to $150 to $165 million.

The articles do not name a single executive who spoke on the results, but the company's management raised 2026 revenue guidance to $150 to $165 million. Management's outlook ties future profitability to sustained generative AI adoption, a favorable revenue mix and effective cost management. The articles frame those factors as necessary for turning gross margin gains into stronger operating profitability. The company's stated view is that the platform and contract wins support its revenue visibility and growth.

Analysts and data providers cited in the articles, including Zacks Investment Research, emphasized the margin trend and valuation. Shares gained 6.5% over the past month, outperforming the Zacks Computers - IT Services industry. BigBear.ai trades at a forward 12-month price-to-sales ratio of 6.98, a discount to industry peers. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for the 2026 and 2027 loss per share widened to 41 cents and 25 cents over the past 30 days. Its Zacks Rank is #4 (Sell).

BigBear.ai's shareholders and investors are directly affected by these figures, as the articles report adjusted EBITDA remained negative at $9.1 million and selling, general and administrative expenses rose to $31.3 million. Government agencies using the platform are also affected by its expanding adoption. The articles note competition from Palantir Technologies and C3.ai in enterprise and government AI markets. Palantir reported third-quarter 2026 revenue up 96% year over year to $2.31 billion, with a gross margin of about 83.4%. C3.ai reported a fiscal 2026 GAAP gross margin of 31%.

The articles describe BigBear.ai's generative AI platform as an emerging growth and margin catalyst within its business. The Ask Sage transaction in December 2025 brought this platform into the company. Its quarterly revenue has grown organically for three consecutive quarters. Earlier in the articles, the company is described as operating in a market for enterprise and government-focused artificial intelligence solutions. The platform's focus on specialized, mission-ready AI solutions is presented as supporting its differentiation in security and defense markets.

The articles leave open whether the margin expansion will be sustained, since they say profitability challenges persist. They do not state when BigBear.ai expects to reach positive adjusted EBITDA. Future revenue depends on converting its backlog and contract wins, but the articles give no timeline for that. Whether Palantir's scalable software model will widen its advantage over BigBear.ai also remains unaddressed. The articles give no further guidance or outcomes beyond the 2026 revenue range and the consensus loss estimates.

stories.Headline: IMF monitoring AI developments, too early to say if AI reassessment underway - CNA
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, the International Monetary Fund said it was closely watching the recent swings in AI stock valuations and a political shift in the United States that could slow data center construction. IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack made the remarks at a regular press briefing in Washington, where she said it was still too early to tell whether investors were turning against the sector over the long term. The trigger for the market moves was the resignation of Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, which sent the company's shares sharply lower on Thursday and pulled down the S&P 500 and Nasdaq indexes. Some major technology firms, including Advanced Micro Devices, Alphabet and Microsoft, rose on the same day.

Kozack said the IMF's earlier view still holds that AI equity valuations remain exposed to a reassessment of how profitable the technology will be over the longer term. She also referred to pledges by newly elected Democratic governors to slow data center development, saying the fund was monitoring their effect on equity markets, the economy and financial stability. She added that it was too early to judge whether a broader reassessment of AI investment, profitability or future productivity gains was under way. Nor could the IMF yet gauge how any shift in AI investment might affect US inflation, given how little data had emerged in recent days.

Kozack described increased demand from AI investment and data center construction as one of two major drivers of US inflation, the other being high energy prices linked to the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. She said the IMF believes the Federal Reserve will need to keep monetary policy restrictive to bring inflation back to its 2 percent target. She added that the fund fully supports the Fed's focus on price stability and its readiness to act to bring inflation down. The Fed's policy-setting committee is next scheduled to meet on December 8 and 9, and the articles give no further detail on the outcome or the IMF's next steps.

stories.Headline: Forget Nvidia. Anthropic is the AI trade’s litmus test
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is preparing an initial public offering that could raise as much as $90 billion, with trading expected to start next Thursday. The move comes as Nvidia Corp., the sector's most valuable company, faces a leadership crisis after co-founder Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a woman that US officials reportedly believe to be a Chinese spy. Bankers are weighing plans to raise the price, and the order book is already multiple times oversubscribed. Chip stocks have steadied after last week's sharp selloff. Traders are betting a successful debut can offset the negative headlines around Nvidia.

The IPO matters because the AI labs have depended heavily on Nvidia to back their computing deals. Huang has championed vendor financing, which supports nascent AI labs and data-center developers. Two months ago, Anthropic signed a $35 billion cloud-computing deal with Nvidia-backed neocloud Lambda, and Nvidia, rather than Anthropic, holds the lease on the data center. Once public, Anthropic could use an at-the-market offering, private placements or convertible bonds to raise money directly. The article says it may not receive an investment-grade rating right away, but it would gain more room with loan bankers if its shares trade alongside other mega-caps.

Asian suppliers are especially exposed. South Korea's SK Hynix, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and Japanese test-equipment maker Advantest all rely on Nvidia for a substantial share of their sales. If Nvidia's dealmaking slows or financing for computing hits a snag, these firms could be forced to cut their earnings outlooks. The article notes that a financing channel opening for the labs themselves would benefit the whole semiconductor supply chain. For now, investors are giving the AI trade the benefit of the doubt.

The writer frames the listing as a test of whether the sector can rely on public capital markets rather than a few large backers. US-based tech firms have raised at least $220 billion from follow-on equity offerings so far this year, according to Bloomberg data, and companies have been selling convertible bonds throughout 2026. The article argues the AI industry would no longer need its own central bank if public markets embrace a major pure-play frontier lab. It adds that Anthropic must first deliver a smooth public debut before that baton can be passed.

stories.Headline: HUMAIN Partners with VUZ to Advance a New Generation of Immersive AI Streaming and Learning by Launching HUMAIN Plus
stories.Summary:
HUMAIN, a PIF company, announced on November 12, 2026 a strategic partnership with VUZ to develop immersive AI learning experiences through HUMAIN+, a new immersive streaming and learning platform. The announcement was made in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and was distributed by PR Newswire. The initiative is aimed at equipping leaders, professionals, faculty, and future innovators with practical AI capabilities. The partnership debuted publicly that day with the first showcase of HUMAIN+, a flagship immersive learning experience.

The partnership combines HUMAIN's vision for streaming and applied AI education with VUZ's immersive video technology. Through immersive digital experiences and AI-driven sessions delivered both virtually and in person, participants will engage with AI in more interactive, contextual, and experiential ways. The two companies are jointly designing and delivering educational experiences meant to move beyond traditional online learning. Participants will be able to experience AI concepts, demonstrations, and real-world applications in environments designed to increase engagement. The HUMAIN+ model will be available in the next few months.

Tareq Amin, Chief Executive Officer of HUMAIN, said that AI is changing how the world works and should fundamentally change how the world learns. He said HUMAIN+ was created to build a new generation of AI talent through practical, immersive streaming and learning experiences. Khaled Zaatarah, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of VUZ, said immersive technology and video streaming can transform many industries, including education. He said the partnership lets VUZ apply its latest technology to AI streaming and education. Zaatarah also said the goal is a world-class platform bringing immersive experiences to people everywhere, at global scale.

The partnership is aimed at learners across industries, including leaders, professionals, faculty, and future innovators. HUMAIN says its learning experiences support the development of talent, leadership, and workforce capabilities. The company says this work will help accelerate AI adoption across Saudi Arabia and globally. The articles do not identify specific participating organizations or report any numbers of participants or sessions. The articles say immersive experiences could reach people everywhere, but they give no figures on that reach.

HUMAIN is a global artificial intelligence company that delivers full-stack AI capabilities across four core areas. These areas are next-generation data centers, hyper-performance infrastructure and cloud platforms, advanced AI models including Arabic large language models, and AI solutions for specific sectors. VUZ is a global immersive technology company that holds two USPTO-granted patents in immersive capture, streaming, and playback. VUZ delivers immersive video across education, entertainment, sports, government, and digital infrastructure in 23 markets. VUZ is headquartered in Riyadh and says its mission includes growing Saudi Arabia's digital economy and exporting Saudi-built technology.

The articles do not describe the specific timing of the HUMAIN+ launch beyond saying it will be available in the next few months. They do not state the cost of the partnership, the number of learners expected, or which institutions will host sessions. They also do not explain how the two companies will divide responsibilities for design and delivery. The press release includes a forward-looking statement warning that actual results may differ materially due to various risks and uncertainties. HUMAIN says it undertakes no obligation to update those statements.

stories.Headline: Veterans tour Washington war memorials using AI glasses
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, a group of veterans from across the country toured Washington's war memorials using special sets of AI glasses to help them locate fallen service members. The trip was an honor flight sponsored by Meta, and the veterans spent three days in the capital. Many of them were blind or visually impaired, so each received a pair of Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to help them move through the memorials built in their honor. The glasses use built-in cameras, microphones and AI to sense the wearer's surroundings and describe them aloud.

The glasses could be used to read details about the memorials and to explain what the wearers were facing. Meta has committed to donating 130,000 pairs to visually impaired and blinded veterans nationwide. According to John Bockstanz, an Innovation Policy Manager at Meta, the glasses are already helping users regain independence in places like busy airports, restaurants and clothing stores. He described the effort as an ongoing, year-round commitment rather than a single flight.

John Bockstanz, who is also an Iraq War veteran, said the company worked with the veterans so they could ask the glasses what they were seeing and get more information about each memorial. Victor Dunham, a Vietnam veteran from Texas, used his pair to research a friend named Anthony, known as Tony, who died while serving beside him. The glasses helped him locate Anthony's name on the Vietnam Memorial wall. Dunham said the experience closed a loop he had carried for decades.

The trip also gave Dunham a chance to share the experience with his son Mark, an Iraq War veteran who came along. Dunham called the visit wonderful and said he appreciated it beyond belief. He described it as the most meaningful thing he had ever done with the company. The articles do not describe any further plans for the trip beyond the three days in Washington.

stories.Headline: Cloudflare Jumps 11%, Nebius Surges 9% as AI Cloud Stocks Defy NVIDIA's Slide; CoreWeave Rallies 6% on Wayve Deal
stories.Summary:
AI cloud stocks rose on Monday, November 9, 2026, even as NVIDIA fell. Cloudflare traded at $297.22, up 11% in afternoon trading, as buyers kept piling in after its third-quarter earnings beat. Nebius Group rose 9% to $140.70 ahead of its own quarterly report. CoreWeave gained 6% to $49.18 after signing a multi-year cloud computing deal with British autonomous driving startup Wayve. NVIDIA, meanwhile, slid 5% to $177.40, while the articles say AI shares were drawing buyers back after last week's post-midterm selloff.

Under the deal reported on November 9, Wayve will use CoreWeave's NVIDIA Blackwell-based infrastructure to train and test its driving models. Wayve already uses Weights & Biases, which CoreWeave acquired in 2025, and financial terms were not disclosed. Cloudflare reported revenue of $782.51 million for the third quarter, up 39.2% from a year earlier and above the $738.30 million consensus. Adjusted earnings of $0.38 per share beat the $0.3434 estimate, and the company reported a 17.5% adjusted operating margin. Management raised its full-year 2026 revenue outlook to $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $845 million to $846 million.

Cloudflare reported its results after the close on November 5, and CEO Matthew Prince called it the company's best quarter ever. He credited the company's fastest revenue growth in nearly four years, achieved while profitability expanded. On the earnings call, Prince presented Cloudflare as the first agentic cloud, with developers building AI agents on its Workers platform. Nebius is expected to report before the market opens on November 12, and its investors are likely to focus on capacity guidance, 2027 run-rate projections and infrastructure spending. CoreWeave did not disclose financial terms of the Wayve agreement, and its own quarterly earnings are also coming up.

NVIDIA's decline was described as running on a separate track from the cloud names. Yahoo Finance reported on November 9 that NVIDIA is investigating CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Oracle gained 3% to $119.16, a smaller rise than the neocloud names, and IREN rose 2% to $21.98, also trailing Nebius and CoreWeave. Analysts expect Nebius to post revenue of $905 million to $907 million, which would mean growth of more than 500% from a year earlier. They also expect an adjusted loss of 69 cents to $1.11 per share, and options pricing implies a post-earnings move of 17% or more.

Cloudflare runs a global edge network that sells security, networking and developer tools on a subscription basis to millions of organizations. That model ties its growth to developer adoption and security demand across a broad customer base. Nebius and CoreWeave rent GPU computing capacity to AI labs, hyperscalers and enterprises, and both buy their chips from NVIDIA. CoreWeave reported a revenue backlog of approximately $104 billion as of June 30, while Nebius disclosed $37.5 billion in remaining performance obligations. Oracle pairs its AI cloud with an enterprise software franchise, and IREN owns the land, power and data centers behind its shift from crypto mining.

The next test for Cloudflare is whether its growth can stay near the pace management guided for the fourth quarter. The bulls can point to accelerating revenue, the 17.5% adjusted operating margin and a higher full-year outlook. On the other side, Cloudflare's reported gross margin fell to 71.2% from 74%, and $4.4 billion in convertible notes remain outstanding. For Nebius, the upcoming report could decide whether its run-up holds against high expectations, and the articles suggest a conservative approach may be warranted until results are released. The articles leave open how long NVIDIA's slide will last and what the reported investigation into Huang's ties will find.

stories.Headline: Gov't vows zero tolerance against cheating with AI glasses
stories.Summary:
The South Korean government said on Friday, November 13, 2026, that it would take a zero-tolerance approach to cheating with AI glasses in next week's nationwide college entrance exam. The vow followed suspicions raised by an unusually high score in this year's certified tax accountant exam, where the top scorer earned 397.5 points out of 400 and missed only one of the 160 questions on the first-round test. Many test-takers regard that result as unrealistic, which has fueled concern that similar devices could be used in the College Scholastic Ability Test. The exam is set for Thursday, November 19. The Office for Government Policy Coordination said that AI-glasses cheating infringes on fair opportunities for students who have worked hard.

Specialized personnel will be sent to test sites to detect the glasses, and anyone caught cheating will be dealt with sternly, including through criminal complaints. The office also said it would seek an investigation into the tax accountant exam to clear up the suspicions. If cheating is confirmed there, the government said, accountability will be enforced under relevant laws and regulations. The statement came from the Office for Government Policy Coordination, which spoke on behalf of the government. It said the government takes public concerns about the matter very seriously.

The office stressed that it intends to manage the upcoming college entrance exam thoroughly to protect the fairness of the examination. The articles do not say whether any cheating has been confirmed in the tax accountant exam or whether any suspects have been identified. They also do not describe the findings of any investigation, which has yet to be carried out according to the statement. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Intel and Altera Simplify Sensor Integration for Edge and Physical AI
stories.Summary:
Intel and Altera announced on November 11, 2026, that they will collaborate on a flexible, real-time sensor bridge for edge and physical AI systems. The announcement came from Santa Clara, California, and combines Intel compute, connectivity and software with Altera FPGAs. The companies say the work aims to help equipment makers connect and act on data from increasingly sensor-rich environments. The partnership targets healthcare, aerospace and defense, and robotics applications. The collaboration centers on modular reference solutions that pair programmable hardware with a consistent Intel compute and software foundation.

The articles say these designs are meant to handle sensor data that must be merged while meeting requirements for timing, performance, power and cost. Some applications need very high bandwidth or flexible form factors that place input and output away from the compute board. In those cases, sensor data must be streamed rapidly into memory for the host Intel processor to use. The companies say this approach should let manufacturers adapt as applications and sensors change and move more efficiently from prototype to deployment. Dan Rodriguez, corporate vice president and general manager of Intel's Edge Computing Group, said customers need a simpler way to turn real-world data into timely action as sensors multiply.

Farhad Shafai, head of business solutions and marketing at Altera, said physical AI systems must sense, decide and act in real time, and that Altera FPGAs supply the connectivity, data processing and deterministic control needed for that. Shafai added that the FPGAs remain programmable as sensors and AI models evolve. Both executives framed the combined offering as a flexible foundation that manufacturers can tailor to their needs. The companies plan to apply the work in three areas. In healthcare, they are jointly developing a reference solution aimed at the strict latency and real-time requirements of advanced equipment.

In aerospace and defense, they are working on reference solutions for next-generation mission systems with a focus on size, weight and power for converged AI and signal-processing workloads. In robotics, they plan to combine Intel compute, connectivity and robotics software with Altera FPGA technology to address complex sensing and timing needs. Developers will reach these capabilities through Intel's Open Edge Platform SDK and an Altera SDK. The articles do not give timelines for when the reference solutions will be released.

stories.Headline: LG ELECTRONICS' PRISM AI WINS THREE HONORS AT 2026 AMEC AWARDS
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics said that its PRISM AI platform won three honors at the 2026 AMEC Global Communication Effectiveness Awards. The platform earned Gold in the Best Use of AI in Communication Measurement category and Silver in both the Best Use of a Measurement Framework category and the Step Change Award. The announcement was made in Seoul, South Korea, with the release dated November 12, 2026, and the PR Newswire version dated November 11. The awards are presented by AMEC, the International Association for the Measurement and Evaluation of Communication. The Step Change Award recognizes the best improvement of a measurement journey.

PRISM AI is LG's AI-powered communications measurement platform, and it is built around three core concepts from AMEC's Barcelona Principles 3.0: outcomes over outputs, quality plus quantity, and transparency. The platform uses a dual-metric system made up of the PR Score and the Communications Impact Index. Its AI-powered filtering removes more than 78 percent of spam and irrelevant content with over 95 percent accuracy. Media monitoring now covers 200 countries, up from 53, and tracked brands have grown from 5 to 30. The time spent on reporting has been reduced from approximately one month to one hour.

LG Electronics described the platform as a reference point for the public relations and communications industry. Cho Jung-bum, head of the AX Center at LG Electronics, said that winning three AMEC Awards was especially meaningful because the recognition came directly from the PR industry's most respected global body. Cho said the company will keep refining PRISM AI's methodology while expanding its capabilities and scope. The AMEC awards adopted a threshold-based judging model this year, under which each entry is judged against fixed criteria rather than against other entries. Judges are not permitted to use generative AI tools to support or inform their evaluations.

The platform's recognition affects LG's global communications workflows, which it has made more efficient and reliable since its introduction. The judging placed the greatest emphasis on real-world effectiveness, including how reliable the findings are, whether they were acted on, and how they shape future communications planning and strategy. PRISM AI processes large volumes of articles in real time and uses large language models to interpret coverage across languages and markets. LG Group is advancing AI transformation (AX) across its businesses, and PRISM AI has become an internationally recognized example of AI-driven data collection and analysis in a specialized professional field. The platform also won the Best AI Tool or Product category at the 2026 IN2 SABRE Awards Asia-Pacific, held in Singapore this August.

LG Electronics is a global innovator in technology and consumer electronics, with a presence in almost every country and an international workforce of more than 75,000. Its four Companies, Home Appliance Solution, Media Entertainment Solution, Vehicle Solution and Eco Solution, combined for global revenue of over KRW 89 trillion in 2025. LG is a leading manufacturer of consumer and commercial products, ranging from TVs and home appliances to air solutions, monitors and automotive components. Its premium LG SIGNATURE and intelligent LG ThinQ brands are familiar names worldwide. The articles give no further information on the company's plans for PRISM AI beyond the statement by Cho Jung-bum.

stories.Headline: DGEN TECHNOLOGIES ACQUIRES EXCLUSIVE LICENCE TO HUMANOS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGY
stories.Summary:
DGEN Technologies Corp. announced on November 12, 2026, that it has entered into a licence agreement with HumanOS Technologies Inc., a Vancouver-based arm's length company. Under the agreement dated that day, HumanOS granted DGEN an exclusive and irrevocable licence to its artificial intelligence software, automation technology and related assets. The announcement was issued from Vancouver, British Columbia, through CNW and PR Newswire. DGEN is listed on the Canadian Securities Exchange under the symbol DGEN, and the deal was described as a transaction. The filing gave the agreement's date and parties in the opening statement of the release.

The licensed assets include the software, source code, systems, platforms and tools that HumanOS developed and operates under its name. They cover the HumAIn, Matspace, Media Studio and Automation Lab products and the HumanOS scan tool. The package also includes the HumanOS trade name, the 1humanos.com domain, associated websites and social media accounts, and client lists limited to names and contact details. The licence lets DGEN and its affiliates use, commercialize, further develop and sublicense these assets, while HumanOS keeps ownership. Improvements made by or for DGEN will belong to DGEN.

As consideration, DGEN will issue 4,000,000 common shares at a deemed price of $0.25 per share, along with 4,000,000 common share purchase warrants. Each warrant allows the holder to buy one DGEN common share at $0.32 for three years from issuance. The shares, warrants and any shares issued on exercise are subject to a statutory hold period of four months and one day. Closing requires approval from the Canadian Securities Exchange and delivery to DGEN of the source code and other materials, and it is expected in the coming week or weeks. The release also states that no finder's fees are payable on the transaction.

The release was issued by DGEN Technologies Corp., which describes itself as a Vancouver-based technology company. The company says it is developing a cloud-based payment platform that would integrate point-of-sale, kiosk and mobile payment systems. stories.Headline: Australian companies face 'AI washing' claims after wave of job cuts, offshoring
stories.Summary:
Australian blue-chip companies are increasingly citing artificial intelligence as they cut jobs and move work offshore, according to unions and experts. On Tuesday, Qantas said it would cut 850 jobs and outsource some corporate functions offshore as part of an AI-driven overhaul with consulting firm Accenture. That move has drawn accusations of "AI washing," a term for attributing layoffs to AI when broader cost-cutting may be the main driver. Tech companies WiseTech and Atlassian have cut jobs this year and attributed the losses to AI. Telstra has also cut jobs linked to an AI joint venture with Accenture, with some work offshored to India.

Other firms across corporate Australia have slashed domestic headcounts while expanding operations in India, the Philippines and Vietnam, though they did not explicitly mention AI in their announcements. When asked about the Qantas cuts, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said AI "represents an enormous opportunity and a major economic issue." Qantas said it would continue consulting with unions and was focused on "redeployment opportunities" and support for affected staff. Qantas did not respond to the concerns about AI washing. Atlassian, WiseTech and Telstra did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Labour unions argue that Australian workers are being replaced not by AI but by lower-paid offshore employees. Australian Council of Trade Unions Secretary Melissa Donnelly said unions worry companies are using AI as cover to cut Australian jobs without accountability. The Australian Services Union, which represents the affected Qantas workers, accused the airline of using AI to launder its cuts to Australian jobs. Senator Barbara Pocock of the Australian Greens said she was concerned about big companies engaging in AI washing. Further job cuts could pose headaches for Australia's centre-left Labor government, whose approval ratings have been falling amid high cost-of-living pressures.

The central bank has raised interest rates five times so far this year, to their highest level in 18 years, amid persistent inflation. The latest data showed the unemployment rate at a five-year high of 4.7%. University of Sydney Business School professor Uri Gal said companies may face less criticism for presenting job cuts as part of an AI transformation than for citing cost reduction. Gal said the Qantas decision appeared to reflect conventional outsourcing, with corporate functions transferred to Accenture, primarily in India. The Reserve Bank of Australia said this week that AI had not yet led to widespread job losses, though it noted "tentative signs of adjustment."

A government spokesperson said it expected Australian workers to share the benefits of new technologies and that employers should invest in upskilling them to adopt AI. The articles do not say whether the government will take further action on the job cuts or the AI washing claims. They also do not say whether Qantas will reverse or revise its plan. Whether other companies will follow the Qantas model of offshoring with AI attribution is not addressed. The articles also do not give the timing of the Qantas cuts beyond the announcement made on Tuesday.

stories.Headline: HEARTBOT AI Launches AnyInsight Edge, Ending the Trade-Off Between Private AI and Agentic Productivity
stories.Summary:
HEARTBOT AI announced AnyInsight Edge on November 12, 2026, in Taipei, extending its AnyInsight enterprise AI security and governance platform to on-premises environments and AI servers. The product applies one control plane to private on-premises models and cloud AI, so enterprises no longer have to choose between the two. Until now, private large language models kept data in-house but lacked the productivity of AI agents, while cloud AI offered stronger agents but could not always receive regulated data. With Edge, policy is managed centrally and enforced across cloud and on-premises environments at once. Every AI interaction, agent action and workflow execution is inspected in real time, access-controlled and fully logged, leaving no gaps in control.

AnyInsight Edge is delivered as a container with a hardware-agnostic design and can run on-premises or integrate with an AI server's operating system. Edge itself requires no GPU, leaving compute resources entirely for model inference. It acts as the policy enforcement point in the on-premises AI traffic path, and it can also run in fully air-gapped environments with no cloud connection. Through Edge, on-premises models such as Gemma, TAIDE and Mistral gain access to AnyInsight's more than 350 ready-to-use AI agents and over 500 application connectors. Edge also routes requests by policy to more than 20 leading cloud models when needed, and it keeps company databases, AI conversations, transferred data and audit logs on-premises if an enterprise chooses.

HEARTBOT AI, whose CEO is Nathan Yen, presents the product as the next step after earlier security changes, arguing that AI now needs a control point where its work actually happens. Yen compared the moment to the convergence of firewalls, intrusion prevention and VPNs into UTM twenty years ago. He said models will keep changing and agents will keep multiplying, so enterprises need policy enforced at the point of AI activity. The company describes AnyInsight Edge as turning every AI server into that control point. Its statement frames the product as addressing enterprises bound by data residency rules, regulation or customer contracts.

Enterprises that run private LLMs, including manufacturing and semiconductor supply chains, banks and insurers, and government agencies and hospitals, are the groups the announcement names as affected. Manufacturers can keep process parameters, yield data and customer drawings inside the plant while still generating production reports. Banks and insurers can mask customer personal data before it reaches a model and keep an auditable record of every AI use. Government and healthcare users can keep official documents and medical records within the agency or hospital, and the platform supports disclosure and human review in line with Taiwan's AI Basic Act and the EU AI Act. The articles give no outside reactions from customers, analysts or regulators.

Earlier, the articles say, many enterprises and institutions bound by data residency rules had already invested in AI servers and deployed private LLMs, but those models often stayed internal chatbots cut off from ERP, MES and CRM systems. Shadow agents built by departments and shadow AI on personal accounts created risks that IT could not see. AnyInsight is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and its governance and data protection mechanisms are designed on the principles of the EU AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation. The articles do not state the product's price or availability dates.

The articles leave open when AnyInsight Edge will be generally available and how it will be priced. They also do not say how many enterprises have adopted AnyInsight so far or how the product performs against competing platforms. The articles do not describe any customer deployments in detail or any independent verification of the security claims. How the platform will be updated as Taiwan's AI Basic Act and the EU AI Act take effect is also not addressed.

stories.Headline: IBM report finds 94% of surveyed enterprises faced a sovereignty challenge, with AI the most common
stories.Summary:
The IBM report, Proof, Not Promises: The Digital Sovereignty Index, was released on November 11, 2026, and it finds that 94% of the enterprises it surveyed faced at least one sovereignty challenge over the previous three years. Those challenges included AI-provider failures, regulatory conflicts, critical vendor disruption, government restrictions such as export controls, and data-access problems. Of the organizations affected, 81% had to supply formal evidence of control to regulators, customers, auditors or internal stakeholders. IBM describes the gap it has found as an "overconfidence gap," in which leaders believe they can prove sovereign control but the evidence often falls short of the Index's highest standards.

The report measures whether an organization can retain and prove control over its critical AI, technology, operations and data, especially when conditions change or dependencies come under pressure. It assesses six areas: responsibility, which asks whether the organization can prove who was accountable; trace, which asks whether it can show exactly what happened; constraint, which asks whether it can prove its controls were working; intervention, which asks whether it can show how it responded and recovered; legitimacy, which asks whether it can explain and justify decisions under scrutiny; and exit, which asks whether it can prove it could change provider or recover operations if needed. The findings suggest that the difficulty is less about control itself than about sovereignty efforts not being built to answer these questions smoothly under pressure. Only a third of respondents, 33%, test their ability to demonstrate sovereignty continuously or as part of regular governance and assurance processes.

IBM's Senior Vice President and Chief Global Affairs Officer, Jonathan Adashek, said that sovereignty should expand future choices rather than restrict them, and that boards need to show how they can adapt, change strategy or change critical provider. He added that the next step is stronger evidence that governance works, including testing exit capabilities, understanding critical dependencies and focusing on where a loss of control would have the greatest impact. Emmanuel Frenehard, Chief Digital Officer at Sanofi, said that digital sovereignty is a business reality rather than a compliance checkbox, and that it is a matter of business continuity as AI becomes embedded across the enterprise. The report itself does not say which organizations or regulators, beyond these two executives, took any position on the findings.

AI emerged as the most common sovereignty problem, with AI-related issues, including incorrect outputs, explainability problems, model or provider failures and governance concerns, cited by 44% of respondents. That figure was ahead of significant provider changes at 35%, formal audit or regulatory events at 38%, data-access or transfer issues at 33%, and government restrictions such as export controls or sanctions at 30%. An average of 82% of respondents said they were very or extremely confident they could provide evidence of sovereign control. However, only 26% of enterprises reached the Index's Leading Digital Sovereignty tier, and enterprises in that tier were more than twice as likely to resolve their most testing challenge without material disruption, at 52% compared with 22% of establishing enterprises.

The research behind the Index combined a review of 27 sources, including legislation, standards, governance frameworks and academic research, with 25 interviews with policymakers, regulators, public-sector officials and policy experts, and perspectives from 17 senior customer leaders across five countries. Its quantitative survey covered 2,003 senior decision-makers at large enterprises in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Saudi Arabia, India and Japan. Among the barriers that respondents reported to proving sovereignty were manual or time-consuming evidence collection, cited by 56%, and fragmented evidence across teams and systems, dependence on third parties for records, and legacy systems or inconsistent standards, each cited by 53%. Half of respondents, 50%, pointed to untested controls, recovery or exit arrangements. The report does not describe any specific steps that organizations are scheduled to take next.

stories.Headline: Public funds ploughing cash into AI will 'own' megatrends shaping economy
stories.Summary:
Sovereign wealth funds and public pension funds are pouring money into artificial intelligence and infrastructure, and a PwC report released on Thursday, November 12, 2026, projects that state-backed investors will reshape the economy. Sovereign wealth fund assets are expected to rise nearly 50% to $22.4 trillion by 2030, up from about $15.2 trillion. Public pension assets are forecast to climb to $36.3 trillion from about $27.6 trillion, and central bank assets to about $20.9 trillion from about $17.3 trillion. The report, which analysed the world's 350 largest public investors, was reported by Reuters and carried by CNBC Africa.

The report says these investors have moved from passive stakes to what it calls principal investors that originate deals themselves and take controlling positions with operational roles. Eric Janson, PwC's global private equity and principal investors leader, said these investors no longer rely only on external managers. Assets are becoming concentrated in a small group, with the top 10 institutions holding about 41% of combined sovereign wealth and pension assets and the top 50 holding 77%. The report says a few dozen large institutions are positioned to set the tone, adding that they will enable, accelerate and own the megatrends shaping the global economy.

In 2025, state investors channelled roughly $66 billion into AI and digitisation, and most of it went to the United States, while flows to China slipped to around $4 billion. The report found Gulf state funds were tilting hard toward the US, pointing to pledges from Qatar's QIA and Abu Dhabi's MGX and ADIA. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund was an exception, cutting foreign allocations to roughly 20% from a peak near 30% as it shifts toward a domestic focus. The article does not describe any formal rule or requirement that these shifts impose on governments or institutions.
